title: Maine man riding electric unicycle killed in collision
text:
An Augusta man riding an electric unicycle was killed in a Saturday afternoon collision.
Johnathan Bauer, 28, was riding the unicycle near Western Avenue and Melville Street about 3:22 p.m. when he collided with a vehicle driven by 26-year-old Rhysonne Bishop of Mississippi, according to Jesse Brann, deputy chief of the Augusta Police Department.
Bauer died at the scene, Brann said.
Bishop wasn’t injured in the crash.
The crash remains under investigation.

title: Turkeys stolen from Thomaston farm, property damaged; police release pictures of suspect vehicle
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Turkeys stolen from Maine farm, property damaged; police identify suspect vehicle
Police in Thomaston say are investigating the theft of a dozen turkeys from a local farm as well as damage to the property.
On Monday, police shared pictures of a pickup truck believed to be involved in the crime at Grace Pond Farm on Main Street in Thomaston. The truck was caught on camera passing the Maine State Prison showroom on Main Street at about 2:29 a.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 27. By Monday afternoon, police said they had identified the vehicle. However, they did not announce any arrests.
The farm posted on Facebook that the value of the stolen turkeys and damage to the farm is close to $1,500.
"That does NOT include our time in dealing with it all, or the stress of knowing someone was AT OUR HOME in the middle of the night stealing, or the expense in additional cameras and security subscriptions," the farm wrote.
The farm owners did say that, as a small farm, any loss of income is hard to absorb, but that they would be able to absorb this and continue on.
They said the support from the community has been incredible. They said the best support people could provide is to continue to shop with them and all local farms.
Anyone with information about the people or vehicle involved should reach out to Thomaston Police and Detective Ron Wood at 207-593-9132.

title: Judge tosses charges for ex-FBI agents accused of lying about Hunter Biden
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge on Monday dismissed a criminal complaint against two former FBI officials accused of making false statements to Congress about Hunter Biden, saying the investigation that produced the charges was rushed, overtly political and dogged by “critical mistakes.”
“What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization,” U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said in a scathing ruling from the bench that dismissed the case against former officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides.
He noted that the investigation was opened a day after a primetime speech by President Donald Trump in which he rehashed grievances over his 2020 election loss and that it was mandated and closely tracked by FBI Director Kash Patel. He also pointed out that the Justice Department could have brought the case, which arises from statements made in 2023, at any time but opted to do so two weeks ago, in the run-up to Tuesday’s midterm voting.
“I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend that I cannot read a calendar,” Faruqui said.
The decision followed a dramatic hearing in which he scolded prosecutors for their unorthodox maneuvers and an FBI agent who worked the case testified that he had been concerned the investigation would be seen as “political.”
The Justice Department may still have an opportunity to pursue a grand jury indictment against the two former officials, whose lawyers had pressed for dismissal of the charges. But the judge’s ruling nonetheless represents an unmistakable setback for the Justice Department, particularly given the difficulty it has had in persuading grand juries in the nation’s capital to return indictments in politically charged prosecutions like this one.
The judge’s concerns about the case were apparent almost immediately, when he raised questions about why the Justice Department had charged the case through a criminal complaint — which is more typically done when investigators have a pressing need to take a defendant into custody — as opposed to an indictment that requires a grand jury’s approval.
Then, at a preliminary hearing last week, he criticized the Justice Department for filing overnight an amended complaint with an additional criminal charge straight to the docket instead of first clearing the new charge with the court — something he said he had never seen before.
The hearing also featured testimony from an FBI agent who worked the case, who said that the investigation had been opened right after Trump gave an election security speech last July and that it had been mandated by FBI Director Kash Patel, who kept close watch on it.
The case accused the two former FBI officials of misleading Congress in 2023 about their involvement in, and knowledge of, efforts to investigate a laptop the Justice Department says was dropped off by Hunter Biden, former President Joe Biden’s son, at a Delaware computer repair shop in 2019.
But it also sought to echo longstanding grievances by Trump and his Republican allies that the FBI attempted to suppress information during the 2020 presidential campaign that was seen as potentially harmful to the Biden family. Candidate Joe Biden, a Democrat, ultimately defeated Trump, the Republican incumbent, in the 2020 election.
The Justice Department’s case noted, for instance, how Floris and Benavides had given lawmakers in 2020 a “defensive briefing” that Republican Sens. Chuck Grassley of Iowa and Ron Johnson of Wisconsin have said was used to undermine their investigation into the Biden administration and link it to Russian disinformation.

title: More clouds today with a few showers possible, some wet weather for Election Day
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Monday will be a warmer day with the chance for a few showers. Overnight showers into Tuesday especially up to the north look likely as well. Election Day will be a bit cooler with some clouds and the chance for a shower but generally a seasonable fall day. Some showers may stick around Wednesday then calm conditions until Friday into the weekend where the next chance for substantial rain comes into play.
Monday: More clouds than this weekend and warm, a late shower possible
A nice day with highs getting into the 60s for most with a few more clouds for some areas. But generally a slightly warmer than average day with decent sunshine for most. Chance for a few late showers towards the evening hours.
Monday night: A few showers around
A few showers may drift around on Monday night especially to the north but otherwise some in and out clouds. Lows into the upper 30s and 40s for most.
Tuesday: A decent day for Election Day with some showers possible
Tuesday looks mainly cloudy with a few showers possible around especially for the north and eastern regions as a system passes to our north. They will mainly be light and won’t have much of an effect on the day. Just be aware of wet roads potentially. Highs will be again near 60 for most with some in the 50s.
Wednesday and beyond: Some showers early Wednesday, next substantial rain possible for Friday and the weekend
These showers may stick around into early Wednesday for some leading to slightly more wet weather, but temps will be near 70 for some again. Thursday looks pretty quiet while Friday into next weekend holds the next chance for significant rain, which would be the first in quite some time. It is still some ways out and there are a lot of details to iron out before then however.

title: President Trump reopens Reflecting Pool in final midterm pitch
text:
President Trump reopens Reflecting Pool in final midterm pitch
President Donald Trump celebrated the reopening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on the eve of the midterm elections, using the Washington landmark as the backdrop for an appeal to voters as polls show widespread economic concerns.
President Trump reopens Reflecting Pool in final midterm pitch
President Donald Trump celebrated the reopening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool on the eve of the midterm elections, using the Washington landmark as the backdrop for an appeal to voters as polls show widespread economic concerns.
President Donald Trump made his final public appearance before the midterm elections Monday at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, announcing its reopening before urging supporters to help Republicans maintain control of Congress.
Rather than travel to a battleground state, Trump remained in Washington to celebrate a renovation he personally championed.
The project ran months behind schedule and exceeded Trump's original cost estimate. It also required additional repairs after the pool's new blue lining began peeling. Federal prosecutors attributed the damage to problems with the installation, contradicting Trump's claims that vandals were responsible.
"And the pool is now better and more beautiful than it's ever been before," Trump said.
The president also used the occasion to warn about the consequences of Democrats gaining power in Congress and to encourage his supporters to vote.
“So we’ll defend our country, our culture, and our heritage for generations to come. We’re going to keep it the way it is. We’re going to make it better. And just,” Trump said.
Although Trump isn't on Tuesday's ballot, the outcome could determine how much of his agenda he can advance over the next two years.
Republicans are fighting to maintain control of both the House and Senate. A Democratic takeover of the House could block Republican legislation and give Democrats the power to launch congressional investigations into Trump administration officials. Control of the Senate would also give Democrats authority over the confirmation of judges and senior administration officials. Democrats argue change is needed.
"Democrats are united in trying to lower costs for families. We're united in holding this corrupt administration accountable," said Kendall Witmer, deputy communications director for the Democratic National Committee.
Over the past month, Trump has traveled across the country campaigning for Republicans while highlighting economic growth and his administration's tax cuts.
But economic concerns remain prominent heading into Election Day. Americans continue to face inflation and higher gasoline prices driven up by the war in Iran.
An October AP-NORC poll found that 74% of U.S. adults disapproved of Trump's handling of the economy, while 64% disapproved of his overall job performance.
A separate NPR/PBS News/Marist poll found that 44% of likely voters considered their congressional vote mainly a vote against Trump, compared with 21% who described it as a vote for him. Another 35% said the president wasn't much of a factor.
And while Republicans and Democrats battle for control of Congress, Americans have their own priorities for the lawmakers who will take office.
The AP-NORC survey found 80% of respondents believe lowering the cost of living should be one of Congress's highest priorities, while 68% say the same about ending the war in Iran.
By comparison, 36% consider investigating the Trump administration a highest priority, and just 18% say the same about supporting the president's agenda.

title: What the final Pine Tree State Poll shows in Maine's major races
text:
Final Pine Tree State Poll before Election Day released: Here's what it shows in Maine's major races
The University of New Hampshire Survey Center has released its final Pine Tree State Poll before Election Day, which is Tuesday, Nov. 3.
The poll shows that in Maine's high-profile U.S. Senate race, 54% of likely voters said they will vote or already have voted for Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, while 45% said they will vote or already have voted for Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins. Less than 1% of likely voters support another candidate and less than 1% are undecided. In the previous Pine Tree State Poll released in September, 51% of those surveyed supported Jackson while 47% supported Collins.
According to the latest poll, 60% of Jackson supporters said their vote is more against Collins, 38% said their vote is more for Jackson and 2% said neither of those things is true or they were unsure.
While the poll shows that Jackson is leading in the race, 56% of likely voters in Maine believe that Collins will win the election while only 26% think that Jackson will be victorious. The remaining 18% of voters are unsure about the outcome.
The poll also shows that 48% of likely voters said their vote is in opposition to President Donald Trump while 14% said their vote is in support. The remaining 37% said their vote is unrelated to Trump.
Polling on Maine governor's race
Democratic candidate Hannah Pingree continues to lead in the gubernatorial poll, as 51% of likely voters said they will vote or have voted for the former Maine House speaker. This marks an increase from the 48% she received in the September poll.
The latest poll shows that 40% of likely voters said they will vote or have voted for Republican candidate Bobby Charles, who also received 40% in the previous poll.
Independent candidate Rick Bennett received 7% of the vote, an increase of 2% from the September poll.
The remaining 2% of likely voters surveyed were split between supporting another candidate and being undecided about their vote.
In addition, the poll found that 61% of likely voters believe that Pingree will win the race for governor, while 26% believe that Charles will be victorious. Only 1% of likely voters think that Bennett will win the gubernatorial election, while the remaining 12% of those surveyed are unsure about the outcome.
Polling for congressional races
The race for Maine's 2nd Congressional District seat will help determine the balance of power in the U.S. House, as incumbent Rep. Jared Golden, a Blue Dog Democrat, decided not to run for reelection.
The final Pine Tree State Poll shows that former Gov. Paul LePage, a Republican, holds a lead over Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap in the race. According to the poll, 52% of likely CD2 voters said they will or have voted for LePage, while 47% said they will or have voted for Dunlap. The remaining 1% either support another candidate or are undecided. In the September poll, Dunlap (51%) had a lead over LePage (45%) with a larger margin (approximately 5%) of undecided voters.
The poll also found that in the race for Maine's 1st Congressional District seat, Democratic incumbent Rep. Chellie Pingree holds a sizeable lead (65%) over Republican challenger Ron Russell (32%) with 3% of likely CD1 voters supporting another candidate and less than 1% of likely voters were undecided. This marks an increase in support for Pingree from the previous poll, where she had 57% to Russell's 35%.
More about the Pine Tree State Poll
The UNH Survey Center said that 1,722 Maine residents completed the survey online between Tuesday, Oct. 27, and Saturday, Oct. 31. The margin of sampling error for the survey is +/- 2.4%.
"We try to be pretty careful when we characterize something as a lead or as tied," said Sean McKinley, project director at the UNH Survey Center. "We could do this survey again in a week and nothing might have changed in the fundamentals of the race, but we might have a different result. When the races are close, that could mean that the other person is now ahead."
McKinley said that while all of the polls strive to be as accurate as possible, none of the results should be taken as gospel.

title: The key governor races to watch in the 2026 midterm election
text:
The key governor races to watch in the 2026 midterm election
Thirty-six states have gubernatorial contests on the ballot this year.
Ahead of Election Day, there were 26 Republican governors and 24 Democratic governors.
With 19 incumbents leaving office, there will be a lot of turnover – and an opportunity for Democrats to hold a majority of the posts for the first time since 2010.
The races will also test whether Democrats can capitalize on a midterm environment that has put several Republican-held seats in play. Some campaigns have grown especially bitter, with personal attacks and family history pulled into the fight.
The most competitive contests will offer an early read on both parties’ strength ahead of the 2028 presidential race.
Below are some of the top races to watch in 2026.
- Alaska | Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is challenging three Republicans — Dave Bronson, Treg Taylor and Bernadette Wilson — for the seat being vacated by term-limited Gov. Mike Dunleavy. Kreiss-Tomkins led the crowded August primary, and Democrat Tom Begich later withdrew to consolidate support behind him; Alaska uses ranked-choice voting in the general election.
- Florida | Republican U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds faces Democrat David Jolly, a former Republican congressman who joined the Democratic Party in 2025. Republicans have dominated Florida statewide races for years, and Donalds has campaigned with President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance.
- Georgia | Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson and Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, are competing to succeed Republican Gov. Brian Kemp. Jackson won a bruising Republican runoff against Trump’s pick, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones; Bottoms won the Democratic primary in a seven-candidate field.
- Iowa | Republican Zach Lahn is challenging Democrat Rob Sand, the state auditor and Iowa’s only Democrat holding statewide office, for the open seat left by retiring Gov. Kim Reynolds. Lahn upset Trump-endorsed U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra in the Republican primary, giving Democrats hope of winning the governorship for the first time in 16 years.
- Kansas | Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly is term-limited, leaving Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson and Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher to compete for the open seat. Republicans see the race as a pickup opportunity, though Kansas has a long pattern of electing governors from the party opposite the president’s.
- Michigan | Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Republican U.S. Rep. John James are running to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. The contest is part of a broader battle in a closely divided state where control of the governor’s office and Legislature is at stake.
- Nebraska | Republican Gov. Jim Pillen is seeking another term against Democrat Lynne Walz, a former state senator. Republicans have held the governorship since 1999, but the race has drawn added attention amid a difficult national climate for the party and a campaign visit from Trump.
- Nevada | Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo is seeking reelection against Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford in a race rated a tossup by election forecasters. Lombardo won the governorship in 2022 by defeating an incumbent, and Democrats are trying to reclaim the office in a key swing state.
- Ohio | Democrat Amy Acton, a physician and former state public health director, is challenging Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a former presidential candidate and Trump ally. The campaign drew national attention after Ramaswamy’s ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother prompted backlash.
- Oregon | Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek is seeking reelection in a rematch with Republican Christine Drazan, whom she narrowly defeated in 2022. Recent polls have shown a close contest, with the candidates emphasizing concerns ranging from the economy to conditions in Central and Eastern Oregon.
- Texas | Republican Gov. Greg Abbott is seeking a fourth term against Democrat Gina Hinojosa, a state representative. Hinojosa has mounted a spirited challenge in a state where Democrats have not won a statewide election in more than three decades, while recent polling has suggested a tighter contest than expected.
- Wisconsin | Democrat David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, faces Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany in the race to succeed retiring Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. Wisconsin’s narrow recent election margins make it a key battleground, and Tiffany has Trump’s endorsement.

title: Bodycam video shows aftermath of fatal shooting by National Guard in Memphis
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Tennessee National Guard troops in Memphis last summer trained their handguns on a man as he lay dying on a sidewalk after a guard member shot him in the back, video released Monday by county prosecutors shows.
A Memphis police officer can be heard in the footage from an officer’s body camera calling for an ambulance and then asking the troops, “Hey, you guys got a medical kit or anything?”
The Shelby County District Attorney’s Office released the videos, which also include footage from stationary cameras and a cellphone from a bystander, as the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation continues its investigation into the July 5 shooting of Tyrin Johnson.
Johnson, 20, who had been armed, died at the scene from a single gunshot wound, according to investigators. An autopsy report shared by Johnson’s family found that he was shot in the back, contradicting police and National Guard accounts that said he was facing the guard members with a gun when they fired at him.
The footage did not show Johnson’s initial encounter with the guard members or them firing at him.
The guard members were part of a federal task force created by President Donald Trump, who last year sent troops and federal agents to Democrat-run cities that he described as overrun with crime. Tennessee’s Republican Gov. Bill Lee had deployed the Guard to support the effort. The task force was involved in four fatal shootings between May and July.
District Attorney Steve Mulroy said he has not yet decided whether to file charges in connection with the death.
A spokesperson for the Tennessee National Guard did not immediately respond to email and phone messages seeking comment. Ed Yarbrough, an attorney for the two guard members, said they have no comment at this time.
Authorities said the troops were responding with local police to reports of gunshots around 4 a.m. when they began pursuing an armed man fleeing on foot.
Footage from stationary street cameras shows a person in dark clothing firing shots through an empty parking lot at three people walking on a sidewalk. Two Memphis police officers hear gunshots nearby and start walking and then running in that direction, a body camera worn by one of the officers shows. The officers say on their radio that they are pursuing a man who is running and armed with a gun.
The video, which is blurry from the officer’s movement, captures yelling and the sound of a single gunshot, followed by several additional gunshot noises.
A Tennessee National Guard report obtained by The Associated Press via a public records request said two guard members responded to the Memphis police radio call, left their vehicle and approached the suspect, who “rounded on them and pointed a tan handgun at them.” Both guard members fired their service weapons — M17 handguns — and Memphis police arrived shortly after, the report stated.
Police body camera footage shows guard members at the scene shouting “Hands!” and “Turn over!” as they point their handguns at a man lying on his back on the sidewalk.
André C. Wharton, an attorney for Johnson’s family, noted that the videos do not show the moments immediately before the shooting, or the shooting itself.
“This investigation must stay focused on the moment the guardsman fired the fatal shot and whether that action was reasonable,” Wharton said.
Johnson was the father of a young child and was preparing to help lead the family construction business, his grandfather, Evaniel Johnson, said.
At least six guard members were on the scene immediately after the shooting, the body camera video shows. One can be seen moving a handgun that is on the ground until a police officer tells him to leave it alone. An officer calls for an ambulance over the radio, and a guard member begins to cut off the man’s shirt just before the video ends.
___
Schoenbaum reported from Salt Lake City.

title: “You Can See Everything”: Another victory for A24
text:
A24 must be allergic to making bad films. I say this with a particular air of sincerity because it seems as though this studio can only produce films of a high or mid-high quality. “Uncut Gems,” “Primetime,” “Backrooms” and even “Marty Supreme” are all films with superb camera work, competent acting and typically an engaging story. Being an A24 film is a badge a movie can wear proudly on its chest and one that tells the audience, “Hey! You’re in for a good time!”
But as you all surely know, with expectations come eager moviegoers, and with eager moviegoers come spent dollars and spent time. If the film fails to exceed or even meet expectations, a poor director somewhere in Hollywood gets executed and we can’t have that, can we? So the question is, is this film, “You Can See Everything,” another win for our good old A24? Yes! I’d say so, and we’ll get into that now.
“You Can See Everything” is an interesting film, as it is difficult to describe its plot presentation. Essentially, the entire film is a documentary about the days leading up to the arrest and subsequent 11-year prison sentence of Theranos founder and local fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, who, in her withdrawal from the public eye, has allowed the film’s directors, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, to film her and her partner, Billy Evans, along with their two children in a rented beach house. In many recreated scenes, Elizabeth Holmes and Billy Evans are portrayed by Amanda Seyfried and Christopher Abbott, respectively.
It’s a fascinating piece of filmmaking, which acts as a legitimate documentary, with the majority of the events depicted in the film having actually occurred in real life. Since the subjects of the film have largely disappeared from the public eye or have been incarcerated, the film uses reenactments to show us what happened, much like a docudrama. Something I have not seen in quite a while and found refreshing is that this film is 75% silence. Not normal silence, but reflective silence.
Much of the film is focused on its director, Nathan Fielder, who, while asking Elizabeth and Billy questions, consistently feels as though he is actively being manipulated. He believes that the pair aren’t being entirely forthcoming with him, especially when Holmes continues to deny she ever did anything wrong and Evans attempts to build a new company off the fraudulent technology from Theranos. A lot of this frustration is later explored in the film when Fielder is speaking to Seyfried over the transcripts of his and Holmes’ conversations. At the same time, those conversations don’t give much away, leaving the audience in suspense, all the while filling our ears with spine-chilling music that I’d argue doesn’t fit the film, yet works beautifully with it.
Of course, I’d be remiss if I didn’t mention the audience reactions when I went to see this film. I saw this on a Tuesday and there were plenty of people in the theater. There was quite a lot of laughing in the audience. I cannot blame them because this film can be a tad goofy at times. Fielder has an odd habit of looking like a lost child in wide shots of contemplative silence. Amanda Seyfried’s wide-eyed, grinning expressions also got a few laughs out of the audience, but so did the silent scenes, which got me thinking further.
Films such as these are usually relegated to the fringe; they are the brainchildren of European avant-garde filmmakers inspired by Scandinavian film artists. I couldn’t believe this was a mainstream release. Watching this movie in a theater that also played films like “Scream 7” just felt wrong. The eerie music, the long shots of silence and the deep introspectiveness of the main character all build this air of sophistication and brilliance. I by no means imply that this film is wrong for it, but I do wonder if mainstream audiences are ready for movies that break conventional standards of American film writing and cinema that leaves the audience wondering hours afterward, “Was she really lying?”
I’d certainly like to think so, but I suppose we’ll just have to wait and see, won’t we?

title: Letter to the Editor: Reflection on recent history
‘They were just kids’: 2 teens killed after late-night Halloween shooting outside restaurant
text:
SPARTANBURG, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) — Authorities in South Carolina are investigating a shooting that killed two teenagers over the weekend.
Spartanburg Police Chief Art Littlejohn said officers were called to the Cook Out restaurant on John B. White Sr. Boulevard around 11:30 p.m. Saturday for multiple shots being fired.
When officers arrived, they found two people suffering from gunshot wounds in the parking lot.
While at the scene, the victims were given first aid before being taken to the Spartanburg Regional Medical Center, where they later died, Littlejohn said.
The Spartanburg County Coroner’s Office identified those shot as 15-year-old Jayden Marek Watson and 17-year-old Shane Carter Dawkins.
Littlejohn said another person was also shot and suffered non-life-threatening injuries. They were taken to the hospital by a family member.
“I want to be totally clear, the young people that were out here were not bad young people; they were just kids. After Halloween night, going trick-or-treating, going out to get something to eat, and then someone being irresponsible, pulled out a gun and started shooting,” Littlejohn said.
At this time, Littlejohn said no arrests have been made, nor have any suspects been identified.
Spartanburg authorities said the shooting remains under investigation.

title: Is El Niño making storms and flash floods in the Southwest worse?
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A chaotic climate phenomenon is intensifying heavy rains and floods in the Southwest, experts say.
A natural warming cycle called El Niño is sizzling Pacific Ocean waters, leaking moisture into the air that can fuel passing storms. Such El Niño events can happen irregularly every couple of years, but scientists say the latest iteration is particularly extreme.
“We’ve had super El Niños in the past, but this is a super duper El Niño,” said meteorologist Jeff Masters of Yale Climate Connections.
The phenomenon wasn’t the only cause of the severe storms, but scientists say it’s making heavy rains more likely and intense across the Southern U.S.
Flash floods on Sunday prompted evacuations across northern New Mexico and central Arizona, and a Colorado ski town braced for its main river to rise to catastrophic levels. And just last week, another wet storm subjected southwestern states to days of flooding.
Over 20 trillion gallons of water have fallen on the Four Corners states and Nevada in the past two weeks, according to calculations by former National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration chief scientist Ryan Maue.
Experts say this year’s extreme El Niño is adding more moisture to the air and shifting atmospheric winds toward the Southwest, creating more ideal conditions for storms.
“The likelihood of big precipitation in the Southwest interior does go up this time of year, but we’re seeing it to a degree we actually haven’t seen before,” said climate scientist Daniel Swain with the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources.
The world’s oceans have already warmed over time because of human-caused climate change, and the El Niño heats things up even more.
“The fact that the ocean temperatures are already warmer than they were, say, 100 years ago, makes these El Niño situations even more intense,” said meteorologist Randy Cerveny with Arizona State University.
The phenomenon is changing weather patterns around the world: regions including Peru and Ecuador are also seeing record-breaking flooding, Swain said. The El Niño event is expected to peak in December, and experts say its onslaught could continue for months afterward.
To stay safe, experts recommended watching the forecast, planning ahead and heeding evacuation warnings from local authorities.
“We’re not at the peak of the heating in the Pacific Ocean. So yes, we will see more of these particular events,” Cerveny said.

title: Officials decry mass shootings that left at least 8 dead and dozens wounded over Halloween weekend
text:
Federal authorities in Texas planned to detail their response Monday to a series of shootings in Dallas, one of numerous gun incidents across the nation on Halloween weekend that left at least eight people dead and dozens more injured.
Many of the mass shootings occurred in entertainment districts and in college towns. The deadliest occurred in Dallas, where the U.S. attorney’s office planned a news conference to discuss federal actions related to three shootings in the city’s Deep Ellum neighborhood, a center of music and restaurants. Those shootings left four people dead and 15 injured and happened over the span of about an hour and 15 minutes early Sunday.
As investigators continued their searches for suspects and the motives for the shootings, word spread of even more mass violence over the weekend along with condemnation from elected officials.
Two separate shootings occurred in Birmingham, Alabama, after the annual “Magic City Classic” college football game on Saturday night. And police in college towns reported shootings in their nightlife districts where annual Halloween gatherings are popular, including in Fayetteville, Arkansas; Birmingham, Alabama; Newark, Delaware; Bloomington, Illinois; and Bloomington, Indiana.
Deep Ellum saw gun violence earlier this year
Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux has said investigators were still trying to determine if the shootings were related and why they started. His department had increased police presence prior to the shootings in the district, which had experienced deadly violence earlier this year.
Two people were fatally stabbed during a fight outside a nightclub in February, and a security guard was shot and killed while trying to break up a fight inside a nightclub in May. There also have been nonfatal shootings, including during Cinco de Mayo festivities in May when five people were wounded outside of a sports bar, police said.
Halloween can be a busy time for gun violence incidents
Multiple academic studies of police department and hospital data from major cities over the last decade have shown gun violence is more frequent at night, on weekends and on holidays. Several studies have pointed to the July Fourth holiday as being one of the most or the most violent holiday because of dark hours for fireworks celebrations, combined with alcohol consumption and other factors. New Year’s and Halloween were also high on the list for gun violence incidents.
Last year the homicide rate in the United States dropped to its lowest point in 75 years, according to FBI numbers on 2025 crime. Those numbers showed homicides decreased by 18% and overall violent crime dropped 9.3% last year.
Cities and municipalities across the country largely have been experiencing drops in homicides and violence, with a few exceptions, for the past few years. Federal authorities and nonprofit groups have noted national violent crime and homicide rates have been declining since 2022. Experts also noted that trend had continued through the first six months of 2026.
Elected officials take to social media after shootings
In Jackson, Mississippi, two people were killed and six others were injured in a shooting during a Halloween costume party at a nightclub early Sunday, police said. Just before the shooting, two men entered the club wearing ski masks. At some point at least one of the suspects opened fire into the crowd, police said. The suspects have not yet been identified.
A 20-year-old man and an 18-year-old woman were killed in the shooting, while six others were taken to hospitals with injuries that didn’t appear to be life threatening, police said.
“No one should have to fear for their life while enjoying an evening out,” Jackson Mayor John Horhn said in a statement following the shooting.
Near Indiana University’s campus, seven people were wounded in a shooting early Sunday in a busy nightlife area. None of the victims were believed to be students, police said.
“This is unacceptable in Bloomington, and in any community,” Bloomington Mayor Kerry Thomson said Sunday in a video address shared on social media.
Even with increased police staffing, no public safety plan can eliminate every act of violence, Thomson said.
Separate shootings occurred outside a college football game
In Birmingham, Alabama, one person was killed and eight others were wounded in two separate shootings just outside Legion Field after the annual “Magic City Classic” football game on Saturday night. Alabama State and Alabama A&M are archrivals whose annual contest has been played for more than 100 years. Nearly 70,000 fans attended Saturday’s game, won by Alabama A&M 31-28. The event draws some of the largest crowds in the country for games played in their college football division.
Michael Pickett, chief of the Birmingham Police Department, said most spectators and families had left the stadium property after the game. The first shooting happened nearby, where vendors were set up along Graymont Avenue.
___
Raby reported from Charleston, West Virginia. AP reporters Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia and Jamie Stengle in Dallas contributed to this report.

title: Looking back week of Nov. 5, 2026
text:
Bar Harbor
They are the best in Maine. And they did it together. The Mount Desert Island High School girls cross-country team captured the girls state Class B championship — the first for MDI in 24 years — on a muddy course at Leavitt Area High School Saturday. The Trojans edged out rival Cape Elizabeth 85-83 for an especially sweet victory. It took a team effort by MDI to capture the win, the strong finishes from all the athletes. Sophomore Heather Spurling, who has been the leader of the pack for MDI much of this season, ran the 5-kilometer race in 20 minutes and 20 seconds to earn to an overall fourth-place finish, improving on past performances with good pacing. “When all classes were combined — A, B and C — the MDI girls were first, so they are the top team in the state regardless of class,” coach Goupee said. Winning the top slot after a hiatus of 24 years is especially sweet for members of the team that last brought home the trophy. “I follow the team in the paper, said 1982 MDI High cross-country state champion Cindy Carey Walls, who ran under the coaching of the late Howie Richards. Ms. Walls, like Heather Spurling, finished fourth at state that year.

title: Ahead of ski season, King leads visa push for foreign seasonal workers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Amid anticipated shortages of seasonal and temporary workers this winter across Maine’s ski and tourism industries, U.S. Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, is leading a bipartisan effort to secure the maximum number of additional H-2B visas for the current fiscal year.
“Chronic labor shortages — faced by seasonal U.S. employers throughout the nation’s history — have evolved into a permanent structural challenge to the American workforce,” King and U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., write in a letter to U.S. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, joined by dozens of fellow lawmakers.
“As this need grows, so does the pressure on U.S. workers, whose employers’ workforce needs cannot be met with American workers alone,” the letter continues.
Maine ranks ninth nationally in demand for H-2B workers, who fill temporary jobs when local workers are unavailable, according to Sen. King’s office.
H-2B ‘critical’ for ski areas
Dirk Gouwens, executive director of the Maine Ski Association, said H-2B employees are critical to the success of the state’s larger ski areas.
“Without the extra help that they provide, ski areas would not be able to meet the needs of guests and this would adversely affect the quality of the ski experience in Maine,” he told Mainebiz.
“While our smaller ski areas, which are mostly located nearer to population centers, rely on them less, our bigger resorts are located in very rural locations that just don’t have big enough populations to fill all the jobs required to provide a top level ski experience,” he noted. “H-2B is critical to helping ski areas meet those needs.”

title: Grow, Give, Gorham: Local nonprofit marks 10 years of serving school community
text:
Grow, Give, Gorham: Local nonprofit marks 10 years of serving school community
Students at Gorham Middle School harvested a total of 1,300 pounds of produce from their Giving Garden this growing season. That food is used in their cafeteria and donated to the town's food pantry.
"That is the ultimate purpose of this garden — to raise food for the community and donate it to the food pantry so that more people will have access to good, fresh produce," said Paula Smeltzer, a master gardener who volunteers at the middle school.
Smeltzer leads other volunteers who help year-round when school is not in session, but during the school year she spends a lot of time working hands-on with the students. She said, "I enjoy being around kids this age that are curious and want to explore and try to learn a little bit."
The Giving Garden was started 22 years ago by teacher Heather Whitaker, who is also co-founder of Grow, Give, Gorham. The nonprofit now oversees the garden and also organizes the town's backpack food distribution program and the Rams Rack, a free thrift shop for students.
"It only works because everyone is doing it together," Whitaker said. According to Smeltzer, the Giving Garden welcomed a record number of volunteers for the 2026 growing season. Others donate their time and money to support the outreach efforts happening inside the school.
Whitaker started Gorham's backpack program 10 years ago alongside Jen Baker, the assistant principal at Village Elementary School. Nonperishable food items are packed into bags and discreetly sent home with students, so they have something to eat over the weekend.
Volunteer Kevin Lambertson said, "Something like this helps to be able to provide food for those families in a way that still gives them dignity... They can receive things that they need without really having to totally give away the situation that they find themselves in."
Lambertson and the other volunteers meet in the middle school cafeteria biweekly to pack the bags. The food is donated or purchased with donated funds.
"It's a powerful reminder of the good that there is in the world," Whitaker said, adding that kids need to have their needs met in order to succeed academically.
Those needs include clothing. The Rams Rack is a free closet resembling a small boutique thrift store in the library. It was started by freshmen Leela Morris and Rataj Zamat after they volunteered at Maine Needs, a Portland-based nonprofit providing free necessities like clothing and hygiene items.
"This isn't a space that's for students who need something," Zamat said. "It's something that anybody could use, anybody could donate to and help out with." They encourage all students, regardless of need, to take advantage of this resource and enjoy shopping secondhand.
Morris said, "I was not picturing like a store type thing or anything like this, so I'm very happy that it turned out this way and that so many people support it."
To support the Rams Rack, clothing donations can be brought to Gorham Middle School. Food donations for the backpack program should be brought there, too. Volunteers can register online.
"It wouldn't be this if it wasn't for the Gorham community and the greater community who donates their time, who donates food items," Whitaker said. "It's a powerful reminder that when we come together and we work together, that we can accomplish really amazing things."

title: Bridge replacement over I-95 underway along Newport, Palmyra town line
text:
NEWPORT, Maine (WABI) - A major bridge replacement project is underway along the Newport and Palmyra town line, state transportation officials announced Monday.
Maine Department of Transportation crews began work on the Exit 157 interchange bridge, which carries routes 100 and 11 over Interstate 95.
Drivers on I-95 should expect lane shifts and periodic closures in both northbound and southbound lanes near the interchange. On routes 100 and 11, traffic will be reduced to alternating one-way lanes during daytime hours, with flaggers directing motorists through the work zone.

title: Supporters resubmit signatures for 2027 ‘Protect Girls’ Sports’ referendum
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Supporters of the “Protect Girls’ Sports” referendum resubmitted thousands of petition signatures Monday for the 2027 ballot and announced a federal civil rights complaint against the state.
New signatures submitted
Campaign organizers said the effort fell 532 signatures short of this year’s ballot because of paperwork tied up in federal court. They said volunteers gathered new signatures on a measure to designate interscholastic sports and school facilities, such as restrooms and locker rooms, by the sex listed on an original birth certificate.
“Today we are submitting 4,836 signatures, almost 10 times what the state has said we need to make sure our petition is validated and goes straight to the 2027 ballot box,” said Leyland Streiff, principal officer of Protect Girls Sports in Maine and leader of Maine Girl Dads.
Local high school athletes were among those who delivered the new signatures to the Secretary of State’s office. They contend that allowing transgender girls to compete in female divisions creates an unfair advantage.
“Men are naturally stronger and faster than women, due to the muscle growth that testosterone creates,” said Reagan Wilson, a junior at Fryeburg Academy. “Naturally, the men I competed against displaced several girls across different sports. This is unacceptable and has deprived me and so many other girls of equal opportunity to compete and win.”
Federal complaint filed
The citizen initiative is paired with a formal federal challenge.
Alliance Defending Freedom, a national conservative Christian legal group, filed a Title IX complaint with the U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights. The complaint was filed on behalf of two female athletes from Fryeburg and Windham. It targets the state, two school districts and the Maine Principals’ Association.
The Maine Principals’ Association previously argued it lacks federal funding for Title IX jurisdiction.
Opponents respond
Transgender advocates dispute claims of a physical advantage at young ages. They argue the measure violates the Maine Human Rights Act’s protections against gender identity discrimination in extracurricular activities.
“Forcing people to be in spaces where they don’t feel welcome, where they don’t feel safe, where they don’t belong — that don’t align with how they see themselves and how they know themselves to be, is incredibly damaging,” said Kris Pitts, executive director of the Maine Trans Network.
Opponents, including Free and Fair Schools Maine, say the measure could open schools to costly lawsuits.
Next steps
Election officials will now review the petitions to determine whether the initiative qualifies for the November 2027 ballot.

title: Russia bombs aid center and shelter in southern Ukraine, killing 24, authorities say
text:
Russia bombs aid center and shelter in southern Ukraine, killing 24, authorities say
Russia bombed an aid distribution center and neighboring shelter in southern Ukraine on Monday, killing 24 people, Ukraine's emergency services agency said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X that 10 guided bombs targeted an area that included a school building used to distribute humanitarian aid and a nearby shelter.
“This is further proof that Russia wants no de-escalation,” Zelenskyy said.
The attacks in the village of Komyshuvakha, in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, occurred as a limited ceasefire expired Monday in Kherson, a different region in the country's south. The limited ceasefire agreement had allowed humanitarian aid and evacuation missions into front-line areas in Russian-occupied territory.
“There was a moment when the next steps could have shown that progress toward peace was possible,” Zelenskyy said. “With these killings, Russia is sending an entirely opposite signal: Russia is counting on more killings.”
As night fell in Komyshuvakha, emergency responders used flashlights to search through the rubble of collapsed buildings, according to photos and video posted online by local officials. About 20 people are considered missing and the death toll could rise, these officials say.
Efforts to rescue people Monday evening were hindered as Russian drones launched additional attacks in the area that had been bombed, according to Mykhailo Semikin, a military official in Zaporizhzhia.
In other areas of Ukraine, authorities reported multiple Russian drone attacks that injured at least 17 people.
After cyberattacks, false alerts sent in Ukraine and Russia
Earlier, residents of Ukraine and Russia had received phony emergency alerts from government-run mobile apps that were hacked, authorities in both countries said. The phony alerts in Ukraine included a warning about an imminent nuclear threat.
It was not clear if the cyberattacks late Sunday in Ukraine and early Monday in Russia were related. Ukraine said its mobile app, which residents rely on to seek safety from Russian missile and drone strikes, was up and running again after being temporarily suspended. Russian authorities said efforts to restore its emergency alert mobile app were ongoing.
A Russian Telegram channel with links to the country's security services said Monday that a hacking group, Hitcore, claimed responsibility for the breach of the Ukrainian emergency alert system. The Associated Press did not independently verify the claim, and the affiliations or motivations of the purported hackers remained unclear.
The alerts received by Ukrainians — making false claims of high radiation levels, a chemical threat and public disturbances in Kyiv — were written in English, Russian and Ukrainian. The English language alerts contained spelling and grammatical errors.
One of the messages, written in Russian, said: “Hi! There will be a nuclear threat across Ukraine. Do not worry, the Oreshnik is incoming,” a reference to a Russian ballistic missile.
There was little indication the fake alerts caused panic in Ukraine. Instead, there was a flood of humorous posts online, with social media users sharing photos of their pets relaxing and apocalypse-themed images generated by artificial intelligence.
A spokesman for Ukraine’s air force command, Yurii Ihnat, said in a television interview that the cyberattack had no impact on Ukraine’s security and defense operations. The government urged people to monitor other emergency channels on social media while the cyberattack was being addressed.
In Russia, the Emergency Situations Ministry said in a statement that hackers sent a false alert through its app at approximately 2:45 a.m. Moscow time on Monday across 33 of Russia’s 89 regions. It did not say who it believed carried out the attack.
The ministry sought to reassure Russians by noting that the wider public alert system was working normally through SMS messages, media broadcasts and municipal sirens and loudspeakers.
“All government bodies must take steps to improve the cybersecurity of our digital resources,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said.
Limited ceasefire ends in Kherson region
As the ceasefire in Ukraine's Kherson region came to an end on Monday, Ukraine’s general staff said that Russia’s military had used the pause in fighting to bolster its drone defenses and replenish ammunition supplies.
The brief pause in fighting, which began on Oct. 27, was part of a humanitarian aid and evacuation mission in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, and marked the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since Russia’s full-scale invasion began nearly five years ago.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, emergency services reported that drone strikes injured 12 people in the eastern Kharkiv region and damaged a refrigeration facility, greenhouses and residential buildings.
Five people were also reported injured in the Black Sea port city of Odesa, where a warehouse was targeted and homes were damaged.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Monday that it shot down 212 Ukrainian drones overnight. The head of Russia’s Samara region, Gov. Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, said in a statement that local air defenses were repelling an aerial attack, but did not give further details.
Independent Russian media outlets later reported that Ukrainian drones had targeted one of Europe’s largest oil transport hubs in Samara.
Katie Marie Davies contributed to this report from Manchester, England.

title: ‘The right time’: County removes all Flock cameras, ends use over privacy concerns
text:
HENRICO, Va. (WWBT/Gray News) - Crews in Virginia have removed all Flock cameras in a county over the weekend.
According to Henrico County Manager John Vithoulkas, crews removed more than 120 Flock cameras Saturday.
County officials said they had to take down the cameras themselves after Flock failed to fulfill its “contractual obligation” to remove them.
Henrico County ended its use of Flock cameras last month due to privacy concerns.
The county said the cameras were supposed to be gone within two weeks after the contract ended.
However, that was not the case, and officials said the poles holding the cameras remain in place, with it being Flock’s responsibility to remove them.
In a social post on Oct. 6, Henrico County said after talking with other leaders, police cut ties with the automatic license plate reader cameras by mid-October.
Officials said the decision evolved as they heard from residents, police and experts about the benefits of the technology, as well as privacy and data-access concerns.
Leaders described the move as preventative and said there was no evidence Henrico police misused the system.
“Rather be proactive than reactive. And we’re aware of the conversations that are occurring nationally, as well as on the state level. And we just, again, felt that this was the right time to make this decision,” Rev. Roscoe D. Cooper III, chairman of the Henrico Board of Supervisors, said.
The technology has drawn public criticism over privacy and potential misuse.

title: Mortgage closing costs: What they are and how much you’ll pay
text:
Mortgage closing costs: What they are and how much you’ll pay
Key takeaways
- Closing costs are the fees you pay to get a mortgage and finalize the purchase, and most of them are due on closing day.
- Costs typically range from 2% to 5% of the total loan amount, or about $8,000 to $20,000 for a $400,000 loan.
- The biggest line items are lender origination fees, title services, the appraisal and the prepaid taxes and insurance that go into your escrow account, and buyers pay most of the fees.
- Your Loan Estimate tells you which fees you can shop for and which are fixed. Comparing that document across at least three lenders is the one step that reliably lowers what you pay.
Closing costs may not be the most exciting part of buying your home, but they are an important expense to plan for. From origination fees and appraisals to title services, they can add up to thousands of dollars, with most being paid by buyers. Some costs are avoidable, others may be negotiable and some are required by your state or county.
Here are the fees to watch for and how to keep them in check.
How much are closing costs?
Buying a home comes with more expenses than just your down payment. Expect to pay about 2% to 5% of your total loan amount in mortgage closing costs. If you’ve taken out a $400,000 loan, that means your closing costs might range from $8,000 to $20,000. How much you’ll end up paying depends on factors like the home’s price, your loan type and where you buy.
According to a 2025 report from LodeStar, the average purchase closing cost total was $4,528 nationally, or about 1% of the average sales price of $433,632. But while LodeStar’s calculation accounts for some common fees, it leaves out origination and underwriting fees, real estate commissions, discount points and escrow prepaids. So, about 1% of the sales price covers title, settlement and government charges. The rest of the way to 2% to 5% of your loan amount is lender fees, points and prepaids, and that’s the part you have the most influence over.
Click the arrow below to compare average closing costs by state.
-  Average closing costs by state Remember, these figures don’t include lender fees or commissions. LodeStar found that closing costs run highest, as a share of sales price, in states where transfer taxes make up the bulk of the bill — Delaware, New York, Vermont, Pennsylvania and Washington, D.C. They run lowest in states with little or no transfer tax. Washington, D.C., and Delaware are the most expensive areas for closing costs. The least expensive were South Dakota, Iowa and Missouri. Source: Lodestar
What’s included in closing costs?
Closing costs can feel like a long list of unfamiliar fees, but nearly all of them fall into one of four buckets:
- Lender fees: Your lender charges these to set up, process and approve your loan. You may also have the option to buy discount points, which are upfront payments that lower your interest rate.
- Third-party services: These pay outside professionals for the home appraisal, title search, title insurance policy, survey and closing agent.
- Government charges: Your city, county or state charges these to record the sale and the mortgage in public records. Many states and counties also charge a transfer tax when the property changes hands.
- Prepaids: These fees cover bills that aren’t due yet. You’ll pay interest from your closing date to your first payment, plus several months of property taxes and homeowners insurance that go into an escrow account.
Not every upfront cost associated with buying a home is considered a closing cost. For example, your down payment will go toward the purchase price of your home and is separate from closing costs.
Two of these four buckets are negotiable. Your lender sets its own fees, and you can compare them and shop for most third-party services. Government charges are set by statute and prepaids are set by your tax bill and your insurer, so neither moves much.
Who pays closing costs?
If you’re the buyer, you’re likely to pay most of the closing costs. Sellers cover some, and in a slower market, they’ll sometimes cover more.
Closing costs paid by the buyer
Buyers may be able to negotiate with the seller to cover some of their costs, called “seller concessions.” The shoppable column below tells you where you have room to move. Some fees you influence by comparing lender offers, some by sourcing the provider yourself and some not at all, because a statute sets them.
Closing costs paid by the seller
Sellers usually pay out of their sale proceeds rather than bringing cash to the table. Sellers can also agree to pay some of the buyer’s closing costs outright as a credit.
Compare your Loan Estimates before you commit
Every lender has to give you the same three-page form within three business days of applying. That’s the point of the Loan Estimate: it’s standardized, so offers line up side by side. To compare offers, read page 2: Section B lists the services you can’t shop for, and Section C lists the ones you can.
Three rules govern what happens between your Loan Estimate and closing day:
- Some can’t increase at all: Your lender’s own charges, discount points, transfer taxes and fees for services you can’t shop, like the credit report and the appraisal.
- Some can increase up to 10%, as a group: Recording fees, plus any Section C service where you used a provider from your lender’s written list.
- Some can change by any amount: Prepaid interest, insurance premiums, escrow deposits and any provider who wasn’t on your lender’s list.
If something material changes on your loan file, your lender can reset those limits, but it must document the reason and send you a revised Loan Estimate.
Your Closing Disclosure arrives at least three business days before closing with the final version of the same numbers. Put the two side by side and look for anything that moved. If a protected fee went up, be sure to ask why — your lender may owe you the difference.
Compare current mortgage rates
Compare mortgage rates from our national marketplace of lenders to find the best rate for your situation.
Learn more
How to lower your closing costs
You won’t avoid closing costs entirely, but you can lower what you pay. These are ordered by how much they typically move.
- Compare lenders and negotiate fees: Look for a mortgage lender that doesn’t charge an origination fee, or one that’ll discount it. Once you have three Loan Estimates in hand, you can show each lender the best offer and ask them to match it. If you’re getting your mortgage at your bank, you can also try asking for a discount or fee waiver, since you’re already a customer.
- Negotiate seller concessions: To encourage a sale, or in a buyer-friendly market, a seller might agree to pay some of your costs. This is often the single largest reduction a buyer can get. Keep in mind that lenders and loan programs limit how much sellers can contribute, and the limit depends on your loan type and down payment, so confirm it with your lender before you write it into an offer.
- Shop around when possible: Section C of your Loan Estimate names the services you can source yourself, typically the title insurance, title search and survey. Comparing providers can reduce your costs, though using your lender’s written list means that fee loses its 10% protection.
- Apply for down payment assistance: Down payment assistance and grants aren’t always limited to your down payment. Depending on the program, some can help with closing costs, particularly if you’re a first-time homebuyer.
- Use a no-closing-cost loan, but run the numbers: Don’t let the name fool you — you’ll still pay closing costs with a no-closing-cost loan. But instead of paying that amount now, you’ll finance it with your mortgage and pay interest on it or pay a slightly higher interest rate. Find your break-even point, or the amount of time it takes for the cost of the loan to make sense. If skipping $6,000 upfront costs you an extra $100 a month, you break even at five years. Stay in the house longer than that, and the loan costs you more.
Frequently asked questions
-  How can I budget for closing costs? Before you start looking at homes, get preapproved for a mortgage so you understand how much you can afford to spend. Knowing your price point can give you a rough sense of what closing costs might be. Since total closing costs are typically 2% to 5% of the loan amount, it might be a good idea to set aside enough funds to cover the high end of that range, on top of your down payment.
-  When are closing costs paid? Most closing costs are paid at the closing, when you sign your final loan and purchase documents. But some of the fees, such as for an appraisal and credit check, are paid ahead of time.
-  How long does the closing process take? Most purchase loans close in about 30 to 45 days from application, though the timeline depends on your loan type, your lender and how quickly you return the requested documents. ICE Mortgage Technology put the average purchase loan at 36.8 days in March 2026, the fastest since it began tracking in 2019. Conventional loans tend to close faster than government-backed loans like FHA and VA loans.
-  Why are closing costs so high? Closing costs, which typically range from 2% to 5% of your mortgage loan, come down to two things: the mortgage amount and where you’re buying. Many of the biggest fees grow with the deal — loan origination is typically a percentage of your loan amount, and title insurance premiums are based on your purchase price or loan amount. Location matters because of taxes: LodeStar found that closing costs run highest, as a share of sales price, in states where transfer taxes make up the bulk of the bill, and lowest in states with little or no transfer tax. Beyond lender charges and third-party services like appraisals and inspections, mandatory escrow prepayments for taxes and insurance can add thousands before you’ve made a single mortgage payment.

title: Reward grows after six dogs found tortured, slain along road
text:
CRETE, Ill. (WLS) - Crime Stoppers of Will County is offering a $25,000 reward for information leading to an arrest in the case of six dogs that were tortured and killed and left on the side of a rural road in Crete. It is the largest reward offered by the organization.
“This is really an important crime to solve,” said David Silverman of Crime Stoppers of Will County.
Two organizations add to reward
Two organizations teamed up to offer reward money in the case.
First Secure Bank Group offered $5,000 in April. Pets and Vets USA, which trains rescued pit bulls to be service dogs for veterans, is adding $20,000.
“Even if you’re not a pet lover, I mean, six little dogs being tortured and killed. How can anybody like anything like that,” said Jay Bergman, First Secure Bank Group board chairman.
Peter Cangelosi, founder of Pets and Vets USA, said, “We got to do something because this progresses from torturing animals to killing animals into human beings.” He said the person or people responsible need to be caught and stopped.
Bags found along Kings Road and Norfolk Avenue
In March, Crete Township workers found black garbage bags on the side of the road at the intersection of Kings Road and Norfolk Avenue in Crete Township. After the workers returned to their office, they discovered the bags had dead dogs inside.
Will County State’s Attorney James Glasgow described what investigators found.
“There were six pit bulls, 45 to 55 pounds, and they showed signs of having been in fighting,” Glasgow said. “I can’t tell you exactly, but they were brutally killed, and then thrown in black trash bags on the side of the road.”
A photo of the dogs has been blurred because of the state of the animals. The photo is being shared to show the coloring of the dogs, which may assist the investigation.
Glasgow: Animal cruelty a danger to society
Glasgow has helped strengthen Illinois animal cruelty laws over the years and is a pet owner. He said people who are cruel to animals pose a danger to society.
“Anybody who is cruel to animals is not just going to stop there, and that’s when you know every serial killer tortured animals as a child or on the way up,” Glasgow said.
How to claim the reward
Will County officials said anyone who claims the reward can remain anonymous. The reward would be paid after someone is charged, with no questions asked.
Anyone with information about the dogs found in Crete can call Crime Stoppers at 1-800-323-6734 or text 274637.

title: Iran has 2-day plan to reopen Strait, resume nuclear talks with US
text:
Iran has 2-day plan to reopen Strait, resume nuclear talks with US
Iran said Monday it had a two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks with the United States if Washington meets its demands, shortening a process originally expected to take seven days.
The announcement came as the region braces for possible renewed fighting, even as Iran’s top diplomat said Sunday that he hoped the U.S. would choose “diplomacy over other paths.”
Iran previously said the plan could be implemented within a week if the U.S. met seven conditions, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports. Iran now says ships passing through the reopened strait would have to follow a route agreed upon by Iran and Oman and travel under Iranian supervision. Separately, Iranian officials have said the U.S. must lift sanctions on Iranian oil sales and agree to a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said the plan remained the basis for negotiations with Washington through mediators, despite the shorter implementation timeline. “This once again demonstrates Iran’s good-faith approach,” he added.
Baghaei gave no indication that Tehran had changed its demands or that Washington had accepted its proposal.
President Donald Trump has alternated between pursuing diplomacy and threatening heavy bombing of Iran in his public comments.
