title: Rock singer addresses rumors of being on board deadly Florida jet crash, reports say
text:
Reports: Singer Lenny Kravitz addresses rumors of being onboard deadly Florida jet crash
Singer and actor Lenny Kravitz is setting the record straight following rumors claiming he died after a jet nose-dived and crashed in Florida on Sunday.
Kravitz's publicist issued a statement to TMZ and local outlet BocaNewsNow, calling the reports "untrue and incorrect."
The Hollywood Reporter, in reference to the New York Post, said the alleged rumors started with a post on X of a purported screenshot of a post by 21-year-old pilot Emily Shelton, who previously went viral in August for making an emergency landing on a highway.
Video: Palm Beach County jet crash witness video
The screenshot, according to reports, made it sound as if Kravitz was on the ill-fated flight that took off from Austin, Texas, and was headed to the Bahamas.
Shelton later posted a statement on TikTok, saying she was not the pilot on the flight.
“I would like to respectfully clarify I was not (the pilot). I ask that people please stop speculating and spreading misinformation on this tragedy and be respectful of those involved. My heart goes out to all those lost and affected,” she wrote.
The rumors come less than a day after a jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood. The aircraft appeared to just miss several homes near a busy road.
All nine people on board were killed. None of the people killed have been publicly identified.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed.
The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 11 kilometers) when pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation and requested to climb another 2,000 feet (about 610 meters).
Moments later, the plane entered a steep dive, first 10,000 feet per minute, then 20,000 feet per minute and up to 30,000 feet per minute, speeding the plane beyond its design limits, according to air traffic control recordings and flight tracking data.
A pilot declared an emergency and issued distress calls. The plane banked sharply to the right before it smashed into the ground.
An investigation is underway.
The Associated Press contributed to this article.

title: Bangor Symphony concert with Gary Sinise to feature his late son’s music
text:
After Gary Sinise’s 33-year-old son died of a rare spinal cancer on Jan. 5, 2024, the actor, best known for his role as Lt. Dan Taylor in the 1994 “Forrest Gump,” went looking for ways to stay connected to McCanna “Mac” Anthony Sinise.
He went through his son’s laptop, phone, tablet and papers. The grieving father found a treasure trove of music Mac had never shared with him. There was sheet music, audio demos and melodies he sang into his phone.
The Bangor Symphony Orchestra will perform some of that music at 7 p.m. Saturday and at 1 p.m. Sunday at the Collins Center for the Arts in Orono. The concert will include Gary Sinise and the Lt. Dan Band, which has performed in all 50 states and more than 600 times for troops around the globe.
Sinise said in a pre-concert interview with Lucas Richman, the conductor and music director for the Bangor Symphony Orchestra, and Executive Director Renia Shterenberg that discovering his son’s music was “a blessing.”
“Often, I think that parents who have lost children may not have that discovery, I have had that blessing,” Sinise said. “It has been so helpful to me [in the grieving process].”
In 2023, Mac recorded an album of his music titled “Resurrection & Revival.” Last year, his father gathered the music he’d found in 2024 in a second album. But Sinise kept finding compositions Mac had written and, earlier this year, recorded a third album.
Richman saw Sinise and his band perform Mac’s music in August in Milwaukee. Richman wanted to bring that music to Maine but felt he needed a personal connection to Sinise to quickly schedule a concert with the Bangor Symphony. It turned out that he had one. Richman’s brother-in-law is a first cousin to Danny Gottlieb, the Lt. Dan Band’s longtime drummer.
“As a father, I was incredibly touched by Mac’s journey and Gary’s dedication to bringing the treasure trove of his son’s music to light,” Richman said in announcing the concert. “It will be such a great honor to have Gary here with the BSO playing his son’s music, as well as paying tribute to the generations of veterans who are the focal point of the work being done by the Gary Sinise Foundation.”
Sinise started the foundation in 2011 to uplift America’s defenders and their families. Its mission statement says: “We serve our nation by honoring our defenders, veterans, first responders, their families, and those in need. We do this by creating and supporting unique programs designed to entertain, educate, inspire, strengthen and build communities.”
This weekend’s concert will be presented in conjunction with Sinise’s upcoming book “Graceful Warrior,” which honors Mac and his own family’s journey of healing. It will officially be released on Nov. 10, on what would have been Mac’s 36th birthday and the day before Veterans Day.
In addition to Mac’s music, the program will include Aaron Copland’s “Fanfare for the Common Man,” Richman’s “A Western Fanfare” and Copland’s “A Lincoln Portrait,” narrated by Sinise. The second half of the concert will feature the Lt. Dan Band playing for the first time with a symphony orchestra.
Richman said the last time he conducted “A Lincoln Portrait” with the Bangor symphony was in October 2010, his first concert conducting. His actor father, Peter Mark Richman, narrated. The elder Richman died in January 2014.
“I have some big shoes to fill,” Sinise told Richman in the pre-concert interview.
A special book signing event with Gary Sinise will be held before each concert. For more information, visit bangorsymphony.org or call the Collins Center box office at 207-581-2787.

title: A play for the times: “Urinetown” should bring sweet relief
text:
BAR HARBOR — The sad news for MDI High School theater lovers is that after directing several successful fall musicals, including 2024’s already legendary production of “Chicago,” Annie Leonardi is moving on to new creative adventures.
The good news is, waiting in the wings for her shot at directing a fall musical was one of the high school’s English teachers, Miranda Snyder.
“As a former theater kid myself, I knew when I applied for the job four years ago, I’d want to get involved in the theater program,” Snyder said.
And she has, assisting with various school productions and participating on and offstage in several Grand productions.
But when she heard Leonardi was stepping down as director, Snyder said she knew she was ready to step up. She also knew exactly what musical she wanted to do. Mark Holmann and Greg Kotis’s Tony Award-winning satire, “Urinetown.”
Despite its off-putting name, Snyder said it is the perfect vehicle for the times we are living in, with its themes of political corruption, controversy, absurdity, and civil protest. It was also perfect for MDI High’s deep pool of talent and generations of theatrical savvy.
“Although ‘Urinetown’ was first produced in 2001, it’s amazing how relevant it is today,” she said. “I first saw it right after the 2024 election when I was feeling pretty demoralized about everything. In addition to being flabbergasted by its relevance, this funny story with its moving, feel-good music and hopeful message somehow made me feel better.”
Curiously, it was not drama department head Casey Rush whom she had to convince — he knew the play and was on board from the get-go — but the students whose initial reaction when she announced they would be doing something called “Urinetown” was pretty much “eewww-ah!”
“But one by one, as they read the script and listened to the music,” Snyder said, “they fell in love with it, too.”
This was made pretty clear at a rehearsal I attended last week in the high school’s dance studio. I arrived mid-first act, just as Fenris Dube, playing officer Lockstock and his towering sidekick, officer Barrell — another fun role for Jorgie Brylen-Waldrop — are exhorting in song an unhappy-looking crowd about what to expect if they don’t obey the rules.
“It’s a hard, cold, tumble of a journey
Worthy of a gurney, a bumble down
A slapped face, smacked with a mace
Certain to debase is our stumble down”
Those of us who saw last year’s Cinderella will recall Dube’s fine, strong baritone, which has only grown stronger, as has his stage presence. He makes it very clear he is a bad guy in this strange story. Officer Lockstock also has a tendency to break through the fourth wall of the theater, to directly address the audience with sardonic updates about the progress of the play.
OK, about that story. Without giving too much away, “Urinetown” takes place in a dystopian future where water has become so scarce that the supply is strictly rationed. As part of that rationing system citizens are also forced to pay to pee and must only do so in public “amenities.” Those who are caught violating these rules are exiled to a mysterious place called “Urinetown,” from which no one returns.
Sadly, as is too often the case (present circumstances not excluded), the people in power, rather than working to make things better for average citizens, devise new ways they can further monetize the situation and line their own pockets.
Inevitably, something’s gotta give, and in this case a young hero, named Bobby Strong, decides enough is enough and leads a grassroots revolution to bring literal relief to the people.
I got to watch as this handsome hero, Bobby, a well-cast Alix Osier, who was a scene stealer as the Page in “Cinderella,” enters the story, realizes something is drastically wrong with the present system, meets the love of his life, Hope, played by Nyeli Monahan — another talented member of that family — discovers she is the daughter of one of the Pay to Pee oligarchs and then abducts her for the cause.
As Hope’s horrible dad, Kevin McDunough is a menacing, powerful presence when he’s speaking. If he can bring that same kind of power and overbearing confidence to his singing, he’s going to scare the, uh, urine out of us all with his song, “Don’t Be the Bunny.”.
After the abduction is accomplished, with a hilarious slo-mo chase scene, officer Lockstock informs us the first act has ended.
I have no idea what happens next, but the glimpses I got of these characters and many others such as Miss Pennywise (the always excellent Molly Dority), Little Sally (adorable Amelia McCane), Little Becky Two Shoes (Liana Johnson, who was hilarious as one of the stepsisters in “Cinderella”), Soupy Sue (Lina Bodge, who made an adorable snowman in the ACT production of “Frozen”) and a bunch of other delightful oddballs.
The score, directed by Annelise Smith, is rousing, and I got to hear some terrific chorus numbers in which everyone seems to be singing at different tempos, but somehow it all worked wonderfully. All this and some fun choreography-in-progress, all make me eager to see how this story plays out.
As this rehearsal was held in the dance studio, I did not get to see any of the production elements they are working on. There has been another changing of the guard in set design, with Thomas Van Gorder taking over for retired Carlene Hirsch. One can only hope he is able to provide this talented cast an environment that matches their energy, excellence and commitment.
Christian Breau will once again conduct the pit orchestra, and we should expect some great evocative costuming from Flannery Lameyer.
Urinetown opens Friday, Nov. 13, at 7 p.m., with evening performances Nov. 14, 20, and 21, with 2 p.m. matinees Sunday, Nov. 15, and Saturday, Nov. 21.

title: Nonprofit packs custom clothing boxes for children in need
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A Virginia nonprofit is using volunteers to pack personalized boxes of clothing and other items for children who lack access to proper clothes.
Boxes of Basics founder Sarah Tyndall started the organization in 2018. A thousand volunteers have since built custom care packages for more than 8,500 children across Virginia.
Clothing insecurity affects children nationwide
An estimated two out of five kids nationwide experience clothing insecurity, meaning they do not have access to clothing that is properly fitted, seasonally appropriate and in good condition.
Clothing insecurity is estimated to affect 20 million children across the country.
Without proper clothes, children can skip school, face bullying and withdraw socially. Clothing insecurity can also lead to lower self-esteem.
Tyndall said she started Boxes of Basics because she saw a need.
“It was the right thing for someone to do. And if I could help these kids, then why wouldn’t I?” Tyndall said.
She described one boy who was affected.
“This little boy didn’t want to go to school because he didn’t have clothes that fit. They were worn. They were small,” Tyndall said. “And after his box of basics, he started waking up 30 minutes early every day. Just to pick out his outfit.”
How the boxes are made
Schools and shelters identify children in need, then share their sizes, favorite colors and favorite characters. Volunteers at a warehouse use that information to select clothing for each child they will never meet.
The clothes are donated. Some are new, and some are gently used.
Tyndall said every box includes:
- Four school outfits
- Four play outfits
- A dress-up outfit
- New shoes, socks and underwear
- Two age-appropriate books
- A set of pajamas
- A hygiene kit
Boxes of Basics also provides a duffle bag for children who need a way to carry their new outfits.
Hand wrapped outfits and love notes
Volunteers hand wrap each outfit and add a love note to every box.
Volunteer Cheryl Burns said the note is the part she likes most.
“I hope you like the clothes and books that I enjoyed picking out for you,” Burns said of the message. “And then I always do a smiley. That’s like my signature. When you see someone smile, it, like, brings joy.”
The organization’s goal is to spread that joy beyond Virginia.

title: Cause of Presque Isle Aprtment house fire released
text:
Presque Isle Apartment House Fire Cause Released
The Maine State Fire Marshal's office says a fire that destroyed a Presque Isle apartment building on Saturday was caused by discarded ashes.
The Presque Isle Fire Department responded around 2:30 a.m. to a three-story apartment building at 572 Main Street that also housed a business.
During the initial response, firefighters determined that the fire originated in an attached shed and was linked to an ash bucket containing discarded ashes, according to Maine Public Safety Department spokesperson Aaron Turcotte.
After extinguishing the blaze, the Presque Isle Fire Department was later called back to the property for a second report of fire in the building. Caribou, Easton, Fort Fairfield and Mapleton, Castle Hill, Chapman Fire departments were called in to help battle the fire.
An excavator was brought in the remove the metal roof to get at the fire in the attic. The area around 572 Main Street was closed until around 11:30 Saturday morning. Crews kept putting water on the fire for several more hours.
The Presque Isle Fire Department requested assistance from the State Fire Marshal's Office to investigate the circumstances of the two fire responses. Investigators determined that the original fire had continued to burn undetected within multiple layers of wall and roof materials, eventually becoming visible and prompting a second fire department response, Turcotte said.
The investigation concluded that the second fire was a continuation of the original one rather than a separate one.
There were no injuries reported. The American Red Cross was offering assistance to the displaced tenants.

title: Police: Several Disney, Universal employees among 281 arrested in Florida sex trafficking sting
text:
17 Disney and Universal employees among 281 arrested in Florida sex trafficking sting, sheriff says
An undercover investigation targeting human trafficking and child sex predators resulted in 281 arrests, including several Disney World and Universal Studios employees, the Polk County Sheriff's Office said Friday.
The operation, called "Polk Around and Find Out II," took seven days, Sheriff Grady Judd said.
The investigation resulted in 239 arrests related to prostitution, 31 arrests related to child sexual predators and 11 other arrests, according to deputies.
Authorities identified 11 human trafficking victims during the investigation.
Attorney James Uthmeier highlighted the range of suspects involved.
"It's theme park employees, it's teachers, it's coaches...it's a wake-up call for parents that you got to be in your kids' lives," Uthmeier said.
According to the sheriff's office, 13 of the suspects arrested were Disney employees and four were Universal Studios employees. Thirty-two of those arrested were living in the U.S. illegally, authorities said.
Among the arrests, Eric Raymond, an Orange County deputy sheriff, was charged with soliciting prostitution.
Another suspect, Rashion Crayton, a youth football coach in Davenport, was caught texting a deputy posing as a 14-year-old girl for sex.
Judd said it was the largest undercover operation his office has ever conducted. Law enforcement uncovered 700 prior charges during the arrests.

title: UMaine men’s hockey falls to BU after three-goal burst in 91 seconds
text:
BOSTON — The University of Maine men’s ice hockey team’s first conference game of the season got off to a rough start on Friday, Oct. 30, as Boston University (BU) scored three goals in 91 seconds and never looked back, handing the Black Bears a 7-2 loss at Agganis Arena. Maine entered the weekend looking to continue its strong start to the season and earn its first win at BU since Nov. 17, 2018, when former goalkeeper Jeremy Swayman made 40 saves. Instead, Maine will have to regroup ahead of Saturday’s rematch.
Maine entered the contest ranked 19th in the USCHO poll and 13th in the NPI, coming off a split weekend against the highly ranked Quinnipiac Bobcats and a double shutout sweep of Colgate. The Black Bears’ 4-2 record gave them reasons to feel optimistic heading into conference play.
Before the game, Maine head coach Ben Barr acknowledged the challenge of playing at BU, a place where the Black Bears have struggled in recent years.
“It’s a place we haven’t been very good, so it’s a great challenge for us,” Barr said. “They’re playing great. I watched both of their games from last weekend. They’re an outstanding team. So it should be fun to be able to go down there and test ourselves against a team like that.”
Barr also emphasized the importance of limiting BU’s opportunities to play an open, fast-paced game.
“If you just have an up-and-down-the-ice game with them, that’s not something that’s going to be probably successful for us,” Barr said. “So we got to try to shrink the game a little bit and play in the trenches as much as we can.”
The Terriers entered the matchup with a 4-2 record, ranking 20th in the NPI and 14th in the USCHO poll. They were coming off a split weekend against No. 17 University of Connecticut, taking four of six conference points. BU lost 5-4 in overtime before winning the second game 6-3.
BU head coach Jay Pandolfo recognized Maine’s defensive strengths ahead of the matchup, noting that the Black Bears had returned to their identity after a difficult previous season.
“It looks like to me they’re playing back to their identity,” Pandolfo said. “I know last year didn’t go well for them. It didn’t go well for us, and to me, just watching them play early on here, they’re bought into the way they need to play.”
However, Pandolfo also knew his team would need to generate sustained offensive pressure against Maine.
“We’re going to have to make sure that we’re not just one-and-done against them,” Pandolfo said. “We got to find a way to create offensive-zone time, create second, third chances, find a way to get inside.”
Boston University wasted little time putting that plan into action, scoring three goals in 91 seconds as second-year forward Tynan Lawrence, first-year defenseman Xavier Villeneuve and second-year forward Ben Merrill put the Terriers ahead 3-0.
Third-year Canisius transfer Petter Wickström Stumer started in net for Maine, splitting starting duties this season with fellow Swede and fourth-year goalie Albin Boija. Wickström Stumer, who started last Friday’s shutout against Colgate, was pulled less than five minutes into the game after first-year forward Viktor Nörringer converted a BU power play to extend the lead to 4-0.
Maine finally responded shortly after, as fourth-year forward Tanner Klimpke gave the Black Bears life and cut the deficit to three.
The Terriers quickly extinguished any hopes of a comeback, adding two more goals in the second period as first-year forward Niklas Aaram-Olsen and third-year forward Brandon Svoboda beat Boija. BU extended its lead early in the final period when second-year forward Conrad Fondrk scored the seventh goal.
Maine added a late consolation goal from fourth-year forward Max Scott, who converted a power play, but the Black Bears could not find another response.
Despite winning 27 faceoffs to BU’s 26, Maine was outshot 37-30. Third-year goalie Mikhail Yegorov stood out for the Terriers, making 28 saves with a .933 save percentage. Wickström Stumer finished with a .333 save percentage, while Boija posted a .903 mark.
The loss dropped Maine to 4-3 on the season and 22nd in the NPI, while BU improved to 5-2 and 16th. The Black Bears will look to avoid the sweep when the teams meet again Saturday.
Maine will then return to Alfond Arena for a two-game series against No. 20 University of Massachusetts on Nov. 6 and 7, with both games scheduled for 7 p.m.

title: Can out-of-state college students vote in Maine?
text:
Yes.
Out-of-state college students attending school in Maine can register and vote if they meet voter eligibility and residency requirements.
Students can establish voting residency at their college address. Paying out-of-state tuition does not disqualify students from registering to vote in Maine.
To qualify, students must be U.S. citizens, at least 18 years old by Election Day and have established a voting residence in the municipality where they register. Students registering in Maine must also provide proof of residency to their municipal clerk.
Registering to vote in Maine establishes a student’s residence, meaning they cannot also vote in their home state in the same election. Students may vote in their home state in future elections if they reestablish residency there.
Students who maintain voting residency in another state may instead vote by absentee ballot in that state.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.
This Fact Brief was produced by students from the Maine Campus, the campus newspaper of the University of Maine, with guidance from journalists at the Maine Trust for Local News. The Maine Trust for Local News partners with Gigafact to produce fact briefs — bite-sized fact checks of trending claims. Read our methodology to learn how we check claims.

title: Monday Five and Five: County Teams Chase Northern Maine Titles
text:
Monday Five and Five: Championship Week Has Arrived
This is it.
After two months of soccer, cross country meets, rivalry games, overtime finishes and tournament runs, we've reached the final week of the fall sports season.
Last week gave Aroostook County an individual state champion, a state runner-up, two very different Wisdom tournament wins and another Presque Isle team headed to a regional championship.
Now eight County soccer teams are still playing, with seven Northern Maine championship games involving local teams coming Tuesday and Wednesday.
Here are my five from last week and five things I'm looking forward to this week.
Five From Last Week
5. Pierce Gorneault Brings Home a State Championship
Pierce Gorneault saved one of his best races of the season for the biggest stage.
The Caribou sophomore won the Class B individual state championship Saturday in Augusta, covering the 5,000-meter course in 16:26.85.
His time was nearly 10 seconds better than the runner-up and was the fourth-fastest time among all classifications Saturday.
And Caribou had plenty more to celebrate.
Emma Graves finished second in the Class B girls race, the Viking boys placed third as a team, the girls finished fifth, and Caribou received both the boys and girls Class B Sportsmanship Awards.
That's a pretty impressive way to finish the season.
4. Houlton/GHCA Finishes State Runner-Up
Houlton/GHCA went to Augusta looking to defend its Class C state championship and came awfully close.
The Shires finished second with 66 points, just 19 behind state champion Winthrop.
What really jumps out is how many Houlton runners finished near the front.
Malachi Witmer placed sixth, Logan Witmer was 12th, Wyatt Quint 16th, Nathan Brady 18th and Brayden Drake 19th.
That's five runners among the top 20 in the state and a runner-up finish to cap another outstanding season for the Shires.
3. Presque Isle Girls Are Playing for A Regional Title
Presque Isle took care of business Saturday afternoon.
The Wildcats shut out Cony 4-0 in the Class B North semifinal, with Hailey Plant, Carrlyn Buck, Bridgid Schupbach and Willow Bugbee all finding the back of the net.
Four goals from four different players is a pretty good formula for tournament soccer.
The win sends Presque Isle into Wednesday's Class B North championship against unbeaten John Bapst.
One more win and the Wildcats are playing for a state championship.
2. Wisdom Survives the Penalty-Kick Pressure
There aren't many more nerve-racking ways to decide a tournament soccer game.
Wisdom and Calais played through regulation and overtime before the Eight-Player North semifinal finally came down to penalty kicks.
James Desjardins scored Wisdom's goal in regulation before Preston Lavoie, Sam Paradis, Zeek Cyr and Cayden Hargrove converted during the shootout.
Then goalkeeper Bentley Nadeau delivered the biggest moment.
Nadeau stopped Calais' final attempt, giving Wisdom the 2-1 victory and sending the Pioneers into the Northern Maine championship.
Wisdom now gets unbeaten PCHS with a regional title on the line.
1. Wisdom Hands Sumner Its Only Loss
Beating an undefeated team in the tournament is impressive.
Beating them 5-0 gets the top spot this week.
Wisdom's girls handed Sumner its first loss of the season Friday and earned another trip to the Eight-Player North championship.
Ellie Cyr scored twice, while Madi Cyr, Libby Cote and Hannah Martin each added goals.
Wisdom has now scored 11 goals in two tournament games while allowing only one.
The Pioneers head into Tuesday's championship at 14-2 with one more win standing between them and a state championship game right here in Presque Isle.
Five to Watch This Week
5. Madawaska and Fort Fairfield Meet Again
It almost feels like these two teams were destined to end up here again.
For the third straight season, Madawaska and Fort Fairfield will meet with the Class D North boys championship on the line.
Madawaska comes in at 14-2 after shutting out Hodgdon 2-0 in the semifinal.
Fort Fairfield earned another shot at the Owls by going on the road and beating Central Aroostook 3-1.
They'll meet Wednesday afternoon in Presque Isle.
The best part for County soccer fans is that we already know one thing.
No matter who wins, an Aroostook County boys team will be playing for the Class D state championship Saturday.
4. Wisdom Has Two Shots at Northern Maine Titles
Tuesday could turn into a memorable day for Wisdom.
Both Pioneer soccer teams are playing for Eight-Player North championships in Brewer.
The boys face 16-0 PCHS after surviving their semifinal in penalty kicks.
The girls take on Dexter after knocking previously unbeaten Sumner out of the tournament.
Two teams. Two championship games.
And there's something extra waiting if either one gets through.
The Eight-Player state championships are being played Saturday at Presque Isle Middle School.
Wisdom has a chance to earn a trip back north to play for a Gold Ball.
3. Fort Kent Has Two Chances at Class C North Championships
Fort Kent also has both soccer teams still playing Tuesday.
The boys face Orono after surviving George Stevens Academy in penalty kicks in the semifinal.
Then the Lady Warriors get their own championship matchup against Orono.
Fort Kent's girls enter at 14-1-2 after turning a scoreless semifinal against Houlton into a 5-0 victory.
Reece Doucette and Hannah Plourde each scored twice in that win, with Avery Werntgen adding another.
One school with two teams playing for Class C North championships on the same day isn't something you see very often.
2. Presque Isle Gets Another Shot at John Bapst
Presque Isle and John Bapst have seen plenty of each other this fall.
Now they meet one more time with the biggest stakes yet.
The Wildcats enter Wednesday's Class B North championship at 11-3-2, while John Bapst comes in unbeaten at 15-0-1.
Presque Isle has won two tournament games to get here, including Saturday's 4-0 semifinal victory over Cony.
This time, there isn't another regular-season meeting waiting afterward.
The winner is the Northern Maine champion and moves on to Saturday's Class B state championship at Cameron Stadium in Bangor.
1. Fort Fairfield Gets a Shot at a Dynasty
This might be my favorite storyline of championship week.
Fort Fairfield faces Penobscot Valley Wednesday night in Presque Isle for the Class D North girls championship.
The Tigers are 14-2 and earned their way here with a 1-0 semifinal victory over Central Aroostook.
Waiting for them is a program that has owned this stage lately.
PVHS is appearing in its sixth straight regional championship game.
The Howlers have won four consecutive Class D North titles, reached the state championship in each of the last four seasons, and won the last three Class D state championships.
That means Fort Fairfield isn't just trying to win Northern Maine.
The Tigers have an opportunity to end one of the best postseason runs in Class D girls soccer and punch their own ticket to Saturday's state championship.
That's a pretty good way to finish our final Five and Five of the fall regular and regional tournament season.
One Last Push
There won't be many games left after this week.
That's what makes these next few days so much fun.
Eight County soccer teams still have a chance to call themselves Northern Maine champions, and every one of them is one victory away from playing for a state title.
Tuesday starts it.
Wednesday keeps it going.
And if things break the right way, Saturday could be a very busy day for Aroostook County sports.
Let's see who gets there.

title: Learn the language of hunting deer
text:
No deer season would be complete without a column on the hunter’s lexicon: those special terms we apply to the sport and the animals we pursue. This lesson is mainly for non-hunters or new hunters hoping to sound more fluent and knowledgeable, but might even help veteran hunters.
We’ll start with simple terms most folks should know. A male deer is a buck, a female is a doe. The plural is bucks and does, unless you’re from Pennsylvania. For some unknown reason, Keystone State hunters shun the “s,” much like everyone does for moose and elk. They’re all members of the deer family, but there are no mooses and elks.
This next term is sometimes misused. A yearling is a deer that is at least 1 but less than 2 years old. This category does not include deer less than 1 year old. Deer younger than a year are fawns, not yearlings and not lambs. The latter refers to sheep, a term that, like moose and elk, can be one or several of the species. Buck fawns may exhibit small tufts of hair or even leathery patches where their antlers will one day grow, which is why they’re sometimes called button bucks.
Yearling bucks typically sport their first set of hard antlers. Those with single-point antlers are referred to as spikes, spike bucks or spike-horns. Those with antlers that split at the tip are called fork-horns, crotch-horns or forkies.
We should perhaps pause and back up a little because I’ve already slipped in a few undefined terms. A buck’s (and on rare occasions, a doe’s) paired antlers are referred to as a rack, at least in the case of deer with more than four points. A point, or tine, is a projection off the main beam, or (on rare occasions) off another point.
The first two points, just above the antler bases, are alternately referred to as brow tines or eye guards. Successive points are most often referred to by less colorful terms based on scoring systems, like G1, G2 and so forth. It’s too bad they can’t have more colorful, descriptive terms.
Among hunters, there is considerable conversation over what defines a point. For some folks, if it’s at least 1 inch tall or something you can hang a ring on, it’s a point. According to the rules of antler scoring systems, which give us the mundane G1, G2, the height of said projection must be longer than its width where it meets the main beam. If you’re not having the rack officially scored, you get to decide.
Not all racks are created equal. Most are fairly symmetrical, with equal number and similar-sized points on either side. Some are less so, and when the asymmetry reaches a certain level, they are referred to as non-typical.
This next point, no pun intended, is worth making for the folks who want to sound well versed in the ways of whitetails but end up doing quite the opposite. We all know deer sport antlers, not horns. Antlers fall off at maturity and a new pair is grown every year, while horns continue growing for the life of the animal. Knowing this, seasoned hunters still refer to antlers as horns. Don’t correct them.
Much more freedom, leeway and creativity can be applied when it comes to big bucks with big horns (or antlers, if you prefer). They are assigned an array of attributions, like staver, sad daddy, gray ghost, slammer, hammer, hat rack and ole mossy horns. Still, it’s best to familiarize yourself with some of the more common ones rather than trying to be original. Otherwise you risk revealing yourself as a nimrod.
Bob Humphrey is a freelance writer and Registered Maine Guide who lives in Pownal. He can be reached at: [email protected]

title: Trapping predators is not the answer
text:
Your Oct. 19 article on Maine’s growing interest in trapping profiles a Belgrade man who plans to trap the predators that have been killing his chickens for years. I understand the frustration. However, the answer is not a trapline; it is a better coop.
Foxes, raccoons, fishers and other predators are doing what they have always done: finding food where it is easiest to get. A sturdy, fully enclosed run with buried hardware cloth and a coop locked at night will protect chickens far more reliably than killing whichever animals happen to wander by. Trap one fox, and another will find the same unprotected flock.
The same is true across our communities. Wildlife-proof garbage cans and secured compost keep raccoons and bears from becoming “nuisances” in the first place. Keeping pet cats indoors protects them from predators, cars and traps, and protects the songbirds they would otherwise kill.
These solutions are not complicated. They simply ask us to take responsibility for our own land and our own animals.
Wildlife should not suffer for hours or days in a trap, and be killed season after season, because we chose not to be good stewards. Before we reach for a trap, we should reach for a hammer and some hardware cloth.
Martha Macdonald
Waterford

title: One person, two dogs die in Belfast fire
text:
One person, two dogs die in Belfast, Maine, fire
One person, two dogs die in Belfast, Maine, fire
One person and two dogs are dead after a fire in a mobile home in Belfast.
Firefighters were first called to Back Searsport Road at about 2:38 p.m. on Friday and found a lot of fire inside the home.
While firefighters were trying to put the fire out, they found a person dead inside.
Investigators from the Maine Fire Marshal's Office say the fire started on a back porch where the laundry area for the home is. The exact cause of the fire was still under investigation over the weekend.
A picture shared by investigators showed significant damage to one end of the home.
The person's name and cause of death will be confirmed and determined by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

title: Connecticut man hid in shrubbery after allegedly crashing into Maine restaurant
text:
A Connecticut man hid in shrubbery after he allegedly crashed into a Naples restaurant early Sunday morning.
Stuart John McClure, 32, of New London was charged with operating under the influence, eluding, aggravated driving to endanger and criminal speeding, according to Maj. Aaron Turcotte, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
McClure was allegedly speeding and driving erratically in a 2015 Jeep Cherokee on Route 302 in Bridgton about 12:30 a.m. He stopped when a trooper pulled him over, but then allegedly sped away, prompting police to pursue him for several miles.
As he entered the causeway in Naples, McClure allegedly crashed into the awning and porch support beams outside Rick’s Cafe.
McClure allegedly fled on foot and was later found hiding in shrubbery along the causeway’s shoreline.
He was taken to Maine Medical Center in Portland, where he was treated for injuries not considered life-threatening.

title: ‘Presidential Campaign Rhetoric’ Puts Bates at Center of Polls
text:
To Professor Stephanie Kelley-Romano, her class Presidential Campaign Rhetoric provides a unique experience for Bates students.
“I want people to see the interdisciplinary nature of a Bates education and the practical real world application. It’s really easy to sit in classes and critique theories and experiences and social movements and politics but when you have to think about how you’re going to do it…it gets a lot harder,” she said.
The class was first offered in 1999, though in a much different capacity.
“It was a really traditional public address class where we looked at all the speeches and ads from past presidential elections, and talked about the rhetoric of the American dream and how citizenship is constructed, but students were incredibly disinterested in reading long, old speeches of dead people,” Kelley-Romano said.
Now, the students run two five-person campaigns spanning nine weeks that involve a presidential candidate, vice presidential candidate, campaign manager, social media manager and speech writer.
This year’s presidential candidates are Charlotte Bernhard ‘28, running as Michelle Foster, and Elias Jones ‘28, running as Andrew Pierce.
“I work on the campaign every day. I do something for it everyday and it sounds terrible working on a class that much, but in this class it’s so much fun,” Jones said.
For both candidates, their interest in the class dates back years.
“I actually have always wanted to take this class since having interest and planning to come to Bates,” Bernhard said. “My babysitter from middle school took this class…and she did it in 2022 and I thought it looked super cool so I looked into it more.”
Over the last several weeks the candidates and their teams have held nominating conventions, town hall debates and traditional debates. All the while doing class visits, creating promotional ads and doing everything they can to fight for the win.
“I’ve learned how to be a better public speaker because I’ve been doing it so much. I think I’ve also learned how to act a little bit because I’m playing a character, I didn’t expect that,” Jones said.
Kelley-Romano values this growth in the class experience.
“I think a lot of them learn about leadership skills that they actually have or strategies that they have for collaboration, that they didn’t realize they were so strong at, so that’s really cool to watch a student kind of come into their own,” Kelley-Romano said.
Presidential Campaign Rhetoric is a class that centers community and collaboration.
“They always get endorsements from past people who have taken the class. There’s a whole day where previous PCRs can come back and give advice and strategy to the campaigns and they stay in touch, which is great,” said Professor Kelley-Romano.
The class works across disciplines, this year bringing in BIO 210 taught by Professor Meredith Greer. Biology students act as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), modeling the expansion of the made-up disease Rabinecromania, to inform candidates and their team as they devise a plan in protecting the people from the outbreak.
“It’s a very unique class experience at Bates and just across all college, as its incredibly immersive, experiential based learning,” Bernhard said.
Behind the heated debates and comedic attack ads, stands a larger purpose.
“The point of the class being so public facing is to get people to vote in the actual election. There’s a really important election in Maine that’s happening right now…so it’s just getting voter outreach and making sure people actually vote,” said Jones.
The past few weeks the candidates have been visiting first year seminars, offering a nonpartisan briefing on the midterm election ballot questions as well as information on how to vote, where to vote, and how to register to vote.
“We do a collaboration with Bates Votes which is super important because the mock campaign does get a lot of energy and attention, which is awesome, but we don’t want to lose sight of the fact that there are actual elections where people can actually vote,” said Professor Kelley-Romano.
Voting for the mock election will take place on Tuesday Nov. 3 from 11:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. in the Fireplace Lounge, open to all first year seminars, Rhetoric classes, Rhetoric majors/minors, and a few select classes across disciplines.
Kelley-Romano hopes this class challenges the Bates community to re-envision modern day politics.
“I think that this class also provides an opportunity to think about how we can do civil discourse and democracy differently,” she said. “Seeing how easy it is to argue to the lowest common denominator when you want to win, we must ask how do we not do that. How do we have a politics of care and a capacious politics of intellectual debate?”

title: Feds declare drought a natural disaster in much of Maine, unlocking relief in 14 counties
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture has designated seven Maine counties as natural disaster areas due to the ongoing drought, unlocking relief for farmers, businesses and nonprofits throughout most of the state.
The primary counties designated as natural disaster areas by the USDA last week are Cumberland, Hancock, Kennebec, Knox, Lincoln, Sagadahoc and Waldo.
The federal agency cites the U.S. Drought Monitor’s designations of these areas as being either in severe or extreme drought for eight or more consecutive weeks during the growing season.
Many of the aforementioned counties have been at least partially under severe conditions since mid-August, according to the Drought Monitor, and the drought has expanded and worsened since then: A stretch of the coastline from Cumberland to Hancock County has been under an extreme designation since mid-September.
“Contiguous counties,” or counties bordering those designated as disaster areas, are also eligible for relief: Androscoggin, Franklin, Oxford, Penobscot, Somerset, Washington and York counties. Some of those areas were also at least partially under severe drought since mid-September, according to the Drought Monitor.
Aroostook and Piscataquis counties are currently left off the eligibility list. While all of Maine has been under at least moderate drought since Sept. 15, a chunk of northern Maine, including much of Aroostook County and northern Piscataquis County, was not given a severe designation until early October. That designation was expanded deeper into Piscataquis County just last week.
The USDA also declared Maine’s drought a natural disaster last year, unlocking similar forms of relief.
RELIEF PROGRAMS
The USDA’s Farm Service Agency announced the availability of emergency loans in the 14 eligible counties last week, along with an array of other disaster assistance programs.
The emergency loans can be used for a variety of needs, such as replacing equipment and livestock or refinancing debts. The FSA says it will review applications based on the extent of losses suffered, security available and repayment ability.
The USDA and FSA also offer a variety of other assistance programs, including ones specifically for livestock producers, orchards and nurseries.
“Impacted producers should timely report all crop, livestock and farm infrastructure damages and losses to their local FSA county office as soon as possible,” Tommy Higgins, state executive director for FSA in Maine, said in a news release. “As you evaluate your operation, take time to gather important documents you may need to get assistance, including farm records, herd inventory, receipts and pictures of damages or losses.”
Eligibility and deadlines to apply vary by program. More information on the types of assistance available can be found at fsa.usda.gov.
The U.S. Small Business Administration announced on Monday that loans are now available to businesses and nonprofits that suffered operational expenses caused by the drought in the eligible counties since Sept. 15. The SBA also made similar loans available to counties impacted by the drought last year.
Small businesses, agricultural cooperatives and aquaculture enterprises may apply for the loans. Private nonprofits and faith-based organizations may also apply.
Eligible entities may qualify for up to $2 million in loans at interest rates as low as 4%, or just over 3.6% for private nonprofit organizations, with no interest or required payments for the first 12 months of the up to 30-year terms.
More information and applications can be found at sba.gov/disaster.
MAINE’S DROUGHT
Maine’s drought, stemming from a dry summer and fall of 2025 that also triggered a natural disaster declaration, subsided in early 2026 due to a rainy spring.
But another dry summer saw the drought crop up again and worsen through the first half of this fall. A lack of rain and full recovery of Maine’s groundwater from past droughts are to blame, experts say.
More than 55% of the state is under at least severe drought, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor’s latest map released Thursday.
The entirety of Maine has been under at least moderate drought conditions as of Sept. 15, but the drought was considered worse along the coast.
That week, the Drought Monitor gave an extreme designation to a slice of the coast from Cumberland County to Hancock County, and a severe designation outlining it, stretching inland to the greater Augusta and Bangor regions and south into York County.
A large swath of northern Maine was upgraded to the severe drought the first full week of October, and another chunk of central Maine was added last week.

title: Want more affordable homes? Lower the standards
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I learned the state is the enemy of affordable housing from Secretary of State Shenna Bellows and her family.
I was there the first winter when her parents were raising three babies in a tent surrounded by hay bales to block the wind. I was there when they moved into an old stone cellar hole, capped over and covered with tarps. Frequently, the hole would flood and they brought the kids to my house to stay while they dried out the bedding and clothes. I was there when we dragged out the cedar logs for the first-floor walls. I was there teaching the precocious Shenna to read by oil lamp because they did not have electricity until the kids were seven. No electricity, no running water, strictly wood heat in winter.

title: Halloween fire burns Belfast apartment building
text:
A Saturday evening fire burned a Belfast apartment building.
The fire broke out about 5:08 p.m. at the Bluebird Circle apartment building, according to Maj. Aaron Turcotte, a spokesperson for the Maine Department of Public Safety.
When firefighters arrived, they found flames climbing the building’s exterior, Turcotte said Monday morning.
Crews kept the flames from spreading into the apartments.
One person was taken to the hospital with injuries from breaking first-floor windows.
Seven people have been displaced.
Investigators determined that the fire was likely caused by improperly discarded smoking material and ruled the blaze accidental.

title: Trump administration appeals to Supreme Court to sideline 20,000 disputed California mail ballots
text:
Supreme Court rejects Trump administration push to set aside thousands of California ballots
The Supreme Court on Monday rejected a push for California to set aside thousands of mail ballots from people President Donald Trump’s administration claims are noncitizens, a decision that comes on the eve of the pivotal midterm elections.
The high court refused to intervene in a case involving 20,000 people the Republican administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the largely Democratic state’s voter rolls.
It was the latest in a flurry of election-related litigation the day before the midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress for the last two years of Trump’s second term.
In California, the Trump administration had asked the high court to set aside the challenged ballots until the voters’ citizenship status could be verified. But officials there said that the list appeared to be filled with errors and that setting the ballots aside could effectively disenfranchise legal voters.
The high court did not detail its reasoning, as is common in emergency decisions. The justices previously rejected Trump’s push to restrict mail ballots around the country in September, even though the justices have sided with his administration in a series of other emergency docket appeals.
The Republican Trump administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite them being rare.
A district court judge previously denied the Justice Department's request and warned that the demand could disenfranchise citizens in Tuesday's midterm elections to determine control of Congress.
Also on Monday in Washington, another federal judge ruled against the administration’s efforts to make last-minute demands of California election officials, finding they violated the U.S. Constitution.
“The Executive Branch has likely violated the Constitution’s Elections Clause, which commits authority over election rules to the states and Congress alone,” wrote Chief Judge James Boasberg.
The administration, for its part, said segregating the ballots was a modest request that would eventually allow legal votes to still be counted.
The administration has faced a remarkable string of losses in court in its push, as well as criticism for waiting until a few weeks before the election to make its demands of California election officials with a list that even the Department of Justice admits is not entirely reliable.
During a hearing over whether to lift her own order forbidding the administration from threatening to prosecute election workers who let potentially illegal voters cast ballots, District Court Judge Trina Thompson drilled down on reports of widespread inaccuracies in the Justice Department's data.
“Would you agree there's a high error rate?” Thompson asked Kenneth Kao, a Justice Department attorney.
“That's a fair statement,” Kao said. “That's why we ask for the registrars' aid in verifying these are all valid voters.”
At the same time, Bill Essayli, the federal prosecutor running the Justice Department's Los Angeles office, said at a news conference he was highly confident the people on the list were not entitled to vote.
“This isn’t speculation. This isn’t a theory,” Essayli said, later conceding there may be errors on the list.
Voting has been underway in California since early October. All of the state’s roughly 23 million registered voters are mailed a ballot. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. California election officials have said that finding and setting aside the challenged ballots now would be logistically impossible.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said the appeal “reeks of desperation and is another attempt to undermine our elections and trample on the rule of law.”
Lower courts have sided with the state, with a district judge warning that segregating ballots would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections and erode trust in the democratic process.
“If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” wrote U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who was nominated by President Bill Clinton, a Democrat.
A 2-1 appeals court panel upheld his order, with one judge appointed by Trump and another appointed by President Joe Biden, a Democrat, voting in favor. The third judge on the panel, also appointed by Trump, argued in a dissent that California’s unwillingness to separate the ballots encourages the “violation of federal law.”
The Justice Department has sought to move the case along quickly, unsuccessfully asking an appeals court to intervene early.

title: DNA used to identify body found in shallow grave in 1991
text:
DNA used to identify body found in 1991 buried in shallow Massachusetts grave
Now that the victim is identified, investigators are looking for the perpetrator
DNA used to identify body found in 1991 buried in shallow Massachusetts grave
Now that the victim is identified, investigators are looking for the perpetrator
Thirty-five years after the discovery of a shallow grave in Quincy, Massachusetts, investigators say they've identified the man who was buried inside.
Video on the player at the top: In an unrelated case, investigators seek more information in the 1982 death of a New Hampshire woman
Glenn Powers, who graduated from Randolph High School in 1970, was identified through forensic genetic genealogy, according to Norfolk District Attorney Michael W. Morrissey. The technique combines DNA sequencing with family tree research, utilizing public databases and records.
The grave in which Powers was found was discovered on March 21, 1991, in a wooded area near 270 Quarry Street in Quincy, which is outside of Boston. His cause of death was blunt force trauma, and the case is considered a homicide.
"In this case, we are committed to searching for Glenn’s killer or killers and holding them accountable. We are appealing to the public for help. Someone knows what happened to Glenn or knows information that may help to identify who is responsible for his murder," Morrissey said in a statement.
Anyone with information about the case is asked to call a tip line at 781-830-4990, Quincy Police at 617-745-5768, or the Massachusetts State Police Unresolved Case Unit at 1-855-MA-SOLVE or 1-855-627-6583.

title: Bruins extend home winning streak to 6
text:
BOSTON — David Pastrnak slipped a shot past Carter Hart to break a shootout stalemate and give the Boston Bruins a 3-2 victory over the Vegas Golden Knights on Monday night.
Boston’s Jeremy Swayman stopped Vegas’ Trevor Connelly, Jack Eichel and Mitch Marner to set up Pastrnak for the winner in the third round.
James Hagens scored his sixth goal of the season, and Morgan Geekie added a power-play goal to help Boston to its sixth consecutive home victory.
Elias Lindholm, Nikita Zadorov, Pavel Zacha and Pastrnak had assists for the Bruins, who’ve won two in a row following back-to-back losses. Swayman made 21 saves.
Connelly tied it 7:23 into the third period when he gathered a loose puck in front of the net and slipped it past Swayman. Noah Hanifin and Marner assisted. Mark Stone also scored for Vegas.
The Golden Knights have lost five of their last six since starting the season 8-2. They also continue to struggle killing off power plays, having allowed a power-play goal in seven of their last eight games.
Hart had 25 saves for Vegas.
The Bruins led 2-0 in the second before Stone knocked in a loose puck for a power-play goal, with assists from Tomas Hertl and Marner, to cut Vegas’ deficit to 2-1.
Up next
Golden Knights: At Pittsburgh on Tuesday night.
Bruins: At Pittsburgh on Thursday night.

title: Interesting times at Thompson Free Library
text:
By Kim Brawn, Thompson Free Library
We live in interesting times. Maybe too interesting. We are surrounded by AI: some headlines, news segments, podcasts and social media promote the pros, while others highlight the cons. Meanwhile, chatbots lurk everywhere. Is it an existential threat or a tool to help humanity? Google now offloads our searches to their AI assistant, Gemini. Many use AI to make tasks easier and more efficient. We go about our daily lives and yet there’s this nagging background noise — wondering what to make of this brave (crazy?) new world — and who or what to believe. There’s something comforting about being able to go to a library at a time like this where you can delve into cutting edge topics in a reassuring space, sharing your curiosity and skepticism with others.
November at the Thompson Free Library in Dover-Foxcroft starts up with TFL’s Reading Group on Thursday the 12th at 6 p.m. when they discuss Kristin Hannah’s bestseller “The Women”. It’s the story of one woman who goes to war (Vietnam), but it shines a light on all women who put themselves in harm’s way and whose sacrifice and commitment to their country has too often been forgotten. Nicholas Kristof, with the New York Times, describes the book as “ . . . historical fiction at its very best. So moving, so wrenching, and yet, in the end, uplifting. Brava! I loved The Nightingale and The Four Winds, but The Women is my favorite.”
TFL’s Youth Services librarian Michelle Fagan once again plays international tour guide as she hosts another “Teen Taste Test” on Tuesday, Nov. 17 at 3:30 p.m. This time the Universal Yums Box features snacks from Spain. Ages 12-17 are invited to join Michelle at the biblioteca!
At 6 p.m. on Nov. 17 Library Director Jon Knepp hosts “Making Informed AI Choices” that will cover topics like: What is AI? What’s wrong with AI? Why are tech companies pushing it? How does it appear in devices, programs, and sites we use every day? Are there good and/or ethical uses for AI? Jon has adapted his presentation from the work and slides of Hannah Cyrus at the Bangor Public Library, who is helping to lead the way on AI education in libraries.
“Originally, I wanted Hannah to present on this topic, but she does not have the time. So, I have taken her class, talked with her and adapted the class for our audience. Rather than preach about the potential danger and harms of AI or shame anyone who uses it, I hope to provide information to allow attendees to make informed decisions about using AI or not. I will also have handouts and advice for removing AI from common pieces of technology if you desire to do so,” Jon said.
Get ready for “Glow Party” on Friday, Nov. 20 from 5 to 7 p.m. There will be canvas and face painting under the glow of black lights (like Spencer Gifts back in the day!), snacks and music for ages 12-17. Space is limited so please register by calling TFL or filling out the form you can find on our Facebook page.
Now it’s entirely possible that Santa and those busy elves already use AI to streamline their North Pole operations. Ok, here comes the holiday teaser: on Saturday, Dec. 5 (from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m.) our own library elves join in the Hometown Holidays festivities with ornament making, card creating, and, of course, cooking & eating pizzelles!
Back to November with some important reminders: the library will be closed Wednesday, Nov. 11 for Veterans Day and Nov. 26-28 (Thursday to Saturday) for the Thanksgiving holiday. We apologize for any inconvenience.
Once again, we find ourselves in the wild west (or Westworld?) like in the early days of the internet, unsure of how things will unfold. Will AI agents go rogue and wreak havoc, or will they find cures for deadly diseases — or both? Well, at least we have each other and a library that encourages learning, investigating, and staying informed. A place to find shelter from the storm as well as understand the weather behind it.
TFL hours: Tues. & Thurs. 9-7, Weds. & Fri. 9-5 and Sat. 9-1. Visit our website: www.thompsonfreelibrary.org, our Facebook page, Instagram @tf_library or contact us at thompsonfreelibrary@gmail.com or 207-564-3350. All programs are free & open to the public. Free Wi-Fi available 24/7 in the parking lot.

title: The billion-dollar problem in firehouses: Potentially toxic gear, tight budgets and a fight over who pays to replace it
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — When a vintage B-17 bomber went down during a living history flight at Bradley International Airport in 2019, the response put firefighter and Connecticut fire union representative Chris Albani right in the thick of it.
After racing to the scene, it was his job to coat the wreckage with a special foam used to quickly smother airplane fires.
That foam contains PFAS — man-made, toxic chemicals touted for their ability to resist heat and fire. They’re a lifesaver in aviation disasters, but also a health hazard, with studies linking PFAS to cancer.
Those chemicals that put him at risk aren’t limited to the foam Albani uses in a crisis. PFAS has also been found in the specialized equipment he and thousands of other first responders wear daily on the job.
“It’s in the gear,” Albani said. “It’s the PFAS that is intentionally put in the gear. And it’s poisoning members.”
And court documents show the manufacturers have known for decades that PFAS are toxic but kept that information hidden.
But recent academic research on PFAS that highlighted the link to cancer has raised alarms at firehouses.
Even so, InvestigateTV discovered firefighters across the country are still wearing potentially toxic turnout gear that contains the chemicals – with a battle brewing from coast to coast over the cost of replacement and who should pay it, leaving first responders in limbo.
The cost of protecting the protectors
Cancer fears have long haunted firefighters like Albani, and for good reasons. The disease is the leading cause of line-of-duty deaths for firefighters, according to the International Association of Fire Fighters.
Albani said that fear has stayed with him.
“It’s just that unknown,” he said. “I have 15 years on, and cancer isn’t an immediate thing. It’s a long-term thing. So, I might not know until I’m 60. The mindset people have now - it’s not about if I get cancer, it’s when.”
Those concerns about risks associated with turnout gear were amplified in 2020. That’s when a study from Notre Dame confirmed high levels of PFAS in both new and used turnout gear, with the potential for the cancer-linked chemicals to leach out and soak into first responders’ skin.
But six years later, InvestigateTV found hundreds of thousands of firefighters nationwide are still wearing gear that contains PFAS. Many want to get rid of it, but replacing it could cost billions — and leave taxpayers on the hook.
“Gear - a baseline pants and jacket is anywhere up to $3,000,” Albani said. “And then you start throwing in a helmet, gloves - looking at $5,000-8,000 per member. If you have a department of 200 people, do the math. It’s a big money ticket item for a municipality to cover.”
Massive lawsuit aims to make manufacturers pay
For many departments, it’s a cost they can’t bear.
InvestigateTV surveyed fire departments across the country - half of the chiefs that responded said they haven’t made the switch because their towns and cities can’t afford the cost. Many believe they shouldn’t have to. That’s where a massive class action lawsuit comes in.
“The defendants understood the dangers of PFAS,” said Jennifer Sclar, an attorney representing a growing number of fire unions and municipalities on the East Coast. “This is not like it came out of the sky in 2018. The defendants have long understood what the dangers of PFAS were and are.”
Sclar is suing more than a dozen companies that manufacture turnout gear or the materials and chemicals used to make it. Every company listed in the filing was contacted for comment by InvestigateTV on numerous occasions. Most — including big names like 3M and DuPont — wouldn’t comment.
In legal filings, 3M has argued that it didn’t manufacture any of the gear worn by the firefighters and there’s no proof of a direct link between the company and protective fire gear - also saying firefighters haven’t made allegations of any physical injuries. DuPont previously told another media outlet the complaints were without merit.
Still, the lawsuit against those companies and others claims they knew about health risks with PFAS chemicals and the gear that contains it but kept saying it was safe.
“That never should have happened,” Sclar said. “And it can’t continue to happen. You have to protect the protectors.”
The goal of the recent legal actions isn’t just to get firefighters out of their toxic threads – they seek to make the manufacturers to foot the bill for replacement gear.
Five class action lawsuits filed by cities and towns now have been consolidated into a single case in Minnesota.
“When this first came to light and firehouses started asking some of the defendants, ‘Hey - I’m hearing PFAS may have had some bad health effects, you know what’s the deal?’” Sclar said. “The defendants told these firemen, ‘Don’t worry about it. There’s nothing to worry about. Nothing to see here’. And they knew that wasn’t true.”
Lawsuit claims secrets about PFAS kept for decades
Dozens of documents made public by the Environmental Working Group, cited in the class action suit and analyzed by InvestigateTV, show 3M and DuPont specifically were long aware of the risks associated with PFAS.
Those records show the companies were internally labeling PFAS as “toxic” as far back as the 1960s and 70s.
By the 1980s, documents InvestigateTV examined show both companies started moving women of child-bearing age off certain assignments to limit PFAS exposure. And in the 1990s, their own records show scientists and studies were finding links between PFAS and cancer.
“We want to make sure that these manufacturers who knew full well that this dangerous chemical was harmful to human beings but yet infused that into our gear for decades - that they’re paying for this gear that we need to replace,” said Ed Kelly, who runs the nation’s largest fire union — the International Association of Fire Fighters.
But replacement is complicated. Getting firefighters from coast to coast into PFAS-free gear means giving millions more to the same companies many believe burned them already.
“They can’t be trusted,” Kelly said. “We have to take that gear and get it independently tested to ensure not only that there’s no PFAS but there’s no other negative health impacts infused into this gear.”
Kelly’s skepticism is grounded in reality.
In 2025, the fire department in Quincy, Massachusetts paid millions for new, supposedly PFAS-free gear — only to have independent tests that same year reveal high levels of the chemicals.
“Outrageous,” Mayor Thomas Koch said at a press conference where the discovery was revealed.
The company involved in manufacturing the gear said in a public statement it eliminated PFAS from all of its textiles the same year Quincy bought its gear and recently told InvestigateTV the chemicals were not intentionally added during manufacturing — with testing turning up very low levels.
But the case still captured national headlines and left fire chiefs even more confused and worried.
In InvestigateTV’s national survey, some leaders said there are too many unknowns with the PFAS alternatives, and not enough proof their crews will be protected if they change gear.
“We know we were lied to,” Albani said. “So, we don’t have a level of trust with those companies. We were deceived. We’ve had members pay the ultimate sacrifice because of it. It’s a problem.”
The potential health threat of PFAS is something firefighters like Chris Albani have to face every time they put on their turnout gear.
Walking through the firehouse and looking at the gear, Albani said he tries not even to touch the jackets and pants he knows contain the chemicals until it’s absolutely necessary. It’s a drastic change after decades of donning the suit for every call.
But firefighters are being forced to break old routines because of new science - waiting for safe gear that lets them save lives — without potentially putting their own at risk.

title: Russia's security service detains a teenager planning a 'terror attack' after a US tip-off
text:
Russia’s security service detains a teenager planning a ‘terror attack’ after a US tip-off
A suspect allegedly planning a terror attack on a major Moscow museum was arrested by Russian authorities after a tip-off from the United States, Russia’s security agency FSB announced on Sunday.
The FSB said information shared with Russia by U.S. law enforcement led to the arrest of the Russian citizen, who is a minor. The agency said it was “grateful to the US side for the information provided.”
The arrest came after the U.S. Embassy in Moscow issued a security alert on Saturday, warning it was “aware of a credible threat of a mass casualty event” at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve in Moscow.
CNN contacted the museum after the alert was issued and was told the institution was not aware of any warnings. However, several events scheduled to take place at the venue were later canceled, and security measures were put in place, according to Russian state media.
The unnamed suspect was detained after posting images on TikTok of himself wearing tactical clothing and an “object resembling an automatic weapon” and sharing photos taken at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve with the caption: “I found a place,” according to the FSB.
The FSB said the teenager subscribed to a neo-Nazi channel on Telegram and made “significant number of search queries regarding past terrorist acts, mass murders, and other violent acts.” It said airsoft weapons were found at the suspect’s home.
It is not unusual for the U.S. to share security warnings with other countries — the State Department has a long-standing “duty to warn” policy and is obligated to let U.S. expat communities know of any threats.
The alert issued on Saturday said the U.S. government was “coordinating with appropriate Russian authorities on a response.”
However, Russia has not always received U.S. warnings with thanks. In March 2024, during the Biden administration era, the U.S. embassy in Moscow warned that ISIS militants were determined to target Russia, specifically saying there were “imminent plans to target large gatherings in Moscow,” including at concerts.
Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed that warning as a provocation. Days later, assailants stormed Moscow’s Crocus City Hall venue and killed more than 140 people. ISIS claimed responsibility for the attack.
Putin’s reaction was different in 2017, during U.S. President Donald Trump’s first presidency, when the U.S. warned Moscow about a planned terror attack at the Kazan Cathedral in St Petersburg. According to a Kremlin statement, Putin personally thanked Trump for the information, saying it was enough to locate and detain the suspects.
The latest warning and the FSB’s public statement thanking the U.S. comes at a time of increased scrutiny of the Trump administration’s relationship with Russia.
Trump has made significant concessions to Russia on sanctions in recent weeks, which have triggered criticism on both sides of the aisle in Washington and driven a wedge between the U.S. and its Western allies.

title: Mass shootings over Halloween weekend leave at least 8 dead and dozens injured across US
text:
(AP) - Federal authorities in Texas planned to detail their response Monday to a series of shootings in Dallas, one of numerous gun incidents across the nation on Halloween weekend that left at least eight people dead and dozens more injured.
Many of the mass shootings occurred in entertainment districts and in college towns. The deadliest occurred in Dallas, where the U.S. attorney’s office planned a news conference to discuss federal actions related to three shootings in the city’s Deep Ellum neighborhood, a center of music and restaurants. Those shootings left four people dead and 15 injured and happened over the span of about an hour and 15 minutes early Sunday.
As investigators continued their searches for suspects and the motives for the shootings, word spread of even more mass violence over the weekend along with condemnation from elected officials.
Two separate shootings occurred in Birmingham, Alabama, after the annual “Magic City Classic” college football game on Saturday night. And police in college towns reported shootings in their nightlife districts where annual Halloween gatherings are popular, including in Fayetteville, Arkansas; Birmingham, Alabama; Newark, Delaware; Bloomington, Illinois; and Bloomington, Indiana.
Deep Ellum saw gun violence earlier this year
Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux has said investigators were still trying to determine if the shootings were related and why they started. His department had increased police presence prior to the shootings in the district, which had experienced deadly violence earlier this year.
Two people were fatally stabbed during a fight outside a nightclub in February, and a security guard was shot and killed while trying to break up a fight inside a nightclub in May. There also have been nonfatal shootings, including during Cinco de Mayo festivities in May when five people were wounded outside of a sports bar, police said.
Halloween can be a busy time for gun violence incidents
Multiple academic studies of police department and hospital data from major cities over the last decade have shown gun violence is more frequent at night, on weekends and on holidays. Several studies have pointed to the July Fourth holiday as being one of the most or the most violent holiday because of dark hours for fireworks celebrations, combined with alcohol consumption and other factors. New Year’s and Halloween were also high on the list for gun violence incidents.
Last year the homicide rate in the United States dropped to its lowest point in 75 years, according to FBI numbers on 2025 crime. Those numbers showed homicides decreased by 18% and overall violent crime dropped 9.3% last year.
Cities and municipalities across the country largely have been experiencing drops in homicides and violence, with a few exceptions, for the past few years. Federal authorities and nonprofit groups have noted national violent crime and homicide rates have been declining since 2022. Experts also noted that trend had continued through the first six months of 2026.
Elected officials take to social media after shootings
In Jackson, Mississippi, two people were killed and six others were injured in a shooting during a Halloween costume party at a nightclub early Sunday, police said. Just before the shooting, two men entered the club wearing ski masks. At some point at least one of the suspects opened fire into the crowd, police said. The suspects have not yet been identified.
A 20-year-old man and an 18-year-old woman were killed in the shooting, while six others were taken to hospitals with injuries that didn’t appear to be life threatening, police said.
“No one should have to fear for their life while enjoying an evening out,” Jackson Mayor John Horhn said in a statement following the shooting.
Near Indiana University’s campus, seven people were wounded in a shooting early Sunday in a busy nightlife area. None of the victims were believed to be students, police said.
“This is unacceptable in Bloomington, and in any community,” Bloomington Mayor Kerry Thomson said Sunday in a video address shared on social media.
Even with increased police staffing, no public safety plan can eliminate every act of violence, Thomson said.
Separate shootings occurred outside a college football game
In Birmingham, Alabama, one person was killed and eight others were wounded in two separate shootings just outside Legion Field after the annual “Magic City Classic” football game on Saturday night. Alabama State and Alabama A&M are archrivals whose annual contest has been played for more than 100 years. Nearly 70,000 fans attended Saturday’s game, won by Alabama A&M 31-28. The event draws some of the largest crowds in the country for games played in their college football division.
Michael Pickett, chief of the Birmingham Police Department, said most spectators and families had left the stadium property after the game. The first shooting happened nearby, where vendors were set up along Graymont Avenue.
___
Raby reported from Charleston, West Virginia. AP reporters Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia and Jamie Stengle in Dallas contributed to this report.
