title: Kennedy Center names the 2026 honorees as Trump renovation battle moves the show offsite
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Kennedy Center said Monday that Paul Anka, David Foster, Andy Garcia, David Mamet and Barbara Mandrell would be recognized at this year’s Kennedy Center Honors, which will be held away from the iconic performing arts venue for the first time as President Donald Trump battles with a federal court over his plans to renovate the building and add his name to it.
All of the nominees have had substantial careers in their respective fields. Mamet is among the most acclaimed playwrights of his time, known for his hard-boiled dialogue in “Glengarry Glen Ross” and “American Buffalo” and other works. Mandrell is a member of the Country Music Hall of Fame whose many hits include “Years” and “Sleeping Single in a Double Bed” and Foster is among the most successful producers of the past 50 years, working with everyone from Chicago to Natalie Cole.
Anka has written or co-written such iconic songs as “My Way” and the theme to the “Tonight” show when Johnny Carson was host. Garcia’s acting credits include “The Untouchables,” “The Godfather Part III” and the HBO film “For Love or Country.”
Several are either friendly with Trump or have been outspoken in support of conservative politics. Mamet told Fox News last year that he was once a “brain-dead liberal” who “discovered my conservative beliefs.” Anka is a longtime friend of Trump who once rewrote ”My Way,” originally written for Frank Sinatra, with MAGA-themed lyrics. Foster has performed for Trump in the past.
The Kennedy Center Honors were established in 1978 and have been given to a broad range of artists. Until Trump’s first term, presidents of both major political parties traditionally attended the annual ceremony, even when they disagreed politically with a given recipient.
Prominent liberals such as Barbra Streisand and Warren Beatty were honored during the administration of Republican George W. Bush, and a leading conservative, Charlton Heston, was feted during the administration of Democrat Bill Clinton.
Trump skipped the awards during his first term but has been far more involved with the Kennedy Center since returning to the White House. He fired the institution’s board of directors and replaced them with loyalists who named him chairman. He personally announced last year’s honorees and hosted the show that honored them.
His administration has spent much of this year locked in a legal battle over whether and how to honor Trump, with the president insisting his name be added to the building in some form. As that plays out, the Kennedy Center has closed with its stages absent of performances for months. This year’s honors program will be held on Dec. 7 at Washington’s Capital One Arena.
“We are proud to honor this year’s class and to continue a tradition that has defined the Center for nearly 50 years,” Trump said in a statement.
___
Italie reported from New York.

title: Ash bucket linked to fire at Presque Isle apartment building and business
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine — A fire on Main Street in Presque Isle has left several families without a home.
According to state and local officials, the Presque Isle Fire Department received a report of a structure fire at 572 Main Street at approximately 2:30 a.m. Saturday, Oct. 31. The building housed multiple apartments and a commercial business.
Cause of the fire
Firefighters determined the fire started in an attached shed and was linked to the improper storage of hot wood ash from a wood boiler.
After firefighters extinguished the initial fire, Presque Isle firefighters were called back to the property around 4 a.m. State Fire Marshal investigators determined the initial fire had continued to burn undetected within multiple layers of wall and roof materials. It eventually became visible, prompting a second fire department response.
Firefighting efforts
Crews had to pull off the roofline of the building to reach the flames. Impact Auto brought in excavation equipment to tear open the structure.
Firefighters extinguished the fire around 2 p.m. Saturday and remained on scene looking for hot spots until 1 a.m. Sunday. They contained the fire to the building, and no nearby property was damaged.
Mutual aid was provided by the Caribou, Mapleton, Easton and Fort Fairfield fire departments. Presque Isle police handled traffic control and blocked off the street while firefighters were on scene.
Residents displaced
The Presque Isle Fire Department said there were no injuries and the building is a total loss. The department said about eight apartments had tenants affected, and the families and individuals living in the building have been displaced. All those affected by the fire have been in contact with the Red Cross.
Ash disposal reminder
The Maine Office of State Fire Marshal reminded residents and business owners to properly dispose of ashes from woodstoves, fireplaces and other solid-fuel heating appliances. The office said ashes should be placed in a covered metal container and stored outdoors, away from buildings and flammable materials.
The office said that even if ashes appear cool, they can still retain enough heat to ignite nearby combustible materials.

title: School district addresses candy given out in medicine bottles
text:
'This was not appropriate': School district addresses candy given out in medicine bottles
A school district in South Carolina is addressing concerns after candy was given out in medicine bottles ahead of Halloween.
In a post on Facebook, Laurens County School District 56, located in Clinton, South Carolina, addressed concerns, saying it "does not promote or encourage students to play with medicine bottles. In fact, we teach our students the importance of medication safety and that medicine bottles should never be used as toys."
The post continued, saying, "We understand the concerns that have been raised regarding the recent distribution of candy in medicine bottles at one of our schools. We truly believe those involved had only good intentions and would never knowingly do anything to put a child in harm’s way. However, we recognize that even with the best intentions, this was not an appropriate way to distribute candy to students."

title: 2026 midterm elections
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - With Election Day hours away and control of Congress at stake, political experts are watching Senate races in key states.
Texas
Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democratic state Rep. James Talarico.
An endorsement from President Donald Trump helped Paxton earn the nomination over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. However, Paxton’s political baggage has loomed large over the campaign.
The Republican-controlled Texas House impeached Paxton over corruption allegations. He was later acquitted.
Meanwhile, a Talarico victory would give Texas its first Democratic U.S. senator in more than 30 years.
Michigan
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a public health administrator, is facing Republican Rep. Mike Rogers for an open Senate seat.
El-Sayed’s Muslim faith has become a flashpoint in the race. Trump has accused El-Sayed of extremist ties without evidence. El-Sayed has denied the claims and said his allegiance is to the U.S. Constitution.
Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), who challenged El-Sayed in the primary, withdrew her support for him Sunday and endorsed Rogers.
Ohio
Republican Sen. Jon Husted is facing former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown.
Husted was appointed to replace J.D. Vance when Vance became vice president.
Brown is attempting a political comeback after losing his reelection bid in 2024 to Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno. The winner of the race will serve the remaining two years of Vance’s term.

title: Nonprofit packs custom clothing boxes for children in need
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A Virginia nonprofit is using volunteers to pack personalized boxes of clothing and other items for children who lack access to proper clothes.
Clothing insecurity affects children nationwide
An estimated two out of five kids nationwide experience clothing insecurity, meaning they do not have access to clothing that is properly fitted, seasonally appropriate and in good condition.
Clothing insecurity is estimated to affect 20 million children across the country.
Without proper clothes, children can skip school, face bullying and withdraw socially. Clothing insecurity can also lead to lower self-esteem.
Tyndall said she started Boxes of Basics because she saw a need.
“It was the right thing for someone to do. And if I could help these kids, then why wouldn’t I?” Tyndall said.
She described one boy who was affected.
“This little boy didn’t want to go to school because he didn’t have clothes that fit. They were worn. They were small,” Tyndall said. “And after his box of basics, he started waking up 30 minutes early every day. Just to pick out his outfit.”
How the boxes are made
Schools and shelters identify children in need, then share their sizes, favorite colors and favorite characters. Volunteers at a warehouse use that information to select clothing for each child they will never meet.
The clothes are donated. Some are new, and some are gently used.
Tyndall said every box includes:
- Four school outfits
- Four play outfits
- A dress-up outfit
- New shoes, socks and underwear
- Two age-appropriate books
- A set of pajamas
- A hygiene kit
Boxes of Basics also provides a duffle bag for children who need a way to carry their new outfits.
Hand wrapped outfits and love notes
Volunteers hand wrap each outfit and add a love note to every box.
Volunteer Cheryl Burns said the note is the part she likes most.
“I hope you like the clothes and books that I enjoyed picking out for you,” Burns said of the message. “And then I always do a smiley. That’s like my signature. When you see someone smile, it, like, brings joy.”
The organization’s goal is to spread that joy beyond Virginia.

title: Bangor Mall Condemnation Catches Shoppers And Retailers Off Guard
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Code Enforcement Condemns Bangor Mall Building; Says Unfit For Human Habitation
In a move that caught many off guard, especially those who had just been in the building this past weekend shopping for costumes at Spirit Halloween, the City of Bangor condemned the building Monday, citing that it was "unfit for human habitation or use."
Signs on the door, dated 11/02, state, "This structure has been condemned for human habitation or use in accordance with Chapter 223 of the Laws and Ordinances of the City of Bangor. Occupancy is forbidden until conditions detrimental to life and health have been corrected to the written satisfaction of the Code Enforcement Office."
It goes on to say that anyone who enters the premises or removes the sign could face a fine of between $100 and $2,500.
While the move to condemn the building itself wascame out of left field for many.
Some areas of the mall had already been condemned. But others were still occupied and functioning.
Read More: City Of Bangor Takes Action Against Deteriorating Mall Conditions
Stores like Hot Topic, Spencer's, and Spirit Halloween were still actively bringing people into the space, and local investors were trying to get backing to buy the building and turn it into luxury condos. The investors did lose the backing of one of their major players, and were in the process of trying to secure alternate funding when they got the news.
We're told that the local investment group was unaware of the City's plan to condemn the building this week. We have reached out to the City, but have not heard anything back from them yet.
Read More: 13 Bangor Mall Stores You’ll Remember From the Good Old Days
There's no word yet on where the businesses that had still been operating out of the mall will go, but it sounds like they were not given much notice, if any, before being told to vacate the premises.
The Dicks Sporting Goods store and JCPenney retail spaces did not have any signs on their doors. So far, they seem to be exempt from the City's actions.
Read More: Bangor Mall Christmas Craft Fair 2026: Dates and Details
The 7th Annual Bangor Mall Christmas Craft Fair is scheduled to take place in the Furniture, Mattresses & More space, the building that's attached to the Bangor Mall, on the next two weekends, November 7th and 8th and November 14th and 15th.
There's no indication yet that the closure of the mall building will impact that event, but we will let you know if that changes.

title: Portland City Council approves funding for industrial park warming shelter
text:
PORTLAND — The City Council appropriated $735,000 in opioid settlement funds Monday toward operating a winter warming shelter at 166 Riverside Industrial Parkway, the site of last year’s city-run shelter.
The decision, on a 7-2 vote, was seen by many as the better of two less-than-ideal options after an initial plan for a shelter in the Bayside neighborhood fell through.
City staff said the shelter, which will also use about $300,000 in funding from MaineHousing, would open as soon as appropriate staff is hired and trained, but that it could be mid-December or later before that happens.
The other option debated by officials would have declared a limited emergency in order to expand capacity at the city-run Homeless Services Center on Riverside Street. A staff memo said expanding capacity there would be cheaper and the additional beds would be available sooner.
However, complicating the decision was concern among councilors that it would shut out some of the city’s most vulnerable. Staff said there are 52 people who have criminal trespass orders that prevent them from accessing the Homeless Services Center. The industrial park option would not turn those individuals away.
Staff said the current housing status of the 52 individuals is unknown, but that “the vast majority of these orders were issued in response to violent behavior that caused injury or posed an imminent physical threat to shelter guests and/or staff.”
The council voted 5-4 against the Homeless Services Center option, with councilors Fournier, Sykes, Michniewicz, Bullett and Phillips opposed.
A majority of councilors agreed that there should be a no-barrier option for homeless individuals who can’t access the Homeless Services Center, and shared concerns for overcrowding there.
‘OUT IN THE COLD’
There were audible groans, deep breaths and exits in frustration Monday leading up to the council’s decision regarding the shelter that was originally slated to open this month. The council chamber was filled with homeless and recovery advocates who criticized the use of opioid settlement funds and questioned how officials again found themselves scrambling for a solution with winter approaching.
During public comment, someone who said they were a former housing counselor at the Homeless Services Center said adding more beds there would create “absolute pandemonium.”
Susanna Richer said the two options presented “are not appropriate,” and she argued that the “implication that most are violent and deserve to be left out in the cold” is offensive.
Cheryl Harkins, an advocate with Homeless Voices for Justice and a representative on the statewide homeless council, called Monday’s vote a “critical decision for people’s lives” and said the community as a whole misunderstands the homeless population.
Officials began to consider returning to the industrial park building after a plan to stand up a shelter at Elena’s Way on Portland Street fell through due to a combination of zoning regulations on the property and neighborhood concern.
The council held a special meeting last week to consider funding the Riverside Industrial Park option, but ultimately postponed action following a lengthy executive session. While officials did not comment at the time, a council memo says the decision was made in order to give staff more time to explore alternative options.
The next day, staff was informed that Seeds of Hope, the Biddeford nonprofit that was originally slated to operate the Elena’s Way warming shelter, had withdrawn its application for MaineHousing funding and was no longer interested in operating a shelter in Portland.
The news put the city back to square one roughly two weeks before a shelter was originally slated to open.
Councilor Anna Bullett, chair of the public safety and health and human services committee, and Mayor Mark Dion then held a meeting with more than a dozen healthcare and community organizations. Dion said the organizations all said similar things: they are already stretched thin with staff.
Bullett, who supported the industrial park option, was critical Monday of Cumberland County government, which she said was also invited to the meeting but wasn’t there.
‘DEEPLY SHAKEN’
Others were critical of the city’s process a year after the council was faced with the same options.
Councilor Wes Pelletier, who supported the Homeless Services Center option, said last year he proposed a coordinator position for establishing a warming center, but was told no. When it appeared that the city had an operator and venue in place, he felt good. But since then, he said, “my trust in staff to provide accurate information has been deeply shaken.”
“The laws that made Elena’s Way difficult were passed two years ago and should not have been surprising,” he said. “It’s clear that the two hands of the city are not talking.”
Pelletier also agreed with other commenters who said the opioid funds should be used for recovery programs.
Ryan Paige, co-founder of a Maine recovery nonprofit, told councilors that the funds are meant to help get people “out of the grips of addiction,” and that it would be “egregious” to use them for a short-term shelter.
Terence Miller, advocacy director at Preble Street, said the nonprofit “strongly encourages” the city to make the shelter as accessible as possible, and that an off-peninsula location presents considerable barriers.
Miller said that if the Homeless Services Center option was chosen, staff should find “a creative solution” to allow individuals with trespass orders to access shelter. They also recommended an extended shuttle schedule for bringing shelter guests to and from the peninsula.
Dion, in response to some of the criticism, defended how city staff has handled the process, and said the city has done its best to find a workable solution. He said very few buildings on the peninsula meet the requirements needed, and responding to Pelletier, said a program coordinator would have run into the same situation: people don’t have space and their staff and budgets are stressed.
“We’re here because the old model has failed,” said Councilor Ben Grant.
Grant and others said the city has attempted for years to establish a warming shelter through community organizations, but that after multiple failures, there needs to be discussions on including funding in the city budget.
“This is clearly not something organizations can do,” said Councilor Kate Sykes.
Councilor Regina Phillips, who supported the industrial park option, said she’s not willing to put funding in the budget “if we’re not going to have folks come with us.”
“The minute you mention the county they crawl under a rock,” she said.

title: Mass shootings over Halloween weekend leave at least 8 dead and dozens injured across US
text:
(AP) - Federal authorities in Texas planned to detail their response Monday to a series of shootings in Dallas, one of numerous gun incidents across the nation on Halloween weekend that left at least eight people dead and dozens more injured.
Many of the mass shootings occurred in entertainment districts and in college towns. The deadliest occurred in Dallas, where the U.S. attorney’s office planned a news conference to discuss federal actions related to three shootings in the city’s Deep Ellum neighborhood, a center of music and restaurants. Those shootings left four people dead and 15 injured and happened over the span of about an hour and 15 minutes early Sunday.
As investigators continued their searches for suspects and the motives for the shootings, word spread of even more mass violence over the weekend along with condemnation from elected officials.
Two separate shootings occurred in Birmingham, Alabama, after the annual “Magic City Classic” college football game on Saturday night. And police in college towns reported shootings in their nightlife districts where annual Halloween gatherings are popular, including in Fayetteville, Arkansas; Birmingham, Alabama; Newark, Delaware; Bloomington, Illinois; and Bloomington, Indiana.
Deep Ellum saw gun violence earlier this year
Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux has said investigators were still trying to determine if the shootings were related and why they started. His department had increased police presence prior to the shootings in the district, which had experienced deadly violence earlier this year.
Two people were fatally stabbed during a fight outside a nightclub in February, and a security guard was shot and killed while trying to break up a fight inside a nightclub in May. There also have been nonfatal shootings, including during Cinco de Mayo festivities in May when five people were wounded outside of a sports bar, police said.
Halloween can be a busy time for gun violence incidents
Multiple academic studies of police department and hospital data from major cities over the last decade have shown gun violence is more frequent at night, on weekends and on holidays. Several studies have pointed to the July Fourth holiday as being one of the most or the most violent holiday because of dark hours for fireworks celebrations, combined with alcohol consumption and other factors. New Year’s and Halloween were also high on the list for gun violence incidents.
Last year the homicide rate in the United States dropped to its lowest point in 75 years, according to FBI numbers on 2025 crime. Those numbers showed homicides decreased by 18% and overall violent crime dropped 9.3% last year.
Cities and municipalities across the country largely have been experiencing drops in homicides and violence, with a few exceptions, for the past few years. Federal authorities and nonprofit groups have noted national violent crime and homicide rates have been declining since 2022. Experts also noted that trend had continued through the first six months of 2026.
Elected officials take to social media after shootings
In Jackson, Mississippi, two people were killed and six others were injured in a shooting during a Halloween costume party at a nightclub early Sunday, police said. Just before the shooting, two men entered the club wearing ski masks. At some point at least one of the suspects opened fire into the crowd, police said. The suspects have not yet been identified.
A 20-year-old man and an 18-year-old woman were killed in the shooting, while six others were taken to hospitals with injuries that didn’t appear to be life threatening, police said.
“No one should have to fear for their life while enjoying an evening out,” Jackson Mayor John Horhn said in a statement following the shooting.
Near Indiana University’s campus, seven people were wounded in a shooting early Sunday in a busy nightlife area. None of the victims were believed to be students, police said.
“This is unacceptable in Bloomington, and in any community,” Bloomington Mayor Kerry Thomson said Sunday in a video address shared on social media.
Even with increased police staffing, no public safety plan can eliminate every act of violence, Thomson said.
Separate shootings occurred outside a college football game
In Birmingham, Alabama, one person was killed and eight others were wounded in two separate shootings just outside Legion Field after the annual “Magic City Classic” football game on Saturday night. Alabama State and Alabama A&M are archrivals whose annual contest has been played for more than 100 years. Nearly 70,000 fans attended Saturday’s game, won by Alabama A&M 31-28. The event draws some of the largest crowds in the country for games played in their college football division.
Michael Pickett, chief of the Birmingham Police Department, said most spectators and families had left the stadium property after the game. The first shooting happened nearby, where vendors were set up along Graymont Avenue.
___
Raby reported from Charleston, West Virginia. AP reporters Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia and Jamie Stengle in Dallas contributed to this report.

title: Judge dismisses lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska Senate race if GOP incumbent loses
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses, the latest development in a ballot controversy that has roiled the final days of one of the nation’s most closely watched races.
Sullivan, an ally of President Donald Trump, faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, in a race that is among a handful expected to determine which party controls the Senate for the final two years of Trump’s term.
Tuesday’s ranked-choice election also includes two candidates who have done little campaigning, one of whom shares the incumbent’s name. It was that candidate’s presence on the ballot that prompted Trump to push for the lawsuit out of fear he would siphon votes from the incumbent.
Shortly after the ruling, the Justice Department filed a notice that it would appeal: “Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” a department spokesperson said in a statement.
The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the election and as early voting was underway, called for an investigation into whether votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan were intended for the senator. The state said the case lacked merit and argued there would be no way to determine that without violating voter privacy.
U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason said the relief the federal government sought was “infeasible” because many voters have already cast their ballots.
“More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified ‘investigation’ of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” she wrote.
Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee argued that the case lacked any legal basis and amounted to election interference.
“Today’s ruling is a victory for democracy and a clear message to Donald Trump and Senate Republicans: No one, no matter how powerful, can toss out free and fair elections just because they don’t like the result,” said the committee’s executive director, Devan Barber.
Peltola’s campaign hailed the ruling. “No sham investigation or baseless lawsuit from a weaponized Department of Justice is going to stop Alaskans from electing Mary on Nov. 3 so she can lower costs for Alaska’s working families,” the campaign said in a statement, alluding to a federal probe disclosed after President Donald Trump said last week that he wanted Peltola prosecuted for the scheme.
Attorneys for the state did not immediately return messages seeking comment.
Senator says he expects ‘to lose a lot of votes’ to the other Dan Sullivan
The senator and his allies, including Trump, for months have portrayed Dan J. Sullivan as a sham candidate intent on confusing voters and helping Peltola.
Earlier Sunday, Sen. Sullivan told CNN that he thought the presence of the second Sullivan on the ballot would affect the election.
“I’m sure I’m going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery,” he said.
He also said he doubted claims by Peltola that she had no idea her top political aides were involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to run as a way to confuse voters.
“There is no way this went on for a year that they weren’t informing her,” Sullivan told CNN’s “State of the Union.” “She got caught lying, and she’s still lying to the Alaskan people, the media, to all of us.”
In the week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign was involved in efforts to recruit the second Sullivan. Shortly after entering the race in June, Dan J. Sullivan said he’d had no contact with her campaign about running. He has not responded to multiple messages over the past few days.
His recent public absence prompted a social media post Sunday by the president: “The Fake Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr., has DISAPPEARED! Nobody can find him, including Law Enforcement.”
Peltola’s campaign responded to the Times story by saying it had no involvement in the campaigns for either Sullivan: “I am not interested in tricking voters,” Peltola said during a recent campaign event.
In its statement indicating its plans to appeal, the Justice Department said the federal judge dismissed the case on procedural grounds but did not dispute the government’s argument that Dan J. Sullivan entered the race “as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters.”
Multiple investigations look into whether Dan J. Sullivan was recruited as a decoy candidate
State courts, including the Alaska Supreme Court, rejected an earlier Republican-backed effort to block the retired teacher from the August open primary ballot on which he appeared as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. The senator was listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent.
Both Sullivans appear the same way on the general election ballot. Peltola placed first in the primary, followed by the senator. Dan J. Sullivan received about 2.5% of the primary vote, but that was enough to finish within the top four and qualify for the Nov. 3 ranked-choice election.
Attorneys for the Alaska Department of Law represented state elections officials in the case and asked Gleason, who was appointed by former Democratic President Barack Obama, to toss the lawsuit. They filed a scathing response to the federal government’s complaint, calling it “meritless.”
Alaska also said the state had taken “significant steps” to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. Voters who still might be confused could ask for help or look up candidate biographies and other information in state-distributed election pamphlets.
Republicans, including ones working with Trump, also have a long history of backing decoy candidates in elections. The governor, a Republican, has ordered an investigation and suggested he may not certify a possible Peltola victory.
In her ruling, Gleason wrote that the Trump administration’s attempt to block certification ran counter to the Constitution, which gives states the authority to run elections. She also cited the Supreme Court’s Purcell principle, which holds that federal courts should generally not change election rules too close to an election.
Kristen Clarke, general counsel of the NAACP, which had filed a brief supporting the case’s dismissal, called the judge’s decision “a big win for the voters in Alaska.”
“The law is clear, and the DOJ’s case was a baseless, eleventh-hour attempt to hijack this midterm election,” she said.
On Thursday, the Justice Department escalated a criminal investigation over the presence of Dan J. Sullivan on the Alaska ballot, issuing a raft of new grand jury subpoenas, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press. The FBI also has begun contacting people who donated to him, some of whom told the AP that the agents were asking if they had been misled about which candidate they were supporting.
___
Riccardi reported from Washington. Associated Press photographer Lindsey Wasson in Anchorage, Alaska, and AP writer Ali Swenson in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Taurids, Leonids and a Beaver Supermoon: Astronomical events for November 2026
text:
Taurids, Leonids and a Beaver Supermoon: Astronomical events for November 2026
Three meteor showers and a supermoon
Taurids, Leonids and a Beaver Supermoon: Astronomical events for November 2026
Three meteor showers and a supermoon
Falling back on the clock means more time to look at the stars.
There will be plenty to look up for in November’s night sky. There will also be some clear nights for stargazing before the weather gets too cold for the year. Also, we’ll have three chances to see a meteor shower this month, as well as plenty of chances to spy the planets. We will also cap off the month with a Beaver Moon.
Related video above: The dark energy pushing our universe apart may not be what it seems, scientists say
Read below for the full list of astronomical events in November.
November mornings — Jupiter, Mars, Venus
All eyes will be on the southeastern morning sky. Throughout November, Jupiter and Mars will be paired in the sky as they cross in front of the constellation Leo. Venus will also be visible lower in the sky, crossing near Spica, the brightest star in Virgo.
Later in the month, Mercury will also appear beneath Virgo, before dipping back below the horizon in December.
November evenings — Saturn
Saturn will be visible between the constellations Pisces and Cetus, the Whale, in the southeastern evening sky, just after dusk.
Nov. 5 — Southern Taurids meteor shower
The Taurids are a unique meteor shower that actually presents in two different areas of the night sky. The Southern Taurids occur between Sept. 23 and Dec. 8, but they peak on the evening of Nov. 5. The Taurids’ radiant, or origin point, is the constellation Taurus, for which they are named.
Nov. 9 — New moon
A new moon does not make for a particularly exciting sky, but it does make for a clear one. Use this opportunity to get some stargazing in. This time of year in the Northern Hemisphere, you can see the constellations Andromeda and Cetus. Hopefully, your local weather will cooperate to make for a star-filled evening.
Nov. 12 — Northern Taurids meteor shower
The Northern Taurids range from Oct. 13 to Dec. 2 and peak on the evening of Nov. 12. The northern variant of the meteor shower also originates from the constellation Taurus, this time near the star Atlas.
The Taurids consist of debris from the comet Encke, which orbits around the sun every three years.
Nov. 17-18 — Leonid meteor shower
The Leonids are one of the most prominent meteor showers of the year. According to NASA, they are considered to be some of the fastest meteors and can be quite colorful. This year, we should expect to see anywhere from 3 to 15 meteors per hour. The Leonids usually are active between Nov. 6 and 30, and their peak this year falls on the evening of Nov. 17.
The radiant of the Leonids is the constellation Leo. They will be visible in the eastern night sky after midnight. Jupiter and Mars will also be in conjunction near Leo on that same night, just above Regulus, one of the brightest stars in the sky.
The Leonid meteor shower consists of the debris of the comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. The comet orbits the sun every 33 years. It also causes meteor storms, which are when more than 1,000 meteors can be seen in an hour, every 33 years when it passes by Earth. The latest Leonid meteor storm took place in 2002. According to NASA, comet 55P was independently discovered by both Ernst Tempel and Horace Tuttle just a year apart, so it is named for both of them.
Nov. 24 — Beaver Supermoon
The full moon of November is known as the Beaver Moon. According to The Old Farmer’s Almanac, this was traditionally the time of year when "beavers begin to take shelter in their lodges, having laid up sufficient food stores for the long winter ahead." The general use of the name traces back to explorer Jonathan Carver’s book "Travels through the interior parts of North-America in the years 1766, 1767, and 1768," which lists names for the moons used by some Great Lakes Indigenous tribes. Carver wrote that the name Beaver Moon was used because "for in this month the beavers begin to take shelter in their houses, having laid up a sufficient store of provisions for the winter season."
Other Indigenous names for the moon include the Freezing River Moon (Abenaki, Anishnaabe, Arapaho, Cree), the Frost Moon (Assiniboine, Creek), the Moon of the Panther (Choctaw), the Moon of Fledgling Hawk (Hopi), the Moon of the Turkey (Potawatomi), and the Moon When All is Gathered in (Pueblo).
The Beaver Moon this year is also a supermoon, meaning it will appear 14% bigger and 30% brighter than an average moon, according to NASA.

title: Unaired Jurassic Park Animated Series Trailer Emerges Online
text:
Unaired ‘Jurassic Park’ Animated Series Trailer Emerges Online
In the last few years, Jurassic Park fans have finally gotten several fairly long-running animated series based on their favorite dino-centric property. Netflix aired five seasons of Jurassic World: Camp Cretaceous, followed by four seasons of a sequel series, Jurassic World: Chaos Theory.
It’s kind of wild it took almost 30 years for a franchise as popular as Jurassic Park to spin off an animated series. Kids have always been the brand’s primarily audience, and far less kid-friendly films of the ’90s got animated series, including The Mask, Dumb & Dumber, Ace Ventura: Pet Detective, and even a couple of movies that did not star Jim Carrey.
But it turns out there was an attempt to make a Jurassic Park animated show way back then, one that was development and then shelved without ever making it to air. And now the trailer for that effort has appeared online. Watch it below:
READ MORE: Directors Known For Only Making Bad Movies
According to the Jurassic Park Wiki, the show would have been titled Escape From Jurassic Park. It would have been about John Hammond, Alan Grant, Ellie Sattler, and Ian Malcolm all returning to Isla Nublar, “in order to recapture the dinosaurs and turn the island into a research facility. Joining them on their mission is Tim and Lex Murphy, who stowed away to the island.” (Kids. Can’t live with ’em, can’t go to an island of dinosaurs without them, lest there not be perspective characters for children to identify with on the animated series.)
The dinosaur designs in this animated series, which was developed in 1993 shortly after the film was released, were by famed artist William Stout, who once wrote of the project...
This was not going to be a kiddy show (although kids of all ages, including myself, could enjoy it). They wanted the show to be a mature prime time series with top writers and state-of-the-art television animation augmented with quite a bit of CG animation. Universal Cartoon Studios wanted a “graphic novel look” to the series. I came in, showed my portfolio and was hired. We made a trailer to communicate the look and feel of the series, also showing how we would combine computer animation with traditional animation. All we needed was [Steven] Spielberg’s approval.
According to Stout, he heard that Spielberg never even watched the trailer they produced because “he was burnt out on Jurassic Park merchandising and all of the film’s commercial exploitation. So, it never got made.”
That’s too bad; the trailer looks pretty good, especially by the standards of mid-’90s TV animation. (I watched a lot of cartoons in that period and I can say for certain: Most were junk and looked like garbage.) Then again, it’s not like the world is exactly starved for Jurassic Park material, either. If you want a JP cartoon, there are nine seasons of them on Netflix right now.

title: This state no longer allows candy, soda, energy drink purchases with SNAP benefits
text:
COLUMBIA, S.C. (WRDW/Gray) - SNAP recipients in South Carolina are no longer able to buy some sugary items, including most candy and soda, under the new program.
The Health Food SC Project, approved by the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food and Nutrition Service, excludes candy, energy drinks, soft drinks and sweetened beverages from the list of foods eligible for purchase under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as SNAP or food stamps.
Diet and zero-sugar soft drinks are still allowed to be purchased using SNAP.
South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster announced his intent to pursue a federal waiver for the restrictions in August 2025, issuing an executive order in September directing the South Carolina Department of Social Services to submit the waiver request. The USDA approved the waiver.
All South Carolina SNAP-approved retailers will participate in the program. SNAP households will not have the option to opt out of the food restrictions.

title: United Airlines will add more direct flights between Maine and California
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In response to high demand, United Airlines plans to add 20 more nonstop, roundtrip flights between the Portland International Jetport and two California destinations next summer.
This year, the airline debuted seasonal direct service once a week to Los Angeles and San Francisco. Flights to San Francisco were popular enough that the airline extended that service five weeks longer than anticipated in 2026, jetport officials said.
“United made history earlier this year when they flew our first transcontinental flights,” Airport Director Paul Bradbury said in a news release Monday. “The demand exceeded our expectations and we are now seeing United at 65% more flights to California for summer 2027. We are grateful to United for the continued investment in the Portland market and look forward to the additional flights to California.”
San Francisco flights will resume Saturday-only service on May 8, 2027, and United will add a Wednesday flight for twice-weekly service starting June 23, according to the news release.
Los Angeles flights will resume Saturday-only service on June 26 and United is adding six Wednesday flights during the summer, according to the release.
“These flights make it very easy to move between the East Coast and West Coast,” Assistant Airport Director Zach Sundquist said in the news release. “United’s hubs in San Francisco and Los Angeles allow for one-stop connections to many Pacific Rim destinations, and with Wednesday service being introduced these options become even more appealing to local businesses with connections to Asia.”

title: Grandmother gets Halloween surprise after grandson asks community to trick-or-treat
text:
Grandmother has Halloween of lifetime thanks to social media post
A grandmother had the Halloween treat of a lifetime on Saturday, thanks to a social media post made by her grandson.
Cade Bearfield of New Hampshire told sister station WMUR that his grandmother, Pauline Fiest, known as Meme, loves Halloween.
"Who isn't a fan? It's great. You can pass out candy, see all these cute kids in their costumes; it's fun. It's just a fun time," Fiest said.
But Bearfield said his family hasn't seen many trick-or-treaters since moving to their home in Manchester.
So, Bearfield made a social media post asking for the community's help.
"I said that everyone was welcome to come trick-or-treating at our house on Saturday because, you know, my grandmother, she sits outside in the cold, in costume every year, and, you know, she's turning 70 and she's going to be retiring soon," Bearfield said. "And we just really wanted to make this a big, special Halloween for her."
His post didn't go unanswered. Dozens of trick-or-treaters showed up before dusk.
Charlene from Manchester stopped by with her family.
"I said that's our first stop; before we do anything, we're going to make this woman's Halloween special," Charlene said.
Beatrice Whiteman told WMUR she saw the post on social media and did the same.
"Thought it was a really cool thing that someone was doing and just wanted to come out and support the community," Whiteman said.
Fiest was both surprised and grateful for the outpouring of community support.
"You just see people coming, and they're smiling, and they're happy, and it doesn't matter how old you are or how young you are; everyone just seems to be having a good time. So, it's good," Fiest said.
Fiest was dressed as Elmo for the occasion.

title: Federal judge orders Iowa to allow Satanic Temple to have holiday display at Capitol
text:
Federal judge orders Iowa to allow Satanic Temple to have holiday display at Capitol
A judge says state officials in Iowa cannot deny the Satanic Temple of Iowa a holiday display at the Statehouse.
Sister station KCCI reports that the Iowa Department of Administrative Services has denied the group's application for three years. The temple has sought to have a family-friendly display in the Capitol rotunda, along with other religious or civic groups.
The court order is the latest in a back-and-forth between the religious organization and Republican state officials, who intend to appeal the federal judge’s decision, according to Attorney General Brenna Bird’s office. Iowa’s Republican leaders have barred the Satanic Temple Iowa's holiday observances in recent years, citing the state Capitol building’s policies that prohibit gratuitous violence and obscene displays.
The Satanic Temple and the leader of its Iowa organization in August sued the state in federal court, arguing that current and former Iowa officials discriminated against their religion by repeatedly refusing to permit their holiday event and violated their constitutional rights and state law.
Chief District Judge Stephanie M. Rose said in her order that the Satanic Temple was likely to succeed on its free speech claim and ordered the current director of the Iowa Department of Administrative Services to approve the group’s application for a holiday event within seven days.
Founded in 2013, the Salem, Massachusetts-based Satanic Temple says it doesn’t believe in Satan but describes itself as a “non-theistic religious organization” that advocates for secularism. It is separate from the Church of Satan, which was founded in the 1960s.
The Satanic Temple hasn’t always been barred from participating in the holiday season at the Iowa Statehouse, where a Christmas tree and other religious holiday installations are included in the rotunda. The Satanic Temple Iowa’s display, which depicted the goat-headed figure Baphomet, was vandalized three years ago, leading to increased scrutiny on the group and its observances. In 2024, their application for a display and event was rejected.
The group said its holiday event would include costumes of the European folklore character Krampus, as well as caroling, coloring for kids and ornament making. In denying their application, state leaders have cited policies to protect children that may be present in the public space and point to the costumes' use of sticks, which could be used as weapons. The Satanic Temple members reject that premise.
The chief district judge wrote that Iowa officials' arguments likely don't justify the denials. Rose wrote that concern that the Krampus character may frighten children is “not a permissible basis for excluding speech,” adding that concern surrounding sticks being carried as part of costumes “cannot justify denying the entire event.” She said the state department could impose the same conditions it applies to other events on the Satanic Temple's event, saying props remain subject to the building's regular security screening.
Members of The Satanic Temple celebrated the ruling, as did the American Civil Liberties Union of Iowa, which is representing the religious organization.
“Too often, fear or misunderstanding of the ‘other’ is amplified by petty governmental bureaucrats looking to score cheap political points by portraying unfamiliar beliefs as ‘dangerous,'” said Matt Kezhaya, attorney for The Satanic Temple, in a statement.
“This was always going to be a family-friendly event,” he added. “None of this became ‘harmful’ just because state officials disapproved of our chosen expression.”
Spokespeople for the Iowa Department of Administrative Services and Gov. Kim Reynolds did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
___
The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: The unforetold | Letters To Editor
text:
To the Editor:
It has never been foretold.
No culture knows it yet.
The ancient prophets slept well for
From even them it had been kept.
Long sailing ships could point their way
With their ropes humming night and day.
For the secret had been kept so well
It had not been shared with heaven nor hell.
Cling to and rejoice therefore
In your incomplete knowledge of things.
Be studious yes, but impatient no
For I'm not the one holding the strings.
It is not my place to share at this time.
That which has stayed wrapped through the ages.
Look for it today in a most careful way but
The future will keep turning its pages.
William F. Fuller
Bar Harbor

title: Ash can started Presque Isle building fire
text:
A Saturday fire that destroyed a Presque Isle building started in an ash can in an attached shed, the state fire marshal’s office ruled Monday.
The blaze spread to other parts of the building and continued to burn the roof and walls, so Presque Isle Fire Department personnel returned to the scene later that morning, according to Maine Public Safety Department spokesperson Aaron Turcotte.
The three-story Main Street building housed several apartments and a business on the ground floor.
The blaze started in the early morning, according to city spokesperson Kim Smith.
Fire marshal investigators determined the bucket, which contained discarded ashes, caused the fire.
After the initial fire was extinguished, a second fire appeared to break out, Turcotte said. Investigators found the original fire was still burning, undetected, through “multiple layers of wall and roof materials,” which eventually burst into flames.
No injuries were reported, Smith and Turcotte said. It is not yet known how many people were displaced. The Red Cross was also present Saturday.
The fire marshal’s office urged residents and business owners to dispose of ashes properly, in a covered metal container stored outdoors, away from buildings and flammable materials.

title: Trump rallies in Iowa and Kansas as Republicans fight to keep Senate and House control
text:
DUBUQUE, Iowa (AP) — President Donald Trump closed out the final weekend of a turbulent midterm campaign with rallies in two states he has handily won in the past while Democrats began to fracture in Michigan, risking their effort to retake the Senate.
The president was in Salina, Kansas, and Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday. Republicans in both states are fending off robust challenges from Democrats, threatening GOP majorities in the Senate while they’re already at risk in the House.
But in Iowa, Trump insisted Republicans were on the verge of sweeping victories on Election Day on Tuesday.
“We’re going to elect ‘America first’ Republicans up and down the line,” he said near the start of a speech that lasted two hours, long even for Trump, who is known for his lengthy, free-wheeling rallies.
Later, he arrived tardy in Kansas, where Air Force One performed a theatrical flyover before landing for an outdoor, airport rally. Hundreds of people started leaving midway through his nearly 90-minute speech in rural central Kansas, which didn’t end until nearly 10 p.m. local time.
“This is our last stop. We’re closing it down tonight,” Trump said. He has crisscrossed the country since Oct. 1, holding more than two dozen rallies in 19 states to lift up the GOP. He is scheduled to give his closing pitch of the midterm elections Monday in Washington at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
With more than 54 million votes already cast, the trips reflect the GOP’s defensive posture as the elections become a referendum on Trump’s White House second term.
They are a reminder of how starkly the political environment has changed since Trump’s last campaign. In 2024, he worked to flip states that had previously backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020. This year, Trump has focused largely on states he has dominated before as voters, including previous supporters, question the economic fallout of his decision to impose tariffs and launch the war in Iran.
Democrats struggle with infighting in Michigan
But Democrats who have become increasingly bullish on their prospects were confronting challenges of their own.
In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s onetime opponent in the Senate primary, Haley Stevens, appeared with Republican Mike Rogers at a church service and later endorsed his campaign. Stevens, a congresswoman who has criticized El-Sayed as being insufficiently supportive of Israel, said she backed Rogers after an invitation to a Democratic event was rescinded.
“Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement. “And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.”
The stunning move forced other Democrats to reiterate their support for El-Sayed. Chuck Schumer of New York, the top Democrat in the U.S. Senate, said the party was “united in our support.” U.S. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, who leads the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, said the party would “stand firmly” behind El-Sayed and “reject any efforts to divide Democrats.”
Earlier, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, a top supporter of El-Sayed, dismissed concerns about a Democratic divide.
“Haley Stevens lost a very, very close primary. I can understand being upset about that,” the Vermont independent said on CBS’ “Face the Nation.” “But from what I can see, all over the state, people are standing up; they’re gonna stand with Abdul.”
Michigan plays a key role in the Democratic effort to retake control of the U.S. Senate. If they don’t keep that seat on Tuesday, they would face additional pressure to win races in deeper Republican territory such as Texas, Kansas, Ohio or Iowa.
Midterms test Trump’s strength in GOP
The campaign’s closing stretch has largely become a test of Trump’s enduring strength in a Republican Party he reshaped in his image a decade ago. He’s hoping to energize voters like Jon Lutz, a Dubuque resident who watches videos of Trump all the time but attended his first rally on Sunday.
Lutz said he’s happy with Trump’s second-term record and wants Republicans to keep control of the House and Senate so his agenda will advance.
“He’s done what he’s said he’s going to do,” the 60-year-old civil engineer said. “I want him to keep going.”
Wendy Kuenzler was also seeing Trump for the first time on Sunday. Waiting in line at the concession stand, the 44-year-old from Burlington said she felt that Iowa was at a crossroads with multiple competitive elections. She plans to support Ashley Hinson, the U.S. Senate nominee.
Kuenzler said she doesn’t blame rising gas and grocery prices on Trump. “He’s on the path to correcting it,” she said.
In Kansas, Liz Wagner, a 59-year-old restaurant owner, traveled 165 miles (266 kilometers) from her hometown of Atchison to attend Trump’s outdoor rally at the airport in Salina, Kansas. She said she agrees “with everything he says.”
“I want people to get up and go to work and stop sticking their hands out,” she said while waiting to get into the rally. “The Democrats like to hand things out.”
Trump is betting that he can overcome the headwinds facing Republicans this year by relentlessly appearing before his most loyal supporters. But the more than two dozen rallies he held in October were occasionally overshadowed by Trump’s meandering asides and sometimes graphic descriptions of the physique of the male politicians he was supporting.
Trump paused the rallies on Saturday and spent the evening at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida at a jungle-themed Halloween party, where he bragged about the wealth of his guests and dismissed concerns about the country’s direction.
“The country has never done better,” he said.
Outgoing Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., raised concerns on Sunday that the president’s policies, particularly tariffs, could weigh down the GOP.
“Tariffs are not popular here in the Midwest,” he told CNN’s “State of the Union.” “I tried telling the president that.”
Bacon predicted “there will be a debate in the party” about its future if there are significant losses this week.
Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina was more optimistic. The chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee said he was confident Republicans would keep the Senate and embraced Trump’s role in the campaign.
“There’s no doubt that President Trump has said himself that the midterm election is about him,” he told NBC’s “Meet the Press.” “His agenda, without any question, is on the ballot.”

title: Family of 4 among those killed in Florida jet crash
text:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (Gray News) - A family representative identified the passengers of the Learjet that crashed in a Florida neighborhood on Sunday.
“With broken hearts, our families share that Adam Robinson and Helen Sharp, their children Emma and Charlie, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and Anita Maria Cetina were among those lost aboard the flight that went down near Greenacres, Florida, on November 1,” the statement, posted on Facebook, read in part.
One of the pilots was previously identified by her mother as 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras.
The identity of the second pilot has not yet been confirmed.
All nine people were killed when the plane crashed into the street and exploded in a neighborhood close to West Palm Beach.
The cause of the crash is still under investigation.
Federal investigators outline the probe but decline to speculate
National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said during a news conference Monday that investigators found evidence the aircraft started breaking up before it hit the ground and that debris from the aircraft could be spread far and wide.
“We do have some indication that the aircraft was breaking up before impact,” Chapman said. “We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site.”
Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti said key components of the jet’s tail may have been lost during the turbulence or as it nose-dived.
“If that happens, you cannot control an airplane at that point. And that very well could explain the missile-like profile just before it hit the ground,” said Guzzetti, a former NTSB and the Federal Aviation Administration investigator.
Weather conditions will be a major focus of the investigation, Chapman said. Rain pounded the region on Sunday, and one of the pilots reported icing conditions at a high altitude in communications with air traffic control.
Weather radar maps from the time of the crash that FlightRadar24 combined with the plane’s flight path seem to show it flying directly into a storm cell that was rapidly expanding upward. But Chapman said investigators still have to determine what the weather conditions were at 35,000 feet.
Chapman said the plane was originally equipped with a cockpit voice recorder that investigators hope to recover.
“We have a lot of work to do on scene,” NTSB investigator Timothy Monville said at the news conference. “This will be a several-day process, and the biggest obstacle that we’re going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway.”

title: Former UMaine hockey goaltender Sean Romeo dies at age 31
text:
Goaltender Sean Romeo, who played for the University of Maine for two seasons before transferring to Ohio State, died on Oct. 24 of complications from a stroke he suffered on Oct. 15, according to the Ohio State men’s hockey website. He was 31.
Romeo started 23 games as a freshman at UMaine in the 2014-15 season and posted a 7-13-1 record, a 3.04 goals-against average and a .902 save percentage. He earned UMaine’s lone playoff win in a best-of-three Hockey East first round loss to Vermont.
The following year, freshman Rob McGovern and redshirt junior Matt Morris split the goaltending. Romeo appeared in just two games, and he transferred to Ohio State after the season.
He sat out the 2016-17 season at Ohio State due to NCAA transfer rules but became the starting goalie the following season and led the Buckeyes to their first Frozen Four appearance since 1998. He was a second team All-Big Ten selection and was the first Buckeye to be named a semifinalist for the Mike Richter Award, which is given to the nation’s best goalie.
He was chosen the Most Outstanding Player of the NCAA Midwest Regional.
He posted a record of 22-10-5 with a 2.06 GAA and a .927 save percentage. He had two shutouts. His 22 wins in a single season are tied for second in school history.
In addition, he was also an outstanding student as he earned the NCAA Elite 90 Award with the highest grade-point average among players at the 2018 Frozen Four.
The following year, he shared the goaltending with sophomore Tommy Nappier and was 8-7-2 with a 2.58 GAA and a .902 save percentage. He set the school record in November 2018 for the longest shutout streak, spanning 204 minutes and 27 seconds. He was the first goalie in program history to register shutouts in three consecutive starts.
The Cary, North Carolina, native, who earned a finance degree at OSU and was a three-time Ohio State Scholar-Athlete and two-time Academic All-Big Ten honoree, went on to have a two-year, 30-game professional career for seven teams in the ECHL.
Former University of Maine assistant coach and current Bowdoin College men’s hockey coach Ben Guite said Romeo was the type of goalie you “wanted to run with due to his preparation and work ethic.”
Guite said Romeo not only worked hard on the ice, he spent a lot of time in the gym and workout room.
“He was also an exceptional student,” Guite said.
He also said the fact Romeo was able to flourish at Ohio State after not having a lot of success at UMaine is a tribute to his “resilience and belief in himself. He fought through adversity.”
“It’s a sad day,” Guite said.
Romeo was an organ donor and donated his lungs, liver, heart and kidneys, according to Ohio State.

title: 2026 midterm elections
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - With Election Day hours away and control of Congress at stake, political experts are watching Senate races in key states.
Texas
Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democratic state Rep. James Talarico.
An endorsement from President Donald Trump helped Paxton earn the nomination over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. However, Paxton’s political baggage has loomed large over the campaign.
The Republican-controlled Texas House impeached Paxton over corruption allegations. He was later acquitted.
Meanwhile, a Talarico victory would give Texas its first Democratic U.S. senator in more than 30 years.
Michigan
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a public health administrator, is facing Republican Rep. Mike Rogers for an open Senate seat.
El-Sayed’s Muslim faith has become a flashpoint in the race. Trump has accused El-Sayed of extremist ties without evidence. El-Sayed has denied the claims and said his allegiance is to the U.S. Constitution.
Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), who challenged El-Sayed in the primary, withdrew her support for him Sunday and endorsed Rogers.
Ohio
Republican Sen. Jon Husted is facing former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown.
Husted was appointed to replace J.D. Vance when Vance became vice president.
Brown is attempting a political comeback after losing his reelection bid in 2024 to Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno. The winner of the race will serve the remaining two years of Vance’s term.

title: Monday Five and Five: County Teams Chase Northern Maine Titles
text:
Monday Five and Five: Championship Week Has Arrived
This is it.
After two months of soccer, cross country meets, rivalry games, overtime finishes and tournament runs, we've reached the final week of the fall sports season.
Last week gave Aroostook County an individual state champion, a state runner-up, two very different Wisdom tournament wins and another Presque Isle team headed to a regional championship.
Now eight County soccer teams are still playing, with seven Northern Maine championship games involving local teams coming Tuesday and Wednesday.
Here are my five from last week and five things I'm looking forward to this week.
Five From Last Week
5. Pierce Gorneault Brings Home a State Championship
Pierce Gorneault saved one of his best races of the season for the biggest stage.
The Caribou sophomore won the Class B individual state championship Saturday in Augusta, covering the 5,000-meter course in 16:26.85.
His time was nearly 10 seconds better than the runner-up and was the fourth-fastest time among all classifications Saturday.
And Caribou had plenty more to celebrate.
Emma Graves finished second in the Class B girls race, the Viking boys placed third as a team, the girls finished fifth, and Caribou received both the boys and girls Class B Sportsmanship Awards.
That's a pretty impressive way to finish the season.
4. Houlton/GHCA Finishes State Runner-Up
Houlton/GHCA went to Augusta looking to defend its Class C state championship and came awfully close.
The Shires finished second with 66 points, just 19 behind state champion Winthrop.
What really jumps out is how many Houlton runners finished near the front.
Malachi Witmer placed sixth, Logan Witmer was 12th, Wyatt Quint 16th, Nathan Brady 18th and Brayden Drake 19th.
That's five runners among the top 20 in the state and a runner-up finish to cap another outstanding season for the Shires.
3. Presque Isle Girls Are Playing for A Regional Title
Presque Isle took care of business Saturday afternoon.
The Wildcats shut out Cony 4-0 in the Class B North semifinal, with Hailey Plant, Carrlyn Buck, Bridgid Schupbach and Willow Bugbee all finding the back of the net.
Four goals from four different players is a pretty good formula for tournament soccer.
The win sends Presque Isle into Wednesday's Class B North championship against unbeaten John Bapst.
One more win and the Wildcats are playing for a state championship.
2. Wisdom Survives the Penalty-Kick Pressure
There aren't many more nerve-racking ways to decide a tournament soccer game.
Wisdom and Calais played through regulation and overtime before the Eight-Player North semifinal finally came down to penalty kicks.
James Desjardins scored Wisdom's goal in regulation before Preston Lavoie, Sam Paradis, Zeek Cyr and Cayden Hargrove converted during the shootout.
Then goalkeeper Bentley Nadeau delivered the biggest moment.
Nadeau stopped Calais' final attempt, giving Wisdom the 2-1 victory and sending the Pioneers into the Northern Maine championship.
Wisdom now gets unbeaten PCHS with a regional title on the line.
1. Wisdom Hands Sumner Its Only Loss
Beating an undefeated team in the tournament is impressive.
Beating them 5-0 gets the top spot this week.
Wisdom's girls handed Sumner its first loss of the season Friday and earned another trip to the Eight-Player North championship.
Ellie Cyr scored twice, while Madi Cyr, Libby Cote and Hannah Martin each added goals.
Wisdom has now scored 11 goals in two tournament games while allowing only one.
The Pioneers head into Tuesday's championship at 14-2 with one more win standing between them and a state championship game right here in Presque Isle.
Five to Watch This Week
5. Madawaska and Fort Fairfield Meet Again
It almost feels like these two teams were destined to end up here again.
For the third straight season, Madawaska and Fort Fairfield will meet with the Class D North boys championship on the line.
Madawaska comes in at 14-2 after shutting out Hodgdon 2-0 in the semifinal.
Fort Fairfield earned another shot at the Owls by going on the road and beating Central Aroostook 3-1.
They'll meet Wednesday afternoon in Presque Isle.
The best part for County soccer fans is that we already know one thing.
No matter who wins, an Aroostook County boys team will be playing for the Class D state championship Saturday.
4. Wisdom Has Two Shots at Northern Maine Titles
Tuesday could turn into a memorable day for Wisdom.
Both Pioneer soccer teams are playing for Eight-Player North championships in Brewer.
The boys face 16-0 PCHS after surviving their semifinal in penalty kicks.
The girls take on Dexter after knocking previously unbeaten Sumner out of the tournament.
Two teams. Two championship games.
And there's something extra waiting if either one gets through.
The Eight-Player state championships are being played Saturday at Presque Isle Middle School.
Wisdom has a chance to earn a trip back north to play for a Gold Ball.
3. Fort Kent Has Two Chances at Class C North Championships
Fort Kent also has both soccer teams still playing Tuesday.
The boys face Orono after surviving George Stevens Academy in penalty kicks in the semifinal.
Then the Lady Warriors get their own championship matchup against Orono.
Fort Kent's girls enter at 14-1-2 after turning a scoreless semifinal against Houlton into a 5-0 victory.
Reece Doucette and Hannah Plourde each scored twice in that win, with Avery Werntgen adding another.
One school with two teams playing for Class C North championships on the same day isn't something you see very often.
2. Presque Isle Gets Another Shot at John Bapst
Presque Isle and John Bapst have seen plenty of each other this fall.
Now they meet one more time with the biggest stakes yet.
The Wildcats enter Wednesday's Class B North championship at 11-3-2, while John Bapst comes in unbeaten at 15-0-1.
Presque Isle has won two tournament games to get here, including Saturday's 4-0 semifinal victory over Cony.
This time, there isn't another regular-season meeting waiting afterward.
The winner is the Northern Maine champion and moves on to Saturday's Class B state championship at Cameron Stadium in Bangor.
1. Fort Fairfield Gets a Shot at a Dynasty
This might be my favorite storyline of championship week.
Fort Fairfield faces Penobscot Valley Wednesday night in Presque Isle for the Class D North girls championship.
The Tigers are 14-2 and earned their way here with a 1-0 semifinal victory over Central Aroostook.
Waiting for them is a program that has owned this stage lately.
PVHS is appearing in its sixth straight regional championship game.
The Howlers have won four consecutive Class D North titles, reached the state championship in each of the last four seasons, and won the last three Class D state championships.
That means Fort Fairfield isn't just trying to win Northern Maine.
The Tigers have an opportunity to end one of the best postseason runs in Class D girls soccer and punch their own ticket to Saturday's state championship.
That's a pretty good way to finish our final Five and Five of the fall regular and regional tournament season.
One Last Push
There won't be many games left after this week.
That's what makes these next few days so much fun.
Eight County soccer teams still have a chance to call themselves Northern Maine champions, and every one of them is one victory away from playing for a state title.
Tuesday starts it.
Wednesday keeps it going.
And if things break the right way, Saturday could be a very busy day for Aroostook County sports.
Let's see who gets there.

title: Martha Stewart apologizes for dressing as homeless person for Halloween after getting backlash
text:
(CNN) — Martha Stewart apologized after she dressed as a homeless person for Halloween.
Stewart, 85, posted a photo of herself on Instagram wearing distressed jeans and makeup resembling dirt while holding a sign that read, “I am hungry, help me!!”
The since-deleted Instagram post also promoted her candle collection in the caption.
The costume sparked backlash online, with many people calling it tone-deaf.
Stewart initially told Page Six that the costume was intended to raise awareness about homelessness, saying she was “distressed” that it offended people.
She later acknowledged on Instagram that her first statement to Page Six did not go far enough and issued an apology.
“It’s hard to admit when you’ve really screwed up. My earlier statement didn’t go far enough. I know many people are economically struggling. Wearing a costume like I did was insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry,” she wrote on Instagram.
