title: Old Town bans automatic license plate reader cameras
text:
Automatic license plate reading cameras are now banned in Old Town.
In the last City Council meeting before election day, Councilors Christian Pushor, Linda McLeod, Michael May, David Wight, Charlene Virgilio, Katrina Wynn and Zachary Wyles unanimously approved banning fixed automatic license plate readers.
Old Town is the first Greater Bangor community to ban the technology.
The initial proposal was brought forward in September at a time when Bangor residents were filing complaints about cameras the city did not own. Brewer officials stopped using such cameras after finding out the software for one of its cameras violated state law.
Fixed license plate readers are not currently being used in Old Town. If they are proposed or requested to be used in the city in the future, five of the seven City Council members would need to approve the proposal.
There has been little to no public comment for or against the proposal during the multiple council meetings in which it appeared on the agenda.
Opposition to license plate reading cameras, which capture passing license plate numbers and other identifying information and add them to a network that can track a person’s movements, has grown across the country this year because of reported misuses, including tracking people without any legal cause and wrongly identifying drivers as criminals.
The council has not discussed the proposal much since it was first brought forward. On Monday there was no discussion.
When councilors have talked about the proposal, they have said that they want future councils, and possibly voters, to have the option to approve or deny the use of the technology. That discussion is reflected in the ordinance.
The ordinance does not ban the Old Town Police Department from using mobile license plate readers, which they currently have in their cars. It also does not mean the fixed readers could not be built or operated in the future. It does require approval for any funds to be used for the cameras and for the police department to enter data-sharing agreements with communities that already use the technology. In a reflection of council discussion, it also creates a requirement for a public hearing where information about data retention and the necessity of the cameras would be shared.
Although there were no proposals to bring the technology to the city, Wyles brought forward the ban in September as a proactive measure. It would be easier to create an ordinance before the cameras were installed than try to react to it, he said at the time.
“I think that smooth waters, calm times is the most appropriate time to put forward proposed legislation because it’s much easier to talk about these things when we’re not dealing with a direct third-party contract on our hands because then it becomes more of an issue about a private company,” he said in September.

title: Maine health clinics urge state for cost-of-living increase, predicting loss of services without it
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
In a joint letter late last month, 17 of Maine’s community health centers urged the state health department to pay a $6.5 million cost-of-living adjustment they say is necessary to keep pace with the rising costs of delivering care.
The clinics, called federally qualified health centers, are among 20 that expected the state to pay the inflation adjustment at the beginning of July, relying on state law and two years of precedent for the annual MaineCare rate increases. They budgeted for it, and planned expenses around it.
But the Maine Department of Health and Human Services said the Legislature did not appropriate the funding, and months later the clinics are scraping by without it.
Laurie Kane-Lewis, CEO of DFD Russell Medical Centers, a group of community health clinics in Turner, Leeds and Monmouth, said the organization has held four medical positions open this year because it can’t pay for increases in the costs to provide benefits to staff.
At Community Clinical Services in Lewiston, which should have received $157,000 from the COLA, CEO Coleen Elias said in September the center would not be able to invest in equipment or recruit for open positions.
“The COLA is owed. It is needed. And it should be implemented without further delay,” the centers wrote in the Oct. 20 letter. “Retroactive payment to the July 1, 2026, effective date is necessary to fully implement the adjustment.”
DHHS spokesperson Lindsay Hammes said Monday that the department can’t pay the cost-of-living adjustment because the Legislature did not appropriate the funding this year.
Unlike in the 2025 biennial budget, in which the Legislature appropriated funds for a 1% COLA increase to rates across all MaineCare services, Hammes said the 2026 supplemental budget only funded and directed COLAs for certain services. They did not include federally qualified health centers.
“I just think they’re playing a word game,” said Rep. Jack Ducharme, R-Madison, the ranking Republican on the appropriations committee. Ducharme says he has continued advocating for the clinics to receive the COLA, pushing DHHS for answers about why they can’t fund it out of the MaineCare Stabilization Fund, which is intended to prevent the loss of services to members when general appropriations fall short.
“To use it to implement a COLA, for whatever reason, they say that doesn’t meet that need,” he said.
The fund was sitting at more than $53 million in late September, according to MaineCare transaction data obtained by Ducharme. Officials have transferred tens of millions out of the fund to cover MaineCare cycle payments since 2025, while bringing tens of millions in from unappropriated surpluses from the general fund.
Ducharme said the department has used the fund for a number of purposes and he doesn’t see why COLAs can’t be one of them.
Hammes said total MaineCare spending on community health centers has increased by almost 50% since the beginning of 2023, largely due to rate increases.

title: Doctors prescribe GLP-1 drugs to some children for weight loss
text:
(Aging Untold) — BATON ROUGE, La. — Weight-loss drugs known as GLP-1s, which are popular with adults, are now being prescribed for some children, according to Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician and Aging Untold host.
Students learn healthy habits
Students at Magnolia Woods Elementary in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, are learning about healthy eating and exercise as part of a statewide push to lower obesity rates.
When lifestyle changes are not enough
For some children, healthy eating and exercise are not enough, Rogers said.
“Sometimes that just move more and eat less is not enough because you have genetics and all that,” Rogers said. “And then really, when you get too big, that’s a hormonal dysregulation.”
Rogers said “GLP-1 agonists” are “huge in terms of getting rid of that food noise, that food noise and food chatter.” She said they are also “anti-inflammatory.”
“Some people just need a little bit more help because of that hormonal dysregulation,” Rogers said.
Who may be a candidate
The age requirement for diabetes patients can be 10 and up.
Experts also say the ideal candidate for a GLP-1 for weight loss has a BMI at or above the 95th percentile, and lifestyle changes alone have not worked. This includes patients who have developed hormone problems requiring medical intervention.
“It’s not a miracle drug — it’s a tool, and so you have to treat the whole entire scenario,” Rogers said.
Cost remains a barrier
The price of GLP-1s remains a barrier for many families.
For patients who cannot afford medication or choose not to take any, the option for now is well-balanced meals and a healthy lifestyle.

title: Why High-Net-Worth Investors Are Rethinking Retirement Taxes
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Retirement planning has long centered on a simple idea: save now, spend later. But for today’s affluent and high-net-worth individuals, that equation is more nuanced. It’s no longer just about how much you save, it’s also about how those savings are taxed when you use them. That is where tax diversification comes in: a strategy built around holding retirement assets across taxable, tax-deferred and tax-free accounts to create greater flexibility later in life.
Moving beyond a one-account mindset
Historically, many investors concentrated retirement savings in pre-tax vehicles like traditional 401(k)s and IRAs. Those accounts can provide valuable upfront tax benefits during peak earning years, but withdrawals in retirement are generally taxed as ordinary income. Roth accounts sit at the other end of the spectrum: funded with after-tax dollars but designed to provide tax-free growth and withdrawals.1 Traditional and Roth retirement accounts usually penalize distributions before age 59.5.2 Taxable investment accounts add a third category, with taxes applied to dividends, interest and realized gains along the way, but no age-based distribution penalties. Taxable accounts can also utilize preferential long-term capital gains rates.3 Together, those different structures reinforce a simple truth: not all retirement dollars are created equal.
“Tax diversification is ultimately about maintaining control,” says Ashley Weeks, Wealth Strategist at TD Wealth®. “If all of your assets are concentrated in one tax category, you may have fewer options when it comes to managing income and tax exposure in retirement.”
Why flexibility matters in retirement
For high-net-worth investors, that flexibility can matter in several ways. A mix of taxable, tax-deferred and tax-free Roth accounts can make it easier to manage ordinary income, capital gains, Medicare premium thresholds and other income-sensitive planning decisions.4 With multiple tax buckets available, retirees can be more deliberate about where income comes from in a given year rather than being forced to accept the tax implications of a single account type.
The tradeoffs of tax deferral
Tax-deferred accounts remain a cornerstone of retirement planning, but they can also create complexity over time. Required minimum distributions can push taxable income higher whether or not the retiree needs the cash flow. The impact can be even more pronounced for married couples. Many plan around joint filing thresholds, but when one spouse passes away, the surviving spouse often moves into single-filer tax brackets while maintaining similar income levels — sometimes driven by ongoing RMDs. This ‘widow’s penalty’ can lead to a higher effective tax burden at a difficult time.5
“Having a mix of taxable, tax-deferred and tax-free assets can help investors adapt as their circumstances change,” Weeks explains. “It allows for more thoughtful decisions about which accounts to draw from and when — especially during periods of transition.”
Planning with purpose
For affluent investors, retirement is not static. It can span decades and include changing income needs, market conditions and tax policy. Tax diversification supports a more dynamic planning approach by giving investors more options as circumstances evolve. Rather than relying heavily on one account type, investors can position themselves to draw from different sources depending on what makes the most sense at the time.
A regional lens: Maine
In Maine, tax diversification is less about chasing tax advantages and more about managing income. Those age 65 and older account for nearly one-quarter of Maine’s population, underscoring the importance of strategies that help retirees maintain flexibility as their financial needs evolve.6
For many affluent households across Maine, retirement planning also takes place against a unique economic backdrop. While living costs vary across the state, housing remains a significant consideration, making tax-efficient income strategies increasingly important for retirees seeking to preserve purchasing power over the long term.7
At the same time, Maine exempts Social Security benefits from state income tax, while other retirement income may still be subject to state and federal taxation.8 IRS data also show that retirement-related income is widely distributed across Maine communities, reinforcing the value of having multiple sources of retirement assets available.9 In Maine, tax diversification can help investors navigate changing income needs, manage tax exposure and make more informed decisions about where income is sourced each year.
Looking ahead
As high-net-worth investors refine their retirement strategies, the focus is shifting beyond accumulation to efficiency. Tax diversification offers a way to bring more intention to how wealth is ultimately used — helping investors manage risk, adapt to life changes and preserve more of what they have built. Because in retirement, it’s not just what you’ve saved — it’s what you’re able to keep.

IRS, “Retirement Topics: Tax on Early Distributions,” https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-tax-on-early-distributions. 3. title: Lindsay Clancy appears in court as District Attorney considers retrial
text:
Lindsay Clancy appears in court as District Attorney considers retrial
Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three children in 2023, returned to court on Monday for a motion hearing as she waits for the District Attorney to decide whether he will pursue a second trial.
On his way into court on Monday morning, defense attorney Kevin Reddington told reporters, "It's a beautiful day to continue the journey."
District Attorney Tim Cruz's office has not announced whether it will conduct a second prosecution. Cruz, a Republican who is running unopposed for reelection, was present in the courtroom on Monday.
When Judge William Sullivan asked the prosecutors if they are going to pursue another trial, Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague replied, "We're not at that point yet."
Defense attorney Kevin Reddington, however, was more direct.
"I want a trial, and I want it with you, and I want it this spring," he said.
Clancy, 36, was on trial over the summer for the deaths of 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan at their Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023. Her defense argued she was not criminally responsible for murder because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings.
The jury was ultimately deadlocked, with a reported 11-1 split in favor of acquittal after seven days of deliberations. A mistrial was declared.
In a recent motion, the prosecution argued that the trial ended with a legally justified mistrial. They also argue, citing the Karen Read case, that the Supreme Judicial Court has previously ruled against allowing "post-trial juror revelations about their deliberations to affect the analysis."
Earlier this month, the judge also denied Clancy's request for an evidentiary hearing regarding the holdout juror who caused the mistrial. That ruling also cited the precedent set in the Read case.
Meanwhile, the defense is also asking the judge to reject proposed restrictions on what can be said publicly about the case. They argue the Commonwealth has not shown enough reason to justify limiting what can be said after the mistrial.
Another hearing is being scheduled for 9 a.m. on Nov. 16.

title: Washington state resident dies from bird flu following exposure to infected cattle
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A person in Washington state has died from complications of the bird flu, the first such U.S. death in a year.
The Yakima County resident, who had previous health conditions, was exposed to avian influenza at a dairy with infected cattle and had been hospitalized, county health officials announced Sunday.
Two other U.S. deaths have been tied to bird flu since it became a national public health concern in 2024. The first, announced in January 2025, was an elderly person in Louisiana who had a version of bird flu known as H5N1. The other, in Washington state, died in November 2025 from a rarer version called H5N5.
Yakima County officials did not release any additional details about the person who recently died. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the person was infected with H5N1.
County officials have reported that 33 dairy herds recently have tested positive for H5N1.
They say three human infections have been linked to exposure at a dairy, and that the Yakima Health District is working with the state health department to find people who were in close contact with those people and monitor them for symptoms.
The H5N1 bird flu has been spreading widely among wild birds, poultry, cows and other animals for several years. Health concerns escalated in early 2024 when infections spread among U.S. livestock. Its presence in the environment increases the chances that people will be exposed, and potentially catch it, officials have said.
More than 70 human infections have been reported in the U.S. since the beginning of 2024, according to the CDC. But there is no known person-to-person spread and the risk to the general public is low, the agency says.
The agency analyzed the genetic sequence of the virus from the person who died in Washington and found no changes that would make the virus spread more easily or cause more severe illness, a CDC spokesperson said Monday.
Officials continue to urge people who have contact with sick or dead birds to take precautions, including wearing respiratory and eye protection and gloves when handling poultry. People who work on farms are considered to be at higher risk.

title: Despite higher paychecks, Americans still have less money to spend, Labor Department report says
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) - Although Americans are seeing bigger paychecks on paper, they still have less money to spend.
According to the U.S. Department of Labor’s Employment Cost Index, the total compensation for civilian workers, including wages and benefits, rose 3.4% over the last 12 months, ending in September. Wages and salaries were up 3.1%, while benefit costs climbed 3.9%.
After adjusting for inflation, however, wages are effectively shrinking, according to the report.
For private-sector workers, inflation-adjusted wages and salaries fell 0.6% over the past year, according to the Labor Department. For state and local government workers, real wages slipped 0.5%. That means price increases are outpacing pay gains, lowering workers’ purchasing power even as employers appear to be spending more on compensation.
The report shows that pay raises are not keeping up with the cost of living, which is a major frustration for many American households. The report also highlights a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is trying to tame inflation without triggering a sharp slowdown in hiring or wage growth.
Last month, the government reported that consumer inflation accelerated in September as goods and services became more expensive, according to the Associated Press.
The Employment Cost Index is one of the Federal Reserve’s closely watched barometers of underlying wage and benefit pressures in the economy.
The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time since 2023 six weeks ago. It was an effort to tame high inflation. It said another rate hike could happen later this year.

title: Mom chooses first-of-its-kind robotic double mastectomy: ‘I want to be there for my kids’
text:
Mom chooses first-of-its-kind robotic double mastectomy: ‘I want to be there for my kids’
Kamilla da Escossia Campello Ronchi, 41, chose to undergo a double mastectomy using advanced robotic technology after genetic testing revealed her high risk of developing breast cancer.
"My children are the most important thing to me," Ronchi said.
She explained that her decision was influenced by her mother’s battle with breast cancer, which ended when Ronchi was just 8 years old.
"My mom was diagnosed with breast cancer. She passed away when I was 8," Ronchi said. "Watching my mom suffer and then growing up without her was really hard. She wasn't there in the most important moments in my life. And I want to be there for my kids."
Ronchi’s surgery, performed at AdventHealth, involved removing and reconstructing her breasts. It marked the first time this robotic technology was used for such a procedure in Central Florida.
Dr. Devina McCray, Ronchi’s surgeon, expressed her gratitude for the trust Ronchi placed in her and the medical team.
"I'm just grateful and blessed that you trusted us. You trusted our team. You trusted me," McCray said.
McCray shared a training video of the robot used in the procedure, explaining how it is transforming outcomes for women.
"It enhances my movements, my eyes, and it allows me to make incisions that are smaller," McCray said.
The robot provides a clearer view of tissue layers, enabling surgeons to avoid damaging nerves. This innovation could address a significant side effect of mastectomies, as 60 to 80% of women who undergo the procedure never regain sensation in their breasts.
"That is what we're looking at. Anecdotally, from patients' reports, they are getting their sensation back," McCray said.
In many cases, nipples cannot be preserved, leaving women with permanent scars. However, Ronchi shared her satisfaction with the results of her surgery.
"When you look in the mirror, does it look like you?" she was asked.
"Yeah. It does. Yeah. Completely. I think it's better than before. It's even better than before," Ronchi said.
The technology is helping women think about life beyond cancer and how they feel when they look in the mirror.
"We've been so focused on the treatment of breast cancer and breast cancer treatment. We do so well with breast cancer, even advanced stages. But now we're starting to realize women are living longer, and we really have to focus on what that means and how to help them," McCray said.
She also noted the importance of supporting younger women, as breast cancer diagnoses are increasingly affecting those in their 20s, 30s, and 40s.
"My goal is not for them to just feel like they're themselves, but even feel like they look better than what they used to be," McCray said.
For Ronchi and many women who will follow, the procedure represents a step forward in improving life after cancer.

title: These brothers have been helping planes depart for four decades
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (InvestigateTV) — Brothers Bobby and Lance Snyder have a combined eight decades of service with American Airlines at Charlotte Douglas International Airport.
From Johnson City to the ramp
Bobby Snyder said the brothers grew up in the Johnson City area, close to the Tri-Cities Airport.
“A friend of ours and his dad, they lived beside of us. We used to go out to the airport,” Bobby Snyder said.
Lance Snyder said he has memories of going to the airport as a child and cleaning overnighters.
“Back then, the big thing was getting peanuts off the airplane and maybe finding some pennies or nickels, you know, as we would clean the airplanes,” Lance Snyder said.
Bobby Snyder said that experience drew him to wanting to work for the airline. In 1986, he came to Charlotte and put a resume in to Piedmont Airlines. He was hired the next week.
Lance Snyder said he followed his brother to Charlotte nine months later, taking the same route and applying for a job at the airline.
Bobby Snyder said he started at the freight house in air freight, delivering freight to the gates. He said he wanted to work on the ramp and moved there in 1987. He has worked on the ramp since.
Lance Snyder said his early duties included unloading and loading airplanes, parking and pushing.
“A lot of the same things that we do today. Just loved it,” Lance Snyder said.
Work as crew chiefs
Both brothers are crew chiefs. Bobby Snyder said he has a crew of three, and the brothers work together all day.
Lance Snyder said the crew prepares for arrivals and departures.
“We’re just getting prepared for arrivals and departures, kind of looking ahead and seeing what’s coming off the airplane, what needs to be unloaded, just making sure our crew is in the right place,” Lance Snyder said.
Bobby Snyder described the work as a team effort. He said typically three to four workers, called runners, are assigned to run each flight, along with a crew of three.
“We have to do the water and air and power. And it all just happens. And it’s got to happen quick, like within just a couple of minutes’ time,” Bobby Snyder said.
He said the doors must be shut four or five minutes before departure to get the plane out on time.
“The main thing is we want to keep our passengers happy. Getting their bags, it’s our responsibility to make sure all that works and works in a timely manner,” Bobby Snyder said.
Working with younger co-workers
Lance Snyder said he still enjoys working and being around people. He said the makeup of the workforce has changed.
“Everybody used to be our age and older. Now everybody’s younger. But that’s been a real blessing too, getting to work with young people, getting to work with people from all over the world, and just learning different cultures,” Lance Snyder said.
He said he hopes to be “a bright light” to co-workers and to encourage them. He said he sometimes gets to be “a little bit of a father figure to some.”
Recognition for service
In February 2026, the Charlotte Regional Visitors Authority honored the brothers with the Unsung Heroes Award for their decades of dedication to the job.
“They have a lot of passion for what they do, they also help mentor lots of team members who are working here today,” said Cesar Marchese, American Airlines CLT customer operations managing director.
Luggage tips for travelers
An airport official said travelers who want to help baggage handlers keep luggage on time should remove any loose straps from their bags.
The official said travelers should also try not to keep the luggage tag on the same handle as the airline bag tag so the system can clearly see the barcodes.

title: Community Helps Those Displaced by P.I. Fire
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine — Businesses and organizations are coming together to help those affected by Saturday’s fire in Presque Isle.
Several county businesses and organizations have stepped up to help those displaced by the fire. From giving out gas to supplying dog and cat food and other donations, many are doing their part to help those in need.
Needs of displaced residents
Jacqueline Cyr, owner of Moments of Grace, said she has been in contact with the families.
“We’ve kind of been in contact with all of the different families and saw what their needs were and the majority of it is housing and then of course they need clothes and things like that,” Cyr said. “One of the families had renters’ insurance so they’re all set. They’re staying in an Airbnb and a few of them had families but there’s some that don’t.”
“There’s one lady she has a hotel room until tomorrow morning and she has an apartment coming in 2 weeks but it’s not ready. So, she doesn’t know what she’s gonna do for the next 2 weeks, and then there’s a family that the mom is pregnant. She’s due at the end of the month and she lost everything. So, they have nothing for the baby. It’s a hard thing. There’s a lot of families affected. You know, it was 8 apartments and a lot of them don’t know what they’re gonna do.”
Businesses and organizations helping
Cyr said Aroostook Trusses inspired her to help, but she also has reached out to other businesses and organizations to see who else can contribute.
“Isaac from Aroostook Trusses, he kind of posted a post saying that anybody that needed help they could come by the gas station and he would fill them up,” Cyr said. “We’ve been in contact with ACAP, Pregnancy Center, the Career Center seeing if they could help with work clothes things like that. The Blue Cross Believers; it’s a motorcycle club. They contacted us and said that we have gift cards we’d like to help, how can we help, and then also Northbound Hounds. They’re like a rescue. They reached out and they were able to get cat food and dog food for a couple of the pets. So, we’re just reaching out trying to do what we can.”
Fern & Forest Baking and HUB Coffee also are helping. Fern & Forest Baking is offering free breakfast, and HUB Coffee is handing out free coffee and bagels to those affected.
How to donate
Moments of Grace is still accepting donations to help those affected by the fire. Donations can be dropped off at Moments of Grace at 17 Parsons St. in Presque Isle from 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. Wednesday through Friday.
Cyr said that for those who can donate, any little bit helps.
“It all adds up and it could make the difference in someone’s life,” Cyr said. “Anything could help. Any kind of clothes. Everyone’s just trying to make it through and they’re all struggling and I can’t imagine and it’s scary because it literally is one life event like that that can change everything for a person. You know, they have a home, their family’s fine, and the next day they don’t.”

title: Federal judge dismisses lawsuit against Harvard over federal demand for admissions data
text:
BOSTON (AP) — A federal judge on Monday dismissed a lawsuit against Harvard University over its alleged failure to provide admissions records that the Justice Department had demanded to ensure the Ivy League school stopped using affirmative action in admissions.
The Justice Department said Harvard had “thwarted” efforts to investigate potential discrimination. It accused Harvard of refusing to comply with a federal investigation and asked a judge to order the university to turn over the records.
But U.S. District Judge Myong Joun concluded that the Justice Department didn’t take the necessary procedural steps to obtain the data before filing the lawsuit. “Before taking enforcement action under the statutory framework, the agency must advise the recipient of its failure to comply and determine that compliance cannot be secured by voluntary means,” Joun wrote.
But Joun also said the ruling does not end the dispute over the data.
“I decide a limited question: whether the Government has adequately established, at this stage and on the materials properly considered, that it satisfied the prerequisites to judicial enforcement invoked in this complaint,” he wrote. “The ruling does not determine whether Harvard has discriminated, whether the agencies may lawfully seek appropriately defined applicant-level data, or whether Harvard may ultimately be required to provide such data.”
Neither Harvard nor the Department of Justice responded to a request for comment.
The ruling is the latest setback against the Trump administration over its ongoing battle with Harvard. It has suffered defeats in the federal courts over everything from billions of dollars in funding cuts to a lawsuit accusing the university of antisemitism.
Trump officials have said they’re taking action against Harvard over allegations of anti-Jewish bias on campus. Harvard officials say they’re facing unconstitutional retaliation for refusing to adopt the administration’s ideological views.
In the fight over admissions data, the Justice Department in 2025 launched a compliance review into Harvard’s admissions practices. It told Harvard to hand over five years of admissions data for applicants to its undergraduate, medial and law schools.
It also asked Harvard for applicants’ grades, test scores, essays, extracurricular activities and admissions outcomes, along with their race and ethnicity.
Justice Department officials said they need the data to determine whether Harvard has continued considering applicants’ race in admissions decisions. The Supreme Court barred affirmative action in admissions in 2023 after lawsuits challenged it at Harvard and the University of North Carolina.
The effort against Harvard is part of a broader campaign by the Trump administration against colleges accused of considering race in admissions decisions.
In October, the Justice Department found the law school at the University of California, Los Angeles, illegally considered race in admissions. The announcement follows a similar finding against the university’s medical school.
The administration also has accused the UC Berkeley Law School and the medical school at the University of California, San Diego, of illegally discriminating against white and Asian applicants.

title: FDA approves more affordable version of HIV-prevention shot
text:
(AP) - The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a generic version of the world’s only twice-a-year shot to prevent HIV — a big step toward making the drug available inexpensively and more quickly in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
The announcement was made on Monday morning by the manufacturer and organizations that helped to speed up development of the medication, called lenacapavir.
The drug is expected to cost $40 a year per person in the countries where it will be available, the same price as daily preventive pills available now. But the shots are much more convenient than the pills because they’re needed much less frequently and they nearly eliminated new infections in two groundbreaking studies of people at high risk.
People don’t always take their daily dose of medication, “and if you do not take it, you cannot get protected against HIV,” said Carmen Pérez Casas, HIV lead for the grant-making organization Unitaid, a global health agency. “With lenacapavir, we are much more hopeful.”
Ultimately, advocates said, the medication should help drive down cases of HIV and AIDS — and deaths. According to the WHO, 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV and 570,000 died from HIV-related causes last year.
With an affordable, high-quality generic medication now available, “we could help to scale this to the 20 million people around the world who need PrEP,” prescription medicine taken by people at risk of HIV before being exposed to the virus, said Carolyn Amole, who leads the HIV program for the Clinton Health Access Initiative, a global health organization.
“And if we scale to those levels,” she added, “we can actually begin to bring an end to the HIV epidemic.”
Generic lenacapavir can’t be sold in the U.S. because a brand-name version, Yeztugo, made by Gilead Sciences and approved last year, is still protected by a patent. The U.S. list price for that version, meaning the cost before insurance, is $28,218 a year. Gilead officials say that’s similar to some other types of PrEP, which stands for pre-exposure prophylaxis.
The new generic was approved by the FDA under a longstanding practice designed to ensure the quality of HIV-related drugs provided to other countries by the U.S. government. Approval of a drug by the U.S. FDA can speed regulatory approval in many other countries. The approval is considered “tentative,” the FDA’s standard designation for generics while the originator remains under patent.
Until now, Gilead has been the sole supplier of lenacapavir, and demand has outstripped supply in low- and middle-income countries. Last year, Gilead established royalty-free licensing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable production. Those voluntary licenses cover a specific set of countries in sub-Saharan Africa, Asia and Latin America.
“We share the sense of urgency around expanding access to lenacapavir for HIV prevention,” a Gilead spokesperson said in a statement. “We believe we have enabled the fastest and most sustainable path to expanding access for communities most affected by HIV.”
The generic was developed by India-based Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories under an agreement brokered by Unitaid, the Clinton Health Access Initiative and Wits RHI, a health research institute in Africa. The partners sought to accelerate development and make the drug available at an affordable price.
Common side effects with lenacapavir include injection site reactions, headache and nausea. People also must be tested for HIV prior to starting the drug and with each injection; drug-resistant HIV has been identified when used by people with an undiagnosed HIV infection.
“For any kind of PrEP … you need to have HIV testing in advance,” said Saiqa Mullick, director of implementation science with Wits RHI. “For many of the low- and middle-income countries, that is a rapid test.”
Generic lenacapavir should start to become available in some places within weeks, those helping with the effort said, although it could take a bit longer in countries that require the drug to go through their own approval processes before people can start taking it. Generic versions made by the other manufacturers have yet to be approved by FDA.
“The work is not done. Now, we need the funding to actually buy it for everyone who needs it and then we need to do the hard work of getting it to the millions of people who need it and want it,” Amole said. “But this is a great milestone.”
Casa said she’s optimistic that scientific advances — along with political will and funding — can help the world curb HIV.
“Now,” she said, “we have the tools.”
___
Gerald Imray in Cape Town, South Africa, contributed to this story.

title: Patriots find ways to win despite injuries
text:
The Patriots went from being among the NFL’s healthiest teams last year to one of its most injured during the first half of this season.
It hasn’t stopped them from winning their first three AFC East games.
Working without wide receiver A.J. Brown and an ever-changing group of offensive linemen, quarterback Drake Maye helped New England’s offense figure things out as the Patriots rallied from a 13-3 halftime deficit and through rainy conditions to beat Miami 24-19 on Sunday.
The Patriots (5-3) have won 4 of 5 after a 1-2 start. While his team left Sunday with yet another injury — a foot issue for tight end Hunter Henry — coach Mike Vrabel likes the fight his team has shown.
“I learned that if I can keep my composure, I think they’ll keep their composure,” Vrabel said. “I have to do a better job of understanding that they can make some plays and we can make some plays, too.”
Maye, who finished 16 of 20 for 199 yards and three total touchdowns (two passing, one rushing), has gone without a turnover in three of the last four games.
Maye said when the Patriots remain composed, they can find a way to win no matter what adjustments they have to make in personnel.
“We just started to finish off drives,” Maye said. “We hit some big ones which helped and we had some catch-and-runs which were nice, but we started running the football pretty well. It was nice to see that and then we started playing complementary football.”
What’s working
A week after rushing for a season-low 70 yards in a loss at Chicago, New England found its running game against the Dolphins, Led by Rhamondre Stevenson’s 19 carries for 82 yards, the Patriots finished with 131 yards. With a 7-yard run in the third quarter, Stevenson became the fourth player in Patriots history to eclipse 4,000 yards rushing for his career (he now has 4,036).
What needs help
Ball security. Wide receiver Efton Chism fumbled in the first quarter, and the Patriots have a minus-7 turnover differential this season. Only the Indianapolis Colts are worse with a minus-11 differential.
Stock up
Kyle Williams. The second-year wide receiver continues to make the most of his targets in his second season. His 13 targets and seven receptions this season are the fewest among Patriots receivers, but he is making big plays when he gets the ball. His 43-yard TD reception in the third quarter was his second scoring catch this season of 30-plus yards. All three of his touchdowns during his rookie season also covered at least 30 yards.
Stock down
Kicker Andy Borregales. His miss from 40 yards Sunday dropped his field-goal percentage to 76.9% (10 of 13), including 3 of 5 on attempts of 40-49 yards.
Injuries
Henry left in the second quarter and did not return. Neither did rookie linebacker Gabe Jacas (knee) following his exit in the third quarter.
Key number
27.3 — Williams’ team-leading average yards per reception this season.
Next steps
The Patriots host Green Bay on Sunday.

title: 'Looked like a missile going down': Witnesses recount moments after jet crash in Florida
text:
'Looked like a missile going down': Witnesses recount moments after jet crash in South Florida
No one on the ground was injured.
'Looked like a missile going down': Witnesses recount moments after jet crash in South Florida
No one on the ground was injured.
A business jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball, with witnesses saying they can't unhear the sound, or remove the site of the explosion from their minds.
"I was getting my nails done and we heard a loud zooming sound, and then we felt and heard an impact," Akemi Graham told Hearst sister station, WPBF Sunday night. "We saw a fireball and then the entire building shook. We didn’t know that it was a jet until a little after, but it checks out, the speed of which everything happened."
“I heard and felt the boom,” Andrew Mannino told CNN. “The power immediately went out and is still out.”
Another woman told WPBF that the crash sounded like a bomb exploding.
Watch witness accounts in the playfinder above
The plane erupted in a massive fireball when it made impact in a residential area near Military Trail and 10th Avenue North.
Nine people that were on board died as a result of the crash, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed.
The Bahamas-bound jet departed from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas, the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement.
Video captured from the scene showed chunks of pavement scattered just feet from nearby homes. No injuries were reported on the ground.  
WPBF said Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, after viewing videos and images of the crash, said the crash “looked like a missile going down."
The Associated Press contributed to this article.

title: Aging Untold: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we share strategies to help caregivers communicate effectively and reset interactions when stress and exhaustion take a toll.
We break down the causes of gout, warning signs and the everyday steps that can help prevent painful flare-ups.
Then, we highlight an alliance of compassionate nurses in St. Louis raising the standard of bereavement care for families experiencing pregnancy or infant loss.
When you are caring for a loved one, the stress can turn into sharp words.
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room and let yourself calm down.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said some words can escalate a conversation and cautioned caregivers to choose words with care. She said these words can escalate a conversation: no, you, always, never, don’t and you can’t
Gout is common and painful. When most people think of it, they picture a big toe that is red and throbbing, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
It starts with uric acid building up in the blood and crystals forming in the joints and other tissues, Rogers said, and the immune system treats the crystal as foreign objects.
She said uric acid buildup can point to something bigger.
Labor and delivery nurses in St. Louis who have experienced the emotional toll of caring for mothers who had suffered a loss have created a nonprofit that offers support and resources to families impacted by the death of a baby.
Kayla Hollingshead said with most diagnoses, there is a standard of care within the medical profession, but no real standard has ever existed for those who unexpectedly lose a baby.
The women created a new standard of care that includes how office staff speaks to families. They also create comfort kits containing books, cards and self-care items that are mailed to families around the world.

title: When she wanted to buy a home in Bangor, she turned to AI
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When buying her new home in Bangor’s Little City neighborhood earlier this year, Sierra Rockwell turned to artificial intelligence for guidance.
While this wasn’t her first time buying a home, it was Rockwell’s first experience doing so as a self-employed hairstylist and salon owner. This made her question how to approach mortgage applications with an untraditional income, especially when she decided to turn her previous property into a rental.
So, she opened ChatGPT, a popular AI chatbot, for the first time and typed in her questions. The tool allowed her to analyze potential property expenses and understand appraisal and inspection issues before making important decisions. It even helped her find a local mortgage lender, Rockwell said.
“What I found most valuable was having access to a tool that allowed me to ask extremely specific questions, explore different scenarios, and better understand terminology and lending guidelines without feeling like I was constantly bothering my mortgage broker,” Rockwell said.
Rockwell is among a growing number of Mainers turning to AI to answer questions when buying or selling a home. The trend is one example of how new technology is helping some navigate the confusing and ever-changing real estate market, but agents warn it should be used as another resource rather than a replacement for a licensed professional.
A Bank of America Homebuyer Insights Report published earlier this year found 1 in 5 prospective buyers used AI tools or chatbots for homebuying research in the last year. The practice is most popular among Millennials and Gen Z buyers.
Of those who used it in their house hunt, buyers most often trusted it to estimate affordability, mortgage payments or closing costs, the report found. They also used AI for general education and research about the homebuying process, as well as to research neighborhoods, market trends or property values.
“In the same way Google is ubiquitous, I think AI is dominating the conversation,” said Julie Williams, owner and CEO of ERA Dawson-Bradford Co., REALTORS.
While some people have become reliant on AI to answer questions or provide guidance in all facets of their lives, others might not realize they’re using it, Williams said. For instance, some may search a topic or question on Google and not read beyond the AI overview generated at the top of the webpage.
In Rockwell’s case, she had never used resources like ChatGPT in her daily life, but heard her clients and boyfriend describe how useful it can be, she said.
AI might be most useful as a research tool in the beginning stages of the homebuying process if a prospective buyer needs complicated real estate jargon decoded, real estate agents said. AI could also explain the steps involved in buying or selling a home so a client knows what to expect, said Judy Oberg, president of the Maine Association of Realtors and an agent at Bridgton-based Oberg Real Estate.
It shouldn’t be trusted to direct essential parts of the homebuying process, such as recommending how much a buyer should offer or how much a seller should list their house for, Oberg said.
That’s because AI software likely doesn’t have access to the same information Maine real estate agents use every day to produce a comparable market analysis for clients, Williams said. The information helps buyers make competitive offers or understand what they could get for their home.
“A comparable market analysis looks at the properties that have sold recently and what’s on the market,” Williams said. “AI might help aggregate information from multiple third party platforms, but now that buyer is trying to do a comparable market analysis without having the experience and expertise that a real estate agent does.”
Additionally, real estate agents can weigh other factors that are important to their clients, such as a home’s quality, desired features, the surrounding neighborhood or its proximity to their client’s workplace or an ideal school. A chatbot likely couldn’t consider these elements in the same way a human would, Oberg said.
“It’s important to use the technological tools that we have available to us, but it’s also helpful to have a person who’s able to take you through a property, unlock that door and have you smell the cat odor,” Williams said.
Though Rockwell found AI helpful, she wouldn’t recommend using it as a substitute for a professional and cautioned that its calculations and answers need to be verified. That’s because the chatbot gave Rockwell incorrect information regarding Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac guidelines that her realtor later corrected, she said.
“AI isn’t always right — it’s a tool, not a replacement,” Oberg said. “We can ask AI how to fix our plumbing, but it can’t come fix it for us.”

title: Reward grows after six dogs found tortured, slain along road
text:
CRETE, Ill. (WLS) - Crime Stoppers of Will County is offering a $25,000 reward for information leading to an arrest in the case of six dogs that were tortured and killed and left on the side of a rural road in Crete. It is the largest reward offered by the organization.
“This is really an important crime to solve,” said David Silverman of Crime Stoppers of Will County.
Two organizations add to reward
Two organizations teamed up to offer reward money in the case.
First Secure Bank Group offered $5,000 in April. Pets and Vets USA, which trains rescued pit bulls to be service dogs for veterans, is adding $20,000.
“Even if you’re not a pet lover, I mean, six little dogs being tortured and killed. How can anybody like anything like that,” said Jay Bergman, First Secure Bank Group board chairman.
Peter Cangelosi, founder of Pets and Vets USA, said, “We got to do something because this progresses from torturing animals to killing animals into human beings.” He said the person or people responsible need to be caught and stopped.
Bags found along Kings Road and Norfolk Avenue
In March, Crete Township workers found black garbage bags on the side of the road at the intersection of Kings Road and Norfolk Avenue in Crete Township. After the workers returned to their office, they discovered the bags had dead dogs inside.
Will County State’s Attorney James Glasgow described what investigators found.
“There were six pit bulls, 45 to 55 pounds, and they showed signs of having been in fighting,” Glasgow said. “I can’t tell you exactly, but they were brutally killed, and then thrown in black trash bags on the side of the road.”
A photo of the dogs has been blurred because of the state of the animals. The photo is being shared to show the coloring of the dogs, which may assist the investigation.
Glasgow: Animal cruelty a danger to society
Glasgow has helped strengthen Illinois animal cruelty laws over the years and is a pet owner. He said people who are cruel to animals pose a danger to society.
“Anybody who is cruel to animals is not just going to stop there, and that’s when you know every serial killer tortured animals as a child or on the way up,” Glasgow said.
How to claim the reward
Will County officials said anyone who claims the reward can remain anonymous. The reward would be paid after someone is charged, with no questions asked.
Anyone with information about the dogs found in Crete can call Crime Stoppers at 1-800-323-6734 or text 274637.

title: Court hears Lori Vallow Daybell's appeal in Idaho killings of 2 of her children, romantic rival
text:
BOISE, Idaho (AP) — The Idaho Supreme Court is scheduled Monday to hear Lori Vallow Daybell’s appeal of her convictions in that state for killing her two youngest children and conspiring to murder a romantic rival.
She is asking the court to reverse her convictions in the deaths of Joshua “JJ” Vallow, Tylee Ryan and Tammy Daybell, whose husband married Vallow Daybell weeks later. JJ was 7, and Tylee was 16. Vallow Daybell holds doomsday religious beliefs and has claimed that people in her life were possessed by evil spirits.
The children went missing in 2019. Their bodies were found buried in rural Idaho on the property of Vallow Daybell’s new husband, Chad Daybell, an author of several religious novels about prophecies and the end of the world.
Vallow Daybell was sentenced to three life sentences in the state, while Chad Daybell was sentenced to death for the three killings.
Vallow Daybell was convicted separately in Arizona for conspiring to murder her estranged husband and her niece’s ex-husband, the latter of whom survived.
In the Idaho appeal, her lawyer argued that a lower court denied her a speedy trial, that it would not let her keep the attorney of her choice — the judge ruled that there was a conflict of interest because the lawyer had represented both her and her husband — and that it should not have allowed jurors to hear about the shootings involving Charles Vallow and Brandon Boudreaux in metro Phoenix.
Months after filing for divorce from Vallow Daybell, Charles Vallow was fatally shot in July 2019 in Chandler by Vallow Daybell’s brother, Alex Cox, whose claim of self-defense was later called into question by investigators.
Nearly three months after Charles Vallow’s killing, someone parked in a Jeep fired a gunshot at Boudreaux, the ex-husband of Vallow Daybell’s niece, as he was driving up to his home in Gilbert, another Phoenix suburb. The shot narrowly missed Boudreaux.
Prosecutors say Vallow Daybell conspired with Cox to kill Charles Vallow so she could collect money from his life insurance policy and marry Chad Daybell, then her boyfriend. Cox, who was identified by prosecutors as the person who shot at Boudreaux, later died from a blood clot in his lungs.
Vallow Daybell received two life sentences for her Arizona convictions, and she has appealed those as well.

Expect mostly dry conditions and unseasonably warm temperatures to stick around through the middle of the week. High pressure is keeping things pleasant today, with highs reaching the 60s in northern areas and approaching 70 degrees south of the mountains.
A weather boundary will stall near the Canadian border tonight, bringing extra clouds and a slight chance of precipitation through Tuesday night, primarily from the high peaks down into central regions. Onshore breezes will keep Tuesday's high temperatures slightly cooler along the coast, but sunshine returns Wednesday, pushing thermometers back into the 70s.
The pattern shifts dramatically late Thursday into Friday as a cold front approaches from the west. This system brings our first real chance for a soaking rainfall in several weeks. Scattered showers will begin overnight Thursday, but the heaviest rain depends heavily on exactly where this front decides to park.
If the system stalls over our region and taps into tropical moisture, we could see significant downpours starting Friday. Because forecast models are still divided on the exact track, residents should simply prepare for the possibility of a wet, dreary weekend ahead.

title: Ukraine and Russia both report cyberattacks on emergency apps
text:
Ukraine and Russia both report cyberattacks on emergency apps
Authorities in both Ukraine and Russia say that their emergency alert mobile applications were targeted by cyberattacks late Sunday, with residents in Ukraine receiving messages that there was a high nuclear radiation danger in the capital Kyiv.
In a post late Sunday on Telegram, Ukraine’s air raid alert channel wrote that “unauthorized parties” had interfered with the messaging app’s operation, and that it had been temporarily suspended. It warned users not to click on links contained in “suspicious notifications.”
Authorities in Ukraine said the app, which Ukrainians rely on to seek safety amid daily Russian missile and drone strikes, was restored overnight. The alerts — making false claims of high radiation levels, a chemical threat and public disturbances in Kyiv — were written in English with spelling mistakes and grammatical errors, as well as in a mix of Russian and Ukrainian.
Related video: Trump plays defense in red states, as Democratic rift widens in Senate battleground ahead of Election Day
One of the false posts mentioned the hacking group, Hitcore.
Mash, a Russian Telegram channel with links to the security services, said it had spoken to representatives of Hitcore and that they had claimed responsibility for the attack. That claim could not be independently verified.
Ukraine's state-run Center for Countering Disinformation reported the breach and urged users to monitor emergency channels on social media and rely on physical alerts while the cyberattack was being addressed.
Russian officials said Monday that hackers had sent fake emergency alerts after gaining access to the mobile app for Russia’s Emergency Ministry.
The ministry did not name who carried out the attack. In a statement, it reassured Russians that the wider public alert system was working normally, and that the mobile app acted as a supplementary service alongside alerts shared through SMS alerts, media broadcasts and municipal sirens and loudspeakers.

title: Letter: Bangor doesn’t need more parking
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
I am a Bangor homeowner and taxpayer. I’m concerned by a recent news article saying the Penobscot County Commissioners are considering the possibility of turning the former YMCA lot into a parking lot.
While I understand the county is in need of a financial boost, and I am all for measures that will help reduce property taxes in Bangor, I can’t see how additional parking could make a real difference, especially since a 2025 downtown parking study found an excess amount of parking available compared to need. In fact, the study concluded that there could be up to a 20% growth in residential spaces, office spaces, and retail businesses downtown and the current parking would still suffice. In addition, the section of Court Street that borders the YMCA lot offers free 4-hour parking, which I have never yet seen at capacity.
There are many negatives to taking over valuable land in downtown Bangor for more surface parking — impervious surfaces that promote runoff, flooding, and water pollution and asphalt causing more of a heat island effect — as property in a walkable area could be used for desperately needed housing, or for the economic benefits of office space or retail businesses. And, there are the questionable aesthetics of yet another parking lot in downtown Bangor.
I hope the commissioners can come up with a plan that gives them needed revenue, while meeting the actual needs of downtown Bangor.
Karen Marysdaughter
Bangor

title: Westbrook bans standalone data centers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Westbrook City Council voted unanimously Monday night to prohibit standalone data centers .
The city updated its land use ordinance to remove the use of data centers from the Rock Row Contract Zone. However, it still allows data centers as an accessory use, like server rooms and IT rooms for hospitals and other large organizations.
Previously, the Rock Row Contract Zone was the only place data centers were permitted, and the city’s ordinances didn’t include any additional standards for data centers beyond a usual site plan review.
Mayor David Morse said he supported the ordinance amendment and noted substantial concerns about data centers, such as electricity and water demands, noise and infrastructure burdens.
“First and foremost our resources and infrastructure need to support the people who live here, our existing businesses, and the housing and economic opportunities our community needs,” Morse said. “Resource-consuming data centers are simply not a good fit for Westbrook.”
In June, the Westbrook City Council passed a 180-day data center moratorium on data centers, though the city hadn’t received any applications to build such a facility like some of its neighbors had.
During the moratorium, the planning board was tasked with reviewing the city’s ordinances and providing a recommendation. It recommended only permitting data centers as an accessory use and updating the city’s definition of a data center.
Westbrook now defines data centers as “one or more buildings or spaces on a property that house networked computer systems and associated equipment, such as servers, network hardware, data storage, power generation or cooling systems, to process and manage data.”
Cities and towns across the state have passed temporary moratoriums, and in a handful of others, voters will decide on their ballots Tuesday to temporarily or permanently ban data centers.

title: What safeguards in place to ensure accuracy of election results? Experts explain
text:
What safeguards in place to ensure accuracy of election results? Experts explain
President Donald Trump has repeatedly raised concerns about voting machine security, but experts say there are several safeguards in place to mitigate risks and verify results.
What safeguards in place to ensure accuracy of election results? Experts explain
President Donald Trump has repeatedly raised concerns about voting machine security, but experts say there are several safeguards in place to mitigate risks and verify results.
Americans can have confidence that the midterm election results will be counted accurately, according to groups representing chief election officials in all 50 states.
A joint statement released on Monday from the National Association of State Election Directors and the National Association of Secretaries of State added, "State and local election officials are ready to facilitate a safe and secure 2026 General Election that all Americans can rely on."
President Donald Trump has sent a very different message in the lead-up to the midterm elections. He has repeatedly raised doubts about the security of America's election infrastructure, including during a primetime address over the summer.
"Americans were blatantly lied to about the security of our election infrastructure, including electronic voting machines and ballot counting systems, dishonest, almost all. They're vulnerable, and they're easily compromised, and people within our government knew that," Trump said.
But those vulnerabilities have long been acknowledged, according to Ryan Macias, an election security and technology consultant.
"There is no technology that does not have vulnerabilities," Macias said. "What we are trying to do is mitigate or manage that risk."
Macias said voting machines generally go through a certification process before they're procured, followed by a series of pre-election tests to make sure they're working properly.
A range of systems are used across the country, according to Verified Voting, a non-partisan organization that tracks voting equipment.
The group's database shows that less than 4% of registered voters live in jurisdictions that use direct recording electronic systems for all voters. These devices present candidate options and store voters' answers electronically.
The vast majority of voters live in places where the process has some sort of paper record, which can be used to obtain an accurate count even if there are errors or cyberattacks.
Geoff Hale with the Center for Democracy & Technology said the paper trail promotes transparency.
"You can independently determine whether the software is operating as intended or whether it's going rogue. So in this sense, every single voter who checks their ballot serves as a sensor for the performance of those systems," Hale said.
The work doesn't stop when polls close.
Results on election night are always unofficial, and a lot happens before those vote totals are verified to make sure they're correct.
"Checks and balances continue post-election, testing continues, audits on the paper record continue for days and, in some cases, weeks after the election to ensure that our ballots are tabulated and the outcome is correct once it gets certified," Macias said.

title: Deep brain stimulation surgery allows artist to return to woodcarving
text:
PHOENIX. Ariz. (Aging Untold) — Bill Daggett fell in love with woodcarving decades ago. Then the shaking started.
What doctor saw at an art show saw
A doctor at an art show noticed Daggett’s tremors and urged him to get checked. The diagnosis was Parkinson’s disease.
“I couldn’t even eat, hardly. I was shaking so bad, and I didn’t want to go out anymore. That’s part of the depression. You don’t want to be seen when you can’t hold a fork and get it to your mouth,” Daggett said.
Choosing deep brain stimulation
When medication was not enough, the Arizona artist chose deep brain stimulation, or DBS. The therapy sends electrical pulses to the brain to stop tremors.
Daggett’s hands are now steady as he carves.
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist and host of “Aging Untold,” compared the therapy to a pacemaker.
“What they did was basically give his brain a pacemaker. You know, we’re kind of accustomed to the thought of a pacemaker helping a heart keep rhythm. But this is a new way to go in and help that brain reset and send those electrical pulses out to give the brain the pacemaker to now reduce those tremors, reduce some of the side effects of the disease and the progression of it,” Cradduck said.
‘Quality of life’ breakthrough
Cradduck said DBS is a “quality of life” breakthrough for people who have lived with the disease for years.
“We talk about the physical aspects of disease and aging all the time, but we forget to talk about the emotional loss, and that’s where this guy was at. He was so connected with being the artist and being able to create, and the disease was robbing him of that. We see that it’s robbing him of physical abilities maybe to eat, but we forget that it’s robbing him of a piece of himself,” Cradduck said.

title: ‘I was terrified’: Viral door-kicking challenge concerns. See what to be on the lookout for
text:
HONOLULU (KHNL/Gray News) - Hawaiian residents say a viral social media trend dubbed the “door-kicking challenge” has apparently made its way to their neighborhoods.
Authorities said the trend typically involves teenagers who run up to random residential front doors late at night, deliver a heavy, high-impact kick or bang to the door to simulate a home invasion before running away.
According to Maui Lani residents, this type of behavior has been happening consistently over the last several months, with home surveillance videos capturing teens kicking random doors in the middle of the night.
Homeowner Matt, who asked that his full name not be disclosed because he fears retaliation from the vandals, said something like this has already happened to him.
“When you’re in the house at 1:30 in the morning and you’re sleeping and you hear this violent pounding on the door, it’s a little unsettling,” he said.
Matt said he spent nearly $14,000 repairing damage and trying to safeguard his home.
Ewa Beach resident Mae also said she heard the front door of her home being kicked about five times around 9 p.m. one night.
“It literally was so powerful that it shook the whole house and it felt like somebody was trying to break down the door,” Mae said. “I was terrified.”
Mae was shocked to see the trend was also happening on Maui.
“It happened to another resident in our area. So, I’m sure it’s happening quite often,” Mae said.
Also worried about retaliation, Mae did not wish to share her full name or the specific neighborhood where she lives.
“I really feel so bad for that family that they also have been experiencing forceful kicking on their doors,” she said.
Hoping to raise awareness by speaking out about her experience, Mae had a message for those pulling the pranks, who are believed to be teenagers:
“Times are hard. It is expensive to fix things and it’s very disrespectful.”
Mae urged parents, “Talk to their children about being respectful to neighbors and their property.”
Matt said he has filed multiple police reports and has contacted his homeowners association.
“Of course we want justice,” he said. “In the same breath, I have a heart, and if you strip all of this away from the individual, they’re really just kids ... I’m not sure if this is a cry for help.”
Matt is asking his community for help identifying the criminals.

title: Gout: Causes, warning signs and what you can do
text:
(Aging Untold) — Gout is common, painful and sometimes missed at first, but it is treatable.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, is explaining what gout is, what can trigger it and how to confirm it early.
What gout is
Gout starts with uric acid building up in the blood and crystals forming in the joints and other tissues, Rogers said.
“It triggers a very inflammatory, painful response,” Rogers said.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says gout is painful type of arthritis that will usually affect a single joint at a time.
When most people think of gout, they picture a big toe that is red and throbbing — podagra, Rogers said.
Why the pain is so intense
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said her youngest daughter has had gout twice and describes it as feeling like a shard of glass. Even walking near her daughter’s foot caused her pain, Cradduck said.
Cradduck said the crystal itself is not what causes the pain.
“It’s not actually the crystal. It’s the immune system that’s coming after to attack that,” she said.
Rogers said the immune system treats the crystal as a foreign object.
What gout can signal about your health
And a uric acid buildup can point to something bigger, Rogers said.
“It really is telling you something else. It can be a very significant signal for underlying metabolic disease,” Rogers said.
Many people with gout also have insulin resistance, diabetes or cardiovascular issues, Rogers said.
Uric acid also lowers nitric oxide, which makes arteries relax, Rogers said.
“It’s the same mechanism that’s involved with atherosclerosis, or hardening of the arteries,” Rogers said. “That’s why it’s so significant to recognize.”
Why men get gout more often than women
Men get gout more than women and Rogers said that is because of estradiol.
“Estradiol is protective,” Rogers said.
Premenopausal women have that protection and men do not have the same level of estradiol. Men get some estradiol from the conversion of testosterone, Rogers said.
As men age, they tend to have less testosterone and carry more visceral fat, Rogers said.
For women, the picture changes after menopause.
“After menopause, when the estradiol drops, then that gap closes,” Rogers said.
Diet, lifestyle and getting checked
Gout has long been called “the disease of kings,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said, and has been linked at times to rich foods and alcohol.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said it comes back to what you put in your body and what you do to keep your body healthy.
She said that in her experience, men do not seek treatment as quickly as women. Her advice: If you have a husband, partner or brother, nudge him to see a doctor.
When treating patients, Rogers said some doctors will put them on allopurinol.
“But that same mechanism of action of lowering uric acid with vitamin C, quercetin and luteolin, the three together, there’s some, products that have all three together that you take that will naturally lower the uric acid,” Rogers said.
As always, consult your health care provider for medical advice.
Sugary food and sugary drinks are some of the quickest ways to raise fructose, and that is one of the quickest ways to push insulin high and hold onto uric acid, Rogers said.
Learn more
Learn more about gout through Alliance for Gout Awareness.

title: Flu Takes Out Bangor Area Bus Routes, Parents Scramble For Rides Monday
text:
Flu Outbreak Among Bangor Bus Drivers Prompts Last-Minute Bus Route Cancellations Monday Morning
As if the time change was challenging enough for parents, some families in Eastern Maine woke up to another predicament Monday morning.
What happened?
An outbreak of the flu amongst bus drivers in the Bangor area led to the last-minute cancellation of a number of bus routes in Bangor and Glenburn both for Monday morning and some for Monday afternoon.
The Bangor School Department issued the urgent message to parents and guardians just after 8 AM Monday Morning.
"Due to driver absences caused by the flu at Cyr Bus, the following bus runs are canceled today:
Run B: Morning and afternoon
Run R: Afternoon only
Run C: Afternoon only
Both Glenburn buses: Canceled today
Please arrange alternate transportation for your child if they ride one of these buses.
We apologize for the short notice and appreciate your understanding."
Of course the timing of that all left a lot of parents scrambling to come up with a plan B.
Flu Season Is Here!
According to the Maine CDC, "flu season" officially kicked off October 4th, but many state epidemiologist say they started to see cases earlier this year than years past. While the Maine CDC Respiratory Virus Dashboard shows that the state-wide cases of the flu are still considered at low level, according to data for the last week of October, with only 16 hospitalizations reported, those numbers could rise, and quickly.
Experts say the typical incubation period for the flu is between 1 and 4 days.
"This means that, in most cases, people start to develop flu symptoms a few days after the flu virus enters their body."
What can you do to keep yourself and your family healthy this flu season?
Health professionals recommend lots of handwashing with soap, often. They also say to use alcohol-based hand sanitizers, when soap and water is not available, especially after you cough or sneeze. Try not to touch your face, mouth or eyes with your hands.
It's also advised that folks should avoid contact with individuals who are sick and with large crowds.
If you have a compromised immune system, doctors recommend getting a flu shot.
Symptoms to look for if you think you have the flu:
The Maine CDC says that flu symptoms typically show up within four days of being exposed to the virus, and can come on suddenly. Things to look for include:
"Cough, Headache, Sore Throat, Fever or chills, Congestion or runny nose, Body and muscle aches. People with flu may also experience fatigue (feeling very tired). Some people may have vomiting and diarrhea, but this is more common in children than adults."
It's also advised that if you think you do have the flu to stay home and away from others unless you're seeking medical attention.

title: ‘They were just kids’: 2 teens killed after late-night Halloween shooting outside restaurant
text:
SPARTANBURG, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) — Authorities in South Carolina are investigating a shooting that killed two teenagers over the weekend.
Spartanburg Police Chief Art Littlejohn said officers were called to the Cook Out restaurant on John B. White Sr. Boulevard around 11:30 p.m. Saturday for multiple shots being fired.
When officers arrived, they found two people suffering from gunshot wounds in the parking lot.
While at the scene, the victims were given first aid before being taken to the Spartanburg Regional Medical Center, where they later died, Littlejohn said.
The Spartanburg County Coroner’s Office identified those shot as 15-year-old Jayden Marek Watson and 17-year-old Shane Carter Dawkins.
Littlejohn said another person was also shot and suffered non-life-threatening injuries. They were taken to the hospital by a family member.
“I want to be totally clear, the young people that were out here were not bad young people; they were just kids. After Halloween night, going trick-or-treating, going out to get something to eat, and then someone being irresponsible, pulled out a gun and started shooting,” Littlejohn said.
At this time, Littlejohn said no arrests have been made, nor have any suspects been identified.
Spartanburg authorities said the shooting remains under investigation.
