title: Trump is giving his closing midterm pitch at problem-plagued Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is making his closing pitch of the midterm elections at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, pushing his slow, expensive and problem-plagued efforts to repair it back into the spotlight on the eve of Election Day.
In comments to reporters as he deplaned from Air Force One for a Sunday rally in Iowa, Trump said his speaking at the site would “show how beautiful it is.”
“We might hold it tomorrow or something,” the president added, without giving specifics. Hours later, the White House formally announced he’d be giving a speech there Monday afternoon.
Rather than using Monday to travel to key states and try to energize his “Make America Great Again” supporters as his Republican Party tries to maintain control of Congress, Trump opted for an event at a Washington renovation project that has been embarrassing and contentious.
The unusual move marks a departure from Trump’s month-long race to stage more than 25 rallies in largely conservative areas, hoping the GOP can overcome his own low approval ratings and polls predicting that the Iran war, high energy prices and cost of living increases could spell a strong election night for Democrats.
Trump wrote on his social media site that his Sunday evening rally in Kansas — which followed his Iowa visit — was “my last stop.”
The presidewnt spent a lot of time at those rallies talking about his second-term focus on molding the White House and the surrounding nation’s capital in his own image. He crammed the Oval Office with gold flourishes, demolishing the East Wing to construct a sprawling ballroom, converting the Rose Garden into a patio space reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago estate and erecting a sprawling South Lawn helipad.
Trump also closed the Kennedy Center after failed attempts to add his name to the building, has planned a towering arch just outside the city and is pushing to revamp a century-old public golf course.
He has bristled at criticisms from former President Barack Obama and other Democrats that he’s spent too much time focused on construction projects — insisting that renovations relax him and that he does them quickly and without requiring too much planning time.
Trump said the Reflecting Pool fix would be fast and inexpensive
His Reflecting Pool saga began in April when Trump said he wanted to change its color and would use contractors he knew to fix the monument in mere days and for about $1.5 million before Independence Day.
The repairs wrapped up nearly three months behind schedule and the budget ballooned to more than 10 times Trump’s early estimate — and that’s assuming no more additional work will need to be done in the future.
Trump had initially declared the work was complete in June. But after unveiling the overhaul, the pool was soon choked with algae blooms, and its “American-flag blue” liner began peeling off in sections. The pool was quickly drained anew for repairs in mid-July.
Trump has repeatedly blamed vandals, but the office of U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia — former Fox News host and longtime Trump ally Jeanine Pirro — said the problems were caused by shoddy workmanship.
In his comments Sunday, Trump continued to insist that the Reflecting Pool “was vandalized badly.” He said that security cameras have since been added to stop that.
Still, a particularly ignominious moment came when the Justice Department charged former Olympian David Hearn with intentionally damaging the Reflecting Pool — then abruptly dropped the case this summer — determining he was not responsible.
A judge later permanently dismissed it.
That prompted Trump to fume that Pirro “choked,” and that he was “disappointed with Jeanine Pirro, really disappointed. She folded like an umbrella” — though he stopped short of firing her.

title: Elizabeth “Betty” Bryer
text:
Elizabeth “Betty” Bryer, 88, died peacefully on Oct. 29, 2026, at NL Eastern Maine Medical Center, Bangor. Betty was born in 1937 in North Conway, N.H., daughter of Stanley P. and Ruth H. (Cobb) Brewer.
Betty graduated from Caribou High School in 1955 and Farmington State Teachers College in 1959. She married the love of her life, Dean Bryer, in 1959, beginning a loving partnership that would span more than six decades. Betty taught elementary school in Orono, Windham, and Freeport, before settling in Bar Harbor in 1967. She is fondly remembered by many in the community for her roles as head teacher at Eden Nursery School and Realtor at the Swan Agency. She remembered former students throughout her life and came to call former real estate clients friends. Betty’s real estate career cumulated in receipt of the Maine Realtor of the Year award in 2018.

title: Bangor Mall Condemnation Catches Shoppers And Retailers Off Guard
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Code Enforcement Condemns Bangor Mall Building; Says Unfit For Human Habitation
In a move that caught many off guard, especially those who had just been in the building this past weekend shopping for costumes at Spirit Halloween, the City of Bangor condemned the building Monday, citing that it was "unfit for human habitation or use."
Signs on the door, dated 11/02, state, "This structure has been condemned for human habitation or use in accordance with Chapter 223 of the Laws and Ordinances of the City of Bangor. Occupancy is forbidden until conditions detrimental to life and health have been corrected to the written satisfaction of the Code Enforcement Office."
It goes on to say that anyone who enters the premises or removes the sign could face a fine of between $100 and $2,500.
While the move to condemn the building itself wascame out of left field for many.
Some areas of the mall had already been condemned. But others were still occupied and functioning.
Read More: City Of Bangor Takes Action Against Deteriorating Mall Conditions
Stores like Hot Topic, Spencer's, and Spirit Halloween were still actively bringing people into the space, and local investors were trying to get backing to buy the building and turn it into luxury condos. The investors did lose the backing of one of their major players, and were in the process of trying to secure alternate funding when they got the news.
We're told that the local investment group was unaware of the City's plan to condemn the building this week. We have reached out to the City, but have not heard anything back from them yet.
Read More: 13 Bangor Mall Stores You’ll Remember From the Good Old Days
There's no word yet on where the businesses that had still been operating out of the mall will go, but it sounds like they were not given much notice, if any, before being told to vacate the premises.
The Dicks Sporting Goods store and JCPenney retail spaces did not have any signs on their doors. So far, they seem to be exempt from the City's actions.
Read More: Bangor Mall Christmas Craft Fair 2026: Dates and Details
The 7th Annual Bangor Mall Christmas Craft Fair is scheduled to take place in the Furniture, Mattresses & More space, the building that's attached to the Bangor Mall, on the next two weekends, November 7th and 8th and November 14th and 15th.
There's no indication yet that the closure of the mall building will impact that event, but we will let you know if that changes.

title: University of Maine expands tick lab to add genetic research
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - The University of Maine is expanding its tick lab as ticks become more widespread across the state.
Griffin Dill, tick lab director at UMaine, said the lab has seen more ticks and higher rates of tick-borne disease.
“We’ve really seen increasing tick population, increasing rates of tick-borne disease,” Dill said.
The UMaine tick lab is working to research and understand how to address Maine’s tick problem.
“So trying to get a better handle on what’s causing this expansion, not just in the geography of ticks and their associated pathogens, but also in that increasing rate of tick-borne disease,” Dill said.
The lab is being expanded to add genetic and genealogy research. The research looks at the entire DNA structure of a tick that carries pathogens that could cause Lyme disease.
Tom Rounsville, director of the Applied Genetics and Genomics Lab, said sequencing the genomes of many of these pathogens could lead to new treatments.
“So, if you go through and sequence the genomes of a large number of these pathogens, it’s possible you might be able to find genes to target for new drug development or some other types of therapies that could be created,” Rounsville said.
The research is powered by submissions from Mainers. Anyone can send the lab a tick found on themselves, on someone else or on a pet.
Dill and Rounsville said the lab can receive between a dozen and 100 ticks a day.
Testing the submissions is an opportunity for UMaine students, Rounsville said.
“They’ll identify ticks microscopically when they come into the lab, prep them for testing, and then take them through the testing process,” Rounsville said.
Information from the tests can help determine where in the state a tick bite is more likely to carry an illness.
Dill said the focus is on understanding ticks and tick movement, not on killing the pest.
“We’re never, you know, advocating for the eradication of a species,” Dill said. “But we want people to be aware of this issue. We want to minimize the effects of ticks and tick-borne diseases and really allow people to enjoy the Maine outdoors.”

title: Roughly 300-acre wildfire burning just over Maine border in New Hampshire
text:
A wildfire was raging in roughly 300 acres of the White Mountain National Forest in New Hampshire as of Monday, according to the U.S. Forest Service.
The Forest Service at White Mountain National Forest said in a social media post Monday afternoon that it first responded to the fire in Coos County, New Hampshire, at about 1 p.m. on Sunday.
Located roughly seven miles southeast of Gorham, New Hampshire, the Forest Service estimated the fire at about 300 acres. The agency said the fire is actively burning in timber, snags and leaf litter, and firefighters are still working to contain it.
The fire did not pose any “significant threats to life or property” as of Monday afternoon, the Forest Service said.
The fire is on the northwest side of the Wild River, in an area west of Mount Hastings (which is located just over the state border in Maine’s Oxford County), according to the AirNow Fire and Smoke Map. The map, produced by the Forest Service and the U.S. Department of Environmental Protection, did not show any smoke impacts beyond the immediate area of the fire as of Monday night.
The cause of the fire is under investigation.
Over 40 personnel have been assigned to the fire and access “is difficult due to steep and rugged terrain,” the Forest Service said.
Terri Teller, a Maine Forest Service fire prevention specialist and ranger, said in an email Monday night that the state agency has not provided assistance. The U.S. Forest Service oversees the national forest, which expands partially into Maine.
Teller noted the fire danger rating in the southern half of Maine was high on Monday due to dry conditions, and has been considered either moderate or high throughout the state over the past week.

title: Bail doubled for former Husson professor, prosecutors call case ‘unusual’
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Former Husson University assistant professor Jonathan Houck made his first appearance in a Bangor courtroom Monday. A judge agreed to double his bail to $100,000 at the state’s request.
Houck is charged with 10 felonies: six counts of possession of child sexual abuse material and four counts of violation of privacy.
Prosecutors argued the increased bail is warranted because of what they called a rare, dangerous overlap in Houck’s alleged conduct.
Prosecutors said an investigation into Houck possessing child sexual abuse material uncovered photos he had secretly taken of some of his college students in varying states of undress.
“Throughout the course of that investigation, the detectives realized that he was also preying on adult victims as well, which is unusual to have both this deviant sexual interest in both adults and children that rises to the level of criminality,” Deputy District Attorney Chelsea Lynds said. “He’s also offending both online and in real life. So, it is very unusual and I would say more dangerous than your average offender.”
Bail conditions
If he makes bail, Houck was ordered to follow a number of conditions. They include no contact with minors, no access to the internet, staying off Husson’s campus and remaining at least five miles from schools with young students, among others.
The conditions effectively bar Houck from his Bangor home, which is one street over from an elementary school.
Houck indicated he’ll be hiring a private defense attorney. That attorney was not at Monday’s hearing and was not able to speak on Houck’s behalf.

title: 2026 midterm elections: Senate, House and gubernatorial races to watch
text:
2026 midterm elections: Senate, House and gubernatorial races to watch
Voters across the country will cast their ballots Tuesday to decide control of the Senate and the House of Representatives, along with state and local races.
The Get the Facts Data Team is tracking the 77 competitive races identified by The Cook Political Report's CPR Race Ratings for the Senate, the House and state governorships.
Races to watch in the Senate
In the Senate, Republicans hold the majority with 54 seats. Democrats need to flip a net four Republican-held seats to gain control of the chamber.
The Cook Political Report has rated 11 Senate races as competitive, with six of those being toss-ups.
Races in Alaska, Texas, Maine and Michigan could influence the balance of the chamber.
In Michigan, Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Republican nominee Mike Rogers are competing for the open Senate seat. Democrats need to retain the seat, which was previously held by Sen. Gary Peters.
The Cook Political Report changed its final rating of Michigan's open Senate seat from toss-up to lean Democrat on Monday, based on new public and private polls.
Republicans hold or previously held seats in Alaska, Texas and Maine. These states have seen higher early-voting turnout than in the 2022 midterm elections.
Races to watch in the House
Republicans have a slim majority in the House with 218 seats; Democrats have 214.
The Cook Political Report has rated 54 House races as competitive, 18 lean Democratic, 18 lean Republican and 18 are toss-ups.
Nine states implemented new district boundaries in a wave of mid-decade redistricting ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. The goal of both Republicans and Democrats was to change districts to sway in favor of either party. More than 34 million people were assigned new districts as a result.
California, Texas, Florida, Ohio and North Carolina redrew their congressional boundaries and have competitive races in their states.
Texas' 35th Congressional district was last held by a Democrat and is now a toss-up between Democratic nominee Johnny Garcia and Republican nominee Carlos De La Cruz.
California's 22nd district race between Republican incumbent David Valadao and Democratic nominee Randy Villegas was rated a toss-up.
Gubernatorial races to watch
There are 36 gubernatorial elections in the midterms this year, with 12 of them classified as competitive races. The GOP holds the majority of governors' offices in the U.S. at 26, with Democrats holding 24 of the positions.
The competitive races give Democrats the chance to hold a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010.
Three of the races are toss-ups, occurring in Kansas, Georgia and Nevada. Georgia may be the closest gubernatorial race, according to The Cook Political Report.
Democrats have a chance to take three open seats that previously had Republican governors: Alaska, Iowa and Ohio. However, the races are still rated as competitive.
Republican nominee and former presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and Democratic nominee and former state health director Amy Acton are competing for Ohio's open governor seat.

title: ICE officer accused of hitting immigrant in Houston with an SUV turns himself in
text:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who is accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston turned himself in Monday, his attorney said.
Mario Alberto Morales made his first court appearance on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon for striking Miguel Parra Hernandez with an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as Morales chased the 48-year-old construction worker through a parking lot. A grand jury indicted Morales, 33, on Friday.
During Monday’s hearing, Judge Matthew Peneguy set bond at $30,000. Prosecutors had asked that bond be set at $75,000, according to the Harris County District Attorney’s Office.
Morales is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. Other encounters have come under investigation.
ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of Morales’ vehicle, an account that prosecutors say is contradicted by video. Surveillance camera video shows Morales’ vehicle drive over a median and strike Parra Hernandez as he runs away.
David Lindenmuth, Morales’ attorney, has said his client was “truly a good man” and did not commit a crime.
Parra Hernandez broke his leg and is recovering at a rehabilitation facility while in federal custody, according to Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare.
Morales had worked as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Lindenmuth said. He unsuccessfully ran for Congress this year and previously served in the Army.
Morales was charged with a misdemeanor in 2013 for stealing four DVDs, according to Harris County Court records. Those charges were dismissed under a plea deal in which he paid a $270 fine.

title: Voters fear the America they've known is slipping away. On that, the left and right agree
text:
The stakes in Tuesday’s midterm elections are so high that Shane Dunn voted for the first time in his life, at age 65.
After a career as a cook up and down the East Coast, Dunn moved to the Philadelphia suburbs and voted last week in Levittown. “I was always a busy man,” he said outside his polling place. But now, “I’m learning what’s going on within our country, and this is actually what brought me out.”
Democrats got his vote. “It feels great, to put my word in,” he said, patting the “I Voted” sticker on his black hoodie.
Voters across the United States are getting their word in, too, as they determine which party controls the Senate and the House and takes charge of governors’ offices, legislatures and state leadership posts in the final two years of Republican Donald Trump’s presidency.
What many of them see is that the America they’ve known is slipping away.
They see lawlessness coming from those who create the laws. They see hate stirred by politicians among neighbors, corruption at every turn, billionaires ruling the roost and a culture that doesn’t speak to how they live — in short, American bedrock at risk of crumbling. Not to mention those crazy gas prices.
In dozens of Associated Press interviews with people who cast ballots at advance polling places or drop boxes across the country, the angst was palpable, most sharply from those who oppose Trump but also from many who support him.
A vote is cast to stop the ‘madness’
“I saw my vote today as trying to put the brakes on just the madness,” said Arthur Horner, 59, who runs a food importing and marketing company that has been hurt by tariffs, after dropping his mail ballot at Dauphin County’s election bureau in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. He voted for Democrats.
In Sioux City, Iowa, cattle rancher Elizabeth Marlett, 61, voted in Woodbury County’s historic Prairie-style courthouse and walked out stewing about a variety of things — the chemicals in processed food, her son’s struggles to get his veterans’ benefits and, perhaps most of all, what she sees as society’s leftward lurch. Things seem broken to her, too.
“Family values are going by the wayside, and they need to be brought back,” she said. “Our liberties have been stomped all over. Religion has been stomped all over. And I believe we in the majority need to step up and stop being silent.” She voted Republican.
Voters despair at the stoking of anger by Trump and allies
The anger in the air, stirred by a cursing president who abides no slights, is too much for some people.
“He’s just destroying us,” Democrat Linda Markle, 72, said of the president. She spoke outside the Warminster Township library in Bucks County, Pennsylvania.
“I am so afraid for this country,” she said. “People used to look out for each other. Not anymore.”
“All people do now is just hate each other,” she said, and Trump “seems to have given them the courage to go ahead and be like that. … The division is horrible, absolutely horrible, and I can’t wait to see the back of him.”
Republican Chris Smith, 27, a Harrisburg software engineer who voted for Trump in 2024, sympathizes with Markle’s sentiment, to a point.
“A lot of people hate him for various reasons, and I can understand why,” he said, noting that ”I think he’s kind of going a bit crazy on a lot of things.” But he likes Trump’s effort to return manufacturing to the U.S. along with the goals of his tariffs, and he voted Republican because he still thinks that party is more fiscally responsible than Democrats.
In Ohio, Lori Wilkinson, a retired home health worker from New Pittsburg, and her husband, David, a janitor, consider themselves independents. David recently wrote to their Republican governor, Mike DeWine, to tell him what a good job he’s doing, and they voted for Republican George W. Bush for president in the past.
Trump? “He’s the worst president in United States history,” David said from the Wayne County election center. “You get up every day, and you’re like, ‘What’s he going to do now?’” Said Lori: “He’s got the hate just so bad, it’s just out of hand. It’s just out of control.” She fears that if Democrats win widely Tuesday, Trump will “go fricking berserk.”
Trump supporter Therese Mennell gets it. “There’s that kind of arrogant vibe about him that people don’t like, and sometimes I shut him off because of the way he talks,” the retiree said from the Wayne County center. “But, I mean, he’s doing the right thing. He is saving our country.”
Some pretend Trump is on the ballot
Despite his striking unpopularity in polls, Trump repeatedly asked supporters to pretend he’s on the midterm ballot, betting that would motivate fans to vote who otherwise might not. But that cuts both ways.
Samontae Mwangi, 20, and his brother, Gathenya Mwangi, 19, voted for the first time, casting early ballots Tuesday at their election center in Topeka, Kansas. Both work at a plant that manufactures trackside buildings for railroads.
They went with their grandfather, Lynn Henderson, 68, a retired Goodyear Tire and Rubber Co. worker and a former Marine lance corporal who wore a Marine’s cap. Henderson said he took his grandsons to vote because his own mother died recently and he wanted them to have an event to remember him when he’s gone.
All three are hoping that the election produces Democratic victories and political change. Gathenya said the economy and discontent with Trump could motivate people who’ve voted in the past to show up, as well as those who never have. “It really could change, make a difference, I feel, if a lot of people vote,” he said.
Denise Wunder, a retired sandwich shop manager, pulled up to the center in a van featuring a decorative license plate with an American eagle. The strong Trump supporter is the daughter of Democrats. Illegal immigration is her top issue.
“I think Trump is kind of our last hope, because otherwise this world’s going to go to hell in a handbasket,” she said. “Yeah, he says stupid stuff, but, you know, so do we.”
In the Richmond, Virginia, suburb of Henrico County, voters arrived at a steady clip on a crisp fall afternoon a week from Election Day. The moment of decision found one conservative couple, Joan and Frank Bark, lamenting the country’s direction.
“I’m afraid Trump has gotten so egotistical, it’s affecting his ability to make intelligent or more favorable decisions,” Frank said. But, he said, “I don’t want the decisions that would be generated from that far left side, either.”
Joan, a retiree like her husband, said of Democrats: “I haven’t found very much that they want to change or work with. It’s just mostly, ‘I hate Trump.’” But Trump really isn’t on the ballot. They voted for Republican candidates.
In Nanuet, New York, people streamed into the small room of a community center to vote; some were in Halloween costumes. Primrose D. Sullivan, a nurse, is an independent. She scoffed at Trump’s wish that voters act as if he’s running.
“No, because he’s not,” she said. “When a patient comes into the hospital, you want me dealing in facts, not in, ‘Hmm, let me act like you might have cancer.’ No. Do you or do you not have cancer? We need to proceed based on facts.” She voted for Democrats.
Yet some see a cancer on politics, if not the presidency
Sullivan was among a number of voters who singled out the billionaires Trump has made common cause with and how that might feed into American decline.
“I don’t begrudge any of our wealthy people, Jeff Bezos or, you know, Elon Musk,” she said. “But I do have a certain problem with them wanting more and more and doing things that really don’t help humanity.”
“If we keep going the way these guys are going,” she went on, meaning both the political and CEO classes, “we’re not going to have anything like what we had in the past.” Theirs is a “self-destructive attitude,” she added, “because, honestly, if the whole planet destroys itself, the wealthy go with us.”
Outside the polling station at the YMCA in Fort Mill, South Carolina, Benjamin Updegraft offered a piercing denunciation of the elite as he traced his evolution from a “full-throated young Republican” who voted for Trump as a young man in 2016 to a “lifetime Democrat,” after casting his ballot in the Senate race.
He cited Musk’s throttling of his Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, which disrupted a key defense against Russian attacks, and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad in the Ohio governor’s race featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Amy Acton among the reasons powerful men must be brought to heel.
“That needs to be cut out from this country like a cancer,” Updegraft said. “We have an incredible responsibility to take back the stranglehold that the worst people in this country have on the reins of power and to inflict punishment on them for their actions.”
In Scottsdale, Arizona, David Lee described his conservative upbringing, his past voting for Republicans and now his decision to turn against that party and vote Democratic in the contested races for governors and the House. He considers Trump’s heavy-handed immigration enforcement to be lawless.
“Nobody wants open borders, but you’re treating these people without due process, sending people to countries they don’t even belong to,” said Lee, 63. “There’s no more rules.”
Then there are those prices. And that war
The Trump supporters interviewed by the AP at the polls signaled their tolerance of the surge of gas prices from the Iran war, in some cases blaming factors other than the actual cause. Nor did they break with him on the war itself.
Among them was David Stouffer, 59, branch manager for a mortgage bank and three-time Trump voter, who spoke outside the Harrisburg elections office. “Iran has been killing Americans for 50 freaking years,” he said. “Yeah, I’ll suffer with some higher gas prices in the interim until they get that nonsense figured out.”
Does that put a crunch on your household budget, Stouffer was asked. “Of course it does.” How to cope with that? “I just keep driving.”
“He’s made the tax cuts real,” Stouffer said. “He has secured the borders. That, to me, is a very, very big deal.”
By the dozens, Democrats, independents and Republicans outside the core of Trump’s support differed with that assessment, even as some of them granted the president his achievements on taxes and immigration.
Horner, the food importer, is going “bonkers” with the tariffs and all the other moves bouncing between the Trump administration and the courts while a “feckless” and now electorally endangered Republican Congress largely stands aside.
“You can’t do business when every month you have to readjust your pricing because the president gets a wild hair on something that he’s not even constitutionally allowed to do,” Horner said. He added, “He’s just playing out the clock on all of this stuff — where you just know he knows it’s wrong.
“And what do we have? Higher healthcare, higher food, higher gas, a business environment that is complete chaos.”
But Jerry Casner, 74, of Mechanicsburg, a suburb of Harrisburg, wants as much of Trump as he can get. Alas, “he can’t run again,” Casner noted.
“Well, technically,” Casner said, “he can’t run again.”
___
Hanna reported from Topeka, Kan.; Levy from Harrisburg, Pa.; Catalini from Levittown, Pa.; and Woodward from Washington. Associated Press journalists Julie Carr Smyth in Wooster, Ohio; Erik Verduzco in Fort Mill, S.C.; Thomas Beaumont in Sioux City, Iowa; Joseph Frederick in Nanuet, N.Y.; Tassanee Vejpongsa in Warminster, Pa.; Mikella Schuettler in Scottsdale, Ariz.; and Sarah Rankin in Henrico, Va., contributed to this report.

title: Red Sox pick up Garrett Whitlock’s option
text:
Pitcher Garrett Whitlock’s $8.25 million option for 2027 was exercised Sunday by the Boston Red Sox, preventing the pitcher from becoming a free agent.
A 30-year-old right-hander, Whitlock was 7-2 with a career-best 1.72 ERA and four saves in 54 relief appearances, striking out 59 in 52 1/3 innings.
He didn’t pitch for the Red Sox between May 24 and June 9 because of left knee inflammation and between Aug. 9 and Aug, 29 due to right elbow inflammation.
Whitlock agreed in April 2022 to an $18.75 million, four-year contract that included a pair of club options. The Red Sox would have owed a $1 million buyout if they had declined the 2027 option. Boston has a $10.5 million option for 2028 with a $500,000 buyout.

title: How to plan ahead for the possible cost of IVF
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — About 10% of Gen Z and Millennials say they are putting off having children because they are unsure how they would afford it or what starting a family would mean for their long-term finances, according to new research from Northwestern Mutual.
Kate Michaels, a managing partner at Northwestern Mutual, said money is pushing family plans down the road while another clock keeps ticking in the background: fertility.
If a couple faces infertility, many end up considering IVF, which Michaels said can be emotionally and financially overwhelming.
Planning for it involves more than a single procedure.
“It’s not like you can only plan for an IVF cycle. There may be monitoring appointments and medical exams that you need to account for before you even get to this bigger cost that you might be incurring,” Michaels said. “So, I think it’s really important that couples think about the fact that they may experience the need for fertility treatments going into a relationship.”
Couples do not need to know whether they will need fertility treatments before talking to a financial advisor. An early conversation can help them prepare for a wide range of costs that may come up.
For Michaels, the benefit goes beyond the numbers.
“That’s where I think the partnering with a financial advisor gives a lot of peace of mind, because again, it’s already such an emotional, emotionally taxing and physically taxing process,” Michaels said. “The last thing that you want to be doing with your partner or even yours if you’re going through this process alone or with a significant other, is to be feeling that financial anxiety.
Michaels recommends reviewing insurance coverage as early as possible to understand what it will and will not cover. That can show where out-of-pocket costs, such as travel or extra procedures, may need to be budgeted.
With that picture in hand, couples can have some idea of how much to start setting aside, just in case.

title: Can you vote in Maine without an ID?
text:
Yes.
Maine doesn’t require registered voters to show ID at the polls. Voters state their name and home address, and an election clerk checks the voting list.
People registering on Election Day must provide proof of identity and residency. Those without it may cast a challenged ballot, which is counted normally but may be reviewed if it could affect the result.
Maine voters rejected a 2025 referendum proposing photo ID and absentee-voting restrictions.
As of September, 36 states requested or required voter ID, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Fourteen of them required voters without acceptable ID to take additional steps for provisional ballots to count. The other 22 allowed alternatives that require no follow-up.
Researchers from the center-left Brookings Institution found 36 documented fraud cases in Arizona over 25 years, compared with 42.6 million ballots cast, using records from the right-leaning Heritage Foundation.

title: Supreme Court rejects Trump administration push to set aside thousands of California ballots
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected a push for California to set aside thousands of mail ballots from people President Donald Trump’s administration claims are noncitizens, a decision that comes on the eve of the final day of voting in the pivotal midterm elections.
The high court refused to intervene in a case involving 20,000 people the Republican administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the largely Democratic state’s voter rolls.
The swift rejection was the latest in a flurry of election-related litigation the day before the elections, which will decide control of Congress for the last two years of Trump’s second term. No justices publicly dissented.
In California, the Trump administration had asked the high court to set aside the challenged ballots until the voters’ citizenship status could be verified. But officials there said that the list appeared to be filled with errors and that setting the ballots aside could effectively disenfranchise legal voters.
The high court did not detail its reasoning, as is common in emergency decisions. The justices previously rejected Trump’s push to restrict mail ballots around the country in September, even though the justices have sided with his administration in a series of other emergency docket appeals.
The Republican Trump administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite them being rare.
A district court judge previously denied the Justice Department’s request and warned that the demand could disenfranchise citizens.
Also on Monday in Washington, another federal judge ruled against the administration’s efforts to make last-minute demands of California election officials, finding they violated the U.S. Constitution.
“The Executive Branch has likely violated the Constitution’s Elections Clause, which commits authority over election rules to the states and Congress alone,” wrote Chief Judge James Boasberg.
The administration, for its part, said segregating the ballots was a modest request that would eventually allow legal votes to still be counted.
The administration has faced a remarkable string of losses in court in its push, as well as criticism for waiting until a few weeks before the election to make its demands of California election officials with a list that even the Department of Justice admits is not entirely reliable.
During a hearing over whether to lift her own order forbidding the administration from threatening to prosecute election workers who let potentially illegal voters cast ballots, District Court Judge Trina Thompson drilled down on reports of widespread inaccuracies in the Justice Department’s data.
“Would you agree there’s a high error rate?” Thompson asked Kenneth Kao, a Justice Department attorney.
“That’s a fair statement,” Kao said. “That’s why we ask for the registrars’ aid in verifying these are all valid voters.”
At the same time, Bill Essayli, the federal prosecutor running the Justice Department’s Los Angeles office, said at a news conference he was highly confident the people on the list were not entitled to vote.
“This isn’t speculation. This isn’t a theory,” Essayli said, later conceding there may be errors on the list.
Voting has been underway in California, a largely Democratic state, since early October. All of the state’s roughly 23 million registered voters are mailed a ballot. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. California election officials have said that finding and setting aside the challenged ballots now would be logistically impossible.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said the appeal “reeks of desperation and is another attempt to undermine our elections and trample on the rule of law.”
Lower courts have sided with the state, with a district judge warning that segregating ballots would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections and erode trust in the democratic process.
“If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” wrote U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who was nominated by President Bill Clinton, a Democrat.
A 2-1 appeals court panel upheld his order, with one judge appointed by Trump and another appointed by President Joe Biden, a Democrat, voting in favor. The third judge on the panel, also appointed by Trump, argued in a dissent that California’s unwillingness to separate the ballots encourages the “violation of federal law.”
The Justice Department has sought to move the case along quickly, unsuccessfully asking an appeals court to intervene early.
___
Associated Press writers Sophie Austin in Sacramento and Safiyah Riddle in Los Angeles contributed to this report.
___

title: Brunswick technical high school receives $1M grant to pump people into workforce
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Region 10 Technical High School announced last week that it received a grant of more than $1 million to support career education.
The technical high school serves about 450 students from Brunswick schools, Topsham-based School Administrative District 75 and Freeport-based Regional School Unit 5. Its career education programs include nursing; welding; cybersecurity; heating, ventilation and air conditioning; plumbing and more.
The grant from MELMAC Education Foundation will be used to fund ASPIRE Region 10, a 5-year initiative focused on strengthening Maine’s workforce pipeline, the school said in a press release.
Student experiences supported through the grant could include informational interviews with local employers, connecting students to mentors, and co-op and pre-apprenticeship programs, according to the school. Staff also plans on working with pre-k through middle school students in the coming years to introduce younger students to technical education opportunities.
“Offering (extended learning opportunities) to our students will allow us to expose them to more career options and give them a head start on the career pathway planning that we focus on in our school,” Said Jason Darling, Region 10 co-op and pre-apprenticeship instructor. “It’s an awesome opportunity for them to be able to get a real world look at a potential career and how the skills they are learning translate to the workplace.”

title: The Lincoln County News
text:
Beverly A. (Phipps) Kibby, formerly of Bow, N.H., passed away peacefully on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026 at The Taylor Community in Laconia, N.H. surrounded by the love of family and friends.
Beverly was born in Hartford, Conn. on April 4, 1936 to the late Evelyn Levensaler Phipps and Raymond “Terry” Phipps and grew up in both Connecticut and Waldoboro. She grew up in Waldoboro with her cousins David and Sylvia and graduated from Medomak Valley High School in Waldoboro in 1954. After high school, Bev continued her education at the Maine Medical Center School of Nursing in Portland where she earned her RN designation.
Bev spent her 48-year career as a nurse caring for others, in all areas of the field. Most notably in New Hampshire, she worked for Concord Visiting Nurses, then as a school nurse for Bow Elementary. She concluded her nursing career in 2005 after working 20-plus years at Concord Obstetrics and Gynecology.
Outside of work and enjoying her friends and family, especially being Nana to her grandchildren, Bev enjoyed taking care of her extensive flower gardens, which delighted neighbors and passersby. She also enjoyed reading and loved music, especially show tunes and piano concertos. She took pleasure in traveling, including trips to Europe, Alaska, and throughout the U.S. seeing the sights and visiting friends and family.
Beverly is survived by her son, Scott Kibby (Amanda), of Chelmsford, Mass.; her daughter, Susan Kibby, of Belmont, N.H.; her beloved twin grandchildren, Blake and Evan Kibby; and her former husband, Jim Kibby, of Manchester, N.H. She is also survived by many beloved cousins and lifelong friends she considered family.
A celebration of life will be held on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026 from 2-5 p.m. at the Old Town Hall, at 91 Bow Center Road in Bow, N.H. All are welcome to join us as we share love, stories, and laughs commemorating Beverly.
In lieu of flowers, please support causes dear to her: the Taylor Home Residents-Sunshine Fund c/o Taylor Community, 435 Union Ave., Laconia, NH 03246, or Granite VNA, 30 Pillsbury St., Concord, NH 03301.
Wilkinson-Beane-Simoneau-Paquette Funeral Home & Cremation Services/603cremations.com, 164 Pleasant St., Laconia, NH 03246, is assisting the family with arrangements. For more information and to view an online memorial, please visit wilkinsonbeane.com.

title: ACA and Medicare in 2027: What’s changing and how to prepare
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ACA and Medicare in 2027: What’s changing and how to prepare
From premiums to prescription coverage, here’s what to review before choosing your health plan.
ACA and Medicare in 2027: What’s changing and how to prepare
From premiums to prescription coverage, here’s what to review before choosing your health plan.
Now that you know how to choose the best plan for you, it helps to understand the finer details. Here’s a closer look at what’s coming in 2027 to the ACA Marketplace and Medicare, and what it could mean for your budget.
ACA Marketplace: Higher Premiums and Shifting Subsidies
Premiums are changing, and so is the financial help many people rely on to afford coverage. ACA insurers have proposed median premium increases averaging 15% for 2027. So far, 29 states and Washington, D.C., have finalized their increases.
What you actually pay depends on your subsidy, which varies with your income and your local plan costs. “It's tied to a benchmark plan in your area. So as the benchmark plan premium changes, so does your subsidy amount. So you have to look at how your net premiums are changing for 2027. In virtually all cases, they will change,” said health policy analyst Louise Norris of healthinsurance.org.
“In virtually all cases, they will change. It might go up or down depending on how that subsidy amount is changing in your area and also depending on your income,” she said.
Most enrollees get help. Last year, 87% received subsidies to assist with cost. To find out if you qualify visit healthcare.gov.
Higher Out-of-Pocket Limits
For 2027, the maximum annual out-of-pocket limit for an individual marketplace plan rises from $10,600 to $12,000, and to $24,000 for families.
“They can’t go above $12,000, but they can be below that,” Norris said. “In a lot of cases, you will see increasing deductibles and increasing out-of-pocket costs, but the amount that they change will vary from one plan to another.”
If Your Plan Is Leaving the Marketplace
Insurers are leaving ACA marketplaces in more than 20 states, Norris said. If your plan is ending, the marketplace will, in most cases, pick a replacement for you that comes as close as possible to what you had this year.
“If your plan is ending altogether, you need to just assume you’re shopping from scratch, starting over, looking at all of the available plans, and picking the one that will best meet your needs,” said Norris.
Waiting has a real cost. People whose plans end have until December 31 to pick a new one, and a special enrollment period in the first two months of the year offers a do-over for anyone who missed their notice. But the plan the marketplace auto-selects takes effect January 1, while a plan you choose later wouldn’t start until February or March. That switch resets your spending. “If you end up needing care in January and then you pick yourself a different plan in February, you’re starting over at zero out of pocket,” Norris said. That could leave you paying more than the $12,000 individual out-of-pocket maximum in a single year.
Some Immigrants Lose Subsidy Eligibility
Another major change: some lawfully present immigrants will no longer qualify for federal marketplace subsidies. That includes people with certain student and work visas, refugees and asylum grantees. “They could still use the marketplace, but they would have to pay full price,” said Norris. An estimated one million people are expected to become uninsured by 2035 as a result of this change.
Immigrants who qualify: 
- Lawful Permanent Resident (LPR)
- Cuba/Haitian Entrant (CHE)
- COFA Migrant
Immigrants who no longer qualify:
- Any non-citizens who aren’t in one of the three categories listed above
- Asylees
- Special Immigrant Juvenile and Special Immigrant Visa (Iraq/Afghanistan)
- Paroled into US
- Granted work permit: EAD
- Conditional entrant before 1980
- Battered spouse, child or parent
- Family Unity Beneficiary
- Trafficking victim family
- Withholding of deportation or CAT
- VAWA self-petitioner
- Deferred Enforced Departure
- Refugees
- Tribal member/ American Indian born in Canada
- Lawful Temporary Resident
- Temporary Protected Status (TPS)
- People with various types of temporary visas, such as work visas, student visas, U-visas (for victims of certain crimes) and T-visas (for victims of trafficking). 
Medicare: Read Your Notice of Change
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services reports Medicare Advantage premiums falling about $2 a month on average, while Part D premiums rise about $1. Norris says the averages hide a wider range. “We saw significant increases and significant decreases,” she said. “You certainly should not assume that your plan is going down an average of $2 a month or up an average of $1 a month.”
Some insurers are shrinking coverage areas or consolidating plans. Norris urges people to read their Annual Notice of Change, mailed by September 30 to Medicare Advantage and Part D enrollees. It shows how your deductible, out-of-pocket exposure, provider network and drug coverage are changing. If you didn’t get one, you may have received a non-renewal notice, which was due by October 2. 
If your Medicare Advantage plan is ending, you can pick another Medicare Advantage plan or move to Original Medicare, with guaranteed access to a Medigap policy, which is not normally available in the fall. Doing nothing is the riskiest choice. “If you are on a Medicare Advantage plan and it is ending and you don’t take any action at all by the end of the year, you will be moved to Original Medicare, but you won’t have any drug coverage or supplemental coverage,” Norris said. A January and February special enrollment period can fix that, but there would be a gap of time before new coverage starts.
If your plan is staying, don’t assume you can get a Medigap plan if you switch to Original Medicare. Insurers in most states can review your medical history, so Norris recommends talking to them first. The deadline to change plans is December 7.
The Part D out-of-pocket cap is rising from $2,100 to $2,400. If you take a high-cost drug, you can ask your plan for a payment plan that spreads costs over 12 equal installments of $200. It doesn’t lower your total, but Norris says it helps with budgeting: “It’s easier to budget $200 a month than to spend $2,400 in the first few months of the year.”
Key Dates and Free Help
Medicare
- Oct. 15–Dec. 7, 2026: Medicare open enrollment. Norris recommends making your choice by Dec. 7.
- Jan. 1–Feb. 28, 2027: Special enrollment period for people whose Medicare Advantage plan ended and who didn’t pick a new one.
ACA Marketplace
- Nov. 1, 2026: Marketplace open enrollment begins in most states.
- Dec. 15, 2026: Deadline to choose an ACA marketplace plan that starts Jan. 1, 2027. Norris says every state allows at least until this date.
- Dec. 31, 2026: Deadline to pick a new plan if your current one is ending.
- Jan. 15, 2027: Marketplace open enrollment ends in most states. (A plan chosen after Dec. 15 starts later and out-of-pocket costs don’t carry over.)
- Jan. 1–Feb. 28, 2027: Special enrollment period for people whose ACA plan ended. A plan picked then starts in February or March.
Free help
- Visit HealthCare.gov or your state’s marketplace to compare plans with your 2027 subsidy factored in.
- Medicare beneficiaries can get free, unbiased counseling through SHIP, the State Health Insurance Assistance Program.
Stay Connected With the National Consumer Unit
Get clear, actionable consumer reporting delivered across platforms.
Follow National Consumer Correspondent Allie Jasinski for real-time updates on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube.
Have a question you’d like us to investigate? Email us at askallie@hearst.com.
Subscribe to our twice-weekly consumer newsletter for in-depth explanations and practical guidance.

title: Flash flooding triggers evacuations in Southwest, warning for Colorado spa town
text:
Flash flooding triggers evacuations in Southwest and a dire warning for Colorado spa town
Heavy rainfall produced flash flooding and mandatory evacuations in a swath of the Southwest on Sunday, including in a Colorado tourist town bracing for its main river to rise to historic levels, as weary residents in the normally arid region deal with another massive drenching.
Officials in Pagosa Springs, a town of more than 2,000 in the Rockies located near ski resorts and known for its hot springs, warned of potentially “catastrophic flooding” as the San Juan River was forecast to crest at more than 20 feet (6.1 meters) late Sunday night.
“To put the forecast into perspective, during the devastating 1911 flood that wiped out most of what existed as the town of Pagosa at that time, the San Juan River crested at approximately 17.8 feet (5.4 meters),” the Archuleta County Sheriff’s Office said in a Facebook post. “This is a potentially catastrophic flood event.”
Video above: Flooding in Arizona
By sundown Sunday, the river's crest had reached about 14 feet (4.2 meters), according to Vicky Schaffer, a spokesperson for the county. Roads in and out of the town were closed, and residents who weren't under evacuation orders were urged to stay home.
Communities in northern New Mexico and central Arizona, meanwhile, also issued mandatory evacuations while the rains forced the closure of several highways.
In the picturesque town of Sedona, Arizona, officials ordered residents near Oak Creek to leave immediately as floodwaters trapped multiple people in their homes.
Arizona expects months’ worth of rain in a couple of days
Nearby Yavapai County and the community of Camp Verde issued similar evacuation orders for residents living near swollen rivers and creeks.
More than 100 miles (160 kilometers) southeast of Sedona, officials in Gila County ordered the total evacuation of Gisela, a community of several hundred residents along Tonto Creek. The wet conditions even produced flash floods, river flooding and swift-water rescues in Tucson, some 230 miles (370 kilometers) south of Sedona.
“We are getting two or three months of rain in a span of a couple of days,” said Aaron Hardin, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Tucson.
Rain fell nearly nonstop Sunday in Flagstaff, Arizona, flooding local roads and overwhelming storm drains. Authorities were searching for a man who slipped and fell into fast-moving floodwaters “and was not seen resurfacing,” according to a police statement Sunday evening.
Outside Our Lady of Guadalupe Church, people filled plastic bags with sand to try to prevent further flooding inside. Luke Willson said water got into the garage, the basement and underneath the church building, as well as in an office where the computers are. “The pumps are pumping, but they’re not pumping fast enough,” he said.
To the southeast, in the Pinetop-Lakeside area of central Arizona, “manhole covers are popping up all over” and residents reported sewage backing up into homes because of flooding, the region's sanitary district said in a statement.
The latest round of soaking rains started Saturday evening and was expected to saturate the region through Monday. The weather service estimates as much as 4 inches (10 centimeters) of rain could fall across the region, fueled by a series of Pacific storm systems.
The weather service issued flood warnings and watches for nearly all of Arizona and parts of southern Utah, southwestern Colorado and western New Mexico, in addition to part of southern Nevada. That includes the sparsely populated Four Corners region, where the states meet.
The weather service office for Salt Lake City said previous storms already soaked places like Zion and Capitol Reef National Parks, warning that this could worsen flooding and “backcountry roads will likely become impassable from this excessive runoff.”
Roads into Colorado tourist town closed
Officials in Pagosa Springs said anyone in low-lying areas along the San Juan, Rio Blanco, Navajo and Piedra rivers should head to a designated shelter at a local church.
They advised residents not to wait to leave their homes as emergency crews may be extremely limited during the worst of the storm. The highway entering town also was closed to inbound traffic, and residents were advised to avoid contact with the San Juan River after sewage was discharged into it.
Katie German, owner and chef of Bruin Coffee in Pagosa Springs, said downtown had been evacuated and that there was street flooding. German said she was most worried about the one bridge into town washing out and trucks carrying everything from food to fuel not having a way in.
Town officials had just lifted an evacuation order from flooding last week only to reimpose it Saturday with the San Juan forecast to crest Sunday night at 21.9 feet (6.7 meters).
“I’m worried about my business, worried about my employees, definitely worried for everybody in this town,” German said.
Officials in La Plata County, west of Pagosa Springs, said all public roads were closed due to the flooding.
Evacuations were also ordered in nearby Durango, Colorado, where the Animas River was rising quickly.
Sedona officials rescue residents trapped in homes
In Sedona, longtime resident Michelle Grimm worried about her community after viewing the rushing waters of Oak Creek rising perilously close to the underside of a pedestrian bridge near the center of town.
“I went out at eight this morning and I saw the bridge and I was like, ‘Oh, we’re in trouble,’” she said as she sheltered in place in her home Sunday.
“I’ve never seen them rescuing people with helicopters out of neighborhoods,” Grimm said.
A video shared by the Sedona fire department showed powerful floodwaters inundating vehicles and rushing past homes and other structures. Other videos and photos shared on social media showed people standing on a pedestrian bridge taking photos and videos as churning, brown waters rushed underneath.
By Sunday afternoon, the drenching rains had largely subsided in the Sedona area.
Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs said state air rescue crews were assisting with rooftop evacuations and state transportation crews were helping clear debris.
No injuries or deaths had so far been reported, and nearly 20 homes had residents who needed emergency assistance to relocate, said David McAtee, spokesperson for Yavapai County.
—-
Marcelo reported from New York; Casey from Boston; and Weber from Los Angeles.

title: ‘I was terrified’: Viral door-kicking challenge concerns. See what to be on the lookout for
text:
HONOLULU (KHNL/Gray News) - Hawaiian residents say a viral social media trend dubbed the “door-kicking challenge” has apparently made its way to their neighborhoods.
Authorities said the trend typically involves teenagers who run up to random residential front doors late at night, deliver a heavy, high-impact kick or bang to the door to simulate a home invasion before running away.
According to Maui Lani residents, this type of behavior has been happening consistently over the last several months, with home surveillance videos capturing teens kicking random doors in the middle of the night.
Homeowner Matt, who asked that his full name not be disclosed because he fears retaliation from the vandals, said something like this has already happened to him.
“When you’re in the house at 1:30 in the morning and you’re sleeping and you hear this violent pounding on the door, it’s a little unsettling,” he said.
Matt said he spent nearly $14,000 repairing damage and trying to safeguard his home.
Ewa Beach resident Mae also said she heard the front door of her home being kicked about five times around 9 p.m. one night.
“It literally was so powerful that it shook the whole house and it felt like somebody was trying to break down the door,” Mae said. “I was terrified.”
Mae was shocked to see the trend was also happening on Maui.
“It happened to another resident in our area. So, I’m sure it’s happening quite often,” Mae said.
Also worried about retaliation, Mae did not wish to share her full name or the specific neighborhood where she lives.
“I really feel so bad for that family that they also have been experiencing forceful kicking on their doors,” she said.
Hoping to raise awareness by speaking out about her experience, Mae had a message for those pulling the pranks, who are believed to be teenagers:
“Times are hard. It is expensive to fix things and it’s very disrespectful.”
Mae urged parents, “Talk to their children about being respectful to neighbors and their property.”
Matt said he has filed multiple police reports and has contacted his homeowners association.
“Of course we want justice,” he said. “In the same breath, I have a heart, and if you strip all of this away from the individual, they’re really just kids ... I’m not sure if this is a cry for help.”
Matt is asking his community for help identifying the criminals.

title: Trump administration will cut South Africa and Rwanda from the AGOA trade program
text:
Trump administration will cut South Africa and Rwanda from the AGOA trade program
U.S. President Donald Trump will cut South Africa and Rwanda from a quarter-century-old Africa trade agreement at the end of the year as punishment for not meeting certain criteria, including policies on trade barriers and alignment with U.S. foreign policy, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative said Monday.
In South Africa's case, it's another sanction against Africa's biggest economy by the Trump administration. Last week, the U.S. excluded South Africa from a meeting of foreign ministers from the Group of 20 countries in Atlanta.
The trade deal under the African Growth and Opportunity Act, or AGOA, was introduced by former U.S. President Bill Clinton in 2000 to give some African nations duty-free access to the American market for some of their goods.
Countries have to meet requirements to be members, like establishing a market-based economy, the rule of law, political pluralism and the right to due process while also eliminating barriers to U.S. trade and investment. Countries' memberships are reviewed each year. More than 30 African nations are currently members of AGOA and view duty-free access to the U.S. market for some of their exports as a crucial economic boost.
The suspensions take effect on Jan. 1, 2027
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that Trump had informed Congress and the governments of South Africa and Rwanda that they would be removed from AGOA from Jan. 1 next year.
Greer said that the two countries were removed because of policies that "include, but are not limited to, barriers that undermine American trade and investment and practices that pose a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests in the region."
The statement did not give any specific examples of trade barriers or security and foreign policy issues.
U.S.-South Africa relations have plummeted during Trump's second term, with his administration accusing South Africa's Black-led government of being anti-white over some of its domestic affirmative action policies, and anti-American for its criticism of Israel and diplomatic ties with Iran.
The U.S. last week sanctioned Rwanda's defense ministry over its support of the M23 rebel group fighting government forces in mineral-rich eastern Congo.
There was no immediate reaction from the South African or Rwandan governments, though South African officials said last week they were expecting to be removed from the program.
Several countries have previously been removed from AGOA
The U.S. under former President Joe Biden cut several nations from AGOA for failing to meet democratic or human rights standards. They included Burkina Faso, Gabon and Niger for coups that overthrew their governments, and Uganda for introducing a strict anti-gay law.
Countries can be reinstated to AGOA and Greer said of South Africa and Rwanda that "the Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria."
Trump has pushed for policy changes in South Africa
The Trump administration has been fiercely critical of South Africa and has baselessly accused its government of allowing widespread violence against minority white farmers. It has also said that South Africa's affirmative action laws that promote Black business ownership are a barrier to U.S. investment.
The U.S. has pressed South Africa to enact specific policy changes, including making crime against farmers a priority crime, dropping affirmative action requirements for U.S. businesses operating in the country, and repealing a land law that allows for the expropriation of private land without compensation in some circumstances.
The South African government has denied it is anti-white and has said the U.S. criticism is a result of misinformation. South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola said last month that the country was preparing for the "worst-case scenario" on AGOA but would not "surrender its sovereignty" to U.S. demands.
U.S. Ambassador to South Africa L. Brent Bozell III said in a post on X on Monday that the AGOA suspension was because of South Africa's failure to enact those policy changes.
"This was a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the U.S. Government," the ambassador wrote.
U.S. Rep. Richard Neal, the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Committee, said in a statement that the administration's move against South Africa, the top exporter to the U.S. in the program, could cause chaos to the U.S. economy and that the administration needs to give a clear explanation of how South Africa can be reinstated.
___
Imray reported from Cape Town, South Africa.

title: Researchers uncover clues explaining why immunotherapy fails in many lung cancer patients
text:
BAR HARBOR, Maine (WABI) - New findings from researchers at The Jackson Laboratory could soon help doctors predict which lung cancer patients will benefit from immunotherapy before starting treatment.
Lung cancer is the second most common cancer in the United States and the leading cause of cancer-related deaths. While immunotherapy has revolutionized cancer care, an estimated 60% to 80% of lung cancer patients do not respond to certain types of the treatment.
Now, a study published in the journal Science reveals new insight into why those treatments fall short for so many.
Looking beyond DNA
Researchers at JAX, an NCI-designated cancer center, looked past standard DNA testing to analyze a fundamental cellular regulatory mechanism known as alternative splicing—the way cells process genetic instructions.
They identified previously overlooked cellular changes that influence how lung cancer tumors interact with the immune system and correspond to differences in patient survival after immunotherapy.
Identifying these patterns could eventually give oncologists a reliable roadmap to determine which patients are strong candidates for immunotherapy and who might need alternative therapies.
The path to clinical trials
Researchers emphasize that while the initial findings are promising, more work remains before the discovery can be used in everyday oncology clinics.
“What we’d need would be clinical trials to really show that this biomarker is what we would call it, this marker that helps select which patients should get the immunotherapy and maybe which patient should get something different actually works,” said Ryan Englander, an MD-PhD candidate at The Jackson Laboratory. “We’ve shown that they’re associated with good responses. We aren’t sure if they are the thing that is actually driving the better response and if they are then they may represent kind of a new therapeutic target too which would be really really cool.”
With further clinical trial testing, researchers hope these cellular markers will help doctors personalize treatment strategies, sparing patients ineffective therapies and pointing them toward better outcomes.

title: Ask ACE: My spouse and kids all work in the business. How should I be paying them?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ACE advises: Start with the same principle that would apply to any employee: family members should be paid a reasonable market rate for real work, with that compensation run through payroll.
Define the job first. The IRS looks at whether the work is legitimate and whether the pay is reasonable for the role. A teenager earning $40,000 to occasionally “help with social media” can raise questions. So can a spouse working substantial hours for little or no pay. Each family member should have a defined role, appropriate compensation, time records and a W-2.
From there, the rules differ depending on who is working and how the business is structured. A child’s wages are taxed to the child, and some may be covered by the standard deduction. If the business is a sole proprietorship, or a partnership owned only by the child’s parents, wages paid to children under 18 are generally exempt from Social Security and Medicare taxes. That exemption does not apply if the business is incorporated, including as an S corporation.
There is also an age-related distinction. Federal law generally does not set a minimum age for children working in a business owned solely by their parents, but hazardous occupations are treated differently. State child labor laws can be more restrictive, so check the rules where the business operates.
For a spouse, payroll can also help build Social Security credits and retirement savings.
Finally, keep compensation separate from ownership. Wages reflect the work someone performs; distributions reflect ownership. That distinction matters when one child works in the business and another does not.
Getting this right also helps with succession, financing or a future sale. Buyers and lenders want to understand the business’s true earnings, and inflated or understated family compensation may eventually need to be normalized.
A good starting point is to list each family member, what they do and what an outside employee would reasonably be paid for the same role.

title: 14 treated after accidental pepper spray discharge leads to craft fair evacuation
text:
HONOLULU (KHNL/Gray News) - An accidental pepper spray discharge prompted an evacuation at a community center in Hawaii on Sunday afternoon.
Honolulu police said officers responded to the Neal S. Blaisdell Center after 3 p.m. during the Hawaii Holiday Craft and Gift Fair.
According to a vendor, a customer was examining a pepper spray canister at a booth when they accidentally activated it, releasing its contents into the air.
The incident prompted an evacuation of the event hall as Honolulu firefighters, including the department’s hazardous materials team, and Emergency Medical Services responded.
Honolulu EMS said multiple crews evaluated 14 adults at the scene, and the patients declined transport to a hospital for further treatment.
Attendees said that a chemical smell lingered near the venue’s entrance following the accidental activation.

title: 18 County Standouts Make a Loaded Week Nine Athlete Ballot
text:
Week Nine Is Loaded: 18 County Athletes Up for Athlete of the Week
The deeper we get into the postseason, the harder these Athlete of the Week decisions become.
Fall Week Nine might be the best example yet.
This week's ballot features 18 Aroostook County athletes, with nine boys and nine girls representing some of the biggest tournament, championship and individual performances of the fall.
There are game-winning goals, dramatic penalty shootouts, state championship cross country finishes, postseason shutouts and players who came through when their teams needed them most.
Now it is time for County sports fans to decide the winners.
Voting is open now. Fans can vote once per hour in both polls through Thursday at 3 p.m.
The Week Nine winners will be announced Friday morning.
Boys Athlete of the Week Nominees
Wyatt Oliver, Hodgdon, Soccer
Oliver came through in a huge tournament moment for the Hawks, scoring 2 goals in Hodgdon's quarterfinal victory over Easton.
One of those goals was the game-winner, coming on a header off a cross to help send Hodgdon into the next round.
Mitchell Burtt, Central Aroostook, Soccer
Burtt was right in the middle of Central Aroostook's dramatic tournament victory.
He scored both Panther goals during regulation and then converted again during the penalty shootout as Central Aroostook advanced.
James Baillargeon, Houlton, Soccer
Baillargeon delivered one of the most dramatic goals of the postseason.
With Houlton and top-seeded Mattanawcook tied in overtime, Baillargeon scored the game-winning goal with only four seconds remaining, sending the Shires into the next round.
Grady Kinney, Central Aroostook, Soccer
Kinney stood tall in goal during Central Aroostook's postseason thriller.
After playing through regulation and two overtimes, Kinney made 3 saves during the penalty shootout, helping the Panthers survive and advance.
Bentley Nadeau, Wisdom, Soccer
Nadeau made his impact when the pressure was at its highest.
He recorded a tournament shutout before later making the decisive save in a penalty shootout, sending Wisdom into the regional championship.
Malachi Witmer, Houlton/GHCA, Cross Country
Witmer turned in another outstanding championship performance.
He finished sixth at the Class C State Cross Country Championship in 17:17.24, leading Houlton/GHCA to a state runner-up team finish.
Aiden Ciarleglio, Hodgdon, Soccer
Ciarleglio came up with a strong performance in net during Hodgdon's quarterfinal win over Easton.
He made 9 saves on 14 shots, including several important stops that helped the Hawks protect their lead and move on.
Wyatt Daigle, Fort Kent, Soccer
Daigle stepped to the spot with Fort Kent's season hanging in the balance.
He converted the deciding penalty kick in the Warriors' semifinal shootout victory over George Stevens Academy, sending Fort Kent into the Class C North regional championship.
Paxton Darrell, Presque Isle, Cross Country
Darrell led the Presque Isle boys at the Class B State Cross Country Championship.
He finished 16th overall in 17:55.52, capping a strong postseason run for the Wildcats.
Girls Athlete of the Week Nominees
Lucy Hartvigsen, Madawaska, Soccer
Hartvigsen delivered one of Week Nine's biggest playoff performances.
She scored both Madawaska goals against Ashland, including the game-winner in double overtime, to send the Owls into the semifinals.
Reece Doucette, Fort Kent, Soccer
Doucette helped send the Warriors back to the regional championship.
She scored 2 goals in Fort Kent's 5-0 semifinal victory over Houlton, including the penalty kick that broke a scoreless game in the second half.
Lilly Burtt, Central Aroostook, Soccer
Burtt played a major role in Central Aroostook's quarterfinal victory over Van Buren.
She scored 2 goals in the Lady Panthers' 3-2 win, helping Central Aroostook advance to the semifinal round.
Carrlyn Buck, Presque Isle, Soccer
Buck found the net when the tournament pressure increased.
She scored in Presque Isle's 3-1 quarterfinal victory over Skowhegan and followed it with another goal in the Wildcats' 4-0 semifinal win over Cony, giving her goals in back-to-back playoff victories.
Raina Ezell, Houlton, Soccer
Ezell exploded offensively in the Class C quarterfinals.
She recorded a hat trick as Houlton defeated Central Aroostook 7-2 and advanced to the semifinal round.
Jenna Strid, Caribou, Cross Country
Strid delivered one of the strongest eligible County girls performances at the state cross country championships.
She finished ninth in Class B in 20:06.27, earning a top-10 state finish for the Vikings.
Chloe White, Fort Fairfield, Soccer
White helped power the Tigers through the Class D quarterfinals.
She scored 2 goals in Fort Fairfield's 4-0 victory over Washburn, helping the Tigers continue their postseason run.
Madi Cyr, Wisdom, Soccer
Cyr produced goals in consecutive tournament victories for the Pioneers.
She scored in Wisdom's 6-1 quarterfinal win over George Stevens Academy and found the net again in the 5-0 semifinal victory over previously unbeaten Sumner.

Burgess stepped into a completely different role when Van Buren needed her.
Playing goalkeeper for the first time, she came up with several big saves in the Crusaders' quarterfinal matchup against Central Aroostook and helped keep Van Buren within striking distance.
