title: Is El Niño making storms and flash floods in the Southwest worse?
text:
Is El Niño making storms and flash floods in the Southwest worse?
A chaotic climate phenomenon is intensifying heavy rains and floods in the Southwest, experts say.
A natural warming cycle called El Niño is sizzling Pacific Ocean waters, leaking moisture into the air that can fuel passing storms. Such El Niño events can happen irregularly every couple of years, but scientists say the latest iteration is particularly extreme — and it's just getting started, with impacts expected for several more months.
“We’ve had super El Niños in the past, but this is a super duper El Niño,” said meteorologist Jeff Masters of Yale Climate Connections.
The phenomenon wasn't the only cause of the severe storms and it's difficult to attribute any single event to it. Still, scientists say this supercharged El Niño is making heavy rains more likely and intense across the Southern U.S. The effects of those storms can be felt more strongly in desert regions, where the land doesn't absorb water as well.
Flash floods on Sunday prompted evacuations across northern New Mexico and central Arizona, and a Colorado ski town braced for its main river to rise to catastrophic levels. And just last week, another soaker of a storm subjected southwestern states to days of flooding.
Over 20 trillion gallons of water have fallen on the Four Corners states and Nevada in the past two weeks, according to calculations by former National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration chief scientist Ryan Maue.
Experts say this year's extreme El Niño is creating more ideal conditions for storms. It's adding more moisture to the air, which is perfect fodder for downpours to draw upon. And it's shifting wind patterns across the globe, redirecting strong air currents toward the Southwest that can stir up that moisture.
“The likelihood of big precipitation in the Southwest interior does go up this time of year, but we’re seeing it to a degree we actually haven’t seen before,” said climate scientist Daniel Swain with the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources.
This El Niño is sloshing warmer waters into new places, but the world's oceans are already hotter than they used to be because of human-caused climate change. That means even more sweltering extremes are possible.
“The fact that the ocean temperatures are already warmer than they were, say, 100 years ago, makes these El Niño situations even more intense,” said meteorologist Randy Cerveny with Arizona State University.
The phenomenon is changing weather patterns around the world: regions including Peru and Ecuador are also seeing record-breaking flooding, Swain said. Parts of Southeast Asia, like Indonesia, are drier than usual.
The El Niño event is expected to peak in December, when it can more strongly harness certain air currents called jet streams to produce more extreme storms across the western U.S. After that, experts say its onslaught could continue for months.
“The dice are certainly loaded for more heavy storms this winter and spring,” said Park Williams with UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography in an email.
The impacts of an El Niño aren't wholly bad, Cerveny said: it can bring rainfall and moisture to drier areas like the Southwest and fill up reservoirs. At the same time, storms and floods can pose a danger to people and property.
To stay safe, experts recommended watching the forecast, planning ahead and heeding evacuation warnings from local authorities.
“We’re not at the peak of the heating in the Pacific Ocean. So yes, we will see more of these particular events,” Cerveny said.

title: Meeting the demand: More nonstop flights are coming between Maine and California
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Meeting the demand: More flights are coming between Maine and California
The number of direct flights between the Portland International Jetport and California will significantly expand next summer.
The Jetport announced on Monday that United Airlines is adding another 20 roundtrip transcontinental flights for the summer of 2027, equating to a 65% increase over the options this past summer.
In January of 2026, United first announced nonstop flights from Portland to both Los Angeles and San Francisco with flights on Saturdays starting on June 27.
These flights were the first time there has been direct commercial service between Maine and California. These flights currently use Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft, which can carry up to 178 passengers.
Initially, the flights were scheduled for only 13 weeks in 2026, but demand was so high that an extra five weeks were added for flights between Portland and San Francisco.
On Monday, jetport officials said the seasonal flights on Saturdays to San Francisco will resume on May 8, 2027, and then flights on Wednesdays will be added on June 23, 2027.
Saturday flights to Los Angeles will resume on June 26, 2027 and United will also have six Wednesday flights between Portland and Los Angeles during the peak summer season.
“United made history earlier this year when they flew our first transcontinental flights,” said Paul Bradbury, Airport Director. “The demand exceeded our expectations and we are now seeing United at 65% more flights to California for Summer 2027. We are grateful to United for the continued investment in the Portland market and look forward to the additional flights to California.”
United is increasing service between Portland and San Francisco to 32 flights, a 77% increase over summer 2026. Service between Portland and Los Angeles is increasing to 19 flights, a 46% increase over summer 2026.
“These flights make it very easy to move between the East Coast and West Coast,” said Zach Sundquist, Assistant Airport Director. “United’s hubs in San Francisco and Los Angeles allow for one-stop connections to many Pacific Rim destinations, and with Wednesday service being introduced, these options become even more appealing to local businesses with connections to Asia.”
The addition of the service to California in 2026 means there is now nonstop service from Portland to all seven of United’s domestic hubs, either seasonally or year-round, including Saturday service to Houston Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston, Texas and daily services to Chicago O’Hare, Denver, New York City/Newark, and Washington DC Dulles.
United has the second-most non-stop destination options from Portland, behind only Breeze Airways. Breeze recently announced its 12th nonstop option from Portland, with service to Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, coming in May of 2027.
American Airlines has six nonstop destinations from Portland, Delta Air Lines has five, Southwest Airlines has four, JetBlue Airways has three and Sun Country Airlines has one.

title: Letter: We have the power to change our country
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
In 2024, we voted for a better, more affordable life.
Where are we now? Sadly, it seems we mistakenly elected leaders who now bear responsibility for several painful consequences. We are involved in a war we neither understand nor consent to. We punish beloved neighboring countries and pay exorbitant prices because of tariffs that bring us no benefit.
Our new leaders paint a rosy picture, but let’s examine it carefully. Instead of elected officials representing our welfare and rights, we have a divided House of Representatives. Half stand for the people; half support the government, and we are beginning to distrust both. Who’s in charge?
So far, they have succeeded in pulling the wool over our eyes. They have been spectacularly successful at one thing: perfecting corruption, shifting the country to financial interests where only the wealthy matter. They hold the key to our treasury and spend taxpayers’ money while we lose ground every day in meeting expenses, affording health care for our families, not to mention gas for our cars.
What can be done before we lose the chance to stop a landslide of corruption? There is one solution; it belongs to us. We have the power to change it, but we must act. We must reduce the danger and start correcting it. Let us all work together toward a better future.
Patricia Fogg 
Greene

title: These brothers have been helping planes depart for four decades
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (InvestigateTV) — Brothers Bobby and Lance Snyder have a combined eight decades of service with American Airlines at Charlotte Douglas International Airport.
They help make sure planes arrive and depart safely and on time at the airline’s second-largest hub. Their commitment is inspiring their younger co-workers.
From Johnson City to the ramp
Bobby Snyder said the brothers grew up in the Johnson City area, close to the Tri-Cities Airport.
“A friend of ours and his dad, they lived beside of us. We used to go out to the airport,” Bobby Snyder said.
Lance Snyder said he has memories of going to the airport as a child and cleaning overnighters.
“Back then, the big thing was getting peanuts off the airplane and maybe finding some pennies or nickels, you know, as we would clean the airplanes,” Lance Snyder said.
Bobby Snyder said that experience drew him to wanting to work for the airline. In 1986, he came to Charlotte and put a resume in to Piedmont Airlines. He was hired the next week.
Lance Snyder said he followed his brother to Charlotte nine months later, taking the same route and applying for a job at the airline.
Bobby Snyder said he started at the freight house in air freight, delivering freight to the gates. He said he wanted to work on the ramp and moved there in 1987. He has worked on the ramp since.
Lance Snyder said his early duties included unloading and loading airplanes, parking and pushing.
“A lot of the same things that we do today. Just loved it,” Lance Snyder said.
Work as crew chiefs
Both brothers are crew chiefs. Bobby Snyder said he has a crew of three, and the brothers work together all day.
Lance Snyder said the crew prepares for arrivals and departures.
“We’re just getting prepared for arrivals and departures, kind of looking ahead and seeing what’s coming off the airplane, what needs to be unloaded, just making sure our crew is in the right place,” Lance Snyder said.
Bobby Snyder described the work as a team effort. He said typically three to four workers, called runners, are assigned to run each flight, along with a crew of three.
“We have to do the water and air and power. And it all just happens. And it’s got to happen quick, like within just a couple of minutes’ time,” Bobby Snyder said.
He said the doors must be shut four or five minutes before departure to get the plane out on time.
“The main thing is we want to keep our passengers happy. Getting their bags, it’s our responsibility to make sure all that works and works in a timely manner,” Bobby Snyder said.
Working with younger co-workers
Lance Snyder said he still enjoys working and being around people. He said the makeup of the workforce has changed.
“Everybody used to be our age and older. Now everybody’s younger. But that’s been a real blessing too, getting to work with young people, getting to work with people from all over the world, and just learning different cultures,” Lance Snyder said.
He said he hopes to be “a bright light” to co-workers and to encourage them. He said he sometimes gets to be “a little bit of a father figure to some.”
Recognition for service
In February 2026, the Charlotte Regional Visitors Authority honored the brothers with the Unsung Heroes Award for their decades of dedication to the job.
“They have a lot of passion for what they do, they also help mentor lots of team members who are working here today,” said Cesar Marchese, American Airlines CLT customer operations managing director.
Luggage tips for travelers
An airport official said travelers who want to help baggage handlers keep luggage on time should remove any loose straps from their bags.
The official said travelers should also try not to keep the luggage tag on the same handle as the airline bag tag so the system can clearly see the barcodes.

title: Rockets end Celtics 5-game winning streak
text:
HOUSTON — Alperen Sengun had 26 points, 10 assists and seven rebounds to lead the Houston Rockets to a 109-93 win over the Boston Celtics on Monday night.
The Rockets improved to 7-1, moving into first place in the Western Conference after the previously undefeated Memphis Grizzlies (6-1) lost to New Orleans in overtime. The Celtics lost for the first time since their season opener at Detroit, ending a five-game streak.
Jabari Smith Jr. and Amen Thompson each scored 14 points for Houston. Tari Eason added 13, and Kevin Durant scored 12 on 5-of-6 shooting.
Jayson Tatum led Boston with 19 points on 5-of-16 shooting, including 1 of 7 from 3-point range. Neemias Queta had 16 points, and reserve Luka Garza made four 3s and scored 14 points.
Boston was frequently flustered by former Celtic Marcus Smart, who had eight points, four rebounds and four assists.
The Rockets never trailed and outscored the Celtics 18-2 on the fast break and 50-34 in the paint. The game was tied at 29 at the end of the first quarter, and Houston led 57-50 at halftime.
Paul George (rest) was sidelined for Boston after scoring 17 points in 33 minutes of the Celtics’ 108-97 win at Orlando on Sunday. Clint Capela (right ankle sprain) sat for Houston.
The Rockets are off to their best start since the 2014-15 season.
Up next
Celtics: Host Milwaukee on Wednesday night.
Rockets: Host Minnesota on Wednesday night.

title: Deep brain stimulation surgery allows artist to return to woodcarving
text:
PHOENIX. Ariz. (Aging Untold) — Bill Daggett fell in love with woodcarving decades ago. Then the shaking started.
What doctor saw at an art show saw
A doctor at an art show noticed Daggett’s tremors and urged him to get checked. The diagnosis was Parkinson’s disease.
“I couldn’t even eat, hardly. I was shaking so bad, and I didn’t want to go out anymore. That’s part of the depression. You don’t want to be seen when you can’t hold a fork and get it to your mouth,” Daggett said.
Choosing deep brain stimulation
When medication was not enough, the Arizona artist chose deep brain stimulation, or DBS. The therapy sends electrical pulses to the brain to stop tremors.
Daggett’s hands are now steady as he carves.
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist and host of “Aging Untold,” compared the therapy to a pacemaker.
“What they did was basically give his brain a pacemaker. You know, we’re kind of accustomed to the thought of a pacemaker helping a heart keep rhythm. But this is a new way to go in and help that brain reset and send those electrical pulses out to give the brain the pacemaker to now reduce those tremors, reduce some of the side effects of the disease and the progression of it,” Cradduck said.
‘Quality of life’ breakthrough
Cradduck said DBS is a “quality of life” breakthrough for people who have lived with the disease for years.
“We talk about the physical aspects of disease and aging all the time, but we forget to talk about the emotional loss, and that’s where this guy was at. He was so connected with being the artist and being able to create, and the disease was robbing him of that. We see that it’s robbing him of physical abilities maybe to eat, but we forget that it’s robbing him of a piece of himself,” Cradduck said.

title: Algae bloom is gone, but impacts on clammers and farmers could last for years
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
September’s algae bloom has faded from the waters of Casco Bay, but harvesters and growers in Harpswell are still taking stock of the damage.
Some of the most vulnerable species, like worms and soft-shell clams, appear to have been wiped out in certain areas, while hard clams and oysters mostly survived. But with the bloom happening just before winter, growers and harvesters say they will have to wait till spring to know if the stress and lack of nutrients will lead to more losses.
Clam diggers and others started seeing signs of the bloom around Sept. 8-9. Dead and dying shellfish and worms were found on mudflats at the head of Middle Bay, in Long Cove, and in other areas, while some places in Harpswell saw no impacts at all. Maine’s Department of Marine Resources and other authorities soon confirmed that the bloom was spreading from Casco Bay as far south as New Hampshire and Massachusetts.
Tests revealed that the bloom contained the plankton Karenia mikimotoi, which is toxic to shellfish but not dangerous to humans. In addition to the plankton’s toxicity, any large algae bloom uses up oxygen, suffocating marine life. Those decomposing animals further deplete oxygen, both in the water and the mud, and can increase acidity.
The near-shore bloom appeared to peak around the middle of September. There were fears that a large storm that moved up the East Coast in the last week of September might push offshore algae back into Maine’s bays, but the storm ultimately tracked away from land and had minimal impact on Casco Bay.
On Oct. 9, Harpswell Harbormaster Darcie Couture reported on Facebook that there were no more visible signs of the bloom, even offshore.
Harpswell clam digger David Wilson, who chairs the town’s Marine Resources Committee, said that in Long Cove and Middle Bay, he and other harvesters have found that larger quahogs, also known as hard clams, survived the event, while younger clams and seed clams did not. Wilson said it could take as many as seven years for populations to rebuild. And he worries that even the clams that did survive the bloom might not make it through the winter if they haven’t built up their fat stores sufficiently.
Bloom’s impact extends to sea farms
Harpswell has more than 100 aquaculture leases, with oysters as the main crop, and farmers reported mixed experiences of the bloom.
Kat Lipp, general manager of Mere Point Oyster Company, on Middle Bay in Brunswick, estimated that the farm lost about 20% of its oysters from the bloom. The farm discovered the harm early on, before the bloom was fully evident. When the extent of the threat became clear, staff stopped handling the oysters to reduce stress on them and give them the best chance of survival, Lipp said.
Like Wilson, she said it remains to be seen how many of the oysters will survive the winter.
Snow Island Oysters, which farms oysters on Harpswell Sound near the north end of Orr’s Island, has not seen an unusual die-off, according to Tait Nygaard, farm manager. The farm has been cautious about handling oysters, he said. He speculated that its location closer to the open ocean may have been a safer spot than farther up in the bays.
Another oyster farmer, Seth White, said his shellfish near Little Birch Island in Middle Bay seem to be doing OK. But his other crop, urchins, was hit hard. White said that when he pulled them up in the middle of September, he found many dead urchins. Some of the live ones didn’t look so good either.
White said he only knows of one other urchin farm, in Portland, and he heard that it survived the bloom. He said it may be a few years before he can try to grow urchins again, because their seed can cost 40 times as much as oyster seed.
He got his urchin seed from the University of Maine through a grant. This was his first time trying to grow them, and he had hoped they would be ready to sell next season. Now he’ll have to wait years to see if urchins can be an economically viable crop.
A more immediate concern for many in the aquaculture and harvesting industries is the immediate loss of income. White said that when oyster farms decided to take a break from their usual schedule of harvesting and handling oysters to give the shellfish a better chance of surviving the bloom, farm workers saw their hours cut. He knew of a dozen or more people at the end of September who hadn’t had any work to do.
At Mere Point Oyster Company, Lipp had a similar message. “The folks out there really being affected by this are the diggers, the farmers, the wild harvesters — the individuals, not the companies,” she said. It will likely be months more before the full effect on workers is known.

title: Maine must realize trapping is not stewardship
text:
The Oct. 19 report “Interest in trapping grows in Maine” describes new trappers taking up the practice to build outdoor skills and make hats and mittens. That framing deserves an honest look at what it asks of wild animals.
A trap is violence. A beaver held underwater until they drown, a fox gripped by the leg through a freezing night, a bear restrained by a cable waiting for the person who will kill them; these are not abstractions. They are living beings experiencing pain, fear and death so that someone can enjoy a hobby or own a fur hat. In 2026, no one in Maine needs a trapped animal’s pelt to stay warm.
The article speaks of ethics and good decisions in the field. Real ethics begins with a simpler question: Is this harm necessary? For recreation and fashion, the answer is “no.”
Trapping is often defended as stewardship. True stewardship protects wildlife and the ecosystems they hold together. It solves conflicts with humane tools like education on coexistence, non-lethal repellents, fencing and good old-fashioned tolerance. It would never turn unnecessary pain, terror and premature death into a pastime and call it conservation.
Maine’s wildlife are not raw material for crafts or a challenge to master. They are our neighbors. A state that valued them would stop treating their suffering as recreation.
Serena Ross
Belfast

title: The Bangor Mall has been condemned
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Bangor Mall has been condemned, according to signs posted in the doors on Monday afternoon.
It’s the latest blow to the mall owner, Namdar Realty Group, after more than two years of lawsuits and dwindling businesses inside the nearly 50-year-old mall.
“This structure has been deemed unfit for human habitation or use,” the signs read.
The condemnation comes as Namdar owes more than $2 million to the city and an insurance company after multiple lawsuits. A potential sale appears poised to fall through after one of the main financiers pulled out.
Bangor’s code enforcement office referred a reporter to city spokesperson David Warren, who confirmed that code enforcement was at the site Monday but declined to share any more details.
The signs are on dozens of doors around the mall, including ones that still have graphics from Spirit Halloween, which was temporarily located inside the mall prior to Halloween, on them. Doorways connecting J.C. Penney and Dick’s Sporting Goods to the rest of the mall were shut.
A J.C. Penney worker said the store was open to the rest of the mall Monday morning, but was closed in the afternoon.
Customers can still enter J.C. Penney and Dick’s Sporting Goods from their exterior doors.
A Bangor city employee put up the signs this afternoon and asked customers who were shopping to leave, according to a Spirit Halloween employee. Monday was the last day Spirit Halloween was going to be open in the mall, and a steady stream of people have attempted to get into the store for clearance sales after the signs were posted.
“The mall is shut down,” the employee told people walking by.
One couple who did not share their names said they were at the mall to pick up an order from one of the stores inside, but can no longer go in.
Lights and arcade games inside the mall are still turned on. Gates opening to the various stores are closed.
A spokesperson for Namdar did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
A craft show planned for this weekend at the mall will go on as planned, according to a Facebook post by organizer Kathy Harvey. She owns the now-closed furniture store, where the show will take place.
One wing of the mall was previously condemned in January. The former Sears wing was closed and power was cut to that area. Stores relocated to other wings.
Namdar owes at least $2 million after losing three different lawsuits in just over the last year, two brought by the city of Bangor and one by the insurance company for the furniture store. A judge found Namdar committed multiple code violations, including issues with a leaking roof and a broken sewer line. Nothing has been filed in the city’s lawsuits since April, and it’s unclear if anything changed recently that spurred the city’s decision to condemn the property.
As of August, Namdar had not completed the court ordered repairs or paid the $1.1 million fine to the city.
A local developer was in the process of buying the property in hopes of turning it into a mix of housing and retail, although the deal stalled last month due to the departure of a key investor.

title: Israeli officials say elections will stand after Netanyahu claimed Arabs stole vote
text:
TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ‘s efforts to question last week’s elections weakened Sunday as officials said the vote would not be undermined by the allegations and a court ordered suspects in one case released.
In an image that indicated officials were on the same page, the head of Israel’s elections committee was shown sitting between Israel’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet intelligence service for a statement making clear that even if claims of foreign interference raised last week are substantiated, the vote would stand.
Netanyahu’s Likud party has said, without giving evidence, that Arab-led parties “stole” the elections in which Netanyahu’s bloc lost its majority of seats in parliament. By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appears to be trying to block any potential alliance in the opposition with the Arab parties that could force him from office.
Likud has cited a handful of cases, including the arrests of three political activists before polls opened on Oct. 27 with envelopes of cash, allegedly to bribe voters. Two days later, police arrested four more suspects. Police said the suspects were connected to the Islamist party Ra’am, which denied that it was involved.
A judge on Sunday questioned or rejected police requests for further restrictions on the three suspects. Police later said one was released subject to unspecified “conditions” and another was ordered to remain on house arrest for eight days. The detention of the third suspect was extended for two days.
Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra’am party, which won eight seats in the Knesset, denounced the arrests as undemocratic and “an attempt to influence the election results.”
Netanyahu suggests joining with Arab parties is treason
Netanyahu saw his parliamentary bloc of allies drop to 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, down from a peak of 68 in the outgoing parliament.
A bloc of parties led by his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, won 48 seats, while Arab-led parties, including Ra’am, won the remaining 19 seats. Together, those two blocs opposing Netanyahu have enough seats to form a new government, though it remains unclear whether they will agree to do so.
The results are due to be officially certified this week, and President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday will begin meeting with each of the parties elected to parliament after that to see who they prefer to be the next prime minister.
Following those consultations, he will choose the candidate — most likely Netanyahu or Eisenkot — who he believes has the best chance of forming a coalition government.
That would set the stage for weeks of negotiations. If they are unsuccessful, Herzog could ask another candidate to try. Otherwise, the country would be plunged into a new election early next year.
Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for Eisenkot to join with Arab parties. Some Israelis agree. A few dozen people protested outside Eisenkot’s home on Sunday night.
“We have a tiny country, a very tiny Jewish country. We want to keep it as a Jewish country,” said one protester, Shoshana Idasis. Other, larger rallies in recent days have called for a Jewish-Arab coalition.
Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of trying to delegitimize the vote
Likud also has alleged foreign interference in the vote. The Shin Bet security service, at the request of Israel’s election commission, has opened an investigation.
But the head of the elections committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said that “our position is that even if the suspicions are substantiated, this would not undermine the integrity of the electoral process or the election results as a whole.”
Likud quickly issued a statement asking how the committee chief can acknowledge there are serious allegations while saying there will be no effect on the final outcome.
Eisenkot on Sunday accused Netanyahu of launching an “orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results” by insinuating that Qatar had supported opposition parties to unseat Netanyahu. Eisenkot said that Shin Bet briefed him on the investigation into foreign interference.
Qatar has denied funding any activities meant to influence the election’s outcome. Many Israelis see the Gulf Arab country as a patron of Hamas, and allegations of its influence have roiled Israeli politics in other cases, including one in which close aides of Netanyahu allegedly accepted money from Qatar while working for the prime minister’s office.
Netanyahu’s opponents have accused him of using scare tactics and trying to create a narrative to further discriminate against Arab-led parties and Israel’s Arab citizens, who make up 20% of the population.
Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List of Arab parties, which won 11 seats, noted last week that more than half the content published by Likud and Netanyahu on election day was directed against Arab voters as a tactic to encourage right-wing Israelis to vote.
“In moments of crisis, he reverts to his familiar tactic: racist incitement and the delegitimization of the Arab public,” he said.

title: Washington state resident dies from bird flu following exposure to infected cattle
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A person in Washington state has died from complications of the bird flu, the first such U.S. death in a year.
The Yakima County resident, who had previous health conditions, was exposed to avian influenza at a dairy with infected cattle and had been hospitalized. The person died Sunday, county health officials said.
Two other U.S. deaths have been tied to bird flu since it became a national public health concern in 2024. The first, announced in January 2025, was an elderly person in Louisiana who had a version of bird flu known as H5N1. The other, in Washington state, died in November 2025 from a rarer version called H5N5.
Yakima County officials did not release any additional details about the person who recently died. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the person was infected with H5N1.
County officials have reported that 33 dairy herds have recently tested positive for H5N1.
They say three human infections have been linked to exposure at a dairy, and that the Yakima Health District is working with the state health department to find people who were in close contact with those people and monitor them for symptoms.
The H5N1 bird flu has been spreading widely among wild birds, poultry, cows and other animals for several years. Health concerns escalated in early 2024 when infections spread among U.S. livestock. Its presence in the environment increases the chances that people will be exposed, and potentially catch it, officials have said.
More than 70 human infections have been reported in the U.S. since the beginning of 2024, according to the CDC. But there is no known person-to-person spread and the risk to the general public is low, the agency says.
The agency analyzed the genetic sequence of the virus from the person who died in Washington and found no changes that would make the virus spread more easily or cause more severe illness, a CDC spokesperson said Monday.
Officials continue to urge people who have contact with sick or dead birds to take precautions, including wearing respiratory and eye protection and gloves when handling poultry. People who work on farms are considered to be at higher risk.

title: How a surveillance company pitched itself to Maine police and enlisted officers in the sales effort
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When Flock Safety sought to expand its network of surveillance cameras in Maine last year, a York police officer stepped in.
Detective Sergeant Thomas Cryan was invited to meetings between a Flock salesman and police chiefs in Eliot and Sanford. He talked up Flock on a call with the Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office. He told the salesman when Kennebunk’s chief would come back from vacation and lamented that officials were not keen to get cameras up in Kittery.
As Flock worked to install its automatic license plate readers across Maine over the past two years, the company leaned on local police officers like him for help.
Police across the country have been rapidly deploying Flock cameras, automatic license plate readers that use artificial intelligence and massive databases to help cops identify passing cars. As the technology has spread through police departments, so have legal and privacy concerns.
This year, a firehose of stories from across the country about Flock, including examples of cops tracking their exes and the technology leading police to pursue or arrest the wrong people spurred a nationwide backlash.
York police recently announced plans to take down Flock cameras in response to local pushback, joining other towns in Maine that have moved away from the tech. Residents will vote on whether to ban the cameras on Nov. 3.
Emails obtained by The Maine Monitor, along with documents obtained by the American Civil Liberties Union of Maine, offer a behind-the-scenes look at how the cameras got there: revealing how Flock has marketed directly to Maine police and worked alongside them to sell plate readers as public opinion swung rapidly against them.
Representatives for Flock did not respond to requests for comment or written questions. Cryan and other York Police Department officials did not respond to multiple requests for interviews over the past several months.
Flock markets its cameras as powerful public safety tools that give communities control over the data the cameras gather. The company says it has helped locate thousands of missing people and stolen cars, and has oversight tools built in. But civil rights groups like the ACLU have criticized Flock’s technology in Maine and nationally, arguing that automatic license plate data collection is unconstitutional mass surveillance.
“Flock doesn’t do well when people are watching,” said Michael Kebede, the director of Maine’s ACLU chapter. “Flock does well only when they operate in the shadows, and that, of course, is not how public safety is achieved.”
‘If we had those cameras in town’
Flock salespeople have been cultivating relationships with local police officers in Maine since at least early 2024. When salesman Dan DelGrosso began asking for assistance selling to southern Maine towns, Cryan, the sergeant in York, appeared eager to help.
Cryan discussed Flock cameras with at least six other law enforcement agencies in 2025. Most of the jurisdictions he contacted ultimately did not purchase cameras, though one, Wells Police Department, signed an agreement that allowed its officers to get familiar with the tech and view license plate data collected in other towns. Sanford, which Cyran also contacted, approved Flock cameras but ultimately rescinded that approval under public pressure.
Cryan’s outreach didn’t stop with pitches to area police. He connected a salesman with the owner of a local motel, which overlooks a road the police department hoped to monitor. He also helped facilitate a meeting between a Flock sales rep and a former police chief who was then involved with the town’s parks and recreation board. That introduction led the company to make an $11,000 proposal for cameras on Short Sands Beach, though the plan ultimately went nowhere.
At the Freeport Police Department, Flock’s main booster was Detective Beck Rice, who met with a sales manager as early as February 2024, according to documents obtained by the ACLU. Rice did not respond to repeated requests for an interview.
According to an email from a Flock salesman, Rice had said he anticipated Flock would face “some hurdles” from the town council. So the salesman introduced Rice to Flock’s director of municipal engagement. He asked the director to schedule “a couple prep calls” with Rice.
It’s not clear what became of Flock’s pitch in 2024, but the next April, Rice went to the town manager, Sophia Wilson, and asked for a meeting to “educate” council members.
“A majority of my cases require me spending hours collecting video footage and then hours combing through the video footage,” he wrote. “If we had those cameras in town, I would be able to quickly identify my suspect vehicle, which would cut down on further crimes occurring if they are located quickly.”
“Once criminals know we have these cameras, it will deter them from coming into town,” he added.
Wilson replied that the councilors were aware of the benefits Flock could bring to the department but were concerned about data privacy. She suggested trying again after addressing the council’s privacy concerns.
Nearly a year after Freeport rejected Rice’s plea for Flock funding, the company offered cameras for free.
In February 2026, resistance to Flock was emerging nationwide. DelGrosso, the salesperson who had cultivated a relationship with Cryan in York, invited Rice to a video call. He offered to enroll Freeport in “Project Prove It,” which would allow its police department full use of Flock cameras for one or two months as a free trial, with no commitment.
Free trials and bundling deals are common in police technology sales nationwide and can allow controversial tech to get a foothold in communities without requiring approval from elected officials. The strategy has already been used in Maine towns testing out AI-powered police reports.
Flock has used the strategy in many places, though most Maine towns appear not to have been offered such free trials. Company salespeople bought police officers lunch and invited them to Flock’s annual conference in Georgia. At least one, Deputy Chief Jeff Pardue of Falmouth, attended that conference in 2025; taxpayers footed the bill for his lodging and flights.
Freeport did not ultimately accept the offer of free cameras, though the strategy has worked outside Maine. Texas Christian University criminology professor Johnny Nhan said users say Flock is “like Costco or drug dealers.”
“They’ll give you a free sample, some free cameras, and then you get kind of hooked on it,” Nhan said. “Once they get that, then it’s contract time.”
‘I’m not here to promote’
Across the country, Flock has coached police on how to sell its cameras to an increasingly skeptical public and sometimes sells its tech alongside officers. In Wells, DelGrosso was joined by then-Police Chief Jo-Ann Putnam and another police officer to pitch Flock to the select board in August 2025.
“If you want to solve crime, you gotta go with the wave of the future,” Putnam told the board.
When a select board member raised privacy concerns, Wells Town Manager Michael Pardue, a former police chief who had been in touch with DelGrosso for weeks, jumped in to defend Flock.
“The expectation of privacy is nil if we’re not looking at people,” he said while DelGrosso nodded. “I’m not here to promote one way or the other. I’m very interested of the concerns of the public … but I am comforted by the fact we’re on camera all the time now, anyway. Everyone knows, if you’ve got a cell phone in your pocket, we know where you are.”
The team had come prepared for the select board’s scrutiny. DelGrosso had invited Michael Pardue, Putnam and other police officers to a virtual “presentation review” meeting the week prior.
The town manager told The Monitor it’s not unusual to meet with vendors ahead of a presentation to the select board. Putnam, now retired, could not be reached for comment.
“Oftentimes it’s important to me to know what it’s about and some of the intricacies so that, if I’m asked questions, I’m not blind to what the topic is,” Michael Pardue said in an interview. He said he wasn’t a stalwart supporter of Flock cameras, but he wanted town leadership to evaluate how the new technology could help.
With multiple members expressing skepticism, the board decided to discuss the tech further at a future workshop. But it would never be scheduled, despite prodding from DelGrosso.
‘Get ahead of the big brother is watching us portion’
Taige Foley loved vacationing in Ogunquit, he told the resort town’s police chief, John Lizanecz, in a June 2024 introduction email. The salesman said he was visiting soon and wanted to buy the department lunch.
By the next summer, DelGrosso had taken over the Ogunquit account. He’d discussed sensible locations for a pair of cameras as an “initial deployment” and sent over a contract for Lizanecz to sign.
Talks hit a sticking point that July. Two cameras with a traffic analytics package would cost Ogunquit $8,200. Lizanecz explained that any expenditure over $5,000 would require town manager Matthew Buttrick’s approval. DelGrosso suggested a shortcut.
“I can split the cameras into two different contracts so that both items are less than $5,000, which could bypass the [Town Manager’s] approval,” he said.
Lizanecz thanked him. “I did think of that, but overall, it’s up to him as he approves these no matter what,” he said.
In any case, DelGrosso’s window of opportunity in Ogunquit closed quickly. Within days, Lizanecz informed him that there would likely be protests against the rollout and asked for advice.
“We are ok with funding but just want to get ahead of the big brother is watching us portion,” he wrote to DelGrosso.
The salesman was under pressure to get Ogunquit’s contract signed.
DelGrosso explained that “leadership eyes” were on him after he sent out the contract, and he pushed hard for a signature by the end of the month. Lizanecz appears to have stopped replying as that deadline approached.
On July 30, the town manager sent Lizanecz a memo outlining why he would decline to authorize a contract with Flock over concerns about privacy, data retention and public trust.
“Given the State of Maine’s well-documented hesitancy to allow speed enforcement cameras, stop sign cameras, and its statutory limitations on the use of police-mounted ALPRs, I believe Maine may be among the first to enact state-level restrictions, or outright bans, on this form of surveillance,” he predicted.
Changes coming?
Across the state, Flock cameras are going offline. South Portland pulled its cameras in June. Falmouth said it removed its Flock cameras at the summer’s end.
As public angst over Flock builds, the company is pivoting. In marketing emails received by Wells officials in August 2026, Flock recommended just seven days of data retention, as opposed to the 21-day legal maximum followed in Maine towns. The company is also rolling out an “audit assistance” tool that flags unusual usage of Flock and will require case codes for all searches by police by the end of the year.
“These changes reflect years of work and deliberation,” said the email, signed by Flock’s CEO Garrett Langley. “They are not the end of that work, but simply the continuation of our commitment to both safety and privacy. We are not perfect, so we will keep listening, improving, and building a better standard for public safety technology together.”
In Falmouth, police requested that Flock take down its four cameras at the summer’s end. The department had decided instead to use readers from a competitor, Axon.
Jeff Pardue, deputy chief of the Falmouth Police Department, said that police had found the readers helpful but were not using the system to search for plates in other jurisdictions, one of Flock’s main selling points. In July, the town signed a 10-year contract for Axon to place its own cameras in the same four locations.
Jeff Pardue said that under the department’s policies and new contract, Falmouth’s camera data will not be shared as part of a database.
“We have supervisors who have their hands on the wheel,” he said. “We are making sure that we do not violate the trust that the public has put in us.”
Axon is familiar to many Maine police departments: The company manufactures Tasers and body cameras. Motorola also has automated license plate readers in Maine; Hancock County activated 13 of them in August.
In York, a “yes” vote on Nov. 3’s “Stop ALPRs” referendum would make it difficult for any of these companies to get a plate reader back up in town. The ordinance language would require any future readers to be approved by town residents.
Broader regulation may be coming soon. State Rep. David Boyer, a Republican of Poland, is aiming to introduce a broad ban on automatic license plate readers in the next legislative session. With conservative and liberal parts of the state alike pushing against the tech, the bill is likely to gain support in Augusta.
Maine’s ACLU has worked with Boyer and with activists in York to limit surveillance. Kebede, the chapter’s director, said the broad discontent over Flock is an unusual point of unity in American politics.
“People generally don’t want to live in a police state,” he said. “People generally don’t want to live in a tech dystopia, but that’s where Flock and companies like Flock want to take us. And whenever people learn about that, they want to stop it.”
Daniel O’Connor is a Report for America corps member who covers rural government as part of the partnership between The Maine Monitor and the Bangor Daily News, with additional support from BDN and Monitor readers.

title: Savannah Guthrie renews plea for information in mother's disappearance
text:
'We cry out for answers': Savannah Guthrie renews plea for information in mother's disappearance
Savannah Guthrie continues to seek information surrounding her mother's disappearance, issuing a new post on social media in an effort to bring her mother home.
The "Today" show host made a post on Instagram Sunday, sharing an old drawing from her daughter, which had the words "I know it might not seem like it but, I really need my mommy," written on it.
When talking about the drawing, Savannah said, "It says so much about how I feel. The world goes on, things appear 'normal' - as we try to keep going and be strong, especially for our young kids - but it’s not and it never will be."
The 54-year-old said her family still "aches" for her mother, Nancy, 84, who went missing nine months ago from her home in Tucson, Arizona.
Authorities reviewed a possible new ransom note in September. Officials later said the message was "not credible."
"We ache for her, we cry out for answers, we cannot move forward. We need someone to help us, tell us what you know," Savannah said in the post. "Our mom was a light in this world. We want to celebrate her and give her the dignity she deserves. Please. We are begging you. Please help us.”
Savannah reminded people that a $1 million reward remains available.
Related video: Savannah Guthrie offers up to $1 million reward for information leading to Nancy Guthrie being found
According to the Pima County Sheriff's Department—which has been investigating the case— said it's continuing to work with its labs in hopes of furthering DNA analysis in the investigation.
"Earlier this month, investigators traveled to Florida to meet with lab scientists to see what more could be done to advance the case," the department said. "A number of ideas were discussed, and we continue to work with all of our partners to solve this case."
Savannah concluded her post, saying, "Thank you to all those who have been kind and shown the best of humanity. Join us in praying without ceasing."

title: Popular children’s snack recalled nationwide over choking risk, FDA warns
text:
Popular children’s snack recalled nationwide over choking risk, FDA warns
A popular children's snack has been recalled nationwide, with federal officials warning of a "potentially fatal choking hazard."
The Food and Drug Administration is warning families not to buy or serve Once Upon a Farm’s Tractor Wheels soft-baked bars after reports that toddlers choked on them.
The agency said it received several reports involving children ages 1½ to 2½ who suffered complete airway blockages and could not breathe.
Above video | Recalls explained: How to stay ahead of recalls
The bars can reportedly form a dry, sticky mass when chewed, federal officials said, which may be difficult to dislodge with back blows or the Heimlich maneuver. Some incidents required emergency responders and hospital observation.
Once Upon a Farm said it is voluntarily recalling the bars after receiving three consumer complaints.
The company is working with the FDA and says no other Once Upon a Farm products are affected.
The recall covers all flavors, package sizes, lot codes and expiration dates of Tractor Wheels bars. The flavors are apple, sweet potato and spinach; strawberry, pumpkin and beet; and banana, pumpkin and cauliflower.
The bars were sold nationwide online and through retailers including Costco, Target and Walmart. The company said they were distributed in 47 states and Puerto Rico, and may also have been sold by third-party vendors.
The FDA advises consumers to throw the bars away immediately. Once Upon a Farm says customers can return them to the place of purchase for a full refund or contact the company at care@uponafarm.com. For more information on the recall, click here.

title: Judge dismisses lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska Senate race if GOP incumbent loses
text:
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — A federal judge on Sunday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses, the latest development in a ballot controversy that has roiled the final days of one of the nation’s most closely watched races.
Sullivan, an ally of President Donald Trump, faces Democrat Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman, in a race that is among a handful expected to determine which party controls the Senate for the final two years of Trump’s term.
Tuesday’s ranked-choice election also includes two candidates who have done little campaigning, one of whom shares the incumbent’s name. It was that candidate’s presence on the ballot that prompted Trump to push for the lawsuit out of fear he would siphon votes from the incumbent.
Shortly after the ruling, the Justice Department filed a notice that it would appeal: “Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” a department spokesperson said in a statement.
The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the election and as early voting was underway, called for an investigation into whether votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan were intended for the senator. The state said the case lacked merit and argued there would be no way to determine that without violating voter privacy.
U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason said the relief the federal government sought was “infeasible” because many voters have already cast their ballots.
“More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified ‘investigation’ of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” she wrote.
Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee argued that the case lacked any legal basis and amounted to election interference.
“Today’s ruling is a victory for democracy and a clear message to Donald Trump and Senate Republicans: No one, no matter how powerful, can toss out free and fair elections just because they don’t like the result,” said the committee’s executive director, Devan Barber.
Peltola’s campaign hailed the ruling. “No sham investigation or baseless lawsuit from a weaponized Department of Justice is going to stop Alaskans from electing Mary on Nov. 3 so she can lower costs for Alaska’s working families,” the campaign said in a statement, alluding to a federal probe disclosed after President Donald Trump said last week that he wanted Peltola prosecuted for the scheme.
Attorneys for the state did not immediately return messages seeking comment.
Senator says he expects ‘to lose a lot of votes’ to the other Dan Sullivan
The senator and his allies, including Trump, for months have portrayed Dan J. Sullivan as a sham candidate intent on confusing voters and helping Peltola.
Earlier Sunday, Sen. Sullivan told CNN that he thought the presence of the second Sullivan on the ballot would affect the election.
“I’m sure I’m going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery,” he said.
He also said he doubted claims by Peltola that she had no idea her top political aides were involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to run as a way to confuse voters.
“There is no way this went on for a year that they weren’t informing her,” Sullivan told CNN’s “State of the Union.” “She got caught lying, and she’s still lying to the Alaskan people, the media, to all of us.”
In the week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign was involved in efforts to recruit the second Sullivan. Shortly after entering the race in June, Dan J. Sullivan said he’d had no contact with her campaign about running. He has not responded to multiple messages over the past few days.
His recent public absence prompted a social media post Sunday by the president: “The Fake Daniel J. Sullivan, Jr., has DISAPPEARED! Nobody can find him, including Law Enforcement.”
Peltola’s campaign responded to the Times story by saying it had no involvement in the campaigns for either Sullivan: “I am not interested in tricking voters,” Peltola said during a recent campaign event.
In its statement indicating its plans to appeal, the Justice Department said the federal judge dismissed the case on procedural grounds but did not dispute the government’s argument that Dan J. Sullivan entered the race “as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters.”
Multiple investigations look into whether Dan J. Sullivan was recruited as a decoy candidate
State courts, including the Alaska Supreme Court, rejected an earlier Republican-backed effort to block the retired teacher from the August open primary ballot on which he appeared as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. The senator was listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent.
Both Sullivans appear the same way on the general election ballot. Peltola placed first in the primary, followed by the senator. Dan J. Sullivan received about 2.5% of the primary vote, but that was enough to finish within the top four and qualify for the Nov. 3 ranked-choice election.
Attorneys for the Alaska Department of Law represented state elections officials in the case and asked Gleason, who was appointed by former Democratic President Barack Obama, to toss the lawsuit. They filed a scathing response to the federal government’s complaint, calling it “meritless.”
Alaska also said the state had taken “significant steps” to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. Voters who still might be confused could ask for help or look up candidate biographies and other information in state-distributed election pamphlets.
Republicans, including ones working with Trump, also have a long history of backing decoy candidates in elections. The governor, a Republican, has ordered an investigation and suggested he may not certify a possible Peltola victory.
In her ruling, Gleason wrote that the Trump administration’s attempt to block certification ran counter to the Constitution, which gives states the authority to run elections. She also cited the Supreme Court’s Purcell principle, which holds that federal courts should generally not change election rules too close to an election.
Kristen Clarke, general counsel of the NAACP, which had filed a brief supporting the case’s dismissal, called the judge’s decision “a big win for the voters in Alaska.”
“The law is clear, and the DOJ’s case was a baseless, eleventh-hour attempt to hijack this midterm election,” she said.
On Thursday, the Justice Department escalated a criminal investigation over the presence of Dan J. Sullivan on the Alaska ballot, issuing a raft of new grand jury subpoenas, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press. The FBI also has begun contacting people who donated to him, some of whom told the AP that the agents were asking if they had been misled about which candidate they were supporting.
___
Riccardi reported from Washington. Associated Press photographer Lindsey Wasson in Anchorage, Alaska, and AP writer Ali Swenson in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Amateur historian’s look into murderous pirate finds New York beach namesake may have helped
text:
WANTAGH, N.Y. (AP) — An amateur historian has stumbled upon a provocative clue to the enduring mystery of what became of a notorious pirate who raided a royal Indian treasure ship centuries ago, implicating a co-conspirator whose name is familiar to many New Yorkers.
James Bailey, who five years ago made headlines after unearthing ancient coins believed to be linked to English pirate Capt. Henry Every, now says that colonial-era documents suggest the “King of the Pirates” and his violent crew got an assist from Thomas Jones, the namesake of Jones Beach, New York’s most visited state park after Niagara Falls.
“You have millions of visitors and generations of New Yorkers going to this beach,” Bailey said. “Nobody knew that he was actually a major player in arguably the biggest heist in the history of piracy.”
Since his big find, Bailey has pored through documents to dig even deeper into the bloody 1695 raid of the Ganj-i-Sawai on the Red Sea and the mystery of what happened to Every.
The pirate crew is said to have tortured, killed and raped those aboard the royal ship, sparking global outrage and what is considered the first worldwide manhunt. Some were caught and executed, but many others, including Every, were never heard from again and are believed to have scattered to Europe and the American colonies.
Documents, including depositions from Every’s associates, suggest Jones was recruited to serve as a “wheelman,” helping the pirates evade authorities after they made off with tens of millions of dollars’ worth of gold and silver, according to Bailey.
Other documents show that New York’s governor, charged by the British crown to crack down on piracy, investigated Jones years later after he’d remade himself as the wealthy proprietor of a whaling operation on the barrier beach on Long Island that now bears his name.
Ghost stories and tall tales after Jones’ death
Bailey’s research, which he hopes to have published, sheds light on a part of Jones’ checkered past long alluded to but never quite fleshed out in local history books, says John Hanc, author of “Jones Beach: An Illustrated History,” which includes a chapter on Jones.
Jones was a major in the English military before moving to the American colonies, initially settling in Rhode Island before eventually becoming a prominent businessman and landowner in New York. Jones owned thousands of acres of land on early Long Island, then just a rural expanse well east of the rapidly growing New York City.
But rumors of how he’d initially made his fortune persisted long after his death in 1713. Before it was demolished in the early 1800s, his crumbling mansion was said to be haunted by ghosts and strange occurrences. Jones’ grave was repeatedly desecrated by robbers searching for buried treasure before it was relocated to a family burial plot behind a nearby church.
A family history published in 1906 by one of Jones’ descendants dismissed the pirate tales as “slander” and “improbable fictions.”
“People were disposed to cast slurs upon his memory, either for mischievousness, or a spirit of malice,” Thomas Floyd-Jones wrote. “These myths were cherished for over a century after his death, which ignorance and superstition did not fail to magnify.”
Was Jones a privateer, a pirate or both?
Hanc and other experts say it wasn’t too far-fetched for Jones to have at least dabbled in piracy.
After serving in the British military, Jones made a career as a privateer, or a seafarer authorized by the English crown to raid the commercial ships of its rivals during wartime, said Meagan Schulman, a Fordham University doctoral candidate who specializes in 17th century piracy and wasn’t involved in Bailey’s research.
But when the conflict ended, privateers like Jones lost their special status, she said. Those that continued the high seas raids were branded pirates.
“The reality was that privateers were pirates, just sponsored by a certain government or patron,” explained Schulman, who grew up going to Jones Beach. “So maybe the short answer is, yes. Jones can be called a pirate, by some people, but he probably did not ever see himself as one.”
After helping Every and his crew evade capture, the documents cited by Bailey show Jones briefly returned to Rhode Island.
Then in 1696, Jones’ father-in-law, Thomas Townsend, a wealthy New Yorker, gifted him and his wife a significant tract of land on Long Island’s south shore, property records show.
Bailey, who recently retired from Rhode Island’s corrections department, posits that allowed Jones a fresh start, as authorities continued to scour pirate-friendly New England for Every and his accomplices.
On Long Island, Bailey says Jones built a homestead and raised a family, but his pirate past was never far behind.
Three years after the Ganj-i-Sawai heist, Richard Coote, New York’s colonial governor, described how one of his efforts to root out piracy had led him to Jones.
Citing witness depositions, the governor wrote in 1698 that a certain “barrel of money” traveled from the city to Long Island, where it ended up at Jones’ house. But Jones, who the governor described as “formerly a pirate,” testified that he knew nothing about the barrel.
Piracy built wealth in colonial America
Bailey’s findings are compelling but shouldn’t be considered conclusive, cautions Richard Blakemore, maritime history professor at the University of Reading in the United Kingdom who also wasn’t involved with Bailey’s work. After all, he said, Thomas Jones is a fairly common name.
If anything, Jones’ possible ties to Every underscore how piracy provided “foundational and multi-generational wealth” for many of the prominent families in the Northeast, says Kevin McDonald, a history professor at Loyola Marymount University in Los Angeles who wrote a book about colonial-era piracy but wasn’t involved in Bailey’s research.
“Popular images of pirates show them as outcasts, but many historians have argued the opposite, based on evidence like this,” agreed Blakemore. “It may surprise readers to find just how much early British colonies were both socially and economically connected to piracy.”

title: Doctors prescribe GLP-1 drugs to some children for weight loss
text:
(Aging Untold) — BATON ROUGE, La. — Weight-loss drugs known as GLP-1s, which are popular with adults, are now being prescribed for some children, according to Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician and Aging Untold host.
Students learn healthy habits
Students at Magnolia Woods Elementary in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, are learning about healthy eating and exercise as part of a statewide push to lower obesity rates.
When lifestyle changes are not enough
For some children, healthy eating and exercise are not enough, Rogers said.
“Sometimes that just move more and eat less is not enough because you have genetics and all that,” Rogers said. “And then really, when you get too big, that’s a hormonal dysregulation.”
Rogers said “GLP-1 agonists” are “huge in terms of getting rid of that food noise, that food noise and food chatter.” She said they are also “anti-inflammatory.”
“Some people just need a little bit more help because of that hormonal dysregulation,” Rogers said.
Who may be a candidate
The age requirement for diabetes patients can be 10 and up.
Experts also say the ideal candidate for a GLP-1 for weight loss has a BMI at or above the 95th percentile, and lifestyle changes alone have not worked. This includes patients who have developed hormone problems requiring medical intervention.
“It’s not a miracle drug — it’s a tool, and so you have to treat the whole entire scenario,” Rogers said.
Cost remains a barrier
The price of GLP-1s remains a barrier for many families.
For patients who cannot afford medication or choose not to take any, the option for now is well-balanced meals and a healthy lifestyle.

title: Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu and Caleb Durbin of Red Sox win Gold Gloves
text:
ST. LOUIS — First basemen Christian Walker of Houston and Matt Olson of Atlanta won their fourth Gold Gloves on Sunday while Boston right fielder Wilyer Abreu won the fielding honor for the third year in a row.
The Red Sox and Arizona tied for the high with three Gold Glove winners each. Red Sox center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela earned the honor for the second straight season and third baseman Caleb Durbin was a first-time winner.
Diamondbacks catcher Gabriel Moreno won his second Gold Glove, his first since 2023, while shortstop Geraldo Perdomo and right fielder Corbin Carroll were first-time winners.
Walker added to Gold Gloves he won in 2022, ‘23 and ’24. Olson also earned the honor in 2018, ‘19 and ’25.
Braves utility man Mauricio Dubón won his third Gold Glove after 2023 and ’25.
Other second-time winners included Chicago Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman and center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong; New York Yankees left fielder Cody Bellinger; Detroit catcher Dillon Dingler; and Milwaukee second baseman Brice Turang.
Additional first-time winners included Cleveland pitcher Tanner Bibee; Milwaukee left fielder Jackson Chourio; Texas utility man Ezequiel Duran; New York Mets pitcher Nolan McLean; Tampa Bay shortstop Tanner Walls’ and Seattle second baseman Cole Young.
Voting was conducted among managers and up to six coaches from each team, who can’t select players on their own club. Since 2013, voting has been factored with a Society for American Baseball Research defensive index, which comprises about 25% of the total.
The utility category is based on a SABR formula and additional defensive statistics.
Walker earned a $75,000 bonus for winning the honor, Bibee $50,000 and Turang $25,000.

title: Ex-Cleveland Guardians pitchers, including star reliever, go to trial in New York on fraud charges
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Former Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz go to trial Monday on charges that they accepted bribes as they colluded with gamblers who made hundreds of thousands of dollars betting correctly on individual pitches.
Their careers and possibly their freedom are at stake in the jury trial expected to unfold over the next month in Brooklyn federal court. Several professional baseball players, including catchers and baseball executives, are among witnesses expected to testify.
Clase, the Guardians’ former closer, and Ortiz, a starter, have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges and are on nondisciplinary leave from the club without pay while their fate is determined.
According to an indictment, the pitchers accepted several thousand dollars in payoffs to help two gamblers from their native Dominican Republic win at least $460,000 on in-game prop bets on the speed and outcome of certain pitches.
Prosecutors allege that Clase began providing the bettors with information about his pitches in 2023 and recruited Ortiz into the scheme in 2025. Lawyers for Ortiz unsuccessfully sought to have Ortiz tried separately from Clase.
Judge Kiyo A. Matsumoto said at a conference Friday that she hopes to complete jury selection quickly enough that lawyers can deliver relatively short opening statements in the afternoon.
Clase, 28, is a three-time All-Star and two-time American League Reliever of the Year who had completed his fourth season of a $20 million, five-year contract when charges against the pitchers were revealed in November 2025.
Ortiz, 27, had earned $782,600 as a starting pitcher for the Guardians during the 2025 season.
The pitchers have been charged with wire fraud conspiracy, honest services wire fraud conspiracy, money laundering conspiracy and conspiracy to influence sporting contests by bribery.
Defense lawyers are expected to argue that the pitchers did not collude with gamblers and instead were varying the placement of pitches strategically to fool batters.
On Friday, the judge ruled that prosecutors cannot show the jury proof that Clase owed $500,000 in U.S. taxes because they had only provided the evidence to defense lawyers several days earlier and long after a deadline had passed to turn over evidence to their adversaries.
A prosecutor had argued that the government wanted to put the evidence in the trial to offset any claim by Clase’s lawyers that he had no incentive to collude with gamblers because he had several million dollars in financial accounts in the Dominican Republic.
Major League Baseball and the Guardians have both said they’ve fully cooperated with authorities. MLB has said it contacted federal law enforcement when it began investigating unusual betting activity.

title: 1 dead, 3 injured after shooting at youth football championship game
text:
MADISON, Ill. (First Alert 4/Gray News) - One person died and three others were injured after a shooting at a youth football championship game Sunday night, authorities said.
The shooting occurred at Madison Senior High School around 9:50 p.m. during a football game unrelated to the school.
The three injured victims were taken to local hospitals, while the fourth victim died on scene.
The Major Case Squad of Greater St. Louis is handling the investigation into the shooting. Law enforcement is looking for witnesses and anyone else with information to come forward.
“Someone in that crowd saw something, recorded something, or has heard something since. We are asking those people to come forward,” said Lt. Andrew Pierson, public information officer for the Major Case Squad. “You do not have to have the whole story, a single photo, a short video, or one detail you think is insignificant may be exactly what moves this investigation forward.”
The school district canceled Monday classes and said they will resume Wednesday.
The district released a statement saying it “is deeply saddened by the shooting” and that while the game was not organized or sponsored by the district, “this violence affects our entire school community.”
Counseling and support services will be offered to students and staff.
Authorities ask anyone with information to contact the command post at 618-709-7750 or CrimeStoppers at 866-371-8477.

title: Portland’s Minibar closes after a year in business
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Minibar, an indoor mini-golf course and sports bar on Marginal Way in Portland, closed Sunday, Nov. 1, after a year in business.
Owner Kevin Moschella cited financial challenges, which he said make continuing operations unsustainable.
Moschella announced the closure in an Instagram post on Friday, Oct. 30, saying he fought to avoid closing but hopes another operator might take over the venue and keep the business going.
“Economic challenges have made it impossible for the business to continue in its current state,” he said.
Located at 270 Marginal Way in Portland’s East Bayside neighborhood, Minibar opened in October 2025 in the former World Gym space. The 15,000-square-foot venue combined an 18-hole indoor mini golf course, a restaurant and a course-side bar.
During its year in business, the venue hosted more than 70,000 rounds of mini golf and hundreds of private events, corporate outings and community fundraisers.
Moschella thanked employees, customers, business partners and community members who supported the business, describing the run as a memorable experience despite the challenges.
“The decision to close is a difficult one, and something I fought hard to avoid down to the last few days, but I don’t regret the decision to open minibar,” said Moschella.

title: Pingree, Charles make final push in Maine governor’s race
text:
(WABI) - Maine gubernatorial candidates Hannah Pingree and Bobby Charles are making their final pushes across the state one day before the election.
WABI caught up with Pingree in Orono and Charles in Ellsworth. Both spoke about their platforms, the importance of voting, and the current stakes of the race for governor. Both candidates are also expecting a huge voter turnout.
“We know that there are hundreds of thousands of Maine people who haven’t voted yet. Reminding them the stakes of this election, reminding them how important the governor’s race is, but also the races up and down the ballot. I will say the good news is that people are fired up. They are concerned about what’s happening in this country. They’re concerned about health care, the price of housing, the price of heating oil this winter. They want a governor; they want leaders who will show up,” said Pingree.
“Only two things really matter, affordability and accountability. So, what am I learning in all these 16 counties confirmation over and over again that affordability and accountability are what people want, that they are turning out in huge numbers, that tomorrow we should have a record turnout. And I’m just going to ask everybody -- please go vote,” said Charles.
Independent Rick Bennett did not have any public appearances scheduled Monday.
According to a new poll put out by The New York Times and Siena -- Pingree has a 12-point lead over Charles, 49 to 37 percent. Bennett received 8-percent support.
In October’s Pine Tree Poll put out today, Pingree leads Charles 51 to 40 percent. Bennett secured 7-percent support.

title: Sanford man pleads guilty in connection with four shootings over drug debts
text:
Sanford man pleads guilty in connection with four shootings over drug debts
Federal officials say Benjamin Ball fired into a Lebanon home while residents were sleeping and conspired to carry out additional shootings
Sanford man pleads guilty in connection with four shootings over drug debts
Federal officials say Benjamin Ball fired into a Lebanon home while residents were sleeping and conspired to carry out additional shootings
A Sanford man has pleaded guilty to federal firearm charges in connection with four shootings in York County over drug debts, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office.
Benjamin Ball, 31, fired a 9mm pistol into a home in Lebanon on the evening of Jan. 3, 2024, over a drug-debt-related issue, according to court records.
Prosecutors say Ball fired the gun from the passenger seat of a vehicle as it drove past the home.
The shooting was captured on a motion-activated security camera from a house across the street. Authorities say the residents of the home were inside and asleep at the time.
Ball also conspired with others to carry out additional shootings at the Lebanon home and another shooting at a home in Acton, according to prosecutors.
Authorities say the shootings involved a 9mm pistol, a 12-gauge shotgun and an AR-15. At the time of the shootings, Ball had been convicted of several felonies and was prohibited from possessing firearms.
He faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years in prison for discharging a firearm during a drug trafficking crime.
He also faces up to 20 years in prison on each of the remaining counts.
Two co-conspirators, Jason Fernald, 47, and Evan Chapman, 28, previously pleaded guilty to their involvement in the shootings.
A sentencing date has not been announced.
The York County Sheriff's Office and the FBI's Southern Maine Gang Task Force investigated the case, with assistance from several local, state and federal agencies.
