title: Día de Muertos blends tradition, art, and remembrance
text:
Día de Muertos blends tradition, art, and remembrance
Día de Muertos, or Day of the Dead, is a vibrant tradition that honors loved ones who have passed away through rituals, art, and remembrance.
New Mexico state historian Rob Martinez described the event as transformative. "It's a celebration that takes something that could sometimes be kind of scary and turns it into something beautiful and festive," Martinez said.
The tradition has deep historical roots. Indigenous communities in what is now Mexico held ceremonies honoring the dead, and over time, these customs intertwined with religious observances. "It's actually an amalgamation of multiple cultures," one participant explained. While celebrated across Mexico, different regions have unique ways of observing Día de Muertos.
Central to the celebration are ofrendas, or altars, which feature photos of deceased family members and items they enjoyed during their lives. "You put your family members' pictures on the altar, and then you also want to put things that they liked during their living time," one participant said. Bright orange cempasúchil, or marigold flowers, are often used to guide spirits back home. "In Mexico, they have the marigold flowers to lead the spirits of our dead ancestors to their favorite foods. You put out plates of tamales, bowls of posole, mole in Mexico," Martinez said.
The festivities take place on Nov. 1 and 2, a time when some believe the veil between the living and the dead is thin, allowing spirits to return. "During that time, the veil is thin, and it's an opportunity for our ancestors to come back and visit us," one participant said.
Face painting has become a modern aspect of Día de Muertos. An artist shared her self-taught approach to creating intricate designs inspired by traditional calaveras, or skulls. "I'm kind of self-taught. I saw somebody on Instagram who looked really cool, and I was like, 'I want to do that,' and then I just taught myself," Zamora said. "When you're doing muertos makeup, it's important to carve out where you're not gonna put the white so that you can get really crisp colors," she added. She emphasized the importance of cultural awareness when expressing oneself through art. "Just to have a little cultural awareness, make sure you're not doing anything offensive or derogatory or culturally insensitive, but really just follow your heart and have fun in creating your canvas," Zamora said.
Zamora views the art as a way to confront mortality. "If we can start seeing death as a friend, a next chapter in life, a place of rest, and not as a villain, we can slowly but surely come to terms with it's just the next part of life, and it's beautiful," she said. "One day death is coming for all of us, but it doesn't have to completely destroy us."
Sugar skulls are another iconic element of Día de Muertos. Historically, indigenous communities used amaranth flower and honey to mold skeletons and other figures representing death. "They will take amaranth and honey or amaranth flower and honey. And they would mold them into different skeletons or calacas or different things that represented death," one participant said. During Spanish colonial rule, sugar-paste techniques were introduced and adapted into calaveritas, which are now used to decorate ofrendas.
In Old Town Albuquerque, Debbie Ball, owner of The Candy Lady, makes close to a thousand sugar skulls for Día de Muertos celebrations each year. "When would you say that you start making your sugar skulls?" Ball said. "July or August," she answered. For her creations, she uses two pounds of sugar, a third of a cup of meringue powder, and about eight tablespoons of water, added gradually. "It's like wet sand. If you've ever done wet sand, you want to be able to pack it in a mold and let it dry, and it will look like that mold. If it's too wet, it'll be drippy. It will never look good. If it's too dry, it will fall apart," Ball said.
Once the sugar mixture is ready, it is packed into molds and left to dry. "You're gonna put it in, and you're gonna push it down as hard as you can. Basically, it's just messy. I like messy," Ball said. The drying process typically takes 48 to 72 hours for flat molds.
Decorating the sugar skulls allows for personal creativity and remembrance. "That's basically what they're for, is to honor the dead," Ball said. Designs can reflect the personality of the deceased or the artist's imagination.
For many, Día de Muertos is a way to keep loved ones close.
It's hard to feel like somebody is fully gone. But if you get them one day a year, they are never gone. You get to have them there with you.

title: Trump spends the day before midterm Election Day promoting his Reflecting Pool makeover
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — As Republicans and Democrats were making their final pitch to voters on the eve of Election Day, President Donald Trump opted to forgo the campaign trail and instead focused on his renovations at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, drawing attention to an expensive, problem-plagued repair job in a place far away from most of the people his party wants to persuade.
It was an unusual closing argument for Republicans to keep control of Congress. But it conforms with the way the president has devoted considerable time, attention and money in his second term on beautifying his Washington surroundings.
Trump, wearing a white “USA” hat, even seemed to admit that he had spent much of his time focused on improving the capital city.
“We have a lot of great things planned for Washington, and I could get into the nation, but for that, you don’t have enough time,” Trump said.
Instead of focusing on issues voters have said they’re worried about, Trump dedicated a large portion of his remarks to his D.C. makeover and the pool, announcing its official reopening, joking that he wanted to name it after himself, and repeating his false claims that the repair work he ordered was vandalized.
After he finished his remarks on Monday, Trump’s stood silently while triumphant music played and he held up a poster with an image of the previously algae-clogged pool. It was his last public appearance before Election Day.
Democrats, for their part, were spending the last 24 hours before Election Day making their case in areas where Republicans have long dominated, while trying to contain the fallout from a messy intraparty split in Michigan. Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed was brushing aside concerns that his prospects could be hurt after his former primary opponent threw her support behind his Republican opponent Mike Rogers.
In addition to giving the speech on Monday afternoon, Trump also was scheduled to participate in nine telerallies for Republicans, where he uses brief remarks on a mass phone call to plead for voters’ support.
Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, hit the campaign trail with more traditional stops in New York and Ohio, where Republicans were fighting for House and Senate seats.
Trump touts renovations as voters worry about the economy
The Reflecting Pool, a long, narrow basin at the foot of the Lincoln Memorial, is one of Washington’s most iconic sites. Martin Luther King, Jr. famously gave his “I Have a Dream” speech from the steps of the memorial in 1963, looking out over the pool.
But this summer it became a focus of Trump’s attention, with the president frequently speaking about his plans for the shallow pool on social media, at the White House and beyond. He displayed posters about the project in the Oval Office and even had his motorcade drive him over the resurfaced pool before it was refilled.
The pool was soon clogged with algae blooms, and its “American-flag blue” liner began peeling and floating up in chunks. The Justice Department charged former Olympian David Hearn with intentionally damaging the Reflecting Pool but then dropped the case this summer after determining he was not responsible.
But the president continues to repeat false claims that vandalism — rather than shoddy workmanship — was to blame for a new blue surface peeling away.
On the platform where he spoke Monday, signs were hanging that said “Restoring Our Capitol” and “The Reflecting Pool.” A poster perched on a display board showed the reflecting pool under the words, “Back, and more beautiful than ever!”
He waxed on about the particular color blue he selected to have the bottom of the pool painted, the kinds of grass and types of columns he had selected for repairs around Washington, and held up a series of blown-up images of rusted pipes taken during the renovation process.
He then started repeating some of his midterm elections pitch, defending his record and attacking Democratic nominees, before eventually turning back to the pool.
The president’s message in the closing days of the midterm campaign was similarly detached from voters’ concerns about the high cost of living. He’s called affordability a “hoax” while boasting to audiences far from the nation’s capital about his renovations of the reflecting pool and the White House, along with repeatedly praising the physiques of the GOP’s nominees.
Vance stuck closer to the party message as he campaigned Monday in Rome, New York. As he campaigned for Republican House candidates Kailee Buller and Anthony Constantino, he touted Trump’s moves to end taxes on tips and overtime and secure the border while branding Democrats as “lunatics” who have contempt for American voters.
Democrats try to flip Republican-favored seats while grappling with fractures
Democratic candidates were working to capitalize on widespread disaffection over high prices, the fallout from Trump’s war with Iran and historical trends that typically favor the party out of power in midterm elections.
In places like Iowa, where voters have not elected a Democratic governor in two decades, Democrat Rob Sand was asking canvassers knocking on doors to help break that streak.
“This is it,” said Sand, who faces Republican Zach Lahn. ”We have 30-whatever hours to change the direction of the state of Iowa.”
He was appearing with Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, who cited his own races as proof that a Democrat can win over Trump-backed candidates in states like his own and Iowa.
In Michigan, Democrats deal with fallout from a dramatic split
Democrats in Michigan — a key state in their efforts to try to retake the Senate — were trying to keep their coalition together after a shock on Sunday when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens announced she would back the GOP candidate instead of her party’s nominee, appearing at a church service with Mike Rogers.
Stevens — who lost in the primary to Abdul El-Sayed — is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. He has also been criticized for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker.
El-Sayed, who campaigned on Monday with fellow Michigan Democrat Debbie Dingell and Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, told supporters worried that Stevens’ endorsement could hurt him that “If we’re nervous about where we’re going to go from here, go vote.”

title: Indiana governor says execution will go ahead Thursday against man who killed 2 kids
text:
Indiana’s governor turned down a clemency request Monday and said an execution planned for this week would go forward for a man who set a fire that killed his girlfriend’s two children in 2010.
Gov. Mike Braun said he would follow the Indiana Parole Board’s recommendation to let the death sentence stand for Jeffrey Weisheit.
“The Indiana Department of Correction will continue preparations to carry out the court-ordered sentence of execution” Thursday, said Braun, a Republican.
Weisheit, 50, had a right under Indiana law to ask Braun to reduce the death sentence to a life sentence for his murder and arson convictions.
Weisheit acknowledged his crimes during an Oct. 16 public hearing but said he wanted to live and improve the lives of other people in prison.
The remains of 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and 5-year-old Caleb Lynch were recovered from the ruins of a fire at their home in the Evansville area.
Alyssa’s body was in a closet. Caleb’s body was on a mattress, restrained with duct tape. A railroad flare was in his underwear and another was under his body.
The children’s mother, Lisa Lynch, was at work at the time. She was in a relationship with Weisheit but it was breaking down, investigators said.
Weisheit’s lawyers say he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems that didn’t get enough attention at his 2013 trial. Separately, his legal team has asked the governor to delay the execution and review how the state acquires drugs for lethal injections.
The lawyers said Indiana purchased pentobarbital from a pharmacy that is under scrutiny by the state attorney general. They also cited the recent failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, and Gov. Bill Lee’s decision there to review what happened during the attempted lethal injection.
But Braun spokesperson Griffin Reid said the “process is over.”
“We remain confident in our process and our ability to humanely carry out the lawfully imposed sentence for the murders of two innocent children,” the Indiana Department of Correction said.
___
This story has been updated to correct the spelling of the last name of governor’s spokesperson to Reid, not Reed.

title: GOP closely watching Iowa and Kansas
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - About 50 million Americans have already cast ballots on the eve of the election, and President Donald Trump spent the weekend campaigning in Iowa and Kansas.
Iowa and Kansas are normally Republican wins, but both are now battlegrounds.
Kansas Senate race
Kansas has not sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in nearly a century. That streak could end Tuesday.
Republican incumbent Roger Marshall released a closing argument video Sunday defending his practices as a doctor, which came under criticism on the campaign trail. Marshall’s staff did not want the video released and worry it may have done more harm than good.

Candidates in Iowa are neck and neck.

“I knew Ashley for a long time and she was a little bit heavier,” Trump said. “But Ashley knew the importance of what this was and how important it was and why she put herself, she went on a regimen. She put herself in shape. She’s in perfect shape.”
Trump went on to say Hinson asked him not to bring that up.
Senate control
Democrats need to net four seats to regain control of the Senate. Both parties see value in winning Iowa and Kansas in particular.

title: ‘Drunk History’ reboot introduces Frances Perkins to a new audience
text:
Amanda Hatch serves as executive director of the Frances Perkins Center in Newcastle.
“Drunk History,” an educational comedy TV series (based on the “Funny or Die” web series of the same name created by Derek Waters in 2007) recently re-debuted as a three-part web series on Comedy Central’s YouTube channel.
The premise? Exactly as it sounds. An inebriated narrator humorously retells an event from history, while guest actors act out the story and lip sync the dialogue.
The result is a comedic, somewhat educational show that combines slurred speech and slapstick moments with elements of truth from history.
The reboot version recently featured Maine’s very own trailblazer Frances Perkins, the first woman to hold a U.S. Cabinet position, played by actress Mae Whitman and narrated by actress and comedian Lisa Gilroy. As executive director of the Frances Perkins Center, an organization dedicated to shining a light on the enduring legacy of Frances Perkins (one that is often overlooked by history books), it was imperative, of course, that I watch it.
My takeaway? The complete silliness that is Gilroy’s vodka-induced anecdotes, played out by a bumbling Franklin D. Roosevelt (Chris Parnell) and an overly zealous Perkins, educate a new audience in an unconventional way — but educates them nevertheless.
The webisode showcases how Perkins, when considering FDR’s job offer for the position of U.S. secretary of labor, accepted only after the president agreed to her list of demands that were radical for the time, including: establishing a minimum wage (“You can’t pay people with a piece of string cheese and a cotton ball anymore!” Gilroy narrates); Social Security (“Old people shouldn’t be slogging and bogging and hogging all day long”); the abolition of child labor (“Are you out of your mind?!”); and a 40-hour work week (“Have you ever heard of: ‘it’s five-o’-clock somewhere?'”).
Incredibly, as suggested in the skit, Perkins not only got this ambitious legislation drafted, but also passed and enacted, thus changing the course of history forever. Similarly, it offers insight into the “boys club” that was the U.S. Cabinet at the time, highlighting how Perkins was not welcomed by some of her male colleagues.
Indeed, as suggested in the Comedy Central webisode, there was an attempt to impeach Perkins. (It does not go into further detail about the matter, which was an attempt by a congressional investigative committee to punish her for refusing to deport a union leader who had been accused of being a communist by his opponents — charges that ultimately failed.)
In the skit’s version of events, Perkins is depicted as bold and confident, and though she was — any woman to fulfill such an ambitious agenda at the time in a male-dominated field would have to be — she differs considerably from Whitman’s and Gilroy’s sassy portrayal (“I’m Frances Perkins. You might not have heard of me, but I don’t [expletive] care!”)
In truth, Perkins was careful to play by the “rules” of the time, to get what she wanted done. She avoided speaking unless spoken to during Cabinet meetings so as not to risk alienating her male colleagues, and adopted a “work uniform” of simple, dark clothes and a tricorn hat to appear serious but not threatening. This ultimately earned her the nickname “Ma Perkins,” which she detested.
Despite these obvious and comedic deviations from history (and the many stories left untold), “Drunk History” shines a light on the life and ongoing legacy of Perkins, in a manner that demands viewers’ attention. In an age when many people, especially younger people, may not unfortunately have the time or patience to read at length about Perkins, it offers a unique way to pique their interest.
My hope is that this sketch will serve as a stepping stone, an invitation to learn more about this remarkable woman who we honor at the Frances Perkins National Monument in Newcastle. I hope viewers will also discover the tragic event that set her tireless advocacy of workers’ rights in motion: witnessing young women jump to their deaths during the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire of 1911. Or how, during World War II, she creatively leveraged her Labor Department position to create the Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) to aid those fleeing Nazi persecution.
You may not have heard of her until now, but I hope you’ll take the time to learn more.
She is, after all, as Gilroy ends in her monologue: “Frances Perrr-errr (‘ruff ‘ruff) –
erkins.”

title: Where Maine's high-profile Senate race stands entering Election Day
text:
Where Maine's high-profile US Senate race stands entering Election Day
The U.S. Senate race in Maine between Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson has picked up national attention, given that it will help determine the balance of power in Congress.
If she is reelected to the Senate for a sixth term, Collins would quickly become the longest-serving U.S. senator from Maine.
"What I bring to the job is, obviously, great knowledge of the Senate, of federal issues, relationships with other senators that enabled me to be effective and to pass legislation," she said.
Jackson has only had just over three months to campaign for Senate, as he was chosen as the Maine Democratic Party's nominee on July 25. A special Senate nominating convention was held just over two weeks after the Democratic primary winner, oyster farmer Graham Platner, dropped out of the race following allegations of sexual assault.
"I didn't think it was going to be me. I'd have been happy to go along, be part of this push to change our government. But the fact that I'm now in this position is really exciting for me," Jackson said.
"This race has been the strangest race that I have ever had in my years running for office," Collins said.
As chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Collins wields power in Washington and has been reminding voters about the federal funding she has delivered to the state of Maine. Millions of dollars have already been appropriated for projects in Maine, and Collins said she wants to bring in more money.
"That has allowed me to bring home to Maine funding for more than 670 projects in every county in this state, and it has made a real difference to so many communities and nonprofits," Collins said. "I'm hoping that there'll be even some more fire stations and equipment for rural hospitals."
Jackson is a proud fifth-generation logger from Allagash who served as president of the Maine Senate (2018-24). He said he will work for Mainers if they send him to Washington.
"If you think that where we are right now is good, then you should vote for Susan Collins," Jackson said. "But if you think your life is spiraling and you can't afford the cost of everything and you want healthcare — universal healthcare — I think you better take a chance on voting for somebody like me."
During his campaign, Jackson has poked holes in Collins' work, tying her to President Donald Trump and saying that she is not using her power in Washington correctly, bringing up her voting record.
"She's powerful toward election time, but she's weak every time that we need her to stand up and fight for us," Jackson said. "She still won't admit that she was wrong in putting Brett Kavanaugh on (the Supreme Court)."
Collins has not backed down and has continued to point to the experience she has over Jackson while questioning his ability to be able to make moves in the nation's capital.
"Time after time, I am ranked as the most bipartisan member of the Senate. I work with members on both sides of the aisle, and that's the way you get things done in Washington," Collins said. "He's wrong on every count, and it shows his lack of knowledge of the Senate. He says that Governor Mills vetoed something like 40 of his bills and that Governor LePage vetoed even more. That's not a sign of working together to get things done."
Since Jackson became the Democratic nominee, it has been months of sparring between him and Collins, including a battle during the Maine's Total Coverage debate on Oct. 8. During the debate, Collins fired back at Jackson after he claimed that the senator and her husband are profiting from the war with Iran.
"That is absolutely outrageous, and you owe me an apology," Collins said.
"No, you owe the apology," Jackson replied.
"To say that my husband and I are making money off the war in Iran is absolutely outrageous," Collins answered.
Political analysts are expecting a nail-biter, as poll after poll shows close margins between the two candidates.

title: Jet crashes into a South Florida neighborhood, killing all 9 on board and leaving a fiery crater
text:
A business jet crashed into a South Florida neighborhood and erupted into a ball of flames, killing all nine people on board and leaving a fiery crater. The cause was not immediately clear, but federal investigators are expected to provide an update Monday.
Video recorded by passersby captured the terrifying moment on Sunday afternoon when the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky before slamming into the ground and exploding in Green Acres, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as shocked residents looked on in horror. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.
“Debris was everywhere. Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire,” Anthony Blackmon, who lives near the crash site, told NBC affiliate WTVJ. “I’ve always seen it on the news, never thought it would happen so close to somebody like how it happened today.”
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed. Authorities have not released the names of the people who died.
Palm Beach County authorities were evacuating about 600 people from a nearby mobile home community while the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board investigate the crash.
Authorities have not provided any information about what caused the Bahamas-bound Learjet 60 to crash. NTSB officials planned to hold a news conference in West Palm Beach on Monday.
The jet began its journey at the Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas, and airport spokesperson Jim Reynolds described it as a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on board.
The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 11 kilometers) when the pilot started to report problems.
The pilot said ice was accumulating on the jet and that turbulence was jolting it by as much as 700 feet (213 meters), according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net. Rain pounded the region on Sunday.
“We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” the pilot told controllers.
The situation rapidly deteriorated.
The pilot requested permission to climb another 2,000 feet (about 610 meters) then quickly declared an emergency as the jet lost altitude at an alarming rate.
“We’re descending 8,000 — mayday, mayday — we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed.
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed, before delivering a devastating acknowledgment of what was about to happen. “We’re going to crash into the ground.”
The plane banked sharply to the right before crashing and exploding.
“It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” DeSantis told reporters at the scene. “It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road.”
___
Taxin reported from Santa Ana, California. Associated Press transportation writer Josh Funk in Gretna, Nebraska, contributed.

title: Family says they found a needle in son’s Halloween candy
text:
COLUMBUS, Wis. (WMTV/Gray News) - A family who said they went trick-or-treating in Columbus, Wisconsin, Saturday night reported finding a needle in a Snickers bar after they got home.
The Lanzhammer family said they tested all of their son’s treats with a magnet when they returned home. They said one of the treats stuck to the magnet.

Columbus Police Department confirmed that they received the report, and said they have not received any other reports of items found inside candy.
Police said people should always inspect any candy that comes from people they do not know and dispose of it properly if it has been tampered with.

title: Meet a Model A Ford club keeping the classic cars on the road
text:
GLEN ALLEN, Va. (Aging Untold) — The Model A was the Ford Motor Company’s next big step after the Model T, ushering in a whole new era for drivers.
The Model A was only produced for a limited time, but nearly a century later, clubs like the Old Dominion Model A Ford Club of Greater Richmond are helping to keep the iconic engines running.
“Oh, it’s great, you know, to see the smile on the faces coming here today. Some lady was hanging out the window just waving,” Dennis Stone, president of the Old Dominion Model A Ford Club, said.
Despite being almost 100 years old, the Model A continues to be fun for all ages.
“We get a lot of smiles per mile. People get excited. And then if we blow the ahooga horn, they are ecstatic, especially kids,” Stew Wolfe, vice president of Old Dominion Model A Ford Club, said.
Henry Ford created the Model A as an upgrade to the Model T.
“We’re looking at an advertisement that occurred in the newspaper in December of 1927, advertising the coming of the new Model A Ford,” Henry Nelson, secretary of Old Dominion Model A Ford Club, said.
Between 1927 and 1931, Ford cranked out roughly 5 million of them, but only a fraction of the cars are still around.
Stone said, for the most part, the cars had no radios, air conditioning or power brakes.
“Bare bones driving. They were the cheapest cars on the market back then,” he said.
But the Model A remained innovative, coming standard with an electric start instead of a crank to get it going. It also came with other bells and whistles.
“It had brakes on all four wheels. It had shock absorbers. It had a way to check your oil without having to get under the car. Had a dipstick. Also, it had gauges inside. You could tell how fast you were going,” Nelson said.
And the Old Dominion Model A Ford Club of Greater Richmond is doing its part to keep the old cars cruising into the future.

title: Maine men’s basketball falls to Providence in season opener
text:
The University of Maine men’s basketball team gave up 49 second in the second half and suffered a season-opening 83-56 loss to Providence College on Monday in Providence, Rhode Island.
Malik Mack scored the first five points of the second half and the Friars went on a 13-0 run to build a 47-26 lead. He finished with 12 points, including nine in the second half.
Jacob Bannarbie scored 17 points and grabbed 10 rebounds for Providence. Ryan Mela added 13 points, while Javon Bardwell added 12, all in the second half.
Hudson Franz led Maine with 13 points. Ayden Evans added 11 points and Killian Gribben had 10. Ace Flagg of Newport finished with seven points.

title: 2026 Midterm Election: How many people have voted early in the US?
text:
2026 Midterm Election: How many people have voted early in the US?
Early voting has ended in many states, with more wrapping up Monday ahead of the 2026 midterm election.
Voters will decide control of the Senate and the House of Representatives, along with state and local races.
More than 54 million voters have cast ballots early, either in person or by mail, according to the latest data from the University of Florida Election Lab. The University of Florida Election Lab gathers data directly from state and regional sources and has tracked early voting since 2008.
Early voting this year has nearly reached the number of votes cast early in the last midterm elections in 2022, with 23 states that have exceeded early voting turnout so far.
Early voting data is not election results, and therefore it's not yet known which candidate will win their races. Some states do report voters' party affiliation, which the data includes.
The Get the Facts Data Team is tracking early voting and analyzing trends in the data. All figures are as of Monday morning. Here's what to know.
States with high early voting turnout
With the election just one day away, 54.5 million people have cast early ballots. That's almost 100% of early voting turnout in the 2022 midterm election, and almost half of total votes.
In Texas, early ballots cast in person or by mail have surpassed the number of early votes cast in 2022, making up more than 138%. Texas has a close, competitive Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton.
Texas is one of 10 states that require voters to provide an excuse to vote by mail. About 7.7 million early ballots have been cast in person.
There are 23 states, including Texas, in which early voting this year has surpassed that of the last midterm election in 2022.
Other states like Connecticut, Illinois and Louisiana have also exceeded their 2022 early voting turnout.
Georgia is another state seeing high overall turnout so far, surpassing 2022 early voting with more than 2.8 million ballots already cast. That's about 71% of the total turnout the state saw in the 2022 midterm elections, including in-person election day voting. Georgia has competitive races for the Senate and governor.
Incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is defending his seat against Republican challenger Mike Collins. The governor's race is between former Atlanta Democratic Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican nominee Rick Jackson.
Tennessee and North Carolina also have high turnout, with early voting accounting for 73% and 74% of the 2022 midterm turnout, respectively. Both states have passed 2022 early voting turnout already, too.
How is early voting turnout in competitive states?
Republican nominee and former presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and Democratic nominee and former state health director Amy Acton are competing for Ohio's open governor seat.
In Ohio, more than 1.6 million voters have cast ballots, more than the 1.2 million early votes cast in the 2022 midterms.
The Cook Political Report has called both the race for governor and the U.S. Senate seat in the state as competitive.
About 1.8 million voters in Michigan have voted ahead of Election Day. The state allows voters to vote early in person or by mail. That's about 99% of 2022 early voting turnout.
Democrat nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are competing for the state's open Senate seat.

title: Soaking rain possible in Maine this weekend
text:
Beneficial rain arrives Friday into Saturday
After a warm start to November, needed rainfall on the way to Maine.
Beneficial rain arrives Friday into Saturday
After a warm start to November, needed rainfall on the way to Maine.
Rain chances increase across Maine late Thursday as a slow-moving cold front approaches. We expect wetter weather to continue into Saturday, with several rounds possible as areas of low pressure move along the front.
We’re gaining confidence that much of the state will receive measurable rainfall during that stretch. The timing and totals are less certain, with several parts of the system still needing to come together. This does not necessarily mean steady rain from Thursday night through Saturday.
Rainfall could reach at least a half-inch across much of the area over those three days. Plenty of moisture will be available, but we still need a clearer picture of how the storm systems develop before narrowing down amounts.
The chance of rain drops Sunday, although we may not get a clean break from the unsettled weather. Additional disturbances could keep the pattern active into early next week.

title: Joe Higgins named Lawrence head girls basketball coach
text:
FAIRFIELD, Maine (WABI) - Joe Higgins is taking over for Greg Chesley as head coach of the Lawrence girls basketball team.
Higgins has been the JV head coach and varsity assistant coach of the Bulldogs for the last eight seasons.
He’s been on the staff for two state championships.
Higgins spoke about what it means to be the head coach.
“We’ve been pretty successful for a good many years. We would just like to keep that momentum going. We’ll be younger this year, but there’s opportunities there. But just having the opportunity to work with these girls (is special), and hopefully (we can) get right back to the tournaments,” said Higgins.
Chesley is now the head women’s basketball coach of KVCC after guiding the Bulldogs to a 140-41 record and the two state titles with Higgins.
The Bulldogs are the defending Class B state champions and will look to replace graduated key players Maddie Provost and Ashley Shores this season.

title: There’s no excuse for dumping pets
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Katie D. Lisnik is executive director of Maine Humane.
Many Mainers have seen media coverage of a cat tied in a garbage bag and thrown into a dumpster at the Bingham Transfer Station. The town of Bigham rightly noted that, “human decency and basic compassion should have guided you to a completely different choice.”
Fortunately, the cat was noticed and rescued quickly by transfer station staff (thank you for your diligence and compassion), but this story could have had a much more horrific ending.
While there is no excuse for this action, and the person responsible should be held fully accountable if found, it highlights a broader trend across Maine that we must recognize and address.
During economic downturns, animal shelters and rescues find themselves caught between a rock and a hard place. The numbers of stray and surrendered animals rise as people are no longer able to afford their care. Additionally, animals entering organizations across Maine are in poorer health because families cannot afford necessary veterinary care or nutritious food. Consequently, demand for limited programs to help struggling families such as pet food pantries and low-cost, subsidized veterinary care skyrockets, quickly outpacing the resources available.
At the same time, organizations struggle with the impact of decreasing donor support, as well as slowdowns in adoptions. This leads to shelters trying to do more with less as animals stay longer in shelters and foster homes, waiting for a family to adopt them. Financial constraints coupled with the increased number of animals needing to come into the organization, result in shelters and rescues being unable to meet community needs. When kennels and foster homes are full, organizations face the conundrum of either taking in more animals than they can reasonably care for, or having to say “not now” when requests roll in.
None of these outcomes are what the animal welfare field across Maine wants to see, but it is the current reality.
So what can help right now?
Plan and prepare. Please don’t wait until the last minute to attempt to find a place for an animal you cannot keep. Providing more notice will help ensure that an organization will be able to help you in a timely manner. If organizations cannot assist you in the exact manner you request, please do not threaten the animal’s safety to manipulate the outcome.
Explore the options that exist to help you keep your pet. Maine Humane’s calendar lists all the low-cost spay/neuter clinics and vaccine clinics across the state that we are aware of. Utilize these resources to help keep your pets healthy when dollars are pinched.
Please make an effort to get your pets spayed or neutered. Prevention is key and the only thing that will truly solve these issues is fewer animals needing help.
Treat shelter and rescue staff and volunteers with the compassion and empathy you expect from them.
Support your shelter and rescue in any way you can. Whether it be a financial gift, a donation of some needed supplies, time spent volunteering, or becoming a foster home to provide a needy animal a safe place, all support is appreciated and makes a big difference.
Spread the word. Talk to pet owners you know, share social posts from organizations you follow, and encourage folks to seek help early
If you are witness to neglect or cruelty, report it to your animal control officer and the Maine Animal Welfare Program. If you hear someone threatening to do something, speak up for that animal.
We know that Mainers love animals and want to see them protected. The issues we are dealing with are big and complex, from economic challenges, housing insecurity, veterinary deserts and more. The only way we will see things improve is through better communication, planning, collaboration and support. Let’s seek to understand, and find ways that animals can get the help they need without breaking a field stretched to its limit.

title: Susan Jean (Hewett) Demers
text:
Susan Jean (Hewett) Demers, 70, passed away on Oct. 20, 2026 at Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor.
Born May 1, 1956, she was the first of four children to Walter and Jean (Wheeler) Hewett.
Growing up in Fayette, Susan helped her family run the Fayette Country Store. She often recalled fond memories of working there and living above the store with her parents and siblings. She graduated from Livermore Falls High School in 1974. After graduation, she attended the University of Maine in Augusta for accounting.
In 1987, she married her husband, Ron Demers, and had three children, whom she dedicated her time to homeschooling until high school. Her lessons emphasized creativity and encouraged them to create from their own imaginations.
During the late ‘90s and early 2000s, she attended Calvary Bible Baptist Church in Whitefield and was very active in her church community. As Sunday school superintendent, she helped teach Sunday school classes, and tirelessly put together arts and crafts projects for the children to make with their lessons each week. She also took pride in contributing to the Girls Alive and Daughters of the King clubs, and was in charge of crafts for vacation Bible school each summer.
She had a passion for art, and created many seasonal and holiday displays for herself and her family to enjoy around the home. She also enjoyed knitting and crocheting, often giving her completed projects to friends and family members as gifts. Each year, she knit a variety of mittens to donate to local charities for the cold winter months. She was skilled at knitting mittens and scarves, as well as crocheting afghans.
To her family and friends, she is remembered as having a heart of gold. She loved caring for people and often went the extra mile to help others when she could. In later years, she took up card making and hosted small groups to teach others how to make their own greeting cards. She found joy in sending her homemade cards to others for birthdays and special events.
She had an appreciation for the simple pleasures in life and loved spending time with her grandchildren, often providing fun outdoor and indoor activities to encourage the same creativity and imagination she instilled in her own children.
Susan is survived by her husband of 39 years, Ron Demers; two sons, Josh Demers and his wife, Tiffany, of Windsor, and Matt Demers and his wife, Allison McKeen, of Gardiner; one daughter, Katie Blanchette and her husband, Graham, of Whitefield; one brother, Ron Hewett and his wife, Orra Lee, of Fayette; two sisters, Linda Elliot and her husband, Bob, of Mount Vernon, and Marcia Millet and her husband, Tim, of Whitefield; and her grandchildren, Mack, Landon, Emmaline, and Blakelynn Demers.
Family and friends are encouraged to honor her memory by spending time with loved ones and appreciating the small moments of friendship and fellowship.

title: Man completes 28-year, 31,000-mile walk around the world
text:
HULL, England (AP) — Karl Bushby embraced his weeping mother in his arms Monday as he returned to his northern England home to complete a 28-year odyssey to walk around the world.
“Where have you been?” his mother, Angela, asked as he arrived outside the home he left in 1998 that was now decked with a banner saying “Welcome Home Son.”
He didn’t need to tell her.
Bushby set out from Punta Arenas, Chile, on Nov. 1, 1998, and walked 31,000 miles (50,000 kilometers) across four continents and 30 countries to get home. He navigated shifting ice over the Bering Strait and swam across the Caspian Sea and English Channel to avoid taking a boat or plane — or any transport — to propel him forward.
He vowed not to return until he could complete the journey on foot. It was an eye-opening adventure full of danger and drudgery that was interrupted for years at a time by the unexpected: the 2008 financial crash that sapped funding from sponsors, the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic and mountains of bureaucratic red tape to get across international borders.
A trek made possible by kind strangers
On the final day of the journey, Bushby pushed his cart toward a hero’s welcome at City Hall before setting off for the last stretch to see his mother.
“Sorry to keep you waiting,” he joked to the crowd of hundreds who cheered his arrival. “Is that it, is it done?”
The ex-paratrooper said he looked like he was 10 years old when he left his mother’s row house at the age of 29. He returned at 57 — softer, grayer and weathered, but far more worldly.
“They say it takes a village but literally it took a world to get me here,” Bushby said. “The kindness of strangers, so many, from individuals to nation states to get me back here today. I didn’t do this alone. There was a big team. The biggest team. Earth.”
The idea started with a birthday card from his dad
Bushby had a thirst for adventure, but his mission only came into focus when his father, Keith, sent him a birthday card in the mid-90s. His dad, an army veteran himself, mentioned an argument two special forces troops had about the possibility of walking from London to New York over the Bering land bridge, believed by some scientists to have been used by early humans to migrate from Asia to the Americas at a time of lower sea levels.
Perilous jungles, scorching deserts and frozen tundra slowed him down, but bureaucratic holdups brought his adventure to a halt for long periods.
Bushby originally calculated the distance could be covered in about five years, but he knew that was unrealistic.
“You just dump a whole bucket full of reality on that,” he said. “We suspected that it was 12 years plus. And the plus was a big plus. But never in our wildest dreams would we ever have imagined 28 years.”
Danger on land and sea followed by border problems
He dodged Colombia’s armed conflict in the dangerous Darién Gap, the roadless and rugged jungle, rainforest and mountains between South and Central America in 2001, and was then jailed for 18 days after crossing a restricted border zone in Panama.
After being airlifted to safety during the 56-mile (90-kilometer) Bering Strait crossing in 2006 with American adventurer Dimitry Kieffer, they started again and faced a standoff with a polar bear, survived near-death plunges into freezing waters and almost lost all their supplies when their sleds plunged in the sea. After managing the rare crossing, the pair were jailed and faced deportation for entering Russia illegally.
It took Bushby almost 10 years to make his way through Russia in fits and starts because of visa struggles and weather that only allowed travel a few months a year. When Russia denied him a visa in 2012, Bushby walked in protest from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., which eventually led to him getting the proper paperwork.
Family firsts and a long-awaited reunion
Bushby has met several times over the decades with family members who have met up with him on his journey. He was greeted on the beach in Dover by his father and brothers after crossing the channel last month.
He reunited with Adam, his 36-year-old son from an early marriage whom he had rarely seen, and he met his 12-year-old granddaughter for the first time, which he said was amazing.
Bushby hadn’t seen his mother in a decade, setting the stage for an emotional and somewhat awkward reunion captured amid a throng of cameras and a documentary film crew.
“Behave yourself, mother,” he joked, as his mother wrapped her arms around him and wept. “Get yourself together.”
He said he had long tried to imagine that moment he would return to find his mother at the gate where he left her so long ago. He said it was an emotional reunion that was “one great, big, blurry mess” he was trying to process.
“It was kind of almost shocking to see my mother after so long,” he said at a news conference later. “She’s changed a lot. We’ve all changed a lot in that time.”
Next steps for a man who walked millions
In the final days of his trip, Bushby spoke of his anxiety over the trip ending, not knowing what he would do next and coming to terms with having to live in his mom’s basement.
“It’s like stepping across the event horizon into a black hole,” he told The Associated Press. “I have no idea what’s about to happen in my life.”
There will be plenty to keep him busy. Six speaking engagements are scheduled in the next two months, a sequel to his memoir “Giant Steps” is due and German filmmaker Werner Herzog is making a documentary on his trek.
He expects to struggle with the ups and downs other adventurers have experienced after long journeys.
“The only way I think, you know, you get over that is just get another mission, another passion and get busy,” he said. “That’s what I intend on doing.”

title: Lily Robbins says it's 'surreal' to return home 5 months after Searsmont explosion
text:
Hundreds of well-wishers lined roads from Augusta to Searsmont Friday as Lily Robbins made her way home after 24 weeks of treatment for injuries she sustained in the May 15 fire and explosion at her family’s lumber mill, which killed her father and injured her uncle.
A procession of fire trucks and other emergency vehicles escorted Robbins from the Augusta Civic Center to Searsmont, where a welcome party packed the Searsmont Fire Station.
Robbins, 23, is a volunteer EMT with Searsmont EMS. She had been working at Mosaic restaurant in Camden since it opened in 2023 to help support herself through college, and she had graduated from the University of Maine a week before the explosion. Like so many other volunteers who had no idea what they were heading into that day, she responded to the call.
Mill employees turned hoses on the fire before the first trucks arrived, according to a federal report. As crews worked the fire inside a silo filled with wood shavings, the silo exploded, releasing a massive fireball that killed Morrill firefighter Andrew Cross, 27. Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury, 76, died June 14 of injuries sustained in the blast. In all, 299 firefighters and other first responders from 46 departments across four Maine counties responded.
Badly burned in the explosion, Robbins ended up in Massachusetts General Hospital’s burn center along with her father, Alden Robbins, the company’s vice president and manager of lumber sales, and her uncle, James A. Robbins, its president. Her father died of his injuries July 2 and her uncle is still recovering. The Robbins family members were some of the first to respond to the fire.
Eleven other firefighters were injured, five of them seriously, along with two EMS providers and mill employees, according to the report. Among them were Searsmont Fire Chief James Ames, who was treated and released at the scene, and Thomas Wolf, a Searsmont firefighter and Robbins Lumber employee. Sarah Tompkins, a farmer who sold produce at the Camden Farmers Market and served as Searsmont’s EMS chief, remains in the hospital after numerous surgeries.
The mill, founded in 1881 and owned by the fifth generation of the Robbins family — Alden, James and their sister, Catherine Robbins-Halsted — is one of the biggest employers and economic engines of Waldo County. It returned to full operation May 26.
A GoFundMe campaign to support Lily Robbins’ recovery had raised $81,970 of a $90,000 goal from 542 donors by 4:45 p.m. Saturday. It was organized by Mosaic owner Hannah Scott, who also helped organize a weeklong restaurant fundraiser in June with a dozen other businesses.
Ames and Wolf attended Lily Robbins’ homecoming Friday, as did members of Cross’s family.
With her mother, Amy Robbins, nearby, and between visiting with family, friends, neighbors and colleagues gathered inside the Searsmont Fire Station’s cafeteria, Lily Robbins stepped aside momentarily for a one-on-one interview with the Midcoast Villager to discuss the ordeal — and her resolve and optimism that have kept her going through the pain and grief.
The following conversation has been lightly edited for length and clarity:
Midcoast Villager: I’m sorry for the loss of your father. I lost mine in August. Losing a parent is a profound experience.
Lily Robbins: There’s nothing really like it. It’s taught me a lot of things that I didn’t know about myself, or grief. I never lost someone that close to me, so it’s been really hard navigating that and my own physical healing journey at the same time. It complicated things.
I just feel really lucky, but there’s also an element of wondering why. Why me? Why not Wayne (Woodbury), or Andrew (Cross), or my dad? I wish they got an opportunity to come home too. There’s a lot of mixed emotions.
How does it feel to come home, especially to a welcome like this?
It feels incredible. I’ve lived in this town my entire life, and there’s no place like home. And Searsmont is one special place. We just have incredible neighbors, an incredible community. I feel so loved.
The drive from Augusta was surreal. I just feel grateful for everyone that came out today and all the support I’ve been given, not just today, but the whole summer.
Is this your first time home since May?
I actually came home for a quick 12-hour visit to Searsmont for my dad’s funeral. I was fortunate enough to be discharged temporarily so I could be there on that day. I wouldn’t have wanted to miss it for anything.
Now, I’m probably going to take some time just to heal and recover and stay at home. Spend a lot of time with loved ones. I have five little siblings, and they are just the absolute joy of my life. I adore them. So I am just looking forward to soaking up every moment with them, getting outside, spending time with my dogs, my cat. A lot of time just resting, enjoying the Maine fall. You know, hunting season’s coming up.
Are you going to hunt?
We’ll see. I would like to, but I still have some hand injuries that may make hunting a challenge.
Are you comfortable talking about the nature of your injuries and treatment?
Yeah. It was a really, really long road. I had burns covering over a third of my body. They estimated 30% to 40%, which is pretty significant. I was unable to walk for a really long time. So there were a lot of long, really hard days.
Thankfully, I’ve had the most incredible amount of support. I got hundreds and hundreds of cards from all over the country. To anyone who sent me a card, I just want to say I read every single word of every single card, and I’ve kept them all. So if I didn’t write back to you, it wasn’t because I didn’t want to, it’s because I couldn’t keep up with all of them. Every single one made me smile.
I think staying hopeful has been the most important thing for me. It’s been really hard to, because not only am I dealing with physical pain and suffering, but I’m also dealing with a lot of mental trauma and grief. So staying hopeful and staying positive has been the most important priority for me.
I’ve done that through humor. I was pranking the nurses at Mass General. I was being ridiculous, but that’s what got me through each day, was laughing and smiling. It was not possible without family and friends, for sure.
You’re an emergency medical technician. What was it like being a patient instead of a caregiver?
You know, it’s really interesting. I’ve spent thousands of hours in an ambulance, and I never pictured myself being the one on that stretcher, and I was so used to caring for others that it was actually really hard for me to be taken care of. There was a degree of stubbornness that I had where I was like, “No, I can do it myself.” It was hard for me to let myself be helped in a lot of ways, and a lot of that was just me needing to get over myself a little bit and realize that I do need to be helped.
The day of, I was in the back of the ambulance telling them exactly what I needed. I need oxygen, I need pain relief, and you need to intubate me before I lose my airway. That’s what I told the paramedic in the back, and that’s what I told the doctors at the ER. I knew exactly what I was going through physically. I knew that there was a severe, severe threat to my life. As soon as the accident happened, I was like, I need help, medical help.
It’s not something I ever wanted to experience, but I think if I ever go back to EMS — and I do plan on working in health care in the future — the experience has given me a lot more empathy and compassion. I know how uncomfortable that stretcher is now.
How do you feel about going back into emergency medical services?
It’s hard to imagine life not on an ambulance just because I loved it so much. But there is a degree of trauma and it’s just, it’s hard. I picture myself struggling to go to a fire or struggling to deal with a burn patient just because it might bring back memories of what I dealt with. But in that same regard, I want to be there for my community. I love giving back to the community. It raised me.
My plans are to go to medical school eventually. I studied zoology (as an undergraduate), but I was on the pre-medical track and my goal was always to go to medical school. It’s postponed now, but I have not given up on it. In fact, I’m probably more motivated.
Is there anything else you’d like to say about your father?
Oh, my gosh. I mean, he’s the reason I got into EMS. He was on the volunteer fire department here in Searsmont when I was a kid. And I remember just seeing his selfless spirit and thinking, “Wow, look how much he’s doing for the community. I want to be able to do that for my community too.”
My dad was just an incredible, incredible person, and he’ll be missed. He left a big hole. The grief is unimaginable. I still haven’t processed it. He left behind six young kids and my beautiful mother, and I’m just grateful for the time I had with him and the lessons he taught me because he always taught me, if you ever fall down, you’ve just got to get back up again. There’s no other choice.
I think that it’s kind of the spirit I’ve had throughout all of this. I’ve had no other option but to get back up on my feet and keep going. Everyone says, “Oh, you’re so strong.” But I kind of have to be. There’s no other choice.
How are your uncle, and your EMS colleague Sarah Tompkins?
He’s doing well. Sarah’s also recovering well. I’ve seen both of them in the last few days. We shared some good moments. I look forward to the day when they come home.
Is there a question I didn’t ask that you would like to answer?
I just want to express — again — thank you to my community. Thank you to the whole state of Maine. This support has been unimaginable from day one. People have shown up in ways I never thought possible.

title: 1 dead, 3 injured after shooting at youth football championship game
text:
MADISON, Ill. (First Alert 4/Gray News) - One person died and three others were injured after a shooting at a youth football championship game Sunday night, authorities said.
The shooting occurred at Madison Senior High School around 9:50 p.m. during a football game unrelated to the school.
The three injured victims were taken to local hospitals, while the fourth victim died on scene.
The Major Case Squad of Greater St. Louis is handling the investigation into the shooting. Law enforcement is looking for witnesses and anyone else with information to come forward.
“Someone in that crowd saw something, recorded something, or has heard something since. We are asking those people to come forward,” said Lt. Andrew Pierson, public information officer for the Major Case Squad. “You do not have to have the whole story, a single photo, a short video, or one detail you think is insignificant may be exactly what moves this investigation forward.”
The school district canceled Monday classes and said they will resume Wednesday.
The district released a statement saying it “is deeply saddened by the shooting” and that while the game was not organized or sponsored by the district, “this violence affects our entire school community.”
Counseling and support services will be offered to students and staff.
Authorities ask anyone with information to contact the command post at 618-709-7750 or CrimeStoppers at 866-371-8477.

title: A brief history of yardwork
text:
This past weekend, I was surprised by how early the neighborhood leaf-blowers were fired up. Most days, during my walks with Milo in our back woods, we are serenaded by a chorus of woodpeckers — Downy, Hairy, and Pileated — Black-capped Chickadees, Golden-crowned Kinglets, White-breasted and Red-breasted Nuthatches, Brown Creepers, Dark-eyed Juncos, White-throated Sparrows, and Northern Cardinals. This past weekend, their soundtrack was drowned out by the cacophony of gas-fired, two-stroke engines of leaf-blowers used to clear yards of leaves. This set me to thinking about the ecology of yards, starting with the question: Why do we clear them of autumn’s leaves?
Today, it is cultural to clear every last leaf from our lawns. Once upon a time, yards were kept as bare dirt for critically practical reasons, including pest control, fire safety, and protection from both domestic and wild animals.

title: 'Sorry to keep you waiting': Man completes 28-year walk around world and returns to mother's house
text:
'Sorry to keep you waiting': Man completes 28-year walk around world and returns to mother's house
Karl Bushby completed his 28-year odyssey to walk around the world on Monday by returning to his mother's home in northern England. Bushby embraced his emotional mother, Angela, outside her home in Hull, England, where he left in 1998. Bushby was surrounded by a crowd outside the home that had a banner saying "Welcome Home Son."
On Monday, Bushby took the final steps of his 28-year odyssey to walk around the world and return to his mother's home in Northern England.
Bushby was surrounded by journalists as hundreds of people cheered his arrival at City Hall.
"Sorry to keep you waiting," he joked. "Is that it, is it done?"
Bushby was a 29-year-old ex-paratrooper when he walked from his home to a Royal Air Force base near Oxford and caught a flight to South America. He returned as a 57-year-old — softer, grayer and weathered, but far more worldly.
"They say it takes a village, but literally it took a world to get me here," Bushby said. "The kindness of strangers, so many, from individuals to nation-states, to get me back here today. I didn't do this alone. There was a big team. The biggest team. Earth."
Bushby set out from Punta Arenas, Chile, on Nov. 1, 1998, and has walked 31,000 miles across four continents and 30 countries to get home. He navigated shifting ice over the Bering Strait and swam across the Caspian Sea and English Channel to avoid taking a boat or plane — or any transport — to propel him forward.
The idea started with a birthday card from his dad
He had a thirst for adventure, but his mission only came into focus when his father, Keith, sent him a birthday card in the mid-90s. His dad, an army veteran himself, mentioned an argument among his fellow special forces troops about the possibility of walking from London to New York over the Bering land bridge, believed by some scientists to have been used by early humans to migrate from Asia to the Americas at a time of lower sea levels.
Perilous jungles, scorching deserts and frozen tundra slowed him down, but bureaucratic red tape often brought his adventure to a halt for long periods.
Bushby originally calculated the distance could be covered in about five years, but he knew that was unrealistic.
"You just dump a whole bucket full of reality on that," he said. "We suspected that it was 12 years plus. And the plus was a big plus. But never in our wildest dreams would we ever have imagined 28 years."
He dodged war in the dangerous Darién Gap, the roadless and rugged jungle, rainforest and mountains between South and Central America in 2001, and was then jailed for 18 days after crossing a restricted border zone in Panama.
At first denied a visa, Bushby made a long trek through Russia
After being airlifted to safety during the 56-mile Bering Strait crossing in 2006 with American adventurer Dimitry Kieffer, they started again and faced a standoff with a polar bear, survived near-death plunges into freezing waters and almost lost all their supplies when their sleds plunged in the sea. After managing the rare crossing, the pair were jailed and faced deportation for entering Russia illegally.
It took Bushby almost 10 years to make his way through Russia in fits and starts because of visa struggles and weather that allowed travel only a few months a year. When Russia denied him a visa in 2012, Bushby walked in protest from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., which eventually led to him getting the proper paperwork.
Bushby planned to meet with family, including his son, Adam, whom he had seen only a few times over the journey. He was expected to meet his 12-year-old granddaughter for the first time.
Then he was off to push his two-wheeled cart the final steps across Hull and reunite with his mother, Angela, whom he hadn't seen in a decade.
"It's been a week of lasts," Bushby told the crowd. "The last day in the tent. The last day on the road. After 28 years, you couldn't ask for more than this. This is the last of the last few steps almost to my mother's house."
Bushby's journey by the numbers
75 million
If fitness trackers had been around when Bushby started his trip, it's likely they couldn't have kept up with his cumulative number of steps.
31,000
The total mileage Bushby put on his body is the equivalent of having run 10,000 5K road races.
10,226
Bushby initially estimated the distance could be traversed in five years. "Then you just dump a whole bucket full of reality on that," he said. "We suspected that it was 12 years plus. And the plus was a big plus. But never in our wildest dreams would we ever have imagined 28 years." That adds up to more than 10,220 days.
31
When geopolitical conflicts closed off passage through Russia and Iran, Bushby decided he would swim across the Caspian Sea, the world's largest inland body of water. His 31-day crossing relied on a technique he calls "floatimming," a hybrid of floating and swimming. He wore a flotation vest and wetsuit and plodded backward by flapping his arms in the water.
30
Starting in Chile and ending in the U.K., he has entered or passed through 30 foreign countries before returning home.
10
No country took longer to get through than Russia, where Bushby spent 10 years, was once detained and faced deportation for entering illegally after crossing the Bering Strait. Harsh weather only permitted a few months of travel each year, and there were many bureaucratic delays. Russia denied him a visa in 2012, so Bushby spent a year walking 3,500 miles in protest from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., which eventually led to him getting the proper paperwork. Still, it ended up taking about a decade to be done with the country.
4
The trek has taken Bushby through South America, North America, Asia and Europe — all but three of the world's seven continents.
2
Bushby fell in love twice and had his heart broken each time. He carried on long-term romances with a woman from Colombia and another from Japan. But the relationships couldn't weather the toll of the road.
'A lot'
Bushby estimates he went through 10 pairs of shoes traveling through the Americas but then lost track. That was 20 years ago, though, so who can blame him? "After that we were just in and out of all kinds of different stuff," he said. The total? "A lot."

main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Here’s a roundup of company news — hires, promotions, awards, new offices, performance metrics and more.
We are also working to get more of a geographic representation, so if you have company news that’s not listed, feel free to send it our way, at lschreiber@mainebiz.biz.
Nichole Fecteau, a Realtor at Better Homes and Gardens Real Estate/the Masiello Group in Berwick, received the 2026 Technology Award from Better Homes and Gardens Real Estate at its national convention, held Oct. 19-22 in Las Vegas. The award recognized Fecteau’s use of technology to market homes and generate listings and her eagerness to teach others. Her systems include daily video, automated prospecting, AI-assisted marketing and branding tools for new-construction builders. As a solo agent, she consistently closes $12 million to $16 million in annual sales, about 85% of it listings.
Fecteau also presented two sessions at the convention. “Advanced Lead Generation for Listing Agents” discussed the systems behind her listing business, from daily video to neighborhood prospecting sequences. “Building Culture in the Real Estate Office,” for brokers and company owners, was presented with Josh McGrath of Better Homes and Gardens Real Estate Central in West Virginia.
“In a time where technology and AI are being overused to produce posts and graphics, I have managed to leverage them in my business to create more time and opportunities for me to be more human,” Fecteau said.
Following the convention, Fecteau was invited to teach agents in North Dakota and Florida, where interest centers on her new-construction expertise and builder branding. She also teaches a course on market visibility and listing market share, and works with brokerages nationwide to bring her lead generation program to their agents.
Maine Association of Realtors named Julie Cromwell as its 2026 Maine State Realtor of the Year. Cromwell has been a Realtor since 1996 and is a broker and the owner of Cromwell Coastal Properties in Woolwich.
She served as president of the Lincoln County Council of the Mountains to Shore Board of Reatlors three times, the first in 1999, then 2017 and again in 2025. Over the course of her 30-year career, Cromwell has served as a director for the Maine Association of Realtors for nearly all of those years, and has served her local board, state level committees and task forces, and also for the National Association of Realtors.
The state Realtor of the Year is chosen from among 11 nominees of the local Realtor associations and more than 6,400 Realtors in Maine.
The Boulos Co. dropped its latest episode of its Boulos Beat podcast, featuring George Cacoulidis, CEO of Grand Metro Properties, hosted by Greg Boulos. The firm also published the report “How Much Is Your Land Worth?” by broker John Finegan, who said land valuation depends on more than price per acre and should consider zoning and regulatory timing, construction costs, the planned building’s value and the site’s physical condition. For more information, visit Boulos’s podcast page and market insights page.
Town & Shore Real Estate said its second annual charity event brought together Hearts of Pine, sponsors, partners and the community to raise and donate $8,000 to Full Plates Full Potential. Players from the Portland Hearts of Pine joined the event to meet guests, take photos and spend time with some of their youngest fans. Amy Kayne of 2Gether created the menu. A raffle featured a signed soccer ball and other prizes.

title: Savannah Guthrie renews plea for information in mother’s disappearance
text:
TUCSON, Ariz. (Gray News) - Savannah Guthrie made another public plea Sunday for information about the disappearance of her mother, Nancy Guthrie, 84.
It has been nine months since Nancy Guthrie disappeared.
Plea on Instagram
“Today” host Savannah Guthrie wrote on Instagram, “Our mom was a light in this world. We want to celebrate her and give her the dignity she deserves... Please help us.”
In the post, she also shared a childhood drawing from her own daughter featuring an umbrella in the rain alongside the message, “I know it might not seem like it but I really need my mommy.”
Investigation status
Nancy Guthrie disappeared from her Tucson-area home on Feb. 1.
Local and federal law enforcement officials still do not have a suspect or person of interest.
The Pima County Sheriff’s Department said Friday its investigators traveled to Florida to meet with scientists in hopes of furthering DNA analysis in the case, KOLD reported.
Tips and reward
The sheriff’s department is still seeking tips in Nancy Guthrie’s disappearance.
The Guthrie family is offering $1 million for information leading to the recovery of Nancy Guthrie. 88-CRIME is offering a $102,500 reward and the FBI is offering a $100,000 reward for information leading to Nancy Guthrie’s location or conviction of those responsible.
Anyone with information is asked to call 88-CRIME locally at 520-882-7463, the FBI at 1-800-225-5324 or the FBI’s Phoenix Field Office at 623-466-1999. Tips can also be submitted online at tips.fbi.gov.

title: Rhodes College professors bringing elite education to inmates
text:
HENNING, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - It’s not unusual to see students working on college-level coursework, earnestly taking notes from the professor.
“It was the last decade of 15 years of my career here was looming and I wanted to do something maybe different, challenging,” said Dr. Stephen Haynes, a 30-year professor of religious studies and humanities at Rhodes College.
Haynes is the director of the college’s “Liberal Arts in Prison” program.
“People who were involved in higher education and prison are 43% less likely to go back to prison,” Haynes said.
The program started as a Great Books Discussion Group in the fall of 2016 with about 25 women interested.
Dr. Haynes said it soon became apparent what the inmates really wanted was a program that gave them college credit.
Now, every week, a group of Rhodes professors and students gather on campus at the statue of former college president Charles Diehl to begin their trek to the Women’s Therapeutic Residential Center in Henning, Tennessee, a low-security rehabilitation-focused prison where instructors teach the hallmarks of a Rhodes College curriculum.
“And so, we were able to develop a certificate program,” Haynes said. “At the end, by May, we’ll have about 45 women who have graduated with these certificates of liberal arts.”
Women like inmate Jameshia Davis — serving a 24-year sentence for drug and firearm possession.
“I thought it was hard at first, because when you hear Rhodes College, it makes you think of like Harvard or something,” Davis said. “Education, if you would have mentioned education to me before I came to prison, I would have probably looked at you like you was crazy.”
Davis not only completed the program but also became a tutor for other incarcerated women.
“I would just like to encourage anyone who’s either discouraged about school, education, whatever it may be, to just challenge yourself and to just know that you can do anything that you put your mind to,” Davis said.
Rhodes English professor Dr. Lori Garner has been part of the prison program for about five years.
“I really think they make me a better teacher. When I learn their perspectives, I can bring them back into my classes at Rhodes. And that really helps everyone,” Garner said. “They bring really diverse life experiences to these same stories that I’ve been teaching for decades.”
Rhodes seniors Sophie Stevenson and Laurel Phillips work closely with the inmates, leading discussion groups and other organizational activities — two of the more than 70 students who’ve volunteered for the program.
Both say over the two to three years they’ve been involved, they’ve come to see the women as friends.
“We hear about their kids and their grandkids and the pets and the birthdays and special occasions and when they are going up for parole and like potentially going to be released,” Phillips said.
The student helpers say the program has not only changed their perspectives about prisons and prisoners but also their own lives.
“I would love to keep working in prisons after this, and I’m really grateful to have gotten this opportunity. I think this is not something that I came to college thinking about or knowing was an option, and now it’s sort of defined my entire college career,” Stevenson said.
For inmates like Davis — who has a parole hearing in May — these classes provide a chance to change their futures and perhaps even the futures of those they love.
“I don’t know, it was kind of really encouraging for my oldest son because he’s in high school and he just...when they see good things that I’m doing, it makes them be like, ‘Hey. If mama can do it, I can do it,’” Davis said.
As of spring of 2025, 92 incarcerated women at WTRC had accumulated 765 Rhodes credits, with 32 earning certificates.
It’s a lesson that extends far beyond the walls of a prison.
“They’re human beings with a future. They’re not the worst thing they’ve ever done. Most of them will get out and they have a lot of potential and it’s great to see that potential being realized,” Haynes said.
Jameshia Davis plans to continue her education toward a bachelor’s degree when she gets released.
And thanks to a $500,000 Mellon Foundation grant, a new Bachelor of Arts in Liberal Studies will be offered at WRTC and support the expansion of educational programming in the men’s facility at West Tennessee State Penitentiary.
That means, starting this summer, WTRC inmates will be able to enroll in a full four-year degree program as part of the Liberal Arts in Prison initiative.
Professor Haynes said the program sponsors are looking for ways to help sustain the program into the future and are looking for donors who want to see it succeed.
