title: 18 County Standouts Make a Loaded Week Nine Athlete Ballot
text:
Week Nine Is Loaded: 18 County Athletes Up for Athlete of the Week
The deeper we get into the postseason, the harder these Athlete of the Week decisions become.
Fall Week Nine might be the best example yet.
This week's ballot features 18 Aroostook County athletes, with nine boys and nine girls representing some of the biggest tournament, championship and individual performances of the fall.
There are game-winning goals, dramatic penalty shootouts, state championship cross country finishes, postseason shutouts and players who came through when their teams needed them most.
Now it is time for County sports fans to decide the winners.
Voting is open now. Fans can vote once per hour in both polls through Thursday at 3 p.m.
The Week Nine winners will be announced Friday morning.
Boys Athlete of the Week Nominees
Wyatt Oliver, Hodgdon, Soccer
Oliver came through in a huge tournament moment for the Hawks, scoring 2 goals in Hodgdon's quarterfinal victory over Easton.
One of those goals was the game-winner, coming on a header off a cross to help send Hodgdon into the next round.
Mitchell Burtt, Central Aroostook, Soccer
Burtt was right in the middle of Central Aroostook's dramatic tournament victory.
He scored both Panther goals during regulation and then converted again during the penalty shootout as Central Aroostook advanced.
James Baillargeon, Houlton, Soccer
Baillargeon delivered one of the most dramatic goals of the postseason.
With Houlton and top-seeded Mattanawcook tied in overtime, Baillargeon scored the game-winning goal with only four seconds remaining, sending the Shires into the next round.
Grady Kinney, Central Aroostook, Soccer
Kinney stood tall in goal during Central Aroostook's postseason thriller.
After playing through regulation and two overtimes, Kinney made 3 saves during the penalty shootout, helping the Panthers survive and advance.
Bentley Nadeau, Wisdom, Soccer
Nadeau made his impact when the pressure was at its highest.
He recorded a tournament shutout before later making the decisive save in a penalty shootout, sending Wisdom into the regional championship.
Malachi Witmer, Houlton/GHCA, Cross Country
Witmer turned in another outstanding championship performance.
He finished sixth at the Class C State Cross Country Championship in 17:17.24, leading Houlton/GHCA to a state runner-up team finish.
Aiden Ciarleglio, Hodgdon, Soccer
Ciarleglio came up with a strong performance in net during Hodgdon's quarterfinal win over Easton.
He made 9 saves on 14 shots, including several important stops that helped the Hawks protect their lead and move on.
Wyatt Daigle, Fort Kent, Soccer
Daigle stepped to the spot with Fort Kent's season hanging in the balance.
He converted the deciding penalty kick in the Warriors' semifinal shootout victory over George Stevens Academy, sending Fort Kent into the Class C North regional championship.
Paxton Darrell, Presque Isle, Cross Country
Darrell led the Presque Isle boys at the Class B State Cross Country Championship.
He finished 16th overall in 17:55.52, capping a strong postseason run for the Wildcats.
Girls Athlete of the Week Nominees
Lucy Hartvigsen, Madawaska, Soccer
Hartvigsen delivered one of Week Nine's biggest playoff performances.
She scored both Madawaska goals against Ashland, including the game-winner in double overtime, to send the Owls into the semifinals.
Reece Doucette, Fort Kent, Soccer
Doucette helped send the Warriors back to the regional championship.
She scored 2 goals in Fort Kent's 5-0 semifinal victory over Houlton, including the penalty kick that broke a scoreless game in the second half.
Lilly Burtt, Central Aroostook, Soccer
Burtt played a major role in Central Aroostook's quarterfinal victory over Van Buren.
She scored 2 goals in the Lady Panthers' 3-2 win, helping Central Aroostook advance to the semifinal round.
Carrlyn Buck, Presque Isle, Soccer
Buck found the net when the tournament pressure increased.
She scored in Presque Isle's 3-1 quarterfinal victory over Skowhegan and followed it with another goal in the Wildcats' 4-0 semifinal win over Cony, giving her goals in back-to-back playoff victories.
Raina Ezell, Houlton, Soccer
Ezell exploded offensively in the Class C quarterfinals.
She recorded a hat trick as Houlton defeated Central Aroostook 7-2 and advanced to the semifinal round.
Jenna Strid, Caribou, Cross Country
Strid delivered one of the strongest eligible County girls performances at the state cross country championships.
She finished ninth in Class B in 20:06.27, earning a top-10 state finish for the Vikings.
Chloe White, Fort Fairfield, Soccer
White helped power the Tigers through the Class D quarterfinals.
She scored 2 goals in Fort Fairfield's 4-0 victory over Washburn, helping the Tigers continue their postseason run.
Madi Cyr, Wisdom, Soccer
Cyr produced goals in consecutive tournament victories for the Pioneers.
She scored in Wisdom's 6-1 quarterfinal win over George Stevens Academy and found the net again in the 5-0 semifinal victory over previously unbeaten Sumner.
Gabby Burgess, Van Buren, Soccer
Burgess stepped into a completely different role when Van Buren needed her.
Playing goalkeeper for the first time, she came up with several big saves in the Crusaders' quarterfinal matchup against Central Aroostook and helped keep Van Buren within striking distance.
One of the Deepest Ballots of the Fall
Week Nine shows exactly why picking an Athlete of the Week gets more difficult as the postseason moves along.
Some athletes delivered huge scoring performances. Others produced the one goal, save or penalty kick that changed a tournament game.
Others stood out at the state championship level.
And some made their biggest impact by keeping the ball out of their own net.
Eighteen athletes have earned their place on this week's ballot.
Now the decision belongs to you.
Vote once per hour in both the boys and girls polls through Thursday at 3 p.m.
The Fall Week Nine Athletes of the Week will be announced Friday morning.

title: Family says they found a needle in son’s Halloween candy
text:
COLUMBUS, Wis. (WMTV/Gray News) - A family who said they went trick-or-treating in Columbus, Wisconsin, Saturday night reported finding a needle in a Snickers bar after they got home.
The Lanzhammer family said they tested all of their son’s treats with a magnet when they returned home. They said one of the treats stuck to the magnet.
The family said they opened the candy to inspect it and found a needle inside the Snickers bar. They said they reported it to police.
Columbus Police Department confirmed that they received the report, and said they have not received any other reports of items found inside candy.
Police said people should always inspect any candy that comes from people they do not know and dispose of it properly if it has been tampered with.

title: Family of 4 among those killed in Florida jet crash
text:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (Gray News) - A family representative identified the passengers of the Learjet that crashed in a Florida neighborhood on Sunday.
“With broken hearts, our families share that Adam Robinson and Helen Sharp, their children Emma and Charlie, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and Anita Maria Cetina were among those lost aboard the flight that went down near Greenacres, Florida, on November 1,” the statement, posted on Facebook, read in part.
One of the pilots was previously identified by her mother as 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras.
The identity of the second pilot has not yet been confirmed.
All nine people were killed when the plane crashed into the street and exploded in a neighborhood close to West Palm Beach.
The cause of the crash is still under investigation.
Federal investigators outline the probe but decline to speculate
National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said during a news conference Monday that investigators found evidence the aircraft started breaking up before it hit the ground and that debris from the aircraft could be spread far and wide.
“We do have some indication that the aircraft was breaking up before impact,” Chapman said. “We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site.”
Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti said key components of the jet’s tail may have been lost during the turbulence or as it nose-dived.
“If that happens, you cannot control an airplane at that point. And that very well could explain the missile-like profile just before it hit the ground,” said Guzzetti, a former NTSB and the Federal Aviation Administration investigator.
Weather conditions will be a major focus of the investigation, Chapman said. Rain pounded the region on Sunday, and one of the pilots reported icing conditions at a high altitude in communications with air traffic control.
Weather radar maps from the time of the crash that FlightRadar24 combined with the plane’s flight path seem to show it flying directly into a storm cell that was rapidly expanding upward. But Chapman said investigators still have to determine what the weather conditions were at 35,000 feet.
Chapman said the plane was originally equipped with a cockpit voice recorder that investigators hope to recover.
“We have a lot of work to do on scene,” NTSB investigator Timothy Monville said at the news conference. “This will be a several-day process, and the biggest obstacle that we’re going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway.”

title: Ex-Chicago FBI chief says he was ousted over a failed protesters case, sues Justice Department
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — The former head of the FBI’s Chicago field office says he lost his job after being wrongly blamed for prosecutions that fell apart against six people who protested the federal immigration crackdown in the city, according to a lawsuit he filed Monday.
Douglas DePodesta, a 24-year veteran of the FBI, says in the suit against top Justice Department officials that federal prosecutors pushed “politically motivated prosecutions” against Chicago’s demonstrators before gathering evidence. He says his superiors told him that FBI Director Kash Patel wanted him fired, and he stepped down against his will this summer.
“I saw the writing on the wall,” DePodesta told The Associated Press on Monday.
He accused the top federal prosecutor in Illinois, Andrew Boutros, of starting a “campaign within the Department of Justice to blame” him after the so-called “Broadview Six” case dramatically fell apart earlier this year.
Boutros’ office declined to comment. The FBI and the Justice Department, which are both named in the suit, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Hours after DePodesta filed the suit, U.S. District Judge April Perry ordered Boutros and three of his assistant attorneys to testify under oath on Nov. 16 in the failed case against the protesters.
“There is more than an adequate factual basis for the Court to pursue an inquiry as to whether willful false statements were made to the court,” Perry wrote in the order.
Federal prosecutors brought charges against around 30 protesters during the Chicago immigration enforcement operation, called Operation Midway Blitz. Many of those charges have been dropped or dismissed.
According to DePodesta’s lawsuit, Boutros faced pressure from the Justice Department throughout the crackdown to charge protesters with felonies.
“Boutros sent DePodesta emails demanding that DePodesta open FBI investigations into individuals with political views or affiliations in opposition to the Trump administration,” DePodesta’s attorneys wrote.
Boutros often pressured attorneys under him in the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Illinois to press charges “before investigating the objective evidence,” and he wanted felony charges when assisting attorneys “favored misdemeanors or no charges at all,” the suit alleges.
The office last October charged six people with conspiring to obstruct a federal officer, a felony, for their actions during a protest at a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in the Chicago suburb of Broadview.
Transcripts turned over to the court, which a judge ordered Boutros’ office to remove redactions from, later revealed that a grand jury twice refused to indict the six, despite prosecutors’ urgings and a highly unusual speech Boutros gave to jurors. Boutros dropped all charges against the six in May as the court moved to investigate possible prosecutorial misconduct.
Boutros “repeatedly complained to his superiors in Washington” that the failure was DePodesta’s fault “to deflect attention from his own malfeasance,” DePodesta’s attorneys wrote in the suit. DePodesta denied Boutros’ accusations to his superiors at the FBI, and they conceded that he was only being forced out because of the “political pressure Boutros created,” according to the suit.
The suit alleges Boutros told Justice Department leadership that DePodesta and his sister-in-law Nancy DePodesta, who is an attorney representing one of the six former defendants, “conspired to destroy” the case.
Nancy DePodesta, who represents Michael Rabbitt, one of the former defendants, confirmed to the AP that she is Douglas DePodesta’s sister-in-law.
“There is no one at the FBI who took their oath of office and their ethical and moral responsibilities more seriously than Doug,” Nancy DePodesta said in a statement to the AP. “It is both heartbreaking and shameful that he was forced out of his position based on what appear to be utterly false rumors spread by” Boutros, she added.
In late September, one of the prosecutors on the “Broadview Six” case abruptly resigned, writing in a scathing resignation letter that Boutros had “scapegoated and publicly vilified” her. She filed a motion asking the court to treat her as an independent party going forward.
The former defendants have asked Judge Perry to appoint a special counsel to look into possible misconduct by prosecutors. At an Oct. 1 hearing, Perry ordered further “fact-finding” about communications between Boutros’ office and Justice Department leadership.
___
Mayes-Osterman is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Mortgage closing costs: What they are and how much you’ll pay
text:
Mortgage closing costs: What they are and how much you’ll pay
Key takeaways
- Closing costs are the fees you pay to get a mortgage and finalize the purchase, and most of them are due on closing day.
- Costs typically range from 2% to 5% of the total loan amount, or about $8,000 to $20,000 for a $400,000 loan.
- The biggest line items are lender origination fees, title services, the appraisal and the prepaid taxes and insurance that go into your escrow account, and buyers pay most of the fees.
- Your Loan Estimate tells you which fees you can shop for and which are fixed. Comparing that document across at least three lenders is the one step that reliably lowers what you pay.
Closing costs may not be the most exciting part of buying your home, but they are an important expense to plan for. From origination fees and appraisals to title services, they can add up to thousands of dollars, with most being paid by buyers. Some costs are avoidable, others may be negotiable and some are required by your state or county.
Here are the fees to watch for and how to keep them in check.
How much are closing costs?
Buying a home comes with more expenses than just your down payment. Expect to pay about 2% to 5% of your total loan amount in mortgage closing costs. If you’ve taken out a $400,000 loan, that means your closing costs might range from $8,000 to $20,000. How much you’ll end up paying depends on factors like the home’s price, your loan type and where you buy.
According to a 2025 report from LodeStar, the average purchase closing cost total was $4,528 nationally, or about 1% of the average sales price of $433,632. But while LodeStar’s calculation accounts for some common fees, it leaves out origination and underwriting fees, real estate commissions, discount points and escrow prepaids. So, about 1% of the sales price covers title, settlement and government charges. The rest of the way to 2% to 5% of your loan amount is lender fees, points and prepaids, and that’s the part you have the most influence over.
Click the arrow below to compare average closing costs by state.
-  Average closing costs by state Remember, these figures don’t include lender fees or commissions. LodeStar found that closing costs run highest, as a share of sales price, in states where transfer taxes make up the bulk of the bill — Delaware, New York, Vermont, Pennsylvania and Washington, D.C. They run lowest in states with little or no transfer tax. Washington, D.C., and Delaware are the most expensive areas for closing costs. The least expensive were South Dakota, Iowa and Missouri. Source: Lodestar
What’s included in closing costs?
Closing costs can feel like a long list of unfamiliar fees, but nearly all of them fall into one of four buckets:
- Lender fees: Your lender charges these to set up, process and approve your loan. You may also have the option to buy discount points, which are upfront payments that lower your interest rate.
- Third-party services: These pay outside professionals for the home appraisal, title search, title insurance policy, survey and closing agent.
- Government charges: Your city, county or state charges these to record the sale and the mortgage in public records. Many states and counties also charge a transfer tax when the property changes hands.
- Prepaids: These fees cover bills that aren’t due yet. You’ll pay interest from your closing date to your first payment, plus several months of property taxes and homeowners insurance that go into an escrow account.
Not every upfront cost associated with buying a home is considered a closing cost. For example, your down payment will go toward the purchase price of your home and is separate from closing costs.
Two of these four buckets are negotiable. Your lender sets its own fees, and you can compare them and shop for most third-party services. Government charges are set by statute and prepaids are set by your tax bill and your insurer, so neither moves much.
Who pays closing costs?
If you’re the buyer, you’re likely to pay most of the closing costs. Sellers cover some, and in a slower market, they’ll sometimes cover more.
Closing costs paid by the buyer
Buyers may be able to negotiate with the seller to cover some of their costs, called “seller concessions.” The shoppable column below tells you where you have room to move. Some fees you influence by comparing lender offers, some by sourcing the provider yourself and some not at all, because a statute sets them.
Closing costs paid by the seller
Sellers usually pay out of their sale proceeds rather than bringing cash to the table. Sellers can also agree to pay some of the buyer’s closing costs outright as a credit.
Compare your Loan Estimates before you commit
Every lender has to give you the same three-page form within three business days of applying. That’s the point of the Loan Estimate: it’s standardized, so offers line up side by side. To compare offers, read page 2: Section B lists the services you can’t shop for, and Section C lists the ones you can.
Three rules govern what happens between your Loan Estimate and closing day:
- Some can’t increase at all: Your lender’s own charges, discount points, transfer taxes and fees for services you can’t shop, like the credit report and the appraisal.
- Some can increase up to 10%, as a group: Recording fees, plus any Section C service where you used a provider from your lender’s written list.
- Some can change by any amount: Prepaid interest, insurance premiums, escrow deposits and any provider who wasn’t on your lender’s list.
If something material changes on your loan file, your lender can reset those limits, but it must document the reason and send you a revised Loan Estimate.
Your Closing Disclosure arrives at least three business days before closing with the final version of the same numbers. Put the two side by side and look for anything that moved. If a protected fee went up, be sure to ask why — your lender may owe you the difference.
Compare current mortgage rates
Compare mortgage rates from our national marketplace of lenders to find the best rate for your situation.
Learn more
How to lower your closing costs
You won’t avoid closing costs entirely, but you can lower what you pay. These are ordered by how much they typically move.
- Compare lenders and negotiate fees: Look for a mortgage lender that doesn’t charge an origination fee, or one that’ll discount it. Once you have three Loan Estimates in hand, you can show each lender the best offer and ask them to match it. If you’re getting your mortgage at your bank, you can also try asking for a discount or fee waiver, since you’re already a customer.
- Negotiate seller concessions: To encourage a sale, or in a buyer-friendly market, a seller might agree to pay some of your costs. This is often the single largest reduction a buyer can get. Keep in mind that lenders and loan programs limit how much sellers can contribute, and the limit depends on your loan type and down payment, so confirm it with your lender before you write it into an offer.
- Shop around when possible: Section C of your Loan Estimate names the services you can source yourself, typically the title insurance, title search and survey. Comparing providers can reduce your costs, though using your lender’s written list means that fee loses its 10% protection.
- Apply for down payment assistance: Down payment assistance and grants aren’t always limited to your down payment. Depending on the program, some can help with closing costs, particularly if you’re a first-time homebuyer.
- Use a no-closing-cost loan, but run the numbers: Don’t let the name fool you — you’ll still pay closing costs with a no-closing-cost loan. But instead of paying that amount now, you’ll finance it with your mortgage and pay interest on it or pay a slightly higher interest rate. Find your break-even point, or the amount of time it takes for the cost of the loan to make sense. If skipping $6,000 upfront costs you an extra $100 a month, you break even at five years. Stay in the house longer than that, and the loan costs you more.
Frequently asked questions
-  How can I budget for closing costs? Before you start looking at homes, get preapproved for a mortgage so you understand how much you can afford to spend. Knowing your price point can give you a rough sense of what closing costs might be. Since total closing costs are typically 2% to 5% of the loan amount, it might be a good idea to set aside enough funds to cover the high end of that range, on top of your down payment.
-  When are closing costs paid? Most closing costs are paid at the closing, when you sign your final loan and purchase documents. But some of the fees, such as for an appraisal and credit check, are paid ahead of time.
-  How long does the closing process take? Most purchase loans close in about 30 to 45 days from application, though the timeline depends on your loan type, your lender and how quickly you return the requested documents. ICE Mortgage Technology put the average purchase loan at 36.8 days in March 2026, the fastest since it began tracking in 2019. Conventional loans tend to close faster than government-backed loans like FHA and VA loans.
-  Why are closing costs so high? Closing costs, which typically range from 2% to 5% of your mortgage loan, come down to two things: the mortgage amount and where you’re buying. Many of the biggest fees grow with the deal — loan origination is typically a percentage of your loan amount, and title insurance premiums are based on your purchase price or loan amount. Location matters because of taxes: LodeStar found that closing costs run highest, as a share of sales price, in states where transfer taxes make up the bulk of the bill, and lowest in states with little or no transfer tax. Beyond lender charges and third-party services like appraisals and inspections, mandatory escrow prepayments for taxes and insurance can add thousands before you’ve made a single mortgage payment.

text:
DALLAS — Rookie Darius Acuff Jr. scored 25 points and the Sacramento Kings won for the first time in seven games this season, beating the Dallas Mavericks 115-100 on Monday night.
Malik Monk added 24 points and Zach LaVine had 23 for the Kings, the last NBA team this season to win.
Daniel Gafford and Walter Clayton Jr. each had 20 points for Dallas. Cooper Flagg of Newport added 17 on 3-of-19 shooting. He did make all 11 of his free throws.

The Kings led 54-53 at the half.

title: Tremont resident tags the first deer on MDI in over 90 years
text:
TREMONT — On Nov. 2, at 6:40 a.m., at Gott’s Store, David "Trusty" Trust tagged the first deer legally harvested on Mount Desert Island in almost 100 years.
Reeling with excitement, Trust explained how he stayed up all night excited for the opening of the Special Hunt in Tremont.
“I told myself, I’m gonna get the first one, and I also told others I want to tag the first deer on MDI in over 90 years.”
Trust did exactly that.
He explained that around 5:45 a.m., after first light, he saw six deer pass by his hunting spot before taking number seven.
“This one right here is one of seven that passed through,” explained Trust, standing by his 99-pound tagged deer hanging from his orange tractor. Trust said that before he got out into the woods, he was careful to measure all his distances from his hunting spot and take all the precautions to follow the guidelines set by the town and the state.
“I made sure to cross all t’s and dot my i’s before getting out there,” said Trust. He took the shot from approximately 15 yards with a crossbow. The shot was a clean kill, hitting the deer directly in the heart and passing through. He went back and recovered the crossbow bolt, thinking it was important and possibly a part of MDI history. “After I took the shot, I tracked it around 30 yards,” said Trust. Once he located the deer, he dragged it to his ATV and hauled it out.
Trust took the deer straight to Gott’s Store so he could tag it. “Everything happened perfectly,” he said with a smile. He plans to process the meat and give it to his family and friends in Otis.
At Gott’s Store, Shelby Parsons tagged Trust’s deer. Parsons tagged three of the four deer brought in so far on the first day of the hunt.
Trust is a Tremont resident and a carpenter who specializes in fabricating staircases. After getting this deer processed, he plans to get back in the woods to claim his second tag.
The Islander also spoke with Game Warden Will Nichols at Gott’s Store. Nichols wants hunters to follow all the hunt's guidelines so it succeeds and keeps everyone safe.
“You can't shoot over bait; you can't shoot too close to anybody's house without permission. So there are all these things that you have to be cognizant of when you're hunting a deer, and just because we have a special hunting area doesn't mean you can go off and do whatever you want. You still have to read the law book and be aware of all these regulations that we have in place.”
He also wanted hunters to know that if they make a mistake, they should reach out to the game wardens to try to resolve any issues.
“People make mistakes; we'd like to think they would reach out to us and let us know. It's not to say that you won't get anything out of that, and we'll have to handle it accordingly. But if we have to track someone down and figure this out on their own as a violation, It's much less likely to go in a way that they like in terms of what may result from that.”
Nichols said most of the interactions he has with the public and hunters are positive and that people do like seeing them around. At press time, Nichols noted that four tags had been claimed at Gott’s. The wardens will be in the area making sure hunters follow the guidelines and can answer any questions if needed.
He also noted that if residents or hunters see someone illegally hunting, they should connect with Operation Game Thief at maineogt.org to report poachers.
The Special Hunt in Tremont has seen its fair share of opposition, as critics of the hunt want to protect the deer population and do not see a need. At a past public hearing in Tremont, one of the critics of the hunt, George Sanker, said he was firmly against it. “I love white-tailed deer and pretty much all wildlife.”
Sanker then referenced a 1931 law banning deer hunting on Mount Desert Island, adding that the founders of Acadia National Park envisioned a safe, peaceful place where wildlife could live without fear. “The 1931 law did not declare no hunting in Tremont. It declared no hunting anywhere on MDI.”
On the other side of the issue, Tremont resident Corey Walker supports the hunt and thinks it's a good thing for the town. Walker spent the early morning hours of Monday trying to get a deer himself but only saw bucks, which could not be shot.
"I did not see any does, I did see a 4-pointer walk right by my blind about 10 feet away from me."
Walker said that he understands the hunt is a touchy subject, but he also believes that the deer here are causing issues, mainly car accidents and spreading Lyme disease.
"Deer are wild animals, not pets. I understand that it is an emotional subject for many people. Deer are beautiful animals, and many of us enjoy seeing them in our yards and throughout our community. However, we also need to recognize that when deer populations grow beyond what the available habitat can comfortably support, problems can develop for both the animals and the people who live here.”
First, Walker explained his safety concern: “Deer crossing our roads create dangerous situations for drivers, passengers, and the deer themselves. Vehicle collisions can result in serious injuries, costly damage, and unnecessary suffering for the animals.”
He then noted that the overpopulation makes the deer compete for food. “There is impact on our natural environment. When there are too many deer competing for limited food, vegetation and natural habitats can suffer. Deer can also experience poor health and inadequate nutrition when food becomes scarce. Third, is ticks and Lyme disease are a real concern in our communities. Although deer are not the source of Lyme disease, they play a role in supporting the adult ticks that spread it," explained Walker via text.
A total of 200 deer can be harvested during the month of November, with two per hunter.

title: Savannah Guthrie renews plea for information in mother’s disappearance
text:
TUCSON, Ariz. (Gray News) - Savannah Guthrie made another public plea Sunday for information about the disappearance of her mother, Nancy Guthrie, 84.
It has been nine months since Nancy Guthrie disappeared.
Plea on Instagram
“Today” host Savannah Guthrie wrote on Instagram, “Our mom was a light in this world. We want to celebrate her and give her the dignity she deserves... Please help us.”
In the post, she also shared a childhood drawing from her own daughter featuring an umbrella in the rain alongside the message, “I know it might not seem like it but I really need my mommy.”
Investigation status
Nancy Guthrie disappeared from her Tucson-area home on Feb. 1.
Local and federal law enforcement officials still do not have a suspect or person of interest.
The Pima County Sheriff’s Department said Friday its investigators traveled to Florida to meet with scientists in hopes of furthering DNA analysis in the case, KOLD reported.
Tips and reward
The sheriff’s department is still seeking tips in Nancy Guthrie’s disappearance.
The Guthrie family is offering $1 million for information leading to the recovery of Nancy Guthrie. 88-CRIME is offering a $102,500 reward and the FBI is offering a $100,000 reward for information leading to Nancy Guthrie’s location or conviction of those responsible.
Anyone with information is asked to call 88-CRIME locally at 520-882-7463, the FBI at 1-800-225-5324 or the FBI’s Phoenix Field Office at 623-466-1999. Tips can also be submitted online at tips.fbi.gov.

title: Community members push back as Mount Vernon Select Board to choose Town Clerk Monday night
text:
Community members push back as Mount Vernon Select Board to choose Town Clerk Monday night
On Monday night, the Mount Vernon Select Board will choose the town's next town clerk, the night before the Midterms.
It comes after the previous clerk, who began in June, was let go in mid-October, according to Select Board Chair Carl Rogers, who did not want to be interviewed on camera.
Rogers said that the labor agreement included a 6-month probationary period that allows for the clerk to be let go if the Select Board decides it's best for the town. Rogers cited a "personnel matter" as the reason.
According to Rogers, Deputy Clerk Brenda Hopkins has been filling in and will be named Clerk on Monday night while the town's registrar will lead most election responsibilities.
Rogers stated that, like many Maine communities, Mount Vernon has seen a large number of early voters and there have been no problems despite the lack of a town clerk.
However, some in the town of 1,800 are left with questions.
"There is no communication as to where we're voting, what time we're voting," said Mount Vernon resident Karen Mairs. "We don't know who is running the voting."
While the town has updates on its website and its Facebook, Mairs said that's not where the aging population of Mount Vernon is looking.
She is hoping for more signage around the town and the polling place. The Community Center, where Mount Vernon residents can vote from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Tuesday, did not have signage indicating that it is where voting will be held as of Monday afternoon.
"It doesn't have to be this dysfunctional," said resident Ona Fast. "And so I wish I could say, yes, I believe that it will be absolutely fair and a good process, but I really don't have that faith."

title: OUI Arrest During Fort Fairfield Trick-or-Treating
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Calls from Fort Fairfield residents helped police take a suspected drunk driver off the road on Halloween night.
According to the Fort Fairfield Police Department, around 6 p.m. on Halloween night they received multiple calls reporting a driver on the back streets of town that was driving while intoxicated during peak trick-or-treat hours. Police say the driver had children in the vehicle at the time and was quickly arrested for Operating Under the Influence while families were out walking around the neighborhood.
In a Facebook post, Fort Fairfield police said quote: “The situation could have ended tragically. We are deeply grateful to the vigilant community members who spoke up and reported this, as well as our dedicated officers for acting quickly to remove the driver from the road and keep our children safe.”

title: Bangor, Portland and Augusta courts will stay open late on Election Day
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Maine courthouses in Portland, Bangor and Augusta will stay open until 9 p.m. Tuesday to accept emergency filings related to the election, according to a release from the Maine Judicial Branch.
The announcement comes as several Maine cities expect federal election monitors at the polls and numerous lawsuits in federal court across the country continue to develop in the final few days before the midterms.
The Maine Judicial Branch said a judge, clerk and marshal will be on duty at each courthouse to accept and act on any emergency filings.
Maine Superior Court Chief Justice Robert Mullen and Maine District Court Chief Judge Brent Davis also issued an order Thursday that all filings pertaining to the election must be filed with paper documents at a clerk’s office, not through the state’s electronic filing system.
Paper filings will be immediately reviewed by the clerk and directed to the appropriate judge for timely review. The judicial branch is also urging filers to include cell phone numbers on any filings, so that they can be reached after hours.
All public documents related to election filings will then be posted on the judicial branch’s high-profile cases webpage, as soon as possible.
A spokesperson for the Maine secretary of state’s office said the courts have always been open and available to the office until polls close on Election Day.
“We appreciate the partnership with the courts to ensure that every voter’s constitutional right to vote is protected,” the spokesperson said in an email.
The state court plans come as federal courts across the country continue to consider a bevy of lawsuits related to the Trump administration’s sweeping efforts to combat noncitizen voting and assert authority over elections, as Democrats and voting rights groups allege federal election interference.
Election monitors
The U.S. Department of Justice will also send election monitors to South Portland, the secretary of state’s office confirmed Friday.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows previously said that election monitors will be in Portland and Lewiston.
The Department of Justice has in recent years sent observers to other states on a smaller scale, usually in response to a civil rights violation. But this comes amid the Trump administration’s efforts to assert authority over the election and following an attempt to force Maine, among other states, to hand over voter information.
“Any monitors are subject to the same laws and rules as any other observer at the poll,” Bellows told Maine Morning Star last week. “That means they can observe what’s taking place, but they may not interact with voters, handle ballots or equipment, or disrupt voting in any way.”
“We will monitor the monitors very carefully to ensure that they don’t cross any lines,” Bellows added.
South Portland Mayor Elyse Tipton told Maine Morning Star about a meeting held Thursday where the city learned that election observers would be at their polling places from 7 a.m. until polls close.
The Department of Justice let city staff know the observers would be in plainclothes, she said, but she did not know why South Portland had been chosen in addition to the state’s two largest cities.
It’s a small piece of the federal agency’s plan to send 1,000 monitors to locations in all 50 states, Justice Department spokesperson Kiersten Pels told States Newsroom on Monday.
The Justice Department for decades has deployed monitors across the country to watch the voting process. During President Joe Biden’s administration, the DOJ sent monitors to 64 jurisdictions across 24 states for the 2022 midterm elections.
Maine Morning Star Senior Reporter Eesha Pendharkar contributed to this report.

title: Admiring Brunswick’s November beauty, thankful 3 times over
text:
BENCHED
Three, sometimes five, times a week, I find myself walking in the Brunswick Town Commons. Other Commons-walkers may also have noted the recent appearance of a fourth bench offering a seat for rest, contemplation, or awaiting the simple emergence of bird voices that come on five minutes after a person stops moving and settles in the woods.
A couple of years ago, when the first three of these benches appeared, I sent a query, and then thanks, to conservationist Jym St. Pierre, a member of the Town Commons Committee at the time. I learned a bit about these repurposed, peg-fastened benches. I also named them (quietly) St. Pierre Benches (even as I knew they were the gifts of many). So now, the number risen to four, I send on general thanks to our Parks and Recreation Department, and (quietly) to the new bench’s namesake.
My favorite bench is in mid-Commons at what I call the Triangle of Confusion — three paths converge there, raising the question I sometimes field while sitting there: Which way should I go? Perhaps you, too, think through that question often. This bench is a best seat for it.
VISITING EDDY
On a mid-October walk, and near its end, I drop into the nearby Mere Brook gully to check on the water level after our very dry summer and to see the seasonal outcry of colors. It is beauty time at the brook: light ricocheting wildly, blue sky peering down through the treetops just to see the display.
It seems odd, even a bit presumptuous, to name this patch of water. But there, close to the bank where I stand, is Eddy.
Leaves, often pale yellow, float downstream, speckling the dark, transparent waters with light. The leaves shine in contrast. They could be little footlights, spotlights facing up.
At a 90-degree stream bend, the current takes its usual course along the outer side of the curve, and there it encounters the partial block of a sunken log, which shunts the surface water to my right; the deeper water flows beneath the wood. And so the upper water begins a lazy spin, finding and re-finding its upstream self. And in its slow circle — diameter around 2 feet — the water captures a collection of yellow leaves. A wheel of light. I have found, re-found, Eddy.
Eddy’s face shifts constantly, so many leaf-eyes nudging into surface space, wobbling slightly atop the water. And every so often some yellow leaves align as a smile that spins then slowly up to become a lined forehead. Ears, varying noses, a mouth, Eddy is a jostle of personalities.
Is it any wonder then, that I begin to talk to Eddy?
A day later I return. Eddy is still there, although a blush of red leaves have entered the circle.
SAY IT SLANT — TAWNY TIMES
Every fall, I await my favorite month. November nears. I revel, as we all do, in the the colorful trek through October, but then the muted, tawny landscape rises, showing its bones and stones, its definition. Bouldery land becomes the main show in its ridges and furrows; even the trees seem to attend, peering down without their expressive leaves, their rustling vocabulary, as if to say, “When will it be leaf time again?” “Later,” the land answers, and the trees go stoic, mimic their stony friends.
Then there is the fresh cold. On some days it sharpens the air and the edges of every blade of dried grass. It even calms our aggressive interloper, the tick. Walking in fields becomes low risk, long sighted, lovely.
But November’s show, its big act, is its light. The year’s round has no light like November light.
I got my first look at oncoming November’s light in early October (though a friend points out that August is first to offer slant-light’s harbinger of fall). It was a clear day, ebbing, and we were at one of our region’s many Land’s Ends, with water stretching to our east, south and west. We’d not seen a cloud all day; the sky had been faultless blue … still was. Except, to our west-southwest a pencil-thin mustache of cloud drew a line across the sun as it neared the far ridges and water. The land darkened. I noticed an involuntary hesitation to breathe out. The world stilled, the few people nearby quieted. Inhale … hold breath … still.
Then the sun dropped a few more degrees, the mustache became a toupee, which, for reasons unknown, seemed to return us all to voice. Vermillion sunset stretched across the sky. Then darkness edged out from the bushes along the ground. But the light held sway for minutes more.
Sandy Stott is a Brunswick resident, chair of the town’s Conservation Commission and its Steering Committee for the Restoration of Mere Brook, a board member of Free the Andro, and a member of Brunswick-Topsham Land Trust’s board of directors. He writes for the AMC’s Appalachia and a variety of publications. He may be reached at [email protected].

title: Windham’s new middle school could be named after late Sen. Bill Diamond
text:
Windham resident John Cressey is spearheading an effort to name the combined Windham-Raymond middle school, due to open next year, after late local politician Bill Diamond.
Diamond, who died last year at 80, served in Maine government for nearly half a century. First elected as a Democrat to the Maine House of Representatives in 1976, he was elected in 1982 to the first of 10 non-consecutive terms in the state Senate, representing a district encompassing Windham, Raymond, Standish and Casco, among other towns. From 1989 to 1997, he served as Maine’s secretary of state under Govs. John McKernan and Angus King.
In addition to his public service, Diamond was, in his later years, particularly devoted to the cause of preventing child abuse. He was the founder of Walk a Mile in Their Shoes, a nonprofit dedicated to advocating for the welfare of Maine’s children, as well as the Windham Neighbors Helping Neighbors nonprofit to provide emergency assistance for Windham residents in need of heating fuel. Diamond was also a lifelong educator, serving as principal of Jordan Small Middle School and superintendent of Raymond public schools.
Cressey, president of Beacon Environmental Consultants and longtime friend of the Diamond family, said the grassroots effort is the best opportunity the town has to honor the work Diamond did for Windham and Raymond.
The Regional School Unit 14 School Board is set to meet on Wednesday, Nov. 4, and vote on the name of the new middle school.
Karyn Diamond, Bill Diamond’s eldest daughter, said she supports the renaming effort, recalling how her father represented both towns as an educator, and saying that his work reflected what a school should stand for, including educating children, protecting them, and teaching them to care for others.
“It would be great just to honor his legacy,” said Cressey.

title: WATCH LIVE: Lindsay Clancy returns to court, but prospect of retrial remains unclear
text:
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.
PLYMOUTH, Mass. (AP) — Lindsay Clancy ‘s lawyer urged a judge Monday to either the dismiss the murder charges against her, or get on with the business of putting her back on trial.
This was the second time the Massachusetts mother has been in court since her first trial with ended with a deadlocked jury unable to agree whether she was legally responsible for killing her three young children. Jurors were split 11-1 in favor of acquittal when the judge declared a mistrial.
Clancy’s defense team moved to dismiss the charges on double jeopardy grounds, based on an unusual argument that the judge should have removed the one juror who favored conviction, then allowed jury deliberations to continue.
Judge William Sullivan did not immediately rule on Monday. Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, implored him to decide quickly, and also pressed the Plymouth District Attorney to reveal soon whether he plans to try Clancy on murder charges again.
“I am not going to have this woman sit incarcerated for the next year, or two or three,” Reddington said. Putting aside his sharp disagreement with the judge about the way the first trial ended, he said he wants Sullivan to preside over a second trial, if one happens. “I want a trial and I want it with you and I want it this spring.”
Sullivan scheduled another hearing for Nov. 16 and suggested a retrial could begin in March.
Prosecutors said they intend to retry Clancy if the case proceeds, but haven’t yet settled on whether they would pursue the same charges, or opt for a reduced charge that might be more palatable for the jury.
Clancy’s lawyer has argued that she had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behavior when she killed her three children in 2023. Prosecutors have acknowledged that Clancy had mental health problems, but said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong.
Hearing had heated moments
Reddington has staked part of his post-trial defense on assailing the one juror who wanted to convict Clancy.
He urged the judge again on Monday to investigate that juror, whom he accused of being untruthful on his jury questionnaire and improperly using his cell phone during jury deliberations.
At one point, Sullivan admonished Reddington to stop using the juror’s name in open court. Sullivan has a standing order sealing the names of the jurors temporarily to protect them from harassment — though several have done media interviews, including the holdout, Michael Desronvil. Reddington protested that the juror’s name “was all over the internet.”
“Why don’t we all dial this back a little bit,” Sullivan said at one point.
Defense challenges judge’s handling of deadlocked jury
Another of Clancy’s lawyers, Martin Weinberg, argued Monday that a mistrial could have been avoided had the judge more thoroughly interrogated jurors about their breakdown in deliberations after the foreperson sent two notes indicating that the lone holdout wasn’t following the court’s instructions on reasonable doubt.
After receiving the notes, Sullivan spoke with each juror, reminded them of their duties and explained what constitutes reasonable doubt. He asked whether they could apply the law to the case, and all said yes.
Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague argued Monday that Sullivan had struck the right balance — and that pressing further would have required delving into the substance of the jury’s deliberations, which isn’t allowed.
Juror’s lawyer defends his conduct
Desronvil said in a recent interview that he was certain of Clancy’s guilt, but other jurors wouldn’t listen.
His lawyer, Heather O’Connor, urged the judge Monday not to investigate his conduct any further, saying he had simply done his duty as a juror.
She disputed the allegations of improper cellphone use, saying all jurors were allowed to keep their phones and there was no evidence Desronvil had used his device to improperly research the case.
“If that’s enough to put a juror under oath, to search their phone, to pull their history, then the lesson (for) every future juror in this Commonwealth is simple: Agree with the majority or potentially be investigated,” O’Connor said.
Sullivan also heard arguments on the prosecutors’ request for a gag order while the case remains pending, to avoid influencing a future jury. Reddington gave interviews during the trial, while prosecutors generally did not speak to reporters. Clancy’s lawyers argued that it would amount to an unconstitutional restraint on speech.
__
AP journalist Leah Willingham contributed from Boston.

title: Maine dairy farmers embrace progressive management, technologies to ensure a future
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
At Fisher Farms, Carmen Fisher’s Facebook page, “CFF Farming,” shares insights on daily farm life.
Georgie, a milk cow “that has my heart,” was recently due to calf but wasn’t eating as much as usual. “Perhaps she was lonely. Cows are herd animals after all,” Fisher writes. Taffy, a mild-mannered Holstein, was brought in and Georgie got her appetite back.
A frozen hydraulic cylinder meant a rough couple of days chopping corn silage. “I put out the call for possible help this morning and within a couple hours I had five offers of assistance.”
About a newborn: “The weather isn’t pretty but this little guy sure is cute!”
The dairy diary is meant to reconnect readers with where their food comes from and the people who grow, produce and facilitate it.
“Giving people a glimpse at the people taking care of their dairy animals provides a human side to it so people can see the true compassion and care provided these animals,” says Fisher. “Despite the fact that these cows are considered a commodity, I want to show people they are still provided the respect and dignity they deserve.”

title: Butterfly Kisses Alliance changes the way families are supported after the loss of a child
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (Aging Untold) — Families navigating the tragic and unexpected loss of a baby are receiving an additional support system from the Butterfly Kisses Alliance.
A group of nurses in St. Louis founded the nonprofit in 2023 to offer support and resources to families and people impacted by the death of a baby, whether before, during or shortly after birth.
Kayla Hollingshead, Jennifer Koskela, Janie Mullinnax and Jeannette Hickey work together as labor and delivery nurses at Progress West Hospital. For each of them, the emotional toll of caring for mothers who had suffered a loss prompted them to create a way to help.
“We grieve with these families because we are there with them through the worst day of their life,” Hollingshead said. “We’re humans as well, we have emotions, and we got into nursing because we care and we love hard.”
Hollingshead said with most diagnoses, there is a standard of care within the medical profession, meaning there is a level of skill, knowledge and care a healthcare provider or support staff member is reasonably expected to provide given the situation.
However, she said, no real standard has ever existed for those who unexpectedly lose a baby.
“These families need to be given a standard amount of care and it should be standard across the country,” she said.
So, the women created a new standard of care that has been implemented at the hospital, ranging from how office staff speaks to families, to ultrasound technicians and beyond.
In addition to changing standards of care, the women also create comfort kits containing books, cards and self-care items that are mailed to families around the world.
Kelsey and Greg Fussner suffered an unconscionable loss of their own in 2023. After suffering a miscarriage 2021, Kelsey found out she was pregnant in July of 2022.
“It was such a relief because we made it past what everyone said,” she said. “Because we’d never made it that far before, so making it that far was really fantastic.”
From the beginning, she said her doctor told her she likely would deliver by 38 weeks. However, as the 38-week mark approached, she said her doctor told her she would be scheduled for a C-section at 39 weeks and one day.
But at Fussner’s final appointment before delivery, at 38 weeks and three days, she received unimaginable news.
“The ultrasound tech just looked at the doctor and shook her head and he [my husband] said, ‘No say it out loud, say it out loud,’ and then the doctor said there was no heartbeat,” she said.
Having eaten breakfast before her appointment, Fussner said the next eight hours were agonizing, as she waited for surgery to deliver her baby girl Nora.
“I wanted to see her, I couldn’t wait to see her and see what she looked like, but on the other side of it was completely devastating and hard to grasp that I’m not going to be able to take my baby home,” she said.
What Fussner didn’t know at the time was that her nursing staff consisted of the same women who founded Butterfly Kisses Alliance. Immediately, she said, they showed compassion by removing baby items from her hospital room and closing other patient doors when she walked the halls.
Then, forced to leave the hospital without her baby, the women offered Fussner a weighted stuffed animal, an elephant, stuffed to the exact weight of her daughter Nora, eight pounds, 13 ounces.
They also packed her a comfort kit full of memories of Nora, including her hospital blanket, footprints, a necklace, homemade quilt and pictures in the outfit she was meant to go home in.
“They took lots of pictures, which I hold so dear to me because it’s the only memory I have of her,” she said.
As the couple continued to grieve, a few months later, Kelsey got a surprise - she was pregnant.
“It was fast, and of course, you’re absolutely terrified,” she said. “It’s confusing because you want to celebrate, but at the same time, you feel bad celebrating.”
Under the care of a different doctor, Fussner was scheduled to deliver at 37 weeks via C-section. It just so happened, she said, to fall on April 10, the same month and day Nora was due.
“They asked if we wanted to change it and I said no,” she said.
On April 10, 2024, Kelsey gave birth to Abigail.
“I felt like this was meant to be, that this was Nora’s way of saying she is with us,” Fussner said. “She will always be part of our lives and she’s a part of our story and my life and she’s going to be part of Abigail’s too, just in a different way.”
The Butterfly Kisses Alliance offers online resources for families dealing with pregnancy loss, even when in-person support is not available.
The organization provides materials for mothers seeking advice about physical changes after pregnancy loss and fathers looking to honor their child. Resources are also available for siblings, grandparents and friends wanting to help their loved ones cope.
To learn more about the Butterfly Kisses Alliance, its mission, or to donate, visit here.

title: Discarded ashes spark Presque Isle apartment building fire, investigators say
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WABI) - Discarded ashes sparked a fire at a multi-unit apartment building in Presque Isle, according to officials with the Maine State Fire Marshal’s Office.

title: Couple refuses to leave dog behind during helicopter rescue amid dangerous flooding
text:
SEDONA, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — Rapidly rising floodwaters triggered water rescues and forced residents from their homes in several Arizona communities Sunday.
That included Sedona, where officials ordered residents near Oak Creek to leave immediately as floodwaters trapped multiple people in their homes.
Alexander Dale and his wife were trapped by rising floodwaters. Their home and several Airbnbs they manage sit on a property next to the creek bed.
“We didn’t know what to do. We couldn’t go anywhere,” Dale said.
Dale, his wife and about nine of their guests climbed onto the roof of the home. They waited about three hours for a helicopter to lift them to safety.
“There was a helicopter and it had this huge rope on it, this huge line,” he said.
According to Dale, there was at first a question about whether the family’s dog could be lifted out.
“He told me, ‘Well, we don’t have a harness for a K-9, so I don’t know if we can take him.’ So I’m like, ‘What do we do?’” Dale said.
The couple did not leave the dog behind. They used harnesses they had at home.
“We put like three of them on him and strapped it all together,” Dale said.
Dale and his dog were lifted out together.
“I was sitting in this harness basically holding my dog, praying he doesn’t go anywhere,” Dale said.
Dale and his wife were not the only people forced out.
Cindy Wilmer, a schoolteacher, lives at Red Rock Crossing. She also evacuated with very little.
“The water was just roaring down the street,” Wilmer said. “I just left with the shirt on my back and the keys to the school and my cat ... I’m worried about my house.”
Fernando Leon was also evacuated. He feared his Oak Creek home might be a total loss.
“I opened the door and I saw the river, and I said, ‘Whoa, I need to get out of here,’” Leon said. “From one day to the next you’re at your place and then you have to evacuate and leave all your things behind. It’s just a very sad feeling.”
By Sunday afternoon, the drenching rains had largely subsided in the Sedona area.
Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs said state air rescue crews were also assisting with rooftop evacuations and state transportation crews were helping clear debris.
No injuries or deaths were immediately reported

title: Lindsay Clancy returns to court in a bid to dismiss charges she killed her three young children
text:
PLYMOUTH, Mass. (AP) — Lindsay Clancy returns to court Monday in a bid to dismiss the charges that she murdered her three young children.
The hearing Monday is the second time the Massachusetts mother has been in court since her trial ended with a deadlocked jury in September after jurors were unable to agree on a verdict. Prosecutors have yet to announce whether they plan to retry Clancy. They could choose to retry her on first-degree murder charges or pursue lesser charges, including second-degree murder or manslaughter, or drop the case entirely.
Clancy has never disputed killing her three young children in 2023, but her lawyer has argued she had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behavior. Prosecutors have acknowledged that the 36-year-old Clancy had mental health problems but said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong.
___
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.
___
The focus at Monday’s hearing in front of Judge William Sullivan is expected to be on a motion from the defense to dismiss the charges on double jeopardy grounds.
They argue that the court did not need to declare a mistrial. Instead, it could have questioned the lone holdout juror Michael Desronvil, or the jury foreperson, regarding reports that he was refusing to follow court instructions with regards to reasonable doubt and failing to follow the law as he was instructed. That could have led to Desronvil being removed, thus avoiding the need for a mistrial.
Since the trial ended, Desronvil said he was certain of Clancy’s guilt but that no one would listen to him.
Prosecutors, in their motion to dismiss, argue that double jeopardy “does not bar the Commonwealth from seeking justice on behalf of the three victims.”
They argue it was unnecessary to investigate Desronvil, whom they don’t name but describe as the dissenting juror, because the foreperson complaint did not allege “any personal issue, bias, or extraneous attributable to the dissenting juror.” Singling that juror out, they argued, for an investigation “surely would have led to judicial coercion” and the “impermissible intrusion into the substance of the jury’s private deliberations.”
The other motion expected to be discussed is the Commonwealth’s request for a gag order that would bar attorneys and their supporters “from making extrajudicial statements to the media that would have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing the criminal proceeding.”
Attorney Kevin Reddington has given a series of interviews since the mistrial and held walking news conferences almost every day during the proceedings. Prosecutors, in contrast, never talked to reporters.
In response, Clancy’s lawyers said this motion would amount to prior restraint since it is barring speech before it occurs. “The government bears a heavy burden to justify such an order,” Laura McConnell, who was hired by Clancy’s defense team, wrote. “There is no jury and it is unknown whether one will ever be impaneled. There is no trial date. The motion should be denied.”

title: Freezers at supermarkets in several European countries hit by apparent cyberattacks
text:
Freezers at supermarkets in several European countries hit by apparent cyberattacks
Supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg and Estonia were hit Monday by problems with freezers and fridges that apparently were caused by cyberattacks, forcing some to dispose of ruined food.
The problems follow a case last month in which attackers remotely took control of refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, sending temperatures soaring.
In Sweden, ICA Group supermarket chain spokesperson Gustaf Nilsson told news agency TT that “a limited number” of stores were affected overnight by an incident that affected refrigeration and freezing systems. He declined to give a specific number.
Video above (WGAL): Cyberattack disrupts refrigeration in European supermarkets
The ICA Kvantum branch in Sjöbo in southern Sweden wrote on its Facebook page that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and set to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit). It said it was working to discard the affected items.
The Coop chain said that six of its stores in central Sweden had problems with their fridges and freezers, TT reported, though it didn't immediately have details.
The Delhaize chain said that an “IT incident” had affected refrigeration systems in several dozen of its stores, mostly in Belgium but also a few in neighboring Luxembourg.
“In the affected stores, the range of fresh and frozen products is temporarily somewhat limited. Our distribution centers are operating normally, and there has been no disruption to deliveries to our stores,” spokesperson Sarah De Meester said.
The Carrefour supermarket chain in Belgium said a “cyberattack targeting refrigeration installations only had an extremely limited impact,” affecting 15 of its more than 700 stores.
In Estonia, a company that makes the affected technology said that one of its clients had been hit by a cyberattack in which attackers accessed a computer controlling refrigeration and turned up the temperature to 50 degrees Celsius, public broadcaster ERR reported.
Jann Mutso, the CEO of Kitman Coldtech, declined to say which store's cooling system had been affected but said that the attack was responded to within minutes and there was no significant damage. The Selver chain said one of its outlets was affected.
The cyberattacks in France appeared to target old systems.

title: Video shows Florida deputies rescuing toddler from retention pond; parents arrested
text:
Video shows Florida deputies rescuing toddler from retention pond; parents arrested
Deputies rescued a 4-year-old child from a retention pond in Deltona early Saturday morning, according to the Volusia Sheriff's Office.
Jenexica Rodriguez-Crespo and Fermin Medrano-Perez, the child's parents, were arrested on charges of child neglect and animal cruelty.
VSO responded after a caller reported an unaccompanied toddler walking near the pond. Deputies who heard the call through Live 911 spotted the child in the water and retrieved him.
"For us, that automatically triggers us to get up, move. We got to get there as quick as possible to kind of prevent worst-case scenario," Sgt. Peter Carelli told WESH 2.
After identifying the child’s home, deputies found animal waste, a roach infestation, and mold inside, authorities said. Deltona Animal Control took custody of a caged dog that authorities said had been neglected.
"Walking up to the house, I just got this extreme foul odor from within, and I've been doing this for 13 years, and it was pretty bad enough that I was, I was concerned that someone could have been possibly dead inside. That's how bad it smelled," Carelli said.
"It was just disheveled everywhere. There was stuff on the ground. There was feces that had been there for a long period of time, as well as urine," he said. "There was insects, dead insects inside the house. You know, feces from insects. Just the whole condition."
Deputies say a grandparent took custody of the child, and the Florida Department of Children and Families was contacted for follow-up.
"No child should have to go through that," Carelli said.
Both parents have been released on bond.

title: Character of the County: Christopher Brown Supports the Living Through Connection
text:
Christopher Brown doesn’t think anyone needs to see a medium – or believe in what he does. That said, he knows from his decade of experience that doing so can be useful.
“I’m not trying to convince anybody,” he said. “I’m just trying to give you what I’m giving you in hopes that it helps.
Brown, of Jefferson, has made a living as a psychic medium for a decade. To him, this means he is somebody who connects with the spirit of the deceased, typically friends and family, or even pets, who have died.
Brown believes that the consciousness of living beings passes to a different, but proximal, world when their mortal timer runs out. He used the metaphor of two pieces of paper on top of each other to describe this realm and the next; mediums can connect with both, he said.
Now 41, Brown is new, relatively speaking, to the business of mediumship. A decade ago he had what he described as a “rude awakening” and discovered the intuition present his whole life might not just be his imagination. After a paranormal investigation at Parson Cemetery in York, he discovered on YouTube that his experience of feeling the spirit of a young boy trying to play with him aligned exactly with another medium who visited the site.
“It opened up a world of fascination that I’d never thought of before,” he said.
At the time, Brown was struggling with depression and had cycled through manual labor jobs that he “never really stuck with,” he said. Through mediumship, he was able to find a new cause that could heal both himself and others, so he dove headfirst down that path.
“I’ve had all these different other jobs, and none of them felt right,” he said. “And this one just felt right.”
Brown became an ordained minister through a spiritualist camp meeting in Etna in 2020 after two years of online courses. He also became a Reiki master. But he is always still learning, he said.
“I’m never satiated by my quest for knowledge when it comes to this stuff,” Brown said.
In the same vein, he is also working toward a degree in psychology from the University of Maine at Augusta, with which he hopes to better understand his clients and social psychology.
In Maine and the broader New England region, Brown performs private individual and group readings, and tours performing demonstrations, having built his business and reputation largely through word of mouth. He said that his work is “like interpreting a daydream that isn’t yours,” and that he is able to see, hear, feel, and sometimes even smell things from the spirit world that his client cannot.
With a profession that often involves grieving clients, Brown said it is “extremely difficult” to navigate emotional boundaries in his line of work.
“I try to just be as empathetic and compassionate in the moment, and I try to just acknowledge that this is not for me; it’s for them, which is not easy,” he said. “I can’t always do it. I try my best.”
He said he once had the spirit of a chimpanzee “come through” – the language used to describe the appearance of a spirit in a mediumship reading – when reading for a zookeeper that it was close to.
“The way it presented to me was a nonverbal child,” Brown said. “I just didn’t hear any speaking. It was all more mannerisms and things like that, and at the end of it, she goes, ‘Yeah, that wasn’t a human child.’ She goes, ‘That was a chimpanzee.’”
Some of his readings are more literal than others. Brown described a time when he did a reading for a man whose deceased father came through, and he heard the father mention Garfield, the orange cartoon cat. This didn’t resonate with his client until Brown mentioned lasagna, which was both Garfield and the father’s favorite food.
The accuracy and validity of his readings are important to Brown, as he brings forward details from spirits that can or cannot be confirmed by his clients. He said that if his client can’t corroborate what he brings to them, he won’t charge for the reading.
“If you go to the gas station, you prepay for 20 bucks of gas, and you don’t get the gas, you need to go back in again and get your money back,” Brown said. “I have to validate this stuff for myself too, because I need to know that it’s real.”
All he asks of skeptics of his line of work is, “don’t be cynical.”
“I applaud skepticism,” Brown said. “I appreciate it. I think it’s important and it’s valuable.”
With a growing market of online and virtual-based mediums, witches, and tarot card readers, he emphasized vetting who is offering the service.
“If you sit down with somebody and they say a bunch of vague stuff that could apply to anybody, then maybe think about what you’re getting or what you’re paying for,” he said.
Alongside what he estimates have been thousands of readings, Brown has a YouTube channel called “UnfilteredMediumship,” where he tries to “take a lot of the ‘woo-woo’ out of this stuff,” he said. He has published two books about mediumship, including “The Untrained Medium,” and made several television appearances, including a feature on “Tirdy Works,”
a realty TV show set in Somerville that aired on truTV in 2020.
Brown has been in Jefferson for a little over eight years, after he moved to be with his wife. He was born in Portland, where he lived most of his life, aside from a brief stint in Connecticut as a child with his family.
“My roots are always Maine,” he said about returning to the state.
In contrast to the heart of Portland, Jefferson is “just more peaceful,” Brown said.
“It’s more grounded,” he said. “It’s more my speed.”
Outside of his bookings and readings, Brown is in a death metal band, in which he plays the electric guitar, recently received his black belt, and is part of a paranormal investigation team called 207 Paranormal. His public appearances and demonstrations keep him busy and traveling across New England, and his schedule can be found on his social media pages.
Brown said he hopes that his clients leave their readings “a little lighter.”
“I hope they leave knowing that the people that they love and they care about can hear them, that they know that they’re there,” Brown said.
For more information about Brown and his services, visit psychicmediumchristopher.com or email [email protected]. He can also be found on Facebook at Psychic Medium Christopher and Instagram at @mediumchristopher.
