title: Floodwaters swamp the Southwest, forcing evacuations and altering some Election Day voting
text:
Some rivers began receding in the flood-weary Southwest on Monday, including in a Colorado tourist town that has to alter its Election Day voting plans, while others were still rising, keeping residents on alert as rain began to move out of the area.
Heavy weekend rainfall produced flash flooding and mandatory evacuations across a swath of the Southwest, including parts of New Mexico, Colorado and Utah in the Four Corners region and in northern and central Arizona. The weather service estimated as much as 4 inches (10 centimeters) of rain could fall across the region through Monday, fueled by a series of Pacific storm systems.
Evacuees included some residents along the rising Animas River in southwestern Colorado, where all La Plata County roads remained closed Monday because of widespread flooding and damage to bridges.
Officials warned of “potentially catastrophic” flooding in Pagosa Springs in neighboring Archuleta County, a town of more than 2,000 located near ski resorts and known for its hot springs. But readings late Sunday night showed the San Juan River started to recede after reaching 16.81 feet (5.1 meters) and was forecast to keep dropping Monday, the National Weather Service said. The sheriff’s office had warned that most of the town was wiped out by a 1911 flood that crested at approximately 17.8 feet (5.4 meters).
The flooding prompted the Colorado Secretary of State’s office to set up alternative voting plans for Pagosa Springs residents.
The San Juan River was still rising Monday further downstream, in New Mexico, where new evacuations were ordered for some residents in San Juan County, including some Navajo communities. The Utah Navajo Health System posted several active highway closures, with detours.
Others were evacuated from New Mexico’s Rio Arriba County, where the Rio Chama was under a flood warning through Tuesday. Still farther south, the rising Jemez River made campgrounds and fishing sites inaccessible.
In the picturesque town of Sedona, Arizona, officials ordered residents near Oak Creek to leave Sunday as floodwaters trapped multiple people in their homes.
“Most of the rain is winding down,” David Byers, a meteorologist with the weather service office in Grand Junction, Colorado, said Monday. The next few days look drier.
Flooding in Colorado tourist town affects Election Day voting plans
In Pagosa Springs, town residents impacted by the floods who haven’t voted yet can also “visit any voter center across the state to request and receive a replacement ballot,” the Secretary of State’s office said in a news release.
Those who decide to cast in-person ballots outside their home county can only vote for statewide races, the office said. But if they have access to their mail ballot, they can return that ballot to any drop box or voter center in the state by 7 p.m. on Election Day and it will make it back to their county clerk for signature verification and tabulation, the office said.
Voting centers will still be open in La Plata County, but some county offices, including the clerk’s office, will have special hours on Tuesday.
Katie German, owner and chef of Bruin Coffee in Pagosa Springs, said Sunday that downtown had been evacuated and that there was street flooding. German said she was most worried about the one bridge into town washing out, preventing trucks carrying everything from food to fuel from getting in.
Town officials had just lifted an evacuation order from flooding last week only to reimpose it Saturday.
“I’m worried about my business, worried about my employees, definitely worried for everybody in this town,” German said.
Arizona is getting months’ worth of rain in a couple of days
Arizona’s Yavapai County and the community of Camp Verde ordered evacuations of residents living near swollen rivers and creeks. And Gila County officials ordered the total evacuation of Gisela, a community of several hundred along Tonto Creek.
The wet conditions even produced flash floods, river flooding and swiftboat rescues in Tucson, where weather service meteorologist Aaron Hardin said “we are getting two or three months of rain in a span of a couple of days.”
Rain fell nearly nonstop Sunday in Flagstaff, Arizona, flooding local roads and overwhelming storm drains. Authorities were searching for a man who slipped and fell into fast-moving floodwaters “and was not seen resurfacing,” a police statement said.
And in the Pinetop-Lakeside area of central Arizona, “manhole covers are popping up all over” and residents reported sewage backing up into homes because of flooding, the region’s sanitary district announced.
—-
Marcelo reported from New York; Casey from Boston; and Weber from Los Angeles. Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed to this report.

title: ‘The right time’: County removes all Flock cameras, ends use over privacy concerns
text:
HENRICO, Va. (WWBT/Gray News) - Crews in Virginia have removed all Flock cameras in a county over the weekend.
According to Henrico County Manager John Vithoulkas, crews removed more than 120 Flock cameras Saturday.
County officials said they had to take down the cameras themselves after Flock failed to fulfill its “contractual obligation” to remove them.
Henrico County ended its use of Flock cameras last month due to privacy concerns.
The county said the cameras were supposed to be gone within two weeks after the contract ended.
However, that was not the case, and officials said the poles holding the cameras remain in place, with it being Flock’s responsibility to remove them.
In a social post on Oct. 6, Henrico County said after talking with other leaders, police cut ties with the automatic license plate reader cameras by mid-October.
Officials said the decision evolved as they heard from residents, police and experts about the benefits of the technology, as well as privacy and data-access concerns.
Leaders described the move as preventative and said there was no evidence Henrico police misused the system.
“Rather be proactive than reactive. And we’re aware of the conversations that are occurring nationally, as well as on the state level. And we just, again, felt that this was the right time to make this decision,” Rev. Roscoe D. Cooper III, chairman of the Henrico Board of Supervisors, said.
The technology has drawn public criticism over privacy and potential misuse.

title: UMaine leaders face campus questions on projected $19M budget deficit in info session
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - The University of Maine and the University of Maine at Machias are rolling out plans for widespread non-academic cuts as administrators work to close a projected $19 million budget shortfall for Fiscal Year 2028.
Leadership detailed a roadmap aimed at trimming approximately $6 million from non-academic operations. The move leaves roughly $3 million left to address in the non-academic budget, which officials say will be their primary focus in the coming weeks.
The newly announced measures come on the heels of an earlier announcement by University President Joan Ferrini-Mundy detailing $10 million in cuts to Academic Affairs, which represents roughly half of the institution’s overall budget.
Where cuts will fall
Administrators noted that existing collective bargaining agreements limit the scope of certain staffing adjustments. However, proposed strategies to reduce spending and generate revenue include:
- Eliminating vacant staff positions and scaling back overtime hours
- Adjusting contract lengths for annually appointed personnel
- Consolidating internal units and departments
- Selling university-owned property and surplus assets
- Implementing and raising facility use fees for external groups
- Pursuing private sponsorships and licensing partnerships
- Increasing on-campus conferences and events to bolster revenue
The adjustments will reach across nearly every major branch of the university, including athletics, student life, research and strategic partnerships, finance and administration, facilities management, and the president’s office.
Campus leaders address workload and degree timelines
On Monday, administrators held an informational question-and-answer forum to field campus community concerns regarding budget impacts on workload and course offerings.
During the forum, Executive Vice President of Academic Affairs and Provost Gabriel Paquette addressed worries about academic delivery:
“I promise you, I promise everyone that we are thinking about workload, we are thinking about the ways in which how would we meet our instructional obligations and how would we enable our students to progress through their degree programs and graduate in a timely way,” Paquette said. “All of that is being assessed, and I look forward to talking more with you about that and everyone here at greater length.”
University leaders said long-term planning remains fluid as they monitor enrollment trends alongside fluctuating state and federal funding levels.

title: Meet a Model A Ford club keeping the classic cars on the road
text:
GLEN ALLEN, Va. (Aging Untold) — The Model A was the Ford Motor Company’s next big step after the Model T, ushering in a whole new era for drivers.
The Model A was only produced for a limited time, but nearly a century later, clubs like the Old Dominion Model A Ford Club of Greater Richmond are helping to keep the iconic engines running.
“Oh, it’s great, you know, to see the smile on the faces coming here today. Some lady was hanging out the window just waving,” Dennis Stone, president of the Old Dominion Model A Ford Club, said.
Despite being almost 100 years old, the Model A continues to be fun for all ages.
Henry Ford created the Model A as an upgrade to the Model T.
“We’re looking at an advertisement that occurred in the newspaper in December of 1927, advertising the coming of the new Model A Ford,” Henry Nelson, secretary of Old Dominion Model A Ford Club, said.
Stone said, for the most part, the cars had no radios, air conditioning or power brakes.
“Bare bones driving. They were the cheapest cars on the market back then,” he said.
But the Model A remained innovative, coming standard with an electric start instead of a crank to get it going. It also came with other bells and whistles.
“It had brakes on all four wheels. It had shock absorbers. It had a way to check your oil without having to get under the car. Had a dipstick. Also, it had gauges inside. You could tell how fast you were going,” Nelson said.
And the Old Dominion Model A Ford Club of Greater Richmond is doing its part to keep the old cars cruising into the future.

title: Shower Chances Increasing For Election Day
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A backdoor cold front will slide southward across the region overnight, triggering isolated to scattered rain showers after midnight. Temperatures will remain mild, with overnight lows holding in the 40s and low 50s.
Election Day Tuesday: Increasing Rain Chances
Much of Election Day morning will remain dry for voters heading to the polls, outside of a few scattered spots seeing brief, light showers. Conditions turn wetter by the afternoon as a warm front lifts in, spreading steadier rain showers from northwest to southeast. High temperatures will range from the upper 40s in the far north to the 50s across central areas, reaching the 60s in southern Maine. Steadier rain showers will linger Tuesday evening into early Wednesday morning.
Wednesday: Clouds Yielding to Mild Afternoon Sun
Steadiest rain showers will taper off for most communities by daybreak Wednesday, though isolated showers may linger across the far north through late morning. Cloud cover will gradually decrease from southwest to northeast during the afternoon. High temperatures will depend on how quickly skies clear, with afternoon readings reaching the upper 50s in the north, 60s across central Maine, and 70s toward the southern part of the state.
Expected Rainfall Totals (Tuesday – Wednesday Morning):
Communities from Calais to Millinocket to Jackman north and east of that line should expect 0.50″ to up to an inch of rainfall with the highest totals in The County. South and west of that line including most of Downeast, the Bangor Region, and the Western Mountains expect up to 0.5″. South of Augusta will see less than 0.10″.
Thursday & Beyond: Monitoring Widespread, Beneficial Rain
Thursday features another mild afternoon with highs returning to the 60s under increasing cloud cover. title: Lindsay Clancy returns to court in a bid to dismiss charges she killed her three young children
text:
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.
PLYMOUTH, Mass. (AP) — Lindsay Clancy ‘s lawyer urged a judge Monday to either the dismiss the murder charges against her, or get on with the business of putting her back on trial.
This was the second time the Massachusetts mother has been in court since her first trial with ended with a deadlocked jury unable to agree whether she was legally responsible for killing her three young children. Jurors were split 11-1 in favor of acquittal when the judge declared a mistrial.
Clancy’s defense team moved to dismiss the charges on double jeopardy grounds, based on an unusual argument that the judge should have removed the one juror who favored conviction, then allowed jury deliberations to continue.
Judge William Sullivan did not immediately rule on Monday. Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, implored him to decide quickly, and also pressed the Plymouth District Attorney to reveal soon whether he plans to try Clancy on murder charges again.
“I am not going to have this woman sit incarcerated for the next year, or two or three,” Reddington said. Putting aside his sharp disagreement with the judge about the way the first trial ended, he said he wants Sullivan to preside over a second trial, if one happens. “I want a trial and I want it with you and I want it this spring.”
Sullivan scheduled another hearing for Nov. 16 and suggested a retrial could begin in March.
Prosecutors said they intend to retry Clancy if the case proceeds, but haven’t yet settled on whether they would pursue the same charges, or opt for a reduced charge that might be more palatable for the jury.
Clancy’s lawyer has argued that she had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behavior when she killed her three children in 2023. Prosecutors have acknowledged that Clancy had mental health problems, but said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong.
Hearing had heated moments
Reddington has staked part of his post-trial defense on assailing the one juror who wanted to convict Clancy.
He urged the judge again on Monday to investigate that juror, whom he accused of being untruthful on his jury questionnaire and improperly using his cell phone during jury deliberations.
At one point, Sullivan admonished Reddington to stop using the juror’s name in open court. Sullivan has a standing order sealing the names of the jurors temporarily to protect them from harassment — though several have done media interviews, including the holdout, Michael Desronvil. Reddington protested that the juror’s name “was all over the internet.”
“Why don’t we all dial this back a little bit,” Sullivan said at one point.
Defense challenges judge’s handling of deadlocked jury
Another of Clancy’s lawyers, Martin Weinberg, argued Monday that a mistrial could have been avoided had the judge more thoroughly interrogated jurors about their breakdown in deliberations after the foreperson sent two notes indicating that the lone holdout wasn’t following the court’s instructions on reasonable doubt.
After receiving the notes, Sullivan spoke with each juror, reminded them of their duties and explained what constitutes reasonable doubt. He asked whether they could apply the law to the case, and all said yes.
Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague argued Monday that Sullivan had struck the right balance — and that pressing further would have required delving into the substance of the jury’s deliberations, which isn’t allowed.
Juror’s lawyer defends his conduct
Desronvil said in a recent interview that he was certain of Clancy’s guilt, but other jurors wouldn’t listen.
His lawyer, Heather O’Connor, urged the judge Monday not to investigate his conduct any further, saying he had simply done his duty as a juror.
She disputed the allegations of improper cellphone use, saying all jurors were allowed to keep their phones and there was no evidence Desronvil had used his device to improperly research the case.
“If that’s enough to put a juror under oath, to search their phone, to pull their history, then the lesson (for) every future juror in this Commonwealth is simple: Agree with the majority or potentially be investigated,” O’Connor said.
Sullivan also heard arguments on the prosecutors’ request for a gag order while the case remains pending, to avoid influencing a future jury. Reddington gave interviews during the trial, while prosecutors generally did not speak to reporters. Clancy’s lawyers argued that it would amount to an unconstitutional restraint on speech.
__
AP journalist Leah Willingham contributed from Boston.

title: VIDEO: Man rescued after falling into sinkhole, truck seen teetering on edge
text:
VIDEO: Man rescued after falling into sinkhole, truck seen teetering on edge
A man was taken to the hospital after officials said he fell down a sinkhole in Arizona.
The Phoenix Fire Department said it was called to a home around 3 p.m. Sunday following reports of a man who fell into a sinkhole in his backyard.
When authorities arrived on the scene, they found an adult man who had fallen into a 6-foot-deep sinkhole. He had sustained an injury to his chest and could not get out on his own.
The department said a pickup truck also partially fell into the hole.
Authorities were able to stabilize the vehicle so it would not fall any further.
In a video posted on the department's Facebook, a rescue technician was seen going down into the sinkhole to recover the man.
Watch video of the rescue in the player above
The man was later taken to the hospital for his injuries. No other injuries were reported.

title: Daniel M. Dunn | Obituaries
text:
Daniel M. Dunn, 37, of Bar Harbor, passed away on Oct. 17, surrounded by the family he loved so deeply. Danny was born in Bar Harbor, Maine, to Thomas and Penny (Strout) Dunn. He graduated from MDI High School in 2008 and earned a bachelor’s degree in business administration from Husson University. He worked in the family’s plumbing and heating business, where his knowledge, skill, and work ethic made him exceptionally good at what he did. He took pride in a job well done and in building something meaningful alongside his family.
Danny was a man of extraordinary strength and determination. Time and again, he faced cancer head-on and kicked its ass, showing a resilience that amazed everyone around him. But his life was not defined by his diagnosis. It was defined by the way he lived, the people he loved, the friendships he built, and the countless adventures and memories he made along the way. Above all else, Danny was a family man. He shared a deep and unwavering love with his wife, Hannah. They faced life’s greatest joys and hardest challenges side by side, continuing to choose each other through it all.

title: Most Mainers think Susan Collins will win despite her trailing in polls
text:
Insiders saw this first. 
This story was broken in Maine Politics Insider, the BDN’s daily premium newsletter for the most ardent political news followers. If you are a new BDN subscriber, you can sign up here. Current subscribers can contact our customer service team to upgrade.
Democrat Troy Jackson posted his strongest polling of the Maine U.S. Senate race in two surveys released Sunday, but most voters still don’t think he will beat U.S. Sen. Susan Collins.
A University of New Hampshire poll had Jackson ahead 54% to 45%. A New York Times/Siena College poll conducted with the Portland Press Herald had him leading 51% to 45%. In September, the same Times poll had Collins ahead 49% to 46%.
Yet 56% of likely voters in the UNH poll said the five-term Republican will win Tuesday, compared with 26% who picked Jackson and 18% who were unsure. Nearly all Collins voters, 95%, think she will win. Only 47% of Jackson’s own voters think he will.
The nervousness is probably due to Collins defying polls before. In 2020, Democrat Sara Gideon led every public poll leading up to Election Day. Collins won by nearly 9 points, and the polling misses in that race were among the worst in the country.
This year’s race could decide control of the U.S. Senate. Most October polls had Jackson ahead by 2 to 5 points or tied, and Collins has not led a public poll since late September.
The two new polls split on how voters see her. The Times had Collins nearly even, with 48% viewing her favorably and 49% unfavorably, while UNH had her underwater at 39% to 54%.
Collins led Jackson in the 2nd Congressional District by about 10 points in The Times poll after carrying the area by 23 points in 2020, according to state results. She lost what is now the 1st District by 4 points that year, and The Times had her down 22 there. Former Gov. Paul LePage, the Republican running for the open there, led Democrat Matt Dunlap by 5 points in both polls.
Collins drew 10% of voters who backed Kamala Harris in 2024 in The Times poll, right at the 1-in-10 floor a Bangor Daily News analysis found she needs. But the Democratic electorate looked more energized in both survey. Also, UNH found almost no crossover, with 98% of Democrats backing Jackson.
President Donald Trump is a drag on Collins in both surveys, with about 60% of likely voters disapproving of his job performance. In the UNH poll, 48% said their Senate vote was meant to oppose Trump.
Around her 2020 win, Collins credited the warm reception on her bus tour rather than the polls. She made a similar case in an interview with Fox News on Sunday.
“I’m feeling very optimistic based on the great response I get in visiting communities all over the state,” she said.
Jackson has framed the final days around turnout, spending much of his time in cities and in the Portland suburbs that Collins has always overperformed other Republicans in.
“We will not outspend them, but we will outwork them,” Jackson told volunteers at his Bangor field office Saturday.

title: Trump rallies in Iowa and Kansas as Republicans fight to keep Senate and House control
text:
DUBUQUE, Iowa (AP) — President Donald Trump closed out the final weekend of a turbulent midterm campaign with rallies in two states he has handily won in the past while Democrats began to fracture in Michigan, risking their effort to retake the Senate.
The president was in Salina, Kansas, and Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday. Republicans in both states are fending off robust challenges from Democrats, threatening GOP majorities in the Senate while they’re already at risk in the House.
But in Iowa, Trump insisted Republicans were on the verge of sweeping victories on Election Day on Tuesday.
“We’re going to elect ‘America first’ Republicans up and down the line,” he said near the start of a speech that lasted two hours, long even for Trump, who is known for his lengthy, free-wheeling rallies.
Later, he arrived tardy in Kansas, where Air Force One performed a theatrical flyover before landing for an outdoor, airport rally. Hundreds of people started leaving midway through his nearly 90-minute speech in rural central Kansas, which didn’t end until nearly 10 p.m. local time.
“This is our last stop. We’re closing it down tonight,” Trump said. He has crisscrossed the country since Oct. 1, holding more than two dozen rallies in 19 states to lift up the GOP. He is scheduled to give his closing pitch of the midterm elections Monday in Washington at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
With more than 54 million votes already cast, the trips reflect the GOP’s defensive posture as the elections become a referendum on Trump’s White House second term.
They are a reminder of how starkly the political environment has changed since Trump’s last campaign. In 2024, he worked to flip states that had previously backed Democrat Joe Biden in 2020. This year, Trump has focused largely on states he has dominated before as voters, including previous supporters, question the economic fallout of his decision to impose tariffs and launch the war in Iran.
Democrats struggle with infighting in Michigan
But Democrats who have become increasingly bullish on their prospects were confronting challenges of their own.
In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s onetime opponent in the Senate primary, Haley Stevens, appeared with Republican Mike Rogers at a church service and later endorsed his campaign. Stevens, a congresswoman who has criticized El-Sayed as being insufficiently supportive of Israel, said she backed Rogers after an invitation to a Democratic event was rescinded.
“Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement. “And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.”
The stunning move forced other Democrats to reiterate their support for El-Sayed. Chuck Schumer of New York, the top Democrat in the U.S. Senate, said the party was “united in our support.” U.S. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, who leads the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, said the party would “stand firmly” behind El-Sayed and “reject any efforts to divide Democrats.”
Earlier, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, a top supporter of El-Sayed, dismissed concerns about a Democratic divide.
“Haley Stevens lost a very, very close primary. I can understand being upset about that,” the Vermont independent said on CBS’ “Face the Nation.” “But from what I can see, all over the state, people are standing up; they’re gonna stand with Abdul.”
Michigan plays a key role in the Democratic effort to retake control of the U.S. Senate. If they don’t keep that seat on Tuesday, they would face additional pressure to win races in deeper Republican territory such as Texas, Kansas, Ohio or Iowa.
Midterms test Trump’s strength in GOP
The campaign’s closing stretch has largely become a test of Trump’s enduring strength in a Republican Party he reshaped in his image a decade ago. He’s hoping to energize voters like Jon Lutz, a Dubuque resident who watches videos of Trump all the time but attended his first rally on Sunday.
Lutz said he’s happy with Trump’s second-term record and wants Republicans to keep control of the House and Senate so his agenda will advance.
“He’s done what he’s said he’s going to do,” the 60-year-old civil engineer said. “I want him to keep going.”
Wendy Kuenzler was also seeing Trump for the first time on Sunday. Waiting in line at the concession stand, the 44-year-old from Burlington said she felt that Iowa was at a crossroads with multiple competitive elections. She plans to support Ashley Hinson, the U.S. Senate nominee.
Kuenzler said she doesn’t blame rising gas and grocery prices on Trump. “He’s on the path to correcting it,” she said.
In Kansas, Liz Wagner, a 59-year-old restaurant owner, traveled 165 miles (266 kilometers) from her hometown of Atchison to attend Trump’s outdoor rally at the airport in Salina, Kansas. She said she agrees “with everything he says.”
“I want people to get up and go to work and stop sticking their hands out,” she said while waiting to get into the rally. “The Democrats like to hand things out.”
Trump is betting that he can overcome the headwinds facing Republicans this year by relentlessly appearing before his most loyal supporters. But the more than two dozen rallies he held in October were occasionally overshadowed by Trump’s meandering asides and sometimes graphic descriptions of the physique of the male politicians he was supporting.
Trump paused the rallies on Saturday and spent the evening at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida at a jungle-themed Halloween party, where he bragged about the wealth of his guests and dismissed concerns about the country’s direction.
“The country has never done better,” he said.
Outgoing Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., raised concerns on Sunday that the president’s policies, particularly tariffs, could weigh down the GOP.
“Tariffs are not popular here in the Midwest,” he told CNN’s “State of the Union.” “I tried telling the president that.”
Bacon predicted “there will be a debate in the party” about its future if there are significant losses this week.
Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina was more optimistic. The chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee said he was confident Republicans would keep the Senate and embraced Trump’s role in the campaign.
“There’s no doubt that President Trump has said himself that the midterm election is about him,” he told NBC’s “Meet the Press.” “His agenda, without any question, is on the ballot.”

title: Two-time Olympian dead at 34 following cancer battle
text:
Two-time Olympian dead at 34 following cancer battle
Ciara Mageean, a two-time Olympian who won gold in the 1,500 meters at the 2024 European championships, has died. She was 34.
A statement posted on her Instagram page said she died of cancer on Sunday morning.
“At 6:30 a.m. this morning, Ciara lost her battle with cancer surrounded by her loved ones,” the statement said. “A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed.”
Mageean won European gold in Rome two years ago, having clinched silver in the 1,500 in Munich in 2022. She placed fourth at the 2023 world championships and represented Ireland in two Olympics.
Last year, Mageean announced she had been diagnosed with bowel cancer.
“Athletics Ireland is deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Ciara Mageean," a statement from Athletics Ireland read. “Ciara was a much-loved and inspirational figure who touched the lives of so many. Her courage, warmth and spirit will leave a lasting legacy."
World Athletics said it was “deeply saddened” by the news, calling her “an inspiration to many, on and off the track.”
Australian middle-distance runner Jessica Hull posted a tribute.
“There are no words. Just the most beautiful person in every way imaginable,” she wrote on Instagram. “Lucky to have shared some miles with you but even more special to have celebrated milestones at the finish line together, I’m so grateful for every moment, rest easy Ciara.”
Sebastian Coe, the president of World Athletics, also paid tribute.
“It is with great sadness that we learned of Ciara’s passing this morning at such a young age," Coe said. “A European champion and inspiration to many, it is a sad day for our sport — her loss will be felt across the athletics community.”

title: FDA approves more affordable version of HIV-prevention shot
text:
(AP) - The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a generic version of the world’s only twice-a-year shot to prevent HIV — a big step toward making the drug available inexpensively and more quickly in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
The announcement was made on Monday morning by the manufacturer and organizations that helped to speed up development of the medication, called lenacapavir.
The drug is expected to cost $40 a year per person in the countries where it will be available, the same price as daily preventive pills available now. But the shots are much more convenient than the pills because they’re needed much less frequently and they nearly eliminated new infections in two groundbreaking studies of people at high risk.
People don’t always take their daily dose of medication, “and if you do not take it, you cannot get protected against HIV,” said Carmen Pérez Casas, HIV lead for the grant-making organization Unitaid, a global health agency. “With lenacapavir, we are much more hopeful.”
Ultimately, advocates said, the medication should help drive down cases of HIV and AIDS — and deaths. According to the WHO, 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV and 570,000 died from HIV-related causes last year.
With an affordable, high-quality generic medication now available, “we could help to scale this to the 20 million people around the world who need PrEP,” prescription medicine taken by people at risk of HIV before being exposed to the virus, said Carolyn Amole, who leads the HIV program for the Clinton Health Access Initiative, a global health organization.
“And if we scale to those levels,” she added, “we can actually begin to bring an end to the HIV epidemic.”
Generic lenacapavir can’t be sold in the U.S. because a brand-name version, Yeztugo, made by Gilead Sciences and approved last year, is still protected by a patent. The U.S. list price for that version, meaning the cost before insurance, is $28,218 a year. Gilead officials say that’s similar to some other types of PrEP, which stands for pre-exposure prophylaxis.
The new generic was approved by the FDA under a longstanding practice designed to ensure the quality of HIV-related drugs provided to other countries by the U.S. government. Approval of a drug by the U.S. FDA can speed regulatory approval in many other countries. The approval is considered “tentative,” the FDA’s standard designation for generics while the originator remains under patent.
Until now, Gilead has been the sole supplier of lenacapavir, and demand has outstripped supply in low- and middle-income countries. Last year, Gilead established royalty-free licensing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable production. Those voluntary licenses cover a specific set of countries in sub-Saharan Africa, Asia and Latin America.
“We share the sense of urgency around expanding access to lenacapavir for HIV prevention,” a Gilead spokesperson said in a statement. “We believe we have enabled the fastest and most sustainable path to expanding access for communities most affected by HIV.”
The generic was developed by India-based Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories under an agreement brokered by Unitaid, the Clinton Health Access Initiative and Wits RHI, a health research institute in Africa. The partners sought to accelerate development and make the drug available at an affordable price.
Common side effects with lenacapavir include injection site reactions, headache and nausea. People also must be tested for HIV prior to starting the drug and with each injection; drug-resistant HIV has been identified when used by people with an undiagnosed HIV infection.
“For any kind of PrEP … you need to have HIV testing in advance,” said Saiqa Mullick, director of implementation science with Wits RHI. “For many of the low- and middle-income countries, that is a rapid test.”
Generic lenacapavir should start to become available in some places within weeks, those helping with the effort said, although it could take a bit longer in countries that require the drug to go through their own approval processes before people can start taking it. Generic versions made by the other manufacturers have yet to be approved by FDA.
“The work is not done. Now, we need the funding to actually buy it for everyone who needs it and then we need to do the hard work of getting it to the millions of people who need it and want it,” Amole said. “But this is a great milestone.”
Casa said she’s optimistic that scientific advances — along with political will and funding — can help the world curb HIV.
“Now,” she said, “we have the tools.”
___
Gerald Imray in Cape Town, South Africa, contributed to this story.

title: Election Day is Tuesday. Here’s what Mainers need to know
text:
Voters across Maine will have one last opportunity to cast their ballots on Tuesday in state and local elections this cycle, which includes races for U.S. Senate, Maine’s two congressional seats and governor.
Whether Mainers are voting on Tuesday or did so via early voting last month, this election is expected to spur one of the highest turnouts for a midterm election in the Pine Tree State in recent memory.
So whether you’re planning to vote Tuesday, still have that absentee ballot sitting on your counter, or are just eager to see how it all shakes out, here’s what to expect on Election Day.
WHAT’S ON THE BALLOT?
Your ballot will be made up of races on the federal, state, county and local levels. Some municipalities also have local referendum questions.
The race in Maine that has the eyes of the nation on it this season is for U.S. Senate: Republican Sen. Susan Collins is seeking a sixth, six-year term and is being challenged by Democratic candidate and former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson.
All Maine voters will also be asked who they want as their next governor. Republican Bobby Charles, Democrat Hannah Pingree and independent Rick Bennett are vying to replace outgoing Gov. Janet Mills, who is terming out of office.
In Maine’s 1st Congressional District, voters will decide between Democratic U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, who is seeking a 10th, two-year term, and Republican challenger Ronald Russell, who ran for the seat and lost in 2024.
In the 2nd Congressional District race, Democrat and State Auditor Matt Dunlap is facing off against Republican and former Gov. Paul LePage. One of them will replace Democratic Rep. Jared Golden, who is not seeking reelection.
You can get to know the candidates in all of the federal and statewide races, as well as many local contests, via the Portland Press Herald’s free Voter Guide.
HOW DO I VOTE?
Where you vote on Election Day depends on where you live — some municipalities have one central polling location for all residents, while others have multiple places based on districts or wards.
With a few exceptions, municipalities must open their polling locations by 8 a.m. (they can choose to open as early as 6 a.m.) and close at 8 p.m.
The exceptions regard Maine’s smaller communities: Communities with fewer than 500 people may open as late as 10 a.m., and communities with fewer than 100 people may close the polls after all registered voters have voted.
It’s best to check the hours and where to vote before heading out. Most municipalities provide these details on their websites.
And remember: if you’re in line by 8 p.m. on Election Day, you have a right to cast your ballot!
CAN I STILL REGISTER TO VOTE?
Yes.
While most methods of registering to vote (such as by mail or online) have expired, Mainers can register to vote in-person at their polling place on Election Day.
“To register to vote, you need to be 18 years or older on Nov. 3, you need to be a citizen of the United States, and you need to demonstrate proof of identity and proof of residency,” Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, the state’s top election official, said in an interview last week.
There are many means of proving your identity, such as a driver’s license, student or tribal ID, or a Social Security card.
Proof of residency can also be displayed via an ID — as long as it has your current address. Other documents that display your current address, such as a lease, a recent utility bill, or a piece of mail, will also suffice.
WHAT DO I DO WITH MY ABSENTEE BALLOT?
While the deadline to request an absentee ballot was Thursday, you have until the polls close at 8 p.m. on Election Day to turn it in.
Most municipalities accept your absentee ballot right at your polling location — but some require you to still drop it off at a municipal office or a drop box.
That includes Portland, which requires absentee ballots to be turned in to ballot drop boxes, rather than polling locations, by 8 p.m. on Election Day. Portland has a drop box outside City Hall on Myrtle Street and another at 212 Canco Road.
To be safe, it’s recommended to contact your municipality or check its website to determine the correct way to submit your absentee ballot on Tuesday.
More than 313,000 Mainers requested absentee ballots this election cycle, according to the secretary of state’s office.
As of early last week, municipal clerks around the state had accepted more than 222,000 ballots. A week before the most recent midterm election, in 2022, the state had accepted about 168,000 ballots.
WHEN WILL WE KNOW THE RESULTS?
It depends on a number of factors.
Some municipalities share their unofficial results the night of the election or the morning after. They have two business days to report their official results to the secretary of state’s office.
“In the closest of races, it may be a couple of days before we have those preliminary results,” Bellows said.
But it could take more than a week for two of the federal races, should they go to a ranked-choice run-off. That’s because the Senate and 2nd Congressional District races have declared write-in candidates, so voters will be asked to rank their choices among three options.
Ranked-choice voting cannot be used in the general election for state-level offices because of the state constitution. It can only be used in gubernatorial and legislative primaries, as well as federal and municipal races.
If no candidate in the Senate or 2nd Congressional District races ranks first on more than 50% of the total ballots cast in the first round, then the last-place finisher is eliminated, the second-choice votes of that candidate’s supporters are reallocated to the remaining candidates, and the results are retabulated.
That can take more than a week.
“Historically, it has been the Friday of the week following the election,” Bellows said. “But we hope to do it more quickly this year, if possible.”
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Nov. 2 to correct the year of the last midterm election.

title: Hampden Garden Club seeks $50K to finish restoring hall where Susan B. Anthony spoke
text:
HAMPDEN, Maine (WABI) - The Hampden Garden Club needs to raise $50,000 to finish restoring Harmony Hall, where Susan B. Anthony spoke to the Maine Woman Suffrage Association in 1898.
Anthony played a role in women’s suffrage that led to the 19th Amendment. More than a century has passed since women were granted the right to vote. According to the most recent census data, women make up more than half of all registered voters in Maine.
A church, then a suffrage meeting place
Harmony Hall was built as a Universalist church and dedicated in 1828. It remained a church for about 60 years before the Maine Woman Suffrage Association took it over.
In 1898, the group welcomed Anthony to the hall.
“The famous suffragette Susan B. Anthony spoke here,” said Valerie Emerson, team leader for the Hampden Garden Club.
According to local history, the crowd overflowed.
“There was one note that we have from a gentleman who listened to her talk,” says Emerson. “He said that she was a tiny old lady who probably shouldn’t be traveling by herself, but she was a fiery speaker.”
Garden club takes over the hall
Harmoney Hall sat empty for a time after that. In the late 1930s, it was donated to the Hampden Garden Club, which began hosting flower shows there.
“Their first big flower show had 500 people,” says Emerson. “People walked to the flower show, they came by horse and buggy. It was absolutely the in thing to do.”
The Hampden Garden Club took ownership of the hall in 1966.
“There’s a beautiful bell tower up there with a Paul Revere marked bell in our foundry,” notes Emerson. “And the bell does ring.”
The hall has a performance stage with dressing rooms on either side. There is a painted mural that covers the back wall of the stage. It is believed to have been painted in the 1930s.
“And legend says that after the play was chosen and the mural was done, some of the ladies complained because the play was too risque, so they didn’t do it,” says Emerson, smiling.
Restoration work and fundraising
The nearly 200-year-old building requires ongoing maintenance.
“A couple of years ago, part of our ceiling fell in. So last year we had the roof repaired. This year we’ve had attic work, we’ve had sub-flooring work, we’ve had electrical work,” said Emerson. “The painters just finished up.”
The club launched a capital campaign for the final phase of restoration.
“Right now, we need to raise another $50,000,” says Emerson.
The club wants to complete the restoration in time for the hall’s 200th celebration in 2028. And they’d like to see Harmony Hall become a community hub once again.
There is a small kitchen and a working bathroom in the hall. They also have banquet tables, tablecloths and chairs.
“It could be used for a game day, for a movie night, for yoga classes, for craft classes, for just about anything you can think of, ” says Emerson.
How to donate
Donations can be made at hampdengardenclub.org. The club also can be found on Facebook as Hampden Garden Club at Harmony Hall.

title: Jackson, LePage, and Pingree lead in final polls
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Two new polls released Sunday give insight into Maine voters’ closing thoughts just days before election day.
Maine Senate Race
A New York Times/Press Herald/Siena poll shows democrat Troy Jackson leading incumbent senator Susan Collins by 6 points. Jackson garnered the support of 51% of the 714 likely Maine voters surveyed, while Collins was backed by 45% of participants. The margin of error for the NYT poll is 4.3%.
In September’s iteration of that same poll, Collins led Jackson by 3%, showing a 9 point change in the new poll which was conducted between Oct. 27 and Nov. 1.
The University of New Hampshire’s Pine Tree State Poll, conducted between Oct. 27 and Oct 31, shows Jackson sitting at 54% and Collins at 45%, though the majority of voters surveyed say they still expect Collins to win. It widens Jackson’s 4-point lead from UNH’s September poll. 87% of Jackson voters said their vote was to oppose President Donald Trump, while 66% of Collins supporters said their vote was unrelated to the president.
Over 1,700 Maine residents completed the survey for UNH, 802 of which reside in Congressional District 2, and 843 residing in Congressional District 1. Their margin of error for the UNH poll is 2.4%.
Race for Governor
In the gubernatorial race, democrat Hannah Pingree leads with 49% of surveyed voters saying they plan to back her in the NYT/Press Herald/Siena poll. Republican candidate Bobby Charles trails at 37% and independent Rick Bennett at 8%. A recent Marist poll showed a much tighter race, with Charles and Pingree tied at 44%.
UNH’s Survey Center says Pingree also pulled out on top in the Pine Tree State Poll. 51% or likely voters said they have or will vote for Pingree, while 40% of favored Charles and 7% said they will vote or have voted for Bennett.
The Pine Tree Poll also showed 61% of those surveyed think Pingree with win, made up of 91% of Pingree supporters, 93% of Bennett supporters, and 22% of Charles supporters. 60% Charles supporters said they believe Charles will win.
Congressional District 2
In the race for Maine’s second congressional district, republican former Gov. Paul LePage pulled out ahead of Democratic Maine state auditor and former secretary of state Matt Dunlap in the UNH Pine Tree State Poll, with 52% of support compared to Dunlap’s to 47%. In UNH’s September poll, Dunlap had a lead over LePage, 51% to 45%.
The NYT/Press Herald/Siena poll did not conduct separate polls for each congressional district, instead asking residents which party they would vote for. 55% of voters said they would vote for the democratic candidate for congress, and 42% said they would vote for the republican candidate.
Congressional District 1
In the Pine Tree State Poll, the UNH Survey Center says incumbent democrat Chellie Pingree garnered the support of 65% of voters surveyed, with republican Ronald Russell was backed by 32%. In September, Pingree was up 57% to Russell’s 35%.
Polls close at 8 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 3.

title: Deputies arrest 2 and seek information on stolen pickup
text:
Aroostook County sheriff’s deputies have arrested two people for allegedly stealing a pickup, which is still missing.
The department received a report on Oct. 24 about a truck that had allegedly been stolen from behind the Sherman Irving station, Sheriff Peter Johnson said Monday.
The 1994 green short-bed GMC pickup has the Maine license plate 628 LRJ. Police believe it’s still in or near Sherman, according to the sheriff.
Deputy Seraphima Smalley investigated and, with video footage from nearby businesses, identified and arrested two suspects, a 60-year-old man from Reed Plantation and a 41-year-old woman from Sherman, Johnson said.
He did not provide their names.
The two were arrested and charged with theft by unauthorized taking, a Class C crime subject to up to 5 years incarceration and up to a $5,000 fine, and theft by unauthorized use, a Class D crime for which they could face up to a year in prison and up to a $2,000 fine.
Anyone with information on the truck’s location should call the sheriff’s office at 207-532-3471 or Aroostook County Crimestoppers at 800-638-8477.

title: Middle East on edge as fears mount that war in Iran could restart after the midterms
text:
Middle East on edge as fears mount that war in Iran could restart after the midterms
With little transparency from Washington and warmongering from Tehran, people across the Middle East have been left anxious and confused, scanning for signals on whether the conflict between Iran and the United States will reignite.
Related video above: The ongoing conflict in Iran is impacting U.S. borrowing rates, financial experts say
“The mood has definitely shifted,” a 36-year-old American living in Saudi Arabia told CNN. She plans to leave before Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections, after which U.S. President Donald Trump has hinted renewed fighting is possible.
“People are more cautious in general, and it feels like a waiting game to see what happens,” she added.
At homes and workplaces across Gulf Arab countries, questions are swirling. Residents are searching for clues that could help them plan for school closures or travel disruptions.
The war began in February when the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran that killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. It entered its eighth month this week with both sides still locked in a stubborn stalemate, neither making progress diplomatically nor able to break the military impasse.
Trump has offered little clarity on his endgame, oscillating between threats of further strikes and openness to possible diplomacy. Iran has tried to project its own deterrence, claiming it now possesses weaponry capable of striking more targets and inflicting even greater damage than before. Mediation is continuing, but a breakthrough would depend on at least one side breaching its own red lines.
Trump wrote on social media this month that Washington “will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections.” The president neither ruled out nor confirmed that strikes would resume afterward, which is part of the reason for the ongoing nerves.
Trump also spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday. The contents of the call were unclear, though Axios, which first reported it, said the conversation concerned Iran.
Asked Sunday about his conversation with Netanyahu, Trump provided no details, saying only that he “had a very good talk” with the prime minister.
“The U.S. has been actively feeding into this regionwide sense of anxiety as it keeps signaling that another round of escalation might be imminent,” Hasan Alhasan, a senior fellow for Middle East policy at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told CNN. “But it’s becoming difficult to distinguish pressure tactics from genuine signals.”
Adding to a sense that escalation could be imminent, Netanyahu, who partnered with the U.S. in attacking Iran and has been pushing for new strikes, will remain in office despite losing his majority in the recent elections. Negotiations to form a new government in Israel look set to begin in earnest next week, but election results suggest it will be difficult for opposition parties to oust Netanyahu quickly, if at all.
Without clarity, residents in the region often rely on hearsay or search social media for reports on troop movements to determine whether a U.S. strike is imminent.
Over the past month, Iranian military commanders have also intensified a series of public messages claiming that Iran has built up large stockpiles of new weapons, a tactic designed to induce fear among Washington’s allies in the region.
A senior security official in Tehran told CNN that Iran will try to target infrastructure beyond oil facilities in the region, including AI, and warned that if the conflict resumes, it will be a long “war of surprises.” On Saturday, Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered a response “without geographical limitations” to any new threat, an apparent effort to present a leader still yet to be seen in public as playing an active role in military preparations.
Foreign workers drawn to wealthy Gulf Arab states by economic opportunities and a tax-free lifestyle have for decades lived in relative stability in a region mired in conflict. That sense of security was shattered this year after the U.S. and Israel launched the war, prompting Tehran to fire unprecedented barrages of ballistic missiles and drones onto Arab cities, disrupting schools, travel and business and causing multiple casualties.
Yet, despite the war, many residents stayed put, telling CNN they feel confident under the protection of well-armed regional militaries. Practical concerns remain, though.
“I’m actively trying not to think about that happening again because I really don’t want another winter with strikes,” Michelle, a 36-year-old American resident of Abu Dhabi, told CNN. “I’ve always felt safe here… but I’m more concerned that our lives will have to change again.”
This month, people were surprised to learn that families of U.S. diplomats have begun leaving discreetly, with the departures becoming known only after their children started saying goodbye to classmates at school. Many of those leaving had only recently returned to their posts after being ordered out at the height of the Iran war in March, making the exits feel like a frustrating and chaotic déjà vu.
Fueling anxiety among residents are reports of thousands of U.S. troops being dispatched to the region, as reported by the Associated Press.
In Saudi Arabia, where major events have already been canceled and offices closed with staff working remotely after the Iran-allied Houthi rebels intensified strikes, residents told CNN they were concerned that a return to war could increase pressure on a country already embroiled in conflict along its southern border.
“My neighbors and friends are bunkering for November but starting to get concerned about flight disruptions over the holidays,” said a 36-year-old American in Saudi Arabia, comparing it to the Covid era. “A lot of offices have moved to virtual or have reduced staff and remote learning is in place.”
Elsewhere in the region, other international gatherings remain on track, though the risk remains that they could be disrupted if the U.S. launches strikes in the coming week.
In Abu Dhabi, where no attacks have been recorded since May, two U.S. oil firms canceled plans for their executives to attend one of the region’s biggest energy conferences, citing security concerns, Reuters reported. The event will proceed as scheduled next week with “strong” U.S. participation and more than 120 American exhibiting companies, the organizer, DMG, told Reuters.
The conference is expected to host nearly 240,000 people, according to the organizers.
In Bahrain, one of the worst-hit countries by Iran this year, people said they still felt the psychological impact of the war.
“There is still that traumatic effect,” 21-year-old Fawaz told CNN. “When you hear the bombings, it’s kind of like you feel it in your hearts and it’s hard to sleep at night, especially when there are bombings outside.”
“A lot of people have become used to it by now, but it’s still very scary,” he added.
Time Out
Despite growing anxiety over the possible resumption of war, there has been a flurry of quiet diplomacy over the past week.
U.S. Vice President JD Vance sent Iran’s top security official Mohsen Rezaei a letter, which the Islamic Republic is reviewing, according to Iranian media. Trump has claimed the letter related to an Iranian request for medical supplies, but it has raised hopes that a diplomatic breakthrough could still be possible.
Iranian officials are in Qatar for talks, a Qatari official said. Qatar has played a prominent role in mediating, but the official added there was no U.S. delegation present Saturday.
On Monday, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said the ball is “entirely in the U.S.’ court,” as “exchanges of messages” between Washington and Tehran were ongoing, according to Iran’s state news agency, IRNA. Baghaei doubled down on Tehran’s demand that “no agreement can be reached,” nor the key Strait of Hormuz reopened, as long as the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian ports remains.
In stark contrast to Trump’s warnings, the U.S. ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack, told CNN’s Becky Anderson that he thinks there could be “dramatic steps” in the next two weeks
“We’re close. I think we’re very close to a place where we can finally say: Let’s just have a time out,” he said, adding that it is, however, a “matter of trust and who goes first.”
On Saturday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio would not say clearly if progress had been made in the talks over the past 48 hours, but claimed that “if there is a diplomatic solution, we would be open to it.”
Asked by CNN if the Trump administration has any time frame for progress in the talks before it would resume military action, Rubio said, “I don’t know if there’s a time frame,” noting that “it’s up to the president to make decisions with regards to those sorts of things.”
“There are multiple talks. Talks have actually never stopped. There’s been active conversations going, both in some cases directly, but often through intermediaries,” he said at a press conference in Atlanta.
“The president’s preference in any challenge around the world is to try to solve it diplomatically and peacefully, if possible,” Rubio said. “He recognizes there are some issues in the world that cannot be solved peacefully, unfortunately, sadly, but we would prefer to solve it in that manner.”
Rubio said that any diplomatic solution “can’t be one that endangers our national security or one that doesn’t meet our core concerns,” particularly around Iran’s nuclear program.
Iranian officials have said they’re open to diplomacy with the U.S., but they do not trust that talks will stop military strikes, citing several past occasions when the Islamic Republic was struck during negotiations.
And a central figure also warned that Iran was not ready to compromise.
“Iran’s conditions have been repeatedly and clearly stated to the mediators,” said Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the Iranian parliamentary speaker who is leading negotiations with the U.S. “The carrot-and-stick approach has no effect on Iran. Progress can only be achieved once Iran’s seven conditions have been agreed upon.”

title: A West Point cadet drugged his girlfriend to force an unwanted abortion. Then he went to grad school
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A onetime West Point cadet drugged his then-girlfriend in her barracks room, administered abortion pills to her against her will and caused a miscarriage. Then he went on to study at two Ivy League universities, starting at one of them after he pleaded guilty to assault, according to court records and a new lawsuit.
The man, Caleb Suh, graduated from Cornell University this year and was a public health graduate student at Columbia University as of Oct. 28, when the woman sued in a New York court. His current status at Columbia is unclear.
The suit drew attention to a case that had played out quietly at West Point and in federal court, where Suh pleaded guilty this past June to the March 2022 assault on a cadet in the class below him. She was 19 and in her second year at the U.S. Military Academy, according to prosecutors.
She wanted to have the baby. Suh didn’t. Instead, he told the judge, he impersonated the woman to open an online pharmacy account, ordered abortion medications, got Xanax from a friend to use as a sedative, and duped his girlfriend into drinking what she thought was just a prenatal protein shake. After waiting until she fell asleep, he administered the abortion pills orally and vaginally.
According to the woman’s lawsuit, Suh left her alone and incapacitated and ignored her attempts to contact him after she woke and realized she was bleeding. She called 911 and was hospitalized.
Lawyer: ‘She’s suffered a life-changing event’
While she was being treated, Suh went back to the online pharmacy’s website to post questions about whether doctors might detect the pills, according to the lawsuit, first reported by The New York Times.
“She’s suffered a life-changing event that she is still dealing with and will be dealing with for the rest of her life,” her lawyer, Russell Kornblith, said by phone Monday. Her suit against Suh seeks unspecified damages.
Suh, who is awaiting sentencing, told the court in June that he was “deeply and immeasurably sorry for my actions and the pain that I have caused.”
His lawyer, Thomas Kenniff, declined to comment Monday.
The lawsuit, which the woman filed under the alias Jane Doe, comes amid national scrutiny of how universities handle student misconduct complaints. Cornell, in particular, has faced criticism since a former student’s lawsuit alleged that several men raped her at a fraternity house in 2024 and that the university did too little after she reported the accusation.
Woman made report to West Point
In Suh’s case, it’s unclear what discipline, if any, he may have faced at West Point. The woman reported him to the Army Criminal Investigation Division there in May 2022, according to her lawsuit. Assistant U.S. Attorney Marcia Cohen said in court in June that Suh had told a West Point investigator the woman’s miscarriage was accidental, denying that he’d ordered abortion medication.
The military academy didn’t provide information Monday on the probe’s findings or outcome.
Suh was criminally charged in a Manhattan-based federal court in June, court records show.
What Cornell says it was told
In the meantime, he transferred to Cornell during the 2023-2024 school year. The Ithaca, New York-based university said in a statement Monday that he answered “no” to an application question asking whether he’d been found responsible for a disciplinary violation at any previous educational institution. West Point reported that he was in good academic standing and was eligible to return, Cornell said.
Cornell websites indicate he was recognized for his writing in spring 2024 and got involved with the Cornell Center for Health Equity, a research group. He wrote on its site that he was interested in “the intersection of emergency medicine, addiction and public health” and aimed to become a physician.
Suh also briefly worked at Cornell’s medical school, leaving several months ago, the university said. He’s credited among authors of a medical journal report summarizing a 2025 conference on cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
This September, Suh started a master’s program at Columbia University’s Mailman School of Public Health in New York City, his lawyer wrote to the judge in Suh’s federal case.
Sentencing set to let Suh finish semester
Columbia declined to comment Monday, citing educational privacy laws.
A person familiar with the matter but not authorized to comment about it publicly said Mailman applicants aren’t asked about their criminal records but are asked whether they have ever been disciplined for student conduct violations or poor academic performance. Suh’s application never mentioned any disciplinary proceedings, the person said.
At the request of Suh’s lawyer, his sentencing recently was put off until January for him to complete his semester at Columbia. He also has been taking a three-month life skills course for people charged with federal crimes, Kenniff told the court in a letter last month.
Prosecutors didn’t oppose the postponement. They declined to comment Monday.
The woman’s lawyer declined to say whether she ultimately graduated from West Point or what she is doing now.
“We hope that by our client coming forward with this lawsuit, it will, at least, ensure that this never happens to anyone else,” Kornblith said.
___
Associated Press writer Larry Neumeister contributed.

title: Maine island turns shuttered nursing home into apartments at ‘almost unheard of’ cost
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Five years ago, Lori Morey was watching as residents left the Island Nursing Home, the Deer Isle facility where she had worked since graduating high school.
The nursing home, among the last skilled nursing facilities in Hancock County, couldn’t find enough staff to stay open.
It was heartbreaking, said Morey, who was then its human resources director. She described the facility as a “safety net” for islanders.
In the following years, its board met for hours each week, first trying to reopen in some form and then attempting to reuse the building. Their final plan seemed improbable to Morey at first: convert it into housing by themselves, with private funding, bit by bit, using local labor.
“Honestly, I was [like], ‘This is not gonna work. I mean, this is never gonna happen,’” she said.
But it did, and what’s now known as HomePort is accepting applications for 23 units available to seniors and essential workers, who are set to start moving in this December.
The roughly $2 million project is at the intersection of major, intertwined challenges facing the island and its towns of Deer Isle and Stonington. At the root are an acute housing shortage and rising property values that make it increasingly difficult for local seniors and working people to stay, raising serious concerns about the year-round community’s future.
HomePort is the second of two recent privately funded developments on the island trying to help address complicated housing-related challenges that face coastal communities across Maine.
Leaders also hope it could be a model for other communities to provide housing at a lower cost.
“The thing of it is to be smart and clever to see what you can do with [a vacant building], and we probably did one of the smartest and cleverest things you can do with it,” said Kathleen Billings, a board member and Stonington’s town manager.
The Island Nursing Home opened in 1983 with 50 beds and expanded to 70 in the late 1990s. It closed in October 2021 because it couldn’t find enough qualified staff in a remote location with a worsening housing shortage, leaders said at the time.
Board members tried to find ways to reopen, floating ideas like offering less skilled care.
“They did I don’t even know how many budgets of trying to make it work,” Morey said, also noting low state reimbursements as a challenge. “But the money’s just not there.”
Providing housing instead would still benefit seniors, Morey said.
HomePort considered hiring a firm to convert the building, but that proved too costly. State funding requires providing services that the original nursing home struggled to staff. Subsidized housing also has income limits, and going without it provides a more flexible option for people who may be working or have some assets but still need a place to live, Billings said.
They settled on doing it themselves at a low enough cost to keep rents relatively affordable.
Enter project manager Dave Witham, who Morey described as a “magician.”
A Deer Isle general contractor with extensive experience in large buildings and architecture, he coordinated mostly local contractors and did significant hands-on work himself.
With the building and much of the infrastructure in place, plus creative planning and the experience of board members, units were completed around $75,000 each, less than half of most quotes per unit or for new construction.
HomePort is on track to finish before its projected two-year timeline and just under budget at about $2 million, according to Witham. Enough donations have come in that they might not need to secure a separate $2 million loan to get started.
A development of its size for this cost is “almost unheard of,” Billings said.
The project also targets the “missing middle,” or people who make too much money for subsidized housing but not enough for market housing costs, she said. Older people can move in for a lower-maintenance option, potentially freeing up other housing, and younger people can save for a home while escaping the cycle of moving between hard-to-find winter rentals and summer housing.
Applications opened in September and seven have been approved, spanning people from their 20s to 80s, Morey said, mostly seniors. Rooms average $1,400 per month including utilities, with smaller apartments listed at $1,300 and two-bedrooms at $1,700. That’s in line with or less than many local rental listings.
The flood of applications officials expected hasn’t come yet, but Morey thinks people have already secured winter housing and momentum will pick up in the spring, along with word-of-mouth interest.
The facility also features two common rooms, a pavilion, outdoor garden areas, a commercial kitchen and office rentals. Morey, who will become its executive director when the building opens, hopes to offer senior center activities in the future and envisions HomePort as an intergenerational neighborhood.
HomePort needs about 15 tenants to cover costs and anticipates annual fundraising to maintain the 43-year-old building. The board started with funds left over from the nursing facility and a $1.5 million capital campaign is ongoing, but numbers weren’t available before press time.
While considering reopening, the board met with some pushback around its decisions and concerns about its due diligence toward finding ways to stay open.
In 2023, for example, the Bangor Daily News reported it might be challenging for a future project to gain support after the board made a quick change in plans and sold its bed licenses. A plan asking towns to contribute to reopening costs shortly after was met with local skepticism.
Morey said it’s taken this long for people to support the change, and some still view the facility as a nursing home.
“It’s hard to change people’s minds after it was such a longstanding institution, you know, and very much loved and supported,” she said. “But at least this way, we’re doing something for seniors.”
To Billings, negative sentiments seem “long gone” now, and the island’s desperate need for housing is very clear.
More than 40% of homes in Deer Isle and Stonington are occupied only seasonally, a local housing study found last December. The island is short more than 100 units of affordable housing, and home prices make it among the least affordable communities in the state.
Donations for the HomePort were generous and often immediate, Billings said, many of them from people who had supported the nursing home financially.
She feels good about the project and broader efforts underway to address housing needs on the island, but is still “very worried” about the future.
The island is attractive and social media has spotlighted it even more, according to Billings. Homes sell fast, often to out-of-state buyers, she said. She doesn’t blame buyers for that, but local residents get priced out as property values rise.
Deer Isle-Stonington needs year-round residents to help its businesses stay open through winter, its schools staffed and its economy functioning. One of Billings’ biggest worries is balancing economic dependence on tourism with those needs, she said, which is one reason she worked to provide rooms for essential workers.
Billings, Morey and Witham all said local commitment and skill among employees and board members made the HomePort project possible, saving money and navigating obstacles to turn the building into an asset.
“I think it’s possible for any community to do this, if they have the right people,” Witham said.

title: Pres. Trump focuses on Reflecting pool
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - With the 2026 midterms elections just a day away, President Trump on Monday touted the completion the repairs to the Reflecting Pool and also made his closing message to voters.
Off the campaign trail after nearly 30 rallies and with control of Congress at stake, President Donald Trump traveled from the White House to the Lincoln Memorial to tout the improvements to the Reflecting Pool.
It’s a project that took the Interior Department months to complete. The President repeated allegations there was vandalism involved.
“The people from Interior have been incredible. And the pool is now better and more beautiful than it’s ever been before. And we’re very proud of it.”
The President also made his closing message to voters- who will decide which party should control Congress for the next two years. “As you know, this is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime. The Democrat Party is nominated in the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history. These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up.”
While voters tell pollsters that their number one issue this election cycle is the high cost of living, the President did not address that issue during his remarks at the Reflecting Pool. Instead, the President touted what he described as a strong and resilient U.S. economy.
The President acknowledged that typically, historically the party in power loses seats during the Midterms. With a razor thin majority, the President and Republicans are hoping to defy that history. The final polls are pointing to significant Democrat success for the 2026 midterm elections.

title: 1-year-old killed after crawling into road while family was doing yard work, troopers say
text:
JONESVILLE, Fla. (WCJB/Gray News) — Troopers are revealing more details about the death of a 1-year-old boy who was hit and killed on a Florida roadway Friday afternoon.
Troopers with Florida Highway Patrol said the family was doing yard work at their home in the Jonesville area when their 1-year-old wandered off.
