title: I learned my lesson on treestand safety the hard way
text:
This was originally published Nov. 1, 2023.
The setup was ideal and I was excited to see what the morning would bring after spending the better part of an hour carefully sneaking through damp October darkness.
I had found the area several weeks earlier and hung my favorite stand 15 feet up a pine. It overlooked a series of deer trails leading to and from a bedding area, the edge of which was peppered with scrapes and rubs on cedars as thick as fence posts.
The spot was on fire with activity and several mornings in a row, one of the largest bucks I’d ever seen posed handsomely in front of the trail camera well into daylight.
With a light, chilly breeze blowing directly into my face, the stars had aligned, causing the scene to feel eerily perfect. And then it happened.
The noise sounded like paper being quickly torn and I immediately started scanning around to locate the source.
Before I could react, all at once the entire left side of the padded seat gave out, taking me with it.
I scrambled to grab anything I could to keep myself on the platform. I was fortunate to land my left hand securely on the armrest of the stand, preventing what would have been a 15-foot fall to the ground.
Upon inspection, I determined the nylon straps suspending the seat had dry-rotted over the years and were an accident waiting to happen. My failure to check them before the season was complete negligence.
Startled, confused and thankful, I collected myself and took stock of any injuries. Other than a sore left forearm, I was unscathed but much wiser. As I climbed down, I decided maybe those new-fangled treestand harnesses weren’t such a bad idea.
The Occupational Safety and Health Administration requires that “fall protection be provided at elevations of four feet in general industry workplaces, five feet in shipyards, six feet in the construction industry and eight feet in longshoring operations.”
As tree stands go, most are set much higher than eight feet. They are far more commonly found from 12 to 20 feet high, depending on stand type and configuration. A fall from those heights is likely to result in injury at the very least, but could potentially be fatal.
Accordingly, these days most manufacturers include some sort of safety harness system with their stands, as well as warnings, instructions and encouragement to always wear the harness while using the stand.
After that morning, I started wearing one of the included harnesses that came with a hang-on stand I purchased. It was a full-body harness, which took some getting used to. I used it a fair bit but found it to be flimsy, uncomfortable and frustrating.
The following year, I invested in a much more comfortable and well-made full-body harness from an established, reputable company. I use the harness while stand hunting in conjunction with a lineman’s rope or safe line, depending on the type of stand.
The lineman’s rope works great for climbing treestands as well as setting up and taking down hang-on stands and climbing sticks. The safe line is perfect for ladder stands and hang-on stands left in place for the season.
Admittedly, there was a bit of a learning curve when it came to proper deployment and use of all the gear. But with a little practice in the backyard, it wasn’t difficult to become proficient enough to feel comfortable using them in the field.
After a couple of weeks that season, it became second nature.
The hunting industry advocates heavily for harnesses to be worn in any treestand. In a perfect world, we all would. But the reality is, a vast majority of hunters choose not to for a variety of reasons.
Yesterday’s thoughts on treestand safety were simple; just don’t fall out. Until a few years ago, I subscribed to that same line of thinking.
Most of us grew up hunting from 10-foot homemade ladder stands with a simple platform, never giving a single thought to the risks of falling.
Today’s treestands are far more advanced. They can be complicated with lots of moving parts and pieces. That makes them extremely portable and allows quick setups at much higher elevations, which provide excellent hunting advantages.
But approaching today’s treestands with yesterday’s thinking is risky business.
Currently, there is no mandated use of harnesses or safety gear while hunting from treestands and it remains a choice.
Full-body harness systems can be cumbersome, frustrating, annoying, time-consuming and uncomfortable. Most days I hate wearing mine, and I suspect there might even be times I choose not to, but that would be wrong of me.
We love to hunt but we also have people that love us. I live in a world where a young son, another on the way and a loving partner all need me to come home safe. Jeopardizing that for them because of something as trivial as comfort, convenience or laziness just seems selfish.
My close call was the reality check I needed and I’m a better hunter for it.
As for that big buck?
I’m not sure if it was the commotion that morning or not, but to add insult to my almost injury and deservedly so, I never saw him there again.
Be still, be quiet, be patient and have fun, but above all else, be safe this season.

title: Flu Takes Out Bangor Area Bus Routes, Parents Scramble For Rides Monday
text:
Flu Outbreak Among Bangor Bus Drivers Prompts Last-Minute Bus Route Cancellations Monday Morning
As if the time change was challenging enough for parents, some families in Eastern Maine woke up to another predicament Monday morning.
What happened?
An outbreak of the flu amongst bus drivers in the Bangor area led to the last-minute cancellation of a number of bus routes in Bangor and Glenburn both for Monday morning and some for Monday afternoon.
The Bangor School Department issued the urgent message to parents and guardians just after 8 AM Monday Morning.
"Due to driver absences caused by the flu at Cyr Bus, the following bus runs are canceled today:
Run B: Morning and afternoon
Run R: Afternoon only
Run C: Afternoon only
Both Glenburn buses: Canceled today
Please arrange alternate transportation for your child if they ride one of these buses.
We apologize for the short notice and appreciate your understanding."
Of course the timing of that all left a lot of parents scrambling to come up with a plan B.
Flu Season Is Here!
According to the Maine CDC, "flu season" officially kicked off October 4th, but many state epidemiologist say they started to see cases earlier this year than years past. While the Maine CDC Respiratory Virus Dashboard shows that the state-wide cases of the flu are still considered at low level, according to data for the last week of October, with only 16 hospitalizations reported, those numbers could rise, and quickly.
Experts say the typical incubation period for the flu is between 1 and 4 days.
"This means that, in most cases, people start to develop flu symptoms a few days after the flu virus enters their body."
What can you do to keep yourself and your family healthy this flu season?
Health professionals recommend lots of handwashing with soap, often. They also say to use alcohol-based hand sanitizers, when soap and water is not available, especially after you cough or sneeze. Try not to touch your face, mouth or eyes with your hands.
It's also advised that folks should avoid contact with individuals who are sick and with large crowds.
If you have a compromised immune system, doctors recommend getting a flu shot.
Symptoms to look for if you think you have the flu:
The Maine CDC says that flu symptoms typically show up within four days of being exposed to the virus, and can come on suddenly. Things to look for include:
"Cough, Headache, Sore Throat, Fever or chills, Congestion or runny nose, Body and muscle aches. People with flu may also experience fatigue (feeling very tired). Some people may have vomiting and diarrhea, but this is more common in children than adults."
It's also advised that if you think you do have the flu to stay home and away from others unless you're seeking medical attention.

title: $17M Aroostook shortwave superstation is on the market
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A famed Aroostook broadcaster is selling one of the world’s most powerful shortwave radio stations.
Monticello’s WBCQ The Planet, an international AM/FM shortwave radio broadcast station and free speech platform, constructed the $17 million Monticello Maine Superstation for the World’s Last Chance Church in 2019.
“We are selling [or leasing] the assets of what we call the superstation facilities, one of the most powerful radio stations in the world,” said Allan Weiner, who co-owns and operates WBCQ with his wife, Angela Weiner. “The facility that we built for them is surplus to our needs. We’re trying to get the Voice of America, the government or the military to take it over or other private shortwave broadcasters in the country.”
From rural Monticello, just off Route 1, broadcasters transmitted shortwave signals to some of the world’s most remote and sometimes oppressed nations. Now, others have the opportunity to spread their message globally.
The World’s Last Chance Church, operating on 9330 MHz with up to 500 KW of power with its fully rotatable antenna system, broadcast globally for six years. But it ended the contract with the station in January, according to Weiner.
Galal Philip Habib Doss, an Egyptian businessman and former Seventh Day Adventist, founded the end-of-times church.
Word of the alleged sale spread quickly on social media and in shortwave and pirate radio circles. But in the telling of the story, there was some confusion, Weiner said.
Some shortwave enthusiasts thought the Aroostook couple was selling the radio station, but they are not.
“We’re not selling our radio station, just selling one of the assets,“ he said. “We’re not going off the air.”
The Weiners founded WBCQ nearly 30 years ago and it is the only AM/FM shortwave station in the country, Weiner said.
He calls the powerhouse, which beams all over the world with 12 transmitters, a “Ma and Pa radio station.”
In shortwave and pirate radio circles, Weiner is a free speech legend who battled the Federal Communications Commission for decades related to his multiple underground stations. In the 1980s he operated an offshore unlicensed AM/FM radio station, Radio New York International, broadcasting rock’n roll music along the entire East Coast from a ship anchored in international waters four miles off Long Island.
“There is nothing illegal about this station; we are in international waters beyond the jurisdiction of the FCC,” Weiner said in a 1982 news broadcast.
The U.S. Coast Guard eventually arrested Weiner and dismantled RNI. Free speech advocates defended him. After an ongoing battle with the governing body, Weiner received his license for WBCQ in 1998.
He was inducted into the North American Pirate Radio Hall of Fame in 2010.
WBCQ uses shortwave frequencies 9330, 7490, 6160, 5130 and 3265. Locally they are on FM 94.7 and 98.3 and 780 AM. The AM station is 50s, 60s, 70s oldies and the FM station is traditional country, he said.
“We beam all over the place. We have listeners in New York, South America. Heck, we’ve gotten a listenership from the people stationed in Antarctica,” Weiner said.
WBCQ also leases shortwave time by the hour.
Weiner does not censor content and will lease to anyone in the name of free speech, he said. But because of the content of some lessees, such as the Hal Turner Show, Weiner came under fire by hate watch groups, including the Southern Poverty Law Center, because of Turner’s racist ideologies. The Hal Turner show is no longer on the broadcast schedule.
Rumors spread that the superstation was selling for $2 million, but Weiner said that is not accurate and the World’s Last Chance Church is asking for offers. The sale is just for the station and the antennae. The superstation operated under Weiner’s FCC license and that is not included, he said.
“Whoever buys it will have to secure a license,” Weiner said. “They would probably have no trouble getting it licensed by the FCC.”
For more information contact Weiner at 207-889-0039.

title: Trump spends the day before midterm Election Day promoting his Reflecting Pool makeover
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — As Republicans and Democrats were making their final pitch to voters on the eve of Election Day, President Donald Trump opted to forgo the campaign trail and instead focused on his renovations at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, drawing attention to an expensive, problem-plagued repair job in a place far away from most of the people his party wants to persuade.
It was an unusual closing argument for Republicans to keep control of Congress. But it conforms with the way the president has devoted considerable time, attention and money in his second term on beautifying his Washington surroundings.
Trump, wearing a white “USA” hat, even seemed to admit that he had spent much of his time focused on improving the capital city.
“We have a lot of great things planned for Washington, and I could get into the nation, but for that, you don’t have enough time,” Trump said.
Instead of focusing on issues voters have said they’re worried about, Trump dedicated a large portion of his remarks to his D.C. makeover and the pool, announcing its official reopening, joking that he wanted to name it after himself, and repeating his false claims that the repair work he ordered was vandalized.
After he finished his remarks on Monday, Trump’s stood silently while triumphant music played and he held up a poster with an image of the previously algae-clogged pool. It was his last public appearance before Election Day.
Democrats, for their part, were spending the last 24 hours before Election Day making their case in areas where Republicans have long dominated, while trying to contain the fallout from a messy intraparty split in Michigan. Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed was brushing aside concerns that his prospects could be hurt after his former primary opponent threw her support behind his Republican opponent Mike Rogers.
In addition to giving the speech on Monday afternoon, Trump also was scheduled to participate in nine telerallies for Republicans, where he uses brief remarks on a mass phone call to plead for voters’ support.
Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, hit the campaign trail with more traditional stops in New York and Ohio, where Republicans were fighting for House and Senate seats.
Trump touts renovations as voters worry about the economy
The Reflecting Pool, a long, narrow basin at the foot of the Lincoln Memorial, is one of Washington’s most iconic sites. Martin Luther King, Jr. famously gave his “I Have a Dream” speech from the steps of the memorial in 1963, looking out over the pool.
But this summer it became a focus of Trump’s attention, with the president frequently speaking about his plans for the shallow pool on social media, at the White House and beyond. He displayed posters about the project in the Oval Office and even had his motorcade drive him over the resurfaced pool before it was refilled.
The pool was soon clogged with algae blooms, and its “American-flag blue” liner began peeling and floating up in chunks. The Justice Department charged former Olympian David Hearn with intentionally damaging the Reflecting Pool but then dropped the case this summer after determining he was not responsible.
But the president continues to repeat false claims that vandalism — rather than shoddy workmanship — was to blame for a new blue surface peeling away.
On the platform where he spoke Monday, signs were hanging that said “Restoring Our Capitol” and “The Reflecting Pool.” A poster perched on a display board showed the reflecting pool under the words, “Back, and more beautiful than ever!”
He waxed on about the particular color blue he selected to have the bottom of the pool painted, the kinds of grass and types of columns he had selected for repairs around Washington, and held up a series of blown-up images of rusted pipes taken during the renovation process.
He then started repeating some of his midterm elections pitch, defending his record and attacking Democratic nominees, before eventually turning back to the pool.
The president’s message in the closing days of the midterm campaign was similarly detached from voters’ concerns about the high cost of living. He’s called affordability a “hoax” while boasting to audiences far from the nation’s capital about his renovations of the reflecting pool and the White House, along with repeatedly praising the physiques of the GOP’s nominees.
Vance stuck closer to the party message as he campaigned Monday in Rome, New York. As he campaigned for Republican House candidates Kailee Buller and Anthony Constantino, he touted Trump’s moves to end taxes on tips and overtime and secure the border while branding Democrats as “lunatics” who have contempt for American voters.
Democrats try to flip Republican-favored seats while grappling with fractures
Democratic candidates were working to capitalize on widespread disaffection over high prices, the fallout from Trump’s war with Iran and historical trends that typically favor the party out of power in midterm elections.
In places like Iowa, where voters have not elected a Democratic governor in two decades, Democrat Rob Sand was asking canvassers knocking on doors to help break that streak.
“This is it,” said Sand, who faces Republican Zach Lahn. ”We have 30-whatever hours to change the direction of the state of Iowa.”
He was appearing with Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, who cited his own races as proof that a Democrat can win over Trump-backed candidates in states like his own and Iowa.
In Michigan, Democrats deal with fallout from a dramatic split
Democrats in Michigan — a key state in their efforts to try to retake the Senate — were trying to keep their coalition together after a shock on Sunday when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens announced she would back the GOP candidate instead of her party’s nominee, appearing at a church service with Mike Rogers.
Stevens — who lost in the primary to Abdul El-Sayed — is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. He has also been criticized for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker.
El-Sayed, who campaigned on Monday with fellow Michigan Democrat Debbie Dingell and Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, told supporters worried that Stevens’ endorsement could hurt him that “If we’re nervous about where we’re going to go from here, go vote.”

title: Former UMaine Quarterback Makes NFL Debut Against Buffalo
text:
Former UMaine Quarterback Makes NFL Debut Against Buffalo
The former University of Maine Black Bear stepped up against Buffalo on Sunday after injuries affected Baltimore’s quarterback room.

Former University of Maine quarterback Joe Fagnano made his NFL debut Sunday, Nov. 1, for the Baltimore Ravens in a 36-10 loss to the Buffalo Bills in Orchard Park, New York.
The undrafted rookie entered in the second quarter after starter Lamar Jackson suffered a thumb injury on Baltimore’s first offensive play and backup Tyler Huntley left with a toe injury.
Fagnano completed his first two passes for 28 yards and later led a third-quarter drive that ended in a field goal.
He finished with 10 completions on 21 attempts for 91 yards, no touchdowns and one interception, while also losing a fumble and taking three sacks.
Fagnano played quarterback at the University of Maine from 2019 through 2022, appearing in 27 games and throwing for more than 5,600 yards, 46 touchdowns and 12 interceptions.
He was named the Black Bears’ offensive rookie of the year in 2019 and earned second-team All-Colonial Athletic Association honors during the pandemic-delayed spring 2021 season before transferring to the University of Connecticut in 2023.
And there you have it! A former Black Bear reached the NFL stage Sunday and was called on for meaningful snaps in his first appearance.

title: Cause of Presque Isle Aprtment house fire released
text:
Presque Isle Apartment House Fire Cause Released
The Maine State Fire Marshal's office says a fire that destroyed a Presque Isle apartment building on Saturday was caused by discarded ashes.
The Presque Isle Fire Department responded around 2:30 a.m. to a three-story apartment building at 572 Main Street that also housed a business.
During the initial response, firefighters determined that the fire originated in an attached shed and was linked to an ash bucket containing discarded ashes, according to Maine Public Safety Department spokesperson Aaron Turcotte.
After extinguishing the blaze, the Presque Isle Fire Department was later called back to the property for a second report of fire in the building. Caribou, Easton, Fort Fairfield and Mapleton, Castle Hill, Chapman Fire departments were called in to help battle the fire.
An excavator was brought in the remove the metal roof to get at the fire in the attic. The area around 572 Main Street was closed until around 11:30 Saturday morning. Crews kept putting water on the fire for several more hours.
The Presque Isle Fire Department requested assistance from the State Fire Marshal's Office to investigate the circumstances of the two fire responses. Investigators determined that the original fire had continued to burn undetected within multiple layers of wall and roof materials, eventually becoming visible and prompting a second fire department response, Turcotte said.
The investigation concluded that the second fire was a continuation of the original one rather than a separate one.
There were no injuries reported. The American Red Cross was offering assistance to the displaced tenants.

title: Judge tosses charges for ex-FBI agents accused of lying about Hunter Biden
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge on Monday dismissed a criminal complaint against two former FBI officials accused of making false statements to Congress about Hunter Biden, saying the investigation that produced the charges was rushed, overtly political and dogged by “critical mistakes.”
“What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization,” U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui said in a scathing ruling from the bench that dismissed the case against former officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides.
He noted that the investigation was opened a day after a primetime speech by President Donald Trump in which he rehashed grievances over his 2020 election loss and that it was mandated and closely tracked by FBI Director Kash Patel. He also pointed out that the Justice Department could have brought the case, which arises from statements made in 2023, at any time but opted to do so two weeks ago, in the run-up to Tuesday’s midterm voting.
“I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend that I cannot read a calendar,” Faruqui said.
The decision followed a dramatic hearing in which he scolded prosecutors for their unorthodox maneuvers and an FBI agent who worked the case testified that he had been concerned the investigation would be seen as “political.”
The Justice Department may still have an opportunity to pursue a grand jury indictment against the two former officials, whose lawyers had pressed for dismissal of the charges. But the judge’s ruling nonetheless represents an unmistakable setback for the Justice Department, particularly given the difficulty it has had in persuading grand juries in the nation’s capital to return indictments in politically charged prosecutions like this one.
The judge’s concerns about the case were apparent almost immediately, when he raised questions about why the Justice Department had charged the case through a criminal complaint — which is more typically done when investigators have a pressing need to take a defendant into custody — as opposed to an indictment that requires a grand jury’s approval.
Then, at a preliminary hearing last week, he criticized the Justice Department for filing overnight an amended complaint with an additional criminal charge straight to the docket instead of first clearing the new charge with the court — something he said he had never seen before.
The hearing also featured testimony from an FBI agent who worked the case, who said that the investigation had been opened right after Trump gave an election security speech last July and that it had been mandated by FBI Director Kash Patel, who kept close watch on it.
The case accused the two former FBI officials of misleading Congress in 2023 about their involvement in, and knowledge of, efforts to investigate a laptop the Justice Department says was dropped off by Hunter Biden, former President Joe Biden’s son, at a Delaware computer repair shop in 2019.
But it also sought to echo longstanding grievances by Trump and his Republican allies that the FBI attempted to suppress information during the 2020 presidential campaign that was seen as potentially harmful to the Biden family. Candidate Joe Biden, a Democrat, ultimately defeated Trump, the Republican incumbent, in the 2020 election.
The Justice Department’s case noted, for instance, how Floris and Benavides had given lawmakers in 2020 a “defensive briefing” that Republican Sens. Chuck Grassley of Iowa and Ron Johnson of Wisconsin have said was used to undermine their investigation into the Biden administration and link it to Russian disinformation.

title: United Airlines adds more flights between Maine and California
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
United Airlines is adding more flights from Maine to two major California cities this summer.
In January, United Airlines announced Saturday-only service from Portland International Jetport to both San Francisco and Los Angeles for this past summer. But on Monday, the airport announced that United was adding 20 more round-trip flights to California.
Beginning May 8, 2027, United Airlines will offer Saturday flights to San Francisco, expanding that to Wednesdays and Saturdays on June 23. Its Saturday-only Los Angeles service begins June 26, 2027, with an additional six flights coming on Wednesdays during the peak summer travel season.
That will bring United’s flights to San Francisco to 32 and to Los Angeles to 19.
“These flights make it very easy to move between the East Coast and West Coast,” Zach Sundquist, the jetport’s assistant director, said in a statement. “United’s hubs in San Francisco and Los Angeles allow for one-stop connections to many Pacific Rim destinations, and with Wednesday service being introduced these options become even more appealing to local businesses with connections to Asia.”
The Portland airport is the state’s busiest. It saw record traffic in 2025, with nearly 2.6 million passengers, surpassing 2024’s 2.4 million, according to data posted on the Portland International Jetport’s website. Through August of this year, the jetport saw more than 1.7 million passengers.

title: 2026 election endorsements: Who’s backing candidates on Orono ballots
text:
Ahead of Election Day, candidates across Maine have received endorsements from public figures, organizations and other political actors. Running for office often involves outreach and the ability to reach certain audiences and demographics. Endorsements can help facilitate this outreach, offering candidates additional support as they approach the election. The endorsements a candidate receives can also provide insight into the kind of campaign they are running and the priorities they may pursue once in office.
The following is an overview of endorsements received by candidates in several races appearing on Orono voters’ ballots, including state legislative, congressional and statewide elections.
Maine Senate District 8
Democrat Mike Tipping and Republican Leo Kenney are running for Maine Senate District 8, which includes Orono.
Tipping is the incumbent in the race and is a senior strategist for the Maine People’s Alliance, whom he is endorsed by. Tipping is also endorsed by the University of Maine Progressives, Maine State Nurses Association and Maine Service Employees Association. Tipping has a background in community organizing and organized labor, and his endorsements largely reflect this.
Kenney is running for the Maine Legislature for the second time after more than 12 years on the Orono Town Council and school board. Kenney’s highest profile endorsement is from the Maine Chamber of Commerce, but he has also received a large number of individual endorsements from friends and supporters.
Maine’s 2nd Congressional District
Democrat Matt Dunlap and Republican Paul LePage are the two candidates for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, which has been cited as a battleground district.
Dunlap is a Maine state auditor and was previously Maine’s secretary of state. He has received endorsements from political figures such as U.S. Sen. Angus King, Bernie Sanders’ political action organization Our Revolution and U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna, in addition to Maine People’s Alliance.
LePage was formerly Maine’s governor and mayor of Waterville. He has been endorsed by U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, who has also campaigned for LePage in Maine twice. LePage has also received endorsements from the National Federation of Independent Business, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Rifle Association.
Maine governor
Democrat Hannah Pingree and Republican Bobby Charles are their parties’ nominees for Maine governor. Independent Rick Bennett is also running.
Pingree is a former Maine House speaker and chair of her local school board, and she is also the daughter of Chellie Pingree, the U.S. representative for Maine’s 1st Congressional District. Pingree is endorsed by Planned Parenthood, the Maine Education Association and Maine AFL-CIO.
Charles is a lawyer who previously worked for the U.S. State Department. He is endorsed by the National Rifle Association, Vice President JD Vance and a number of individual supporters.
U.S. Senate
Democrat Troy Jackson and Republican Susan Collins are the two leading candidates for Maine’s U.S. Senate race.
Jackson is a former Maine Senate president and union member. Jackson has been endorsed by a number of figures at the local and state level such as Jordan Wood, Mike Tipping and Nirav Shah. Jackson has also received endorsements from nationally recognized figures, ranging from former President Barack Obama, to children’s entertainer Ms. Rachel and actor Hannah Einbinder.
Collins has served in the U.S. Senate since 1997. She has been endorsed by former U.S. Sen. Joe Manchin, the Maine Fraternal Order of Police, the International Association of Fire Fighters and the Chief of Passamaquoddy Tribe at Sipayik.

title: Penquis sets fundraising goal for annual Thanksgiving turkey drive with WABI, partners
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - As Thanksgiving approaches, families across Maine are looking forward to gathering around the table, sharing traditions, and spending time with loved ones. For many households, however, the rising cost of living can make putting together a holiday meal a challenge. Thanks to the generosity of local residents, businesses, and community partners, thousands of families will once again have the opportunity to enjoy a traditional Thanksgiving meal.
This year, Penquis and its partners are working toward a goal of providing turkeys and holiday meal support to 5,500 households through a network of more than 40 local food pantries. For the past nine years, Penquis has coordinated this community-wide effort, helping connect donations with families throughout the region. Key partners in the annual campaign include Townsquare Media, WABI, and First National Bank.
“Thanksgiving is about gathering together, sharing traditions, and creating memories,” said Renae Muscatell, Penquis Community Relations Manager. “Every donation, whether it’s a turkey or a financial gift, helps make it possible for families to celebrate the holiday with dignity and joy. The incredible support we see year after year is a reminder of how much our community cares for one another.”
The impact of the Turkey Drive is felt far beyond the holiday meal itself. Local pantry partners say the program helps families feel connected and supported during a season that can be financially and emotionally difficult.
“This is an incredible program that not only helps families celebrate Thanksgiving together with a turkey they may not have otherwise been able to afford, but it fosters a sense of community. It reminds people in need that they are not alone, and it allows others to do something manageable to pay it forward, show kindness, and be part of something important in their community,” shared a Penquis pantry partner.
The annual drive begins with “Free the Z,” a beloved event hosted by Townsquare Media’s Z107.3. Beginning Tuesday, November 17, radio host Kid will camp out in the Brewer Hannaford parking lot, where he and a dedicated team of volunteers will collect frozen turkeys and monetary donations. Every $15 donation provides one turkey. The goal is to collect at least 2,026 turkeys before passing the baton to WABI on Thursday, November 19.
That same evening, WABI will host its annual Turkey Telethon from 4:00 p.m. to 6:30 p.m., accepting live donations during evening newscasts. Together, these community events help move the region closer to the ambitious goal of ensuring 5,500 households can enjoy a Thanksgiving meal.
First National Bank, a longtime sponsor and supporter of the Turkey Drive, continues to play a vital role in the effort. “Community is what brings programs like this to life,” said Ashleigh Briggs-Davis of First National Bank. “When neighbors come together to support one another, the impact reaches far beyond a single meal. The Turkey Drive helps strengthen connections, offers hope during a challenging season, and reminds families that their community is here for them.”
Ways to Get Involved
- Drop off frozen turkeys or cash donations at the Brewer Hannaford parking lot from Tuesday, November 17 through Saturday, November 21.
- Call during the Turkey Telethon on Thursday, November 19 during the 4 p.m., 5 p.m., or 6 p.m. newscasts to donate by phone.
- Give online at Penquis.org by clicking “Turkeys,” or text TURKEYS to 44321 to make a quick and easy donation.
Every turkey donated represents more than a meal. It helps families gather around the table, continue cherished traditions, and create new memories together. Through the generosity of donors, volunteers, businesses, and pantry partners, thousands of households will experience the comfort and connection that make Thanksgiving special. In today’s challenging economic climate, this support also helps ease the burden of food insecurity, ensuring more families can celebrate the holiday with dignity and hope.

title: 5 injured in Halloween night shootings near Michigan State campus, police say
text:
EAST LANSING, Mich. (WILX/Gray News) - An investigation is underway after two shootings on Halloween night near the Michigan State University campus left five people injured, authorities said.
At a press conference Sunday afternoon, East Lansing Police Chief Jennifer Brown said the department responded to four separate incidents, including two shootings that left a total of five people injured.
Police officers were called to a reported shooting near the intersection of M.A.C. Avenue and Linden Street.
Multiple shots were fired in that incident and three people were taken to the hospital with gunshot wounds, according to Brown.
Officials said two of the victims were listed in stable condition, while the condition of the third was not immediately known.
The chief said later that night, a second shooting was reported and police responded to the area of Stoddard and Frye Avenues, where two more people were shot.
Those two victims are now listed in stable condition. The chief said multiple guns were recovered from the scene, but officials were not sure whether they were the weapons used in the shooting.
Brown said “several individuals were taken into custody” in connection with the violence.
Police have not said whether the shootings are connected. It is unclear whether any of the victims are MSU students.
A spokesperson for MSU said the Department of Police and Public Safety did assist ELPD in response to shootings, but “the criminal activity did not involve a threat to campus and did not take place on MSU’s campus.”
Brown said the East Lansing Fire Department also responded to 91 total incidents over a 24-hour span, including 75 incidents into Halloween night.

title: Couple refuses to leave dog behind during helicopter rescue amid dangerous flooding
text:
SEDONA, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — Rapidly rising floodwaters triggered water rescues and forced residents from their homes in several Arizona communities Sunday.
That included Sedona, where officials ordered residents near Oak Creek to leave immediately as floodwaters trapped multiple people in their homes.
Alexander Dale and his wife were trapped by rising floodwaters. Their home and several Airbnbs they manage sit on a property next to the creek bed.
“We didn’t know what to do. We couldn’t go anywhere,” Dale said.
Dale, his wife and about nine of their guests climbed onto the roof of the home. They waited about three hours for a helicopter to lift them to safety.
“There was a helicopter and it had this huge rope on it, this huge line,” he said.
According to Dale, there was at first a question about whether the family’s dog could be lifted out.
“He told me, ‘Well, we don’t have a harness for a K-9, so I don’t know if we can take him.’ So I’m like, ‘What do we do?’” Dale said.
The couple did not leave the dog behind. They used harnesses they had at home.
“We put like three of them on him and strapped it all together,” Dale said.
Dale and his dog were lifted out together.
“I was sitting in this harness basically holding my dog, praying he doesn’t go anywhere,” Dale said.
Dale and his wife were not the only people forced out.
Cindy Wilmer, a schoolteacher, lives at Red Rock Crossing. She also evacuated with very little.
“The water was just roaring down the street,” Wilmer said. “I just left with the shirt on my back and the keys to the school and my cat ... I’m worried about my house.”
Fernando Leon was also evacuated. He feared his Oak Creek home might be a total loss.
“I opened the door and I saw the river, and I said, ‘Whoa, I need to get out of here,’” Leon said. “From one day to the next you’re at your place and then you have to evacuate and leave all your things behind. It’s just a very sad feeling.”
By Sunday afternoon, the drenching rains had largely subsided in the Sedona area.
Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs said state air rescue crews were also assisting with rooftop evacuations and state transportation crews were helping clear debris.
No injuries or deaths were immediately reported

title: Political analysts predict the winners of Maine's four major races
text:
Political analysts predict the winners of Maine's four major races in the 2026 election
Election Day is now just hours away, and many eyes will be on Maine because the U.S. Senate race between incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson will help determine the balance of power in Washington.
The race for Maine's 2nd Congressional District seat will also have a bearing on the balance of power in the U.S. House, while Rep. Chellie Pingree is seeking her 10th term in Congress.
Maine will also be electing a new governor, as Gov. Janet Mills cannot run for reelection due to term limits.
The In the Arena podcast team broke down the four major races in this election with former State Sen. and Portland Mayor Ethan Strimling, a Democrat, and former State Sen. Phil Harriman, a Republican, offering their predictions on the outcomes.
Maine's CD2: Matt Dunlap (D) vs. Paul LePage (R)
Strimling believes that Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap will edge out Republican former Gov. Paul LePage, 50.5% to 49.5%, to win the U.S. House seat of outgoing Congressman Jared Golden, a Blue Dog Democrat.
"I think (Dunlap) has done a good job, and I think the backlash against Donald Trump is statewide," Strimling said. "He's really got the right profile for that district. He's got the base fired up enough because he's progressive enough, unlike Jared Golden, and he's lived in that district forever. Paul LePage just feels like yesterday's news."
Harriman, however, believes LePage will defeat Dunlap 52% to 48%.
"I think (LePage's) legacy as governor has ingratiated him with the 2nd Congressional District," Harriman said. "Matt Dunlap was hiding, or how should we say, downplaying his progressive agenda, which does play well along the southern coast of Maine, but not in the 2nd Congressional District. I think the fact that Jared Golden didn't endorse Matt Dunlap also has an impact on this race."
Maine's CD1: Chellie Pingree (D) vs. Ron Russell (R)
This is a rematch of the 2024 election for the 1st Congressional District seat, and Harriman believes Democratic Congresswoman Chellie Pingree will once again defeat Republican challenger and Army veteran Ron Russell. Harriman's predicted margin of victory is 58% to 42%.
"I think Chellie Pingree has the base of her district solidly on her side, but I do think there are an awful lot of people who are frustrated with the status quo in Washington, regardless of party affiliation," Harriman said.
Strimling also believes in a Pingree victory, but thinks she will get 60% of the vote and Russell will get 40%.
"There's no doubt she's going to win," Strimling said. "I do think just this year, Democrats are going to be voting a little bit more heavily than 2024, so I think she does a little better."
Maine governor: Rick Bennett (I) vs. Bobby Charles (R) vs. Hannah Pingree (D)
Strimling believes that Democratic candidate and former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree will have a comfortable victory in the governor's race over Republican candidate Bobby Charles, a former assistant U.S. secretary of state, and State Sen. Rick Bennett, an independent candidate who was a longtime Republican. Strimling predicts that Pingree will win with 51% of the vote while Charles will receive 40% and Bennett will get 9%.
"I think there's some Bobby Charles people who have finally just decided: 'We're not comfortable with him,'" Strimling said. "I'm going to throw a few votes to Rick Bennett, so I think (Pingree) wins it with double digits and she gets over that magic 50% mark in a three-way race."
Harriman also believes this is Pingree's place to lose. He predicts that Pingree will receive 50% of the vote while Charles finishes with 43% and Bennett comes in at 7%.
"It's going to be, statistically, I think, a razor-thin election," Harriman said.
Harriman added that if Bennett were not on the ballot, the votes for the state senator would by and large probably go to Charles — a sentiment that Strimling agrees with.
"I think Rick Bennett takes way more from Bobby Charles than from Hannah Pingree," Strimling said. "(Bennett) is a lifetime Republican, and so there are people in the Republican Party who like him and the fact that he's rejected Trump, but not a lot of Democrats."
U.S. Senate: Susan Collins (R) vs. Troy Jackson (D)
Harriman believes that Sen. Susan Collins will be able to win a sixth term in the Senate, something no senator from Maine has done before. He predicts that the Republican incumbent will receive 52% of the vote, Democratic candidate and former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson will get 47% of the vote and the remaining 1% will go to write-in candidates.
"I think the closer people get to the ballot box, the more they're going to recognize that Susan Collins has served with distinction, she works hard and she's delivering for Maine people," Harriman said.
Strimling thinks the race will be tighter, but he also believes that Collins will retain her Senate seat. He predicts that Collins will win with 51.5% of the vote while Jackson receives 48.5%.
"(Collins) really is a very good campaigner. She sort of frames this race as Maine versus the country. I think people feel that and they sort of think that she's going to be the one who's better for Maine," Strimling said. "I don't think that's true, but that's what I think voters come to. Very, very hard fought, but I think in the end, she's going to get it."
"There is a lot of early voting and it's been predominantly Democrats. But if you dive deeper below that, what you discover is that the margin of votes going towards Troy Jackson is not as strong as you might expect for people who are voting early," Harriman added. "I think when we look back on it, I think that will be one of the key factors."
"Now, there are a lot more absentee ballots this time. So if the turnout continues to be that high, then Troy has a much better shot. But if the turnout ends up being at about the same place, then I think you are looking at a 2020 redux," Strimling replied. "I think it's all about turnout. If Democrats turn out in a wave and Republicans stay home in a riptide, then Troy Jackson will win. I mean, he's a very qualified, good candidate. He has done a remarkable job under very tough circumstances."

title: The Rotta the Hutt Halloween Costume Was Just As Bad as the Character in ‘The Mandalorian and Grogu’
text:
The Rotta the Hutt Halloween Costume Was Just As Bad as the Character in ‘The Mandalorian and Grogu’
Every year, the biggest hit movies inspire many of the most popular Halloween costumes. In 2026, that meant a lot of Jessie and Woody from Toy Story, some Minions (and maybe some monsters), and at least a handful of couples where the woman wore a black turtleneck and never blinked, trailed by her boyfriend with a laptop strapped to his chest.
I went in a different direction. I decided to dress as Rotta the Hutt, Jabba the Hutt’s son from The Mandalorian and Grogu.
This choice probably requires a little explanation. It’s not because I relate to the character of a giant slug with incredibly well-toned muscles. (I get the slug part; I sit on my ass watching and writing about movies all day. It’s the well-toned muscles where Rotta and I depart company.)
Every Halloween since 2022, I have worn some sort of inflatable costume. It started as a one-off thing. My wife wanted me to be something that matched our daughter, who dressed that year like a paleontologist. So I was a big inflatable dinosaur skeleton.
(Please note my short T-rex arms in that picture. Richard Jenkins would be proud.)
My kids got a big kick out of watching me lumber down the sidewalk inside a giant balloon with legs. Too big of a kick; in 2023, they demanded I get another inflatable costume. That year I was a cactus (that everyone in New York thought was a pickle).
With that, the tradition was set. I didn’t like the cactus (or the pickle) because people could see my face. That was too embarrassing; at least with the dinosaur, no one outside my family knew it was me. The following Christmas, my in-laws bought me an inflatable costume of Spider-Rex, the character who asks the provocative question “What if Spider-man, but dinosaur?” That became the Halloween 2024 costume.
And last year, I was Gizmo from Gremlins, mostly because I found the suit heavily discounted at an online retailer. Later, I found out why; it was impossible to see out of the head and also the built-in fan struggled to keep the costume inflated. I spent Halloween blindly staggering through Brooklyn, hoping I would get home before midnight so I wouldn’t accidentally eat candy too late and turn into Stripe.
This year’s costume was set from basically the moment I spotted this image back in August: An inflatable Rotta the Hutt costume, based on arguably the goofiest character in Star Wars canon since Jar Jar Binks, rendered even goofier by the fact that the inflatable costume version has two human hands poking out of Rotta’s armpits.
READ MORE: We Ate “Scary” Blumhouse Branded Cheetos
(Note: The costume is out of stock! I’m not the only one that bought this hideous thing!)
Now, as a moron loving father who would do anything to make his children smile, and someone who has worn a ridiculous inflatable costume for four straight Halloweens, I can tell you from a place of authority: Having somewhere to stick your hands out of the costume absolutely comes in handy. Otherwise, you are literally entombed in soft rubber for the duration of trick-or-treating. You can’t eat any candy, you can’t get a tissue to blow your nose, you can’t get assistance stepping over a broken piece of sidewalk or a bewildered kid. You’re completely on your own.
Actually, the serious design flaw in the Rotta suit was below that — and I’m not talking about his incredibly chiseled abdomen muscles. I’m talking about the legs. As you can see from the official online listing, the Rotta the Hutt costume has two little holes in the bottom to stick your feet through. While those feet holes do break the otherwise seamless illusion that this is the famous and beloved Star Wars character Rotta the Hutt asking for a second Fun Size Butterfinger, it would very tricky to walk in an anatomically correct slug costume.
But here is the unfortunate discovery I only made after I Whalefalled myself into this monstrosity: While Rotta the Hutt had holes for feet, there were no legs built into the costume. So it was nearly as hard to walk in it as if the costume had just been a giant slug filled with air. (Rotta also had an incredible long tail that made turning or not hitting small children nigh impossible.)
To see for yourself, scroll to the video in the fourth slide of the Instagram photo below. You will think I am hamming this up for the camera. I am not. That was the widest and most graceful stride I could make. It was like trying to walk with shackles around your ankles.
In short, the Rotta the Hutt costume was an unmitigated trick-or-treating disaster. I literally could not keep pace with my kids. I would say “Slow down! I am a giant slug!” and they would laugh at me and run off to the next house. None of these inflatable costume are easy to go trick-or-treating in, but in five years, Rotta the Hutt was by far the worst and the most difficult to manage.
That said: Rotta the Hutt was easily the worst part of The Mandalorian and Grogu. The character was curiously conceived — Mando is hired to rescue him, Rotta doesn’t want to be rescued because he wants to earn his freedom himself through pit fighting, then Rotta is instantly double crossed in a pit fight and must be rescued anyway — and mostly consisted of a vocally unrecognizable Jeremy Allen White mumbling about how he is nothing like his father, a fact he proved by having well-defined abs and shouting things like “I don’t wanna be anything like my father!”
He just didn’t make much sense as a character. And you know what? Rotta the Hutt did not make much sense as a Halloween costume, either. So while I could not walk in it, or properly supervise my children, or go to the bathroom without enormous difficulty, I must concede it was a fairly accurate film-to-costume adaptation. Indeed, the feeling of walking as if my ankles were shackled must be how Rotta felt to be shacked to his father Jabba’s legacy. He is his own man! And now I am too.

title: How to plan ahead for the possible cost of IVF
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — About 10% of Gen Z and Millennials say they are putting off having children because they are unsure how they would afford it or what starting a family would mean for their long-term finances, according to new research from Northwestern Mutual.
Kate Michaels, a managing partner at Northwestern Mutual, said money is pushing family plans down the road while another clock keeps ticking in the background: fertility.
If a couple faces infertility, many end up considering IVF, which Michaels said can be emotionally and financially overwhelming.
Planning for it involves more than a single procedure.
“It’s not like you can only plan for an IVF cycle. There may be monitoring appointments and medical exams that you need to account for before you even get to this bigger cost that you might be incurring,” Michaels said. “So, I think it’s really important that couples think about the fact that they may experience the need for fertility treatments going into a relationship.”
Couples do not need to know whether they will need fertility treatments before talking to a financial advisor. An early conversation can help them prepare for a wide range of costs that may come up.
For Michaels, the benefit goes beyond the numbers.
“That’s where I think the partnering with a financial advisor gives a lot of peace of mind, because again, it’s already such an emotional, emotionally taxing and physically taxing process,” Michaels said. “The last thing that you want to be doing with your partner or even yours if you’re going through this process alone or with a significant other, is to be feeling that financial anxiety.
Michaels recommends reviewing insurance coverage as early as possible to understand what it will and will not cover. That can show where out-of-pocket costs, such as travel or extra procedures, may need to be budgeted.
With that picture in hand, couples can have some idea of how much to start setting aside, just in case.

title: Poet Andrea Gibson’s legacy celebrated in Portland
text:
Growing up in Calais, renowned poet Andrea Gibson was an outdoor kid.
“Andrea really loved where they grew up,” said their wife, Megan Falley. “They grew up playing in the woods. … They told me stories about never wanting to come home, even in the winter snowstorms. They would huddle by the exhaust from the dryer of their house to get warm so they could continue to play.”
Falley will return to Maine on Nov. 12 for a sold-out event at the State Theatre called “Andrea Gibson’s ‘Love Letter From the Afterlife.'”
Gibson died on July 14, 2025, from ovarian cancer, a diagnosis they’d received four years earlier.
In an interview, Falley explained the purpose of the event. “It feels like really privileged, fortunate and important work to be doing, to continue to elevate Andrea’s voice and message,” she said.
Singer-songwriter and longtime friend of Gibson, Chris Pureka will perform. The highlight of the show is a screening of Gibson’s final performance in 2024 at the Paramount Theater in Denver. The film will include live accompaniment from the five-piece Goosebumps Orchestra, performing a score written by Blake Neely.
Neely also wrote the score to the 2025 Oscar-nominated documentary “Come See Me in the Good Light” which traces Gibson’s cancer diagnosis and how they and Falley faced the darkest time with love and laughter.
At the end of the night in Portland, Falley will read Gibson’s poem, “Love Letter From the Afterlife.”
Gibson was born and raised in Calais, and graduated from St. Joseph’s College in Standish in 1997 with an English degree. Gibson was a star basketball player in high school and college.
In a 1993 Portland Press Herald story, Gibson spoke about the Calais High School women’s basketball Class C championship win. “It was a perfect game, a perfect ending to a perfect season,” they said. In that game, Gibson scored a game-high 20 points.
As a poet, Gibson was known for enthralling, gutsy live performances in which their talent and passion for spoken-word poetry was palpable.
Falley still lives in the home she shared with Gibson in Longmont, Colorado. She keeps up with Gibson’s popular Substack newsletter Things That Don’t Suck and has shared numerous essays and observations since Gibson died.
Falley said the couple watched a recording of the Denver performance in May 2025, just a few months before Gibson died. Falley unpacked what that experience was like.
“It was definitely an emotional time. Their health was really declining and they were sort of tapped into what they were leaving, and leaving behind,” she said. “I think that they felt like it was in many ways, between that show and the documentary, that they had accomplished what they wanted to with both.”
Falley and Gibson visited Maine a number of times, as Gibson’s parents and sister still live here.
The couple were in Calais a few weeks before Gibson’s cancer diagnosis.
“It was really interesting because they were in a lot of pain but felt compelled to return home.” said Falley. “I thought it was so beautiful when I went and I totally understood their love for it and could appreciate the time travel of being shown around the map of their life.”

title: Washington state resident dies from bird flu following exposure to infected cattle
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A person in Washington state has died from complications of the bird flu, the first such U.S. death in a year.
The Yakima County resident, who had previous health conditions, was exposed to avian influenza at a dairy with infected cattle and had been hospitalized. The person died Sunday, county health officials said.
Two other U.S. deaths have been tied to bird flu since it became a national public health concern in 2024. The first, announced in January 2025, was an elderly person in Louisiana who had a version of bird flu known as H5N1. The other, in Washington state, died in November 2025 from a rarer version called H5N5.
Yakima County officials did not release any additional details about the person who recently died. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the person was infected with H5N1.
County officials have reported that 33 dairy herds have recently tested positive for H5N1.
They say three human infections have been linked to exposure at a dairy, and that the Yakima Health District is working with the state health department to find people who were in close contact with those people and monitor them for symptoms.
The H5N1 bird flu has been spreading widely among wild birds, poultry, cows and other animals for several years. Health concerns escalated in early 2024 when infections spread among U.S. livestock. Its presence in the environment increases the chances that people will be exposed, and potentially catch it, officials have said.
More than 70 human infections have been reported in the U.S. since the beginning of 2024, according to the CDC. But there is no known person-to-person spread and the risk to the general public is low, the agency says.
The agency analyzed the genetic sequence of the virus from the person who died in Washington and found no changes that would make the virus spread more easily or cause more severe illness, a CDC spokesperson said Monday.
Officials continue to urge people who have contact with sick or dead birds to take precautions, including wearing respiratory and eye protection and gloves when handling poultry. People who work on farms are considered to be at higher risk.

title: The Latest: Democrats and Republicans make a final push one day before midterm elections
text:
President Donald Trumpclosed out the final weekend of a turbulent midterm campaign with rallies in two states he had handily won in the past. At the same time, Democrats began to fracture in Michigan, risking their effort to retake the Senate. Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers as Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election.
Trump will make his closing pitch of the midterm elections Monday afternoon at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, pushing his slow, expensive and problem-plagued efforts to repair it back into the spotlight on the eve of Election Day.
The Latest:
Justice Department defends voter list that it says contains suspected noncitizens
The Justice Department has defended the accuracy of a list that it says has more than 20,000 suspected noncitizens registered to vote in California and suggested that an immigrant rights group should face contempt charges over an analysis of the names.
U.S. District Court Chief Judge James Boasberg had allowed the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights access to data on people the Trump administration alleges are noncitizen voters. Boasberg ordered the plaintiffs not to disclose any names and to use the data only for arguments about why they have legal standing to challenge its use.
In a Saturday court filing, the group said more than 40% of the people on the list do not appear in the state’s voter file. The filing also identified 22 people who were likely naturalized U.S. citizens while saying that thousands more American citizens appeared to be on it.
The Justice Department argued Sunday that the group’s filing had nothing to do with its legal standing and therefore violated Boasberg’s order. The agency also suggested that Boasberg refer the matter for investigation into possible contempt of court.
Voters on the left and right fear the America they’ve known is slipping away
In dozens of Associated Press interviews across the United States, many voters say the America they’ve known is slipping away.
They see lawlessness coming from those who create the laws, hate stirred by politicians and a culture that doesn’t speak to how they live. The angst was palpable among people who cast ballots at advance polling places or drop boxes ahead of Tuesday’s election, which will determine the political party that controls Congress in the final two years of Republican Donald Trump’s presidency.
“He’s just destroying us,” Democrat Linda Markle, 72, said of the president. She spoke outside the Warminster Township library in Bucks County, Pennsylvania.
“I am so afraid for this country,” she said. “People used to look out for each other. Not anymore.”
Trump supporter Therese Mennell in Ohio said he gets it. “There’s that kind of arrogant vibe about him that people don’t like, and sometimes I shut him off because of the way he talks,” the retiree said in Wayne County. “But, I mean, he’s doing the right thing. He is saving our country.”
In Alaska fishing community, the Dan Sullivan episode takes an ominous turn as FBI comes knocking
In the sleepy Alaskan fishing community of Petersburg, nobody has seen Dan J. Sullivan for weeks.
His rustic home stood dark a day after FBI agents visited friends who donated to his quixotic campaign to unseat the Republican senator with the same first and last name — Dan S. Sullivan. The only display of politics at his home was a yard sign from the League of Women Voters: “Stand Up for Democracy: Vote 2026.”
What may have begun as a ploy to harm the reelection prospects of Sen. Sullivan has taken a serious turn as the Trump administration weighs criminal charges over a campaign tactic known as “ballot stacking.”
“It just seems like such a waste of our taxpayer money,” said Sharon Hunter, a Petersburg resident who, with her husband, donated $1,000 to Dan J. Sullivan, a former elementary school teacher. FBI agents knocked on her door Saturday during a round of interviews with the campaign’s dozen contributors.
“I’m a bit incredulous about their whole angle,” Hunter said, “because they’re targeting a person who’s been a real contributor in this community.”
Trump is giving his closing midterm pitch at problem-plagued Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool
Trump is making his closing pitch of the midterm elections at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, pushing his slow, expensive and problem-plagued efforts to repair it back into the spotlight on the eve of Election Day.
In comments to reporters as he deplaned from Air Force One for a Sunday rally in Iowa, Trump said his speaking at the site would “show how beautiful it is.”
“We might hold it tomorrow or something,” the president added, without giving specifics. Hours later, the White House formally announced he’d be giving a speech there Monday afternoon.
Rather than using Monday to travel to key states and try to energize his “Make America Great Again” supporters as his Republican Party tries to maintain control of Congress, Trump opted for an event at a Washington renovation project that has been embarrassing and contentious.
The unusual move marks a departure from Trump’s monthlong race to stage more than 25 rallies in largely conservative areas, hoping the GOP can overcome his own low approval ratings and polls predicting that the Iran war, high energy prices and cost of living increases could spell a strong election night for Democrats.
El-Sayed’s primary opponent stuns Democrats by endorsing Republican opponent in Michigan Senate race
Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, stunned party officials Sunday by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers as Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill.
Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary.
“Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. “And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.”
El-Sayed dismissed the endorsement when asked about it by reporters later Sunday, saying he’s focused on issues voters care about, such as the high cost of living.
“At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he said, adding later: “None of this matters.”
Trump rallies in Iowa and Kansas as Republicans fight to keep Senate and House control
President Donald Trump closed out the final weekend of a turbulent midterm campaign with rallies in two states he has handily won in the past, while Democrats began to fracture in Michigan, risking their effort to retake the Senate.
The president was in Salina, Kansas, and Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday. Republicans in both states are fending off robust challenges from Democrats, threatening GOP majorities in the Senate while they’re already at risk in the House.
But in Iowa, Trump insisted Republicans were on the verge of sweeping victories on Election Day on Tuesday.
“We’re going to elect ‘America first’ Republicans up and down the line,” he said near the start of a speech that lasted two hours, long even for Trump, who is known for his lengthy, freewheeling rallies.
Later, he arrived tardy in Kansas, where Air Force One performed a theatrical flyover before landing for an outdoor, airport rally. Hundreds of people started leaving midway through his nearly 90-minute speech in rural central Kansas, which didn’t end until nearly 10 p.m. local time.

title: Judge dismisses complaint against ex-FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about Hunter Biden
text:
Judge dismisses complaint against 2 ex-FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about Hunter Biden
A federal judge on Monday dismissed a criminal complaint against two former FBI officials accused of falsely downplaying their knowledge of a laptop the Justice Department says belonged to Hunter Biden.
The decision by U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui followed a dramatic hearing in which he scolded prosecutors for their unorthodox maneuvers and an FBI agent who worked the case testified that he had been concerned the investigation would be seen as “political.”
The Justice Department may still have an opportunity to pursue a grand jury indictment against the two former officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, whose lawyers had pressed for dismissal of the charges. But the judge's ruling nonetheless represents an unmistakable setback for the Justice Department, particularly given the difficulty it has had in persuading grand juries in the nation's capital to return indictments in politically charged prosecutions like this one.
The judge's concerns about the case were apparent almost immediately, when he raised questions about why the Justice Department had charged the case through a criminal complaint — which is more typically done when investigators have a pressing need to take a defendant into custody — as opposed to an indictment that requires a grand jury's approval.
Then, at a preliminary hearing last week, he criticized the Justice Department for filing overnight an amended complaint with an additional criminal charge straight to the docket instead of first clearing the new charge with the court — something he said he had never seen before.
The hearing also featured testimony from an FBI agent who worked the case, who said that the investigation had been opened hours after President Donald Trump gave an election security speech last July and that it had been mandated by FBI Director Kash Patel, who kept close watch on it.
The case accused the two former FBI officials of misleading Congress in 2023 about their involvement in, and knowledge of, efforts to investigate a laptop the Justice Department says was dropped off by Hunter Biden, former President Joe Biden's son, at a Delaware computer repair shop in 2019.
But it also sought to echo longstanding grievances by Trump and his Republican allies that the FBI attempted to suppress information during the 2020 presidential campaign that was seen as potentially harmful to the Biden family. Candidate Joe Biden, a Democrat, ultimately defeated Trump, the Republican incumbent, in the 2020 election.
The Justice Department's case noted, for instance, how Floris and Benavides had given lawmakers in 2020 a “defensive briefing” that Republican Sens. Chuck Grassley of Iowa and Ron Johnson of Wisconsin have said was used to undermine their investigation into the Biden administration and link it to Russian disinformation.

title: Parents of 1-year-old fatally shot by police protest at Mississippi Attorney General's Office
text:
JACKSON, Miss. (AP) — The parents of a 1-year-old boy who was shot and killed by a police officer in Mississippi led a protest Monday at the office of the state’s attorney general, who ruled last month that the shooting was justified.
Cries of “our baby’s life mattered” echoed through the office’s lobby as Kohen Wiley’s parents and a small group of activists demanded to speak to Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch.
Marquell Bridges, an activist who has been working with Kohen’s parents, said they wanted Fitch to look Kohen’s parents in the eyes and tell them why the shooting was justified.
“These people work for us. We pay their salaries. We vote. We put them in office, and our people have to understand that we have the power,” he said.
They were met in the lobby by Fitch’s chief of staff, who said Fitch was not in the office. An email seeking comment was sent to the attorney general’s office Monday.
Kohen Wiley was killed in June when a police officer in the small town of Senatobia about 40 miles (65 kilometers) south of Memphis, Tennessee, fired his gun into a moving vehicle while responding to a shoplifting call.
Body-worn cameras show Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, holding Kohen as she and a friend run across the parking lot of a Senatobia Walmart and enter their vehicle. Wiley and the friend, who was driving, are Black.
Five officers approach the parked car with guns drawn. The car reverses away and crashes into a parked vehicle nearby as officers yell for it to stop.
The vehicle then accelerates forward as Senatobia Sgt. Hunter Foster steps toward it, directly in front, with his gun drawn. The wheels turn away from him, and he appears to put his hands on the hood as he jumps out of the way. He fires his gun, shattering the window of the front passenger side, where Kohen was seated on his mother’s lap.
The shooting sparked months of mourning and calls for justice, both nationally and in Senatobia.
Kohen would have turned 2 on Sunday.
Sitting outside the attorney general’s office, Kohen’s father, Davion Williams, said the passing of Kohen’s birthday was “the worst feeling ever.”
“It’s hard. It’s just hard to even express and talk about,” said Williams. “Now we have to keep his name alive.”
Williams said he wants Foster prosecuted and Fitch out of office. He wore a t-shirt with Kohen’s face that read “Kohen should be 2. Vote in his honor.”
Foster’s attorney, Martin Zummach, has said his client had “no choice” but to shoot at the vehicle because it was going to hit him. The Mississippi Attorney General’s office said its monthslong probe found that Foster’s use of force was appropriate.
The U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, meanwhile, was investigating an arson fire on Saturday that damaged the Senatobia police building. It was unclear what caused the fire. Emails to the ATF and the state fire marshal’s office Monday were not immediately returned.

title: Trapping is an exercise in cruelty that causes animals to suffer
text:
The Oct. 19 report, “Interest in trapping grows in Maine,” presents trapping as a skill that can be learned and practiced responsibly.
There is no responsible way to trap.
Courses can teach someone where to set a trap and how to talk to landowners, but they cannot change what a trap does: it seizes whatever animal steps into it and holds that animal in pain until someone returns.
Maine has seen this firsthand. In 2014, weeks after federal officials approved a permit allowing a number of endangered Canada lynx to be caught, two lynx died in Conibear traps set for fisher and marten. Nearly 20 more were caught that season, and federal officials estimate most trapped lynx are never reported. Bald eagles and other raptors are drawn to baited sets, and family dogs are caught every season.
The animals targeted suffer, too. Maine law requires most foothold traps to be checked only once per calendar day. An animal caught just after a morning check can legally wait until nearly midnight the next day. Killer-type traps and drowning sets can go three days unchecked, or five in unorganized territory. During that time, a fox or coyote held by the leg may break teeth biting at the steel and dislocate joints struggling to escape, while enduring cold, thirst and terror.
Rising interest in trapping is not progress. It is a reason for Mainers to ask whether this practice belongs in a state that claims to value its wildlife.
Mindi Fleming
Livermore Falls

title: This state no longer allows candy, soda, energy drink purchases with SNAP benefits
text:
COLUMBIA, S.C. (WRDW/Gray) - SNAP recipients in South Carolina are no longer able to buy some sugary items, including most candy and soda, under the new program.
The Health Food SC Project, approved by the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food and Nutrition Service, excludes candy, energy drinks, soft drinks and sweetened beverages from the list of foods eligible for purchase under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, commonly known as SNAP or food stamps.
Diet and zero-sugar soft drinks are still allowed to be purchased using SNAP.
South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster announced his intent to pursue a federal waiver for the restrictions in August 2025, issuing an executive order in September directing the South Carolina Department of Social Services to submit the waiver request. The USDA approved the waiver.
All South Carolina SNAP-approved retailers will participate in the program. SNAP households will not have the option to opt out of the food restrictions.
