title: Westbrook canned-water brand to start distributing in Florida
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Jen Millard, a 2026 Mainebiz Business Leader of the Year, founded mainelove in 2024 to package water from Sebago Lake — considered one of the cleanest in the country — in recyclable aluminum cans.
The company recently won double gold for its Perfectly Still Water line in the non-carbonated water category at the inaugural Water Choice Awards presented by New York City beverage media platform the Daily Pour. The February issue of Food & Beverage magazine named mainelove’s Blueberry Lemon Flavored Seltzer as Editor’s Pick.
The recognition comes as the Westbrook startup expands into Florida and grows its hospitality presence, with placements of co-branded cans at the Mandarin Oriental, Boston Harbor Hotel and select Westin locations.
The company is part of 1% For the Planet, giving back 1% of sales (versus profits) to environmental causes.
Mainebiz: Earlier this year, your brand was in 500-plus stores, licensed in 21 states and had expanded into New Hampshire and Massachusetts. What are the trends today?
Jen Millard: We are now in over 1,100 locations, including grocery, restaurants, hospitality and general C stores; licensed in over 30 states with the ability to ship to all 50 states via our partners Amazon and Walmart; and now have full distribution in Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Connecticut.
MB: You sold $500,000 worth of product from May to December in 2025. What are sales today?
JM: From May to December in 2026, we are on pace to finish the year at over $1 million in sales.
MB: You previously raised $2.2 million to fund growth. Where are you now?
JM: We are in a capital cycle now and looking to raise an additional $5 million for growth.
MB: Have you been hiring? You previous had four full-time and three part-time employees.
JM: We employ eight full-time roles, two part-time roles and four contractors. Our growth requires adding additional sales leads in Florida and in the hospitality space.
MB: What does the Florida expansion look like?
JM: Our entry to Florida starts with a team. We are the water of FTLDUTD [Florida soccer organization Fort Lauderdale United], which happens to be in the same league as [Maine men’s and women’s soccer organizations] Hearts of Pine and Maine Wildness. We are already poured and sold at the property. This team sits in south Florida, and we will start our expansion into hotels and hospitality from there. We have over 200 hotels in the pipeline in Florida. The capital raise is key to bringing this alive.
MB: How much product have you sold in Florida so far?
JM: It’s too early to share results. The Florida market really starts in November with the return of snowbirds.
MB: What’s your growth plan for 2027?
JM: We have an aggressive $5 million plan to deliver in 2027, which depends on our capital raise and many other factors.
MB: Why is Florida a target market?
JM: The route from Maine to Florida along the I-95 corridor is a well-known path for Mainers and snowbirds. This I-95 corridor is our focus on expansion and growth.
MB: What’s up next for mainelove?
JM: Our focus is to continue our I-95 expansion, which likely includes the D.C. metro area for the spring of 2027. We shall see. We see continued success with tourists who come to Maine, try our water in a great restaurant or location and then purchase it via Amazon or Walmart when they go home. That is the dream.

title: Martha Stewart apologizes for dressing as homeless person for Halloween after getting backlash
text:
(CNN) — Martha Stewart apologized after she dressed as a homeless person for Halloween.
Stewart, 85, posted a photo of herself on Instagram wearing distressed jeans and makeup resembling dirt while holding a sign that read, “I am hungry, help me!!”
The since-deleted Instagram post also promoted her candle collection in the caption.
The costume sparked backlash online, with many people calling it tone-deaf.
Stewart initially told Page Six that the costume was intended to raise awareness about homelessness, saying she was “distressed” that it offended people.
She later acknowledged on Instagram that her first statement to Page Six did not go far enough and issued an apology.
“It’s hard to admit when you’ve really screwed up. My earlier statement didn’t go far enough. I know many people are economically struggling. Wearing a costume like I did was insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry,” she wrote on Instagram.

title: Getting the facts on common Election Day issues
text:
Getting the facts on common Election Day issues
On Election Day things sometimes go wrong. Whether it be something minor like running out of ballots, or something bigger like allegations of voter fraud or intimidation.
Getting the facts on common Election Day issues
On Election Day things sometimes go wrong. Whether it be something minor like running out of ballots, or something bigger like allegations of voter fraud or intimidation.
It's election eve and election officials across the state are working to ensure everything goes smoothly on Tuesday.
"Worst case scenario, we had such a huge turnout, we would get permission to photocopy them, and they would just have to be hand tallied at the end of the evening," Fran Smith, the town clerk in Brunswick said, talking about solutions if the town were to run out of ballots.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows added that the state printed enough ballots for 100% of Maine's registered voters.
On tabulator malfunctions, Smith said her team has already tested the new tabulators and that they are just an upgrade from the ones Maine has been using for years.
These issues are on the more minor side, but Brunswick and many other communities will have police at the polls just in case.
We've reported throughout this campaign cycle that there have been concerns about some larger issues including immigration enforcement at polling locations in Maine, allegations of voter fraud and intimidation and electioneering.
"If we felt somebody had voted on behalf of somebody else, then we would obviously elevate it to the Secretary of State's office, to do a proper legal investigation. And then they would obviously, in turn turn it to the Attorney General's office," Smith said.
"If the voter feels uncomfortable, they should immediately alert the warden or call my office," Bellows added.
In a press release last week, the United States Attorney's Office for the District of Maine appointed two assistant U.S. attorneys to oversee any election related complaint regarding fraud and voter rights.
There have been isolated incidents of voter fraud in Maine. In 2020, a roommate intercepted a ballot and voted in the roommate's name and in 2024, a man intercepted his late father's ballot and filled it out.
"I think it's really important to know that anyone who tries to cheat by voting in the name of another or voting two ballots would be caught and would be investigated and prosecuted," Bellows said.
She also confirmed that there will be congressional observers in Maine on Election Day as well as DOJ monitors.
If you get to the polls by the time they close on Election Day, you can still cast your ballot as long as you are in line before 8 p.m.

title: Aging Untold: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we share strategies to help caregivers communicate effectively and reset interactions when stress and exhaustion take a toll.
We break down the causes of gout, warning signs and the everyday steps that can help prevent painful flare-ups.
Then, we highlight an alliance of compassionate nurses in St. Louis raising the standard of bereavement care for families experiencing pregnancy or infant loss.
When you are caring for a loved one, the stress can turn into sharp words.
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room and let yourself calm down.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said some words can escalate a conversation and cautioned caregivers to choose words with care. She said these words can escalate a conversation: no, you, always, never, don’t and you can’t
Gout is common and painful. When most people think of it, they picture a big toe that is red and throbbing, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
It starts with uric acid building up in the blood and crystals forming in the joints and other tissues, Rogers said, and the immune system treats the crystal as foreign objects.
She said uric acid buildup can point to something bigger.
Labor and delivery nurses in St. Louis who have experienced the emotional toll of caring for mothers who had suffered a loss have created a nonprofit that offers support and resources to families impacted by the death of a baby.
Kayla Hollingshead said with most diagnoses, there is a standard of care within the medical profession, but no real standard has ever existed for those who unexpectedly lose a baby.
The women created a new standard of care that includes how office staff speaks to families. They also create comfort kits containing books, cards and self-care items that are mailed to families around the world.
The Ford Motor Company produced the Model A for a limited time, but nearly a century later, car clubs are helping to keep the iconic engines running.
“We get a lot of smiles per mile. People get excited. And then if we blow the ahooga horn, they are ecstatic, especially kids,” Stew Wolfe, vice president of Old Dominion Model A Ford Club, said.
Between 1927 and 1931, Ford cranked out roughly 5 million of them, but only a fraction of the cars are still around.

title: Ex-Husson professor’s bail doubled after making 1st court appearance
text:
A former Husson University associate professor is charged with 10 felonies after he was allegedly viewing sexually explicit images of children and filming students at the school.
Jonathan Houck, 33, of Bangor had his first appearance Monday afternoon in Penobscot County court. He is charged with six felony counts of possession of child sexual abuse material and four counts of violations of privacy.
Houck, who was arrested Friday, did not enter a guilty plea because he is charged with felonies. The case will go before a grand jury that will decide whether or not to indict him on the charges.
A police investigation found child sexual abuse material on Houck’s phone, Deputy District Attorney Chelsea Lynds said. There is no indication he produced the images but it did involve children as young as 5 years old.
While investigating that case, police found images on Houck’s accounts of college women who clearly didn’t know they were being recorded, Lynds said. Houck, a professor of exercise science and assistant cross country coach, used his position to have students undress and weigh themselves while a hidden camera recorded them, she said.
Lynds’ description of the Husson allegations align with a student’s TikTok video posted on Thursday. The student accused Houck of filming partially dressed students with hidden cameras in a fall 2025 exercise science class where the students’ body weights were needed. She undressed to her bra and underwear, weighed herself, got dressed and went back to class.
“In this case, the defendant has both a sexual interest in children and a deviant criminal sexual interest in adults, which was demonstrated by using his position of trust as a professor to create this opportunity to capture his own students in states of undress,” Lynds said.
Houck’s lawyer for the day did not make an argument about bail because Houck has retained an attorney who will do so at a later date.
Judge Meghan Szylvian raised Houck’s cash bail to $100,000 at the request of Lynds. He was held on a $50,000 bail over the weekend.
He is held in the Penobscot County Jail. Part of his bail conditions include no contact with any children, no contact with current or former Husson students, and not to go on the campus. If he posts bail, he cannot live within 5 miles of a school.

title: FDA approves generic version of HIV-prevention drug to be sold in low-income countries
text:
FDA approves generic version of HIV-prevention drug to be sold in low-income countries
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved a generic version of the world’s only twice-a-year shot to prevent HIV — a big step toward making the drug available inexpensively and more quickly in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
The announcement was made on Monday morning by the manufacturer and organizations that helped to speed up development of the medication, called lenacapavir.
The drug is expected to cost $40 a year per person in the countries where it will be available, the same price as daily preventive pills available now. But the shots are much more convenient than the pills because they’re needed much less frequently and they nearly eliminated new infections in two groundbreaking studies of people at high risk.
People don’t always take their daily dose of medication, “and if you do not take it, you cannot get protected against HIV,” said Carmen Pérez Casas, HIV lead for the grant-making organization Unitaid, a global health agency. “With lenacapavir, we are much more hopeful.”
Ultimately, advocates said, the medication should help drive down cases of HIV and AIDS — and deaths. According to the WHO, 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV and 570,000 died from HIV-related causes last year.
With an affordable, high-quality generic medication now available, “we could help to scale this to the 20 million people around the world who need PrEP,” prescription medicine taken by people at risk of HIV before being exposed to the virus, said Carolyn Amole, who leads the HIV program for the Clinton Health Access Initiative, a global health organization.
“And if we scale to those levels,” she added, “we can actually begin to bring an end to the HIV epidemic.”
Generic lenacapavir can’t be sold in the U.S. because a brand-name version, Yeztugo, made by Gilead Sciences and approved last year, is still protected by a patent. The U.S. list price for that version, meaning the cost before insurance, is $28,218 a year. Gilead officials say that’s similar to some other types of PrEP, which stands for pre-exposure prophylaxis.
The new generic was approved by the FDA under a longstanding practice designed to ensure the quality of HIV-related drugs provided to other countries by the U.S. government. Approval of a drug by the U.S. FDA can speed regulatory approval in many other countries. The approval is considered “tentative,” the FDA's standard designation for generics while the originator remains under patent.
Until now, Gilead has been the sole supplier of lenacapavir, and demand has outstripped supply in low- and middle-income countries. Last year, Gilead established royalty-free licensing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable production. Those voluntary licenses cover a specific set of countries in sub-Saharan Africa, Asia and Latin America.
“We share the sense of urgency around expanding access to lenacapavir for HIV prevention,” a Gilead spokesperson said in a statement. “We believe we have enabled the fastest and most sustainable path to expanding access for communities most affected by HIV.”
The generic was developed by India-based Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories under an agreement brokered by Unitaid, the Clinton Health Access Initiative and Wits RHI, a health research institute in Africa. The partners sought to accelerate development and make the drug available at an affordable price.
Common side effects with lenacapavir include injection site reactions, headache and nausea. People also must be tested for HIV prior to starting the drug and with each injection; drug-resistant HIV has been identified when used by people with an undiagnosed HIV infection.
“For any kind of PrEP … you need to have HIV testing in advance,” said Saiqa Mullick, director of implementation science with Wits RHI. “For many of the low- and middle-income countries, that is a rapid test.”
Generic lenacapavir should start to become available in some places within weeks, those helping with the effort said, although it could take a bit longer in countries that require the drug to go through their own approval processes before people can start taking it. Generic versions made by the other manufacturers have yet to be approved by the FDA.
“The work is not done. Now, we need the funding to actually buy it for everyone who needs it and then we need to do the hard work of getting it to the millions of people who need it and want it,” Amole said. “But this is a great milestone.”
Casas said she’s optimistic that scientific advances — along with political will and funding — can help the world curb HIV.
“Now,” she said, “we have the tools.”

title: Aquaculture’s challenges must not be swept under the rug
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Kelsey Fenwick lives in St. George.
Academic institutions have a responsibility not only to educate, but to present complex issues fairly and accurately. At a recent conference I attended, however, a program intended to promote lifelong learning instead presented a one-sided perspective on a complex and controversial issue affecting Maine’s coast: aquaculture.
The Wishcamper Center’s SAGE program at the University of Southern Maine describes its mission as providing lifelong learning opportunities for adults aged 50 and older. I believe a recent presentation fell short of that educational mission by featuring Sebastian Belle, executive director of the Maine Aquaculture Association (MAA), without adequately addressing the significant controversies surrounding the industry he represents.
The MAA purports to promote “economically and environmentally sustainable business practices” and has described its advocacy for clean water in strong terms. The presentation, however, did not acknowledge or address alleged Clean Water Act violations and pending litigation involving Cooke Aquaculture, a major player in Maine’s aquaculture industry.
Nor did it address concerns about the ownership and financial interests behind Maine shellfish aquaculture operations, including reports of oyster aquaculture lease interests being controlled by the Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, a multibillion-dollar foreign institutional investor. These issues deserve scrutiny in any discussion of the industry’s environmental and economic sustainability.
The presentation emphasized the need to produce more food, particularly protein, citing population growth, changing diets, land constraints and limits on water resources. Those are legitimate considerations. But a meaningful discussion of sustainability must also examine the environmental and economic trade-offs of expanding industrial-scale aquaculture.
Belle acknowledged that sustainability does not mean having no environmental impact. Nevertheless, the presentation did not address the potential adverse effects of aquaculture on local fishermen, native species, marine ecosystems and coastal communities.
Nor did the conference give sufficient attention to who benefits economically. Cooke Aquaculture operates internationally, and its global scale raises legitimate questions about how much of the economic value generated by its Maine operations remains in Maine and how much flows to interests elsewhere.
The economic and environmental sustainability of open-water salmon aquaculture cannot be assessed solely by examining the environmental effects of net pens in Maine waters. It also requires examining the wild fish used to produce salmon feed, the ecological consequences of removing those fish from marine food webs and whether fish that could feed people directly are instead being diverted to produce a higher-value export commodity. Belle’s presentation acknowledged none of these factors.
Nor did the presentation address Maine’s continued allowance of finfish open net-pen aquaculture, a practice that has been prohibited or phased out in all other coastal states. That distinction is relevant to any balanced assessment of Maine’s approach to the industry.
Maine is fortunate to have an exceptional seafood tradition and independent harvesters whose livelihoods are closely tied to the health of our coastal waters. We should encourage people to support locally harvested, wild seafood while carefully evaluating the environmental and economic consequences of expanding aquaculture. Claims of sustainability should be examined critically, particularly when the interests being represented include large, internationally operating businesses.
In my view, the USM Wishcamper Center’s programming did the public a disservice by presenting an industry advocate’s perspective without adequately exploring the competing evidence and concerns.
Inviting industry representatives to speak is entirely appropriate. Presenting their views as an educational opportunity, however, carries a responsibility to provide context, ask difficult questions and make room for other perspectives.
Lifelong learning should equip Mainers to think critically about consequential public issues, not leave them with an incomplete picture.

title: 14 treated after accidental pepper spray discharge leads to craft fair evacuation
text:
HONOLULU (KHNL/Gray News) - An accidental pepper spray discharge prompted an evacuation at a community center in Hawaii on Sunday afternoon.
Honolulu police said officers responded to the Neal S. Blaisdell Center after 3 p.m. during the Hawaii Holiday Craft and Gift Fair.
According to a vendor, a customer was examining a pepper spray canister at a booth when they accidentally activated it, releasing its contents into the air.
The incident prompted an evacuation of the event hall as Honolulu firefighters, including the department’s hazardous materials team, and Emergency Medical Services responded.
Honolulu EMS said multiple crews evaluated 14 adults at the scene, and the patients declined transport to a hospital for further treatment.
Attendees said that a chemical smell lingered near the venue’s entrance following the accidental activation.

title: Ghost hunter investigates paranormal claims at New Mexico Civil War site
text:
Ghost hunter investigates paranormal claims at New Mexico Civil War site
The Battle of Valverde, a key Civil War conflict fought on Feb. 28, 1862, along the dried riverbank of the Rio Grande in New Mexico, is now the focus of paranormal legends that a ghost hunter recently set out to investigate.
"The Texans coming up through Mesilla and they had their sights set on Fort Union," said ghost hunter and author Cody Polston, who provided historical context for the battle.
Union troops stationed at Fort Craig worked to block Confederate access to Colorado and its resources, including gold. "So there's a lot on the line, and often this battle is kind of underrated because it's like, ah, they're kind of nuts out in the West, too much sun," Polston said.
During the battle, Union forces pulled out of the fort, leading to a major clash. "He pulled his forces out of the fort, and there was a big clash," Polston said. "They ended up bailing out and leaving a unit force at the rear, which is never a good thing." More than 500 soldiers died in the conflict.
Legend has it that cannon fire can be heard at Fort Craig on the anniversary of the battle. Polston decided to investigate. "The old riverbank is back that way, so they were anchored against this, so man, literally their line was kind of right through here," he said. However, after conducting observations, Polston reported, "We just finished with our observations in our area, and we have nothing at all to report, nothing that sounded anything remotely like a cannon."
Polston also shared a story he heard at the Valverde Hotel in Socorro. A cowboy claimed he encountered a headless man with a musket while searching for a lost calf near the historical site of the lancer charge. "The craziest story I ever got, I was at the Valverde Hotel in Socorro. I was looking for ghost stories in the area, and someone pointed out this cowboy to me," Polston said.
The cowboy recounted his experience. "He was near what historically would have been the lancer charge," Polston said. A man reportedly popped out of a bush with a musket, aimed, and fired at the cowboy. "I said, that's pretty scary. He said it's worse. The guy had no head. His horse startles and starts riding into the bosque. Takes a while to calm a horse down. He's like, I really don't want to go back that way," Polston said.
To investigate the cowboy's account, Polston and his team recreated the scene. "The task, the way we're going to do this, we have zeroed in the position where the shooter was, so what we're going to do is time this for four seconds. The reason for four seconds is that's how long he lost sight of the guy mounting, dismounting from the horse, and checking that area," Polston said.
After timing the reenactment, Polston concluded that most paranormal claims could be explained rationally. However, one mystery remained unresolved. "The one we could not figure out was Fort Craig, and I was on that one. We were walking back toward the old magazine, and we could just... there's a gunpowder smell, and it's strong," Polston said. "You can smell clear as day. Stayed around for five or 10 seconds. It was, phew, gone."
Polston has investigated numerous reports of paranormal activity at the battlegrounds, continuing to explore the intersection of history and legend.

title: 5 free guides to help you fill out your Maine ballot
text:
Election 2026
Visit the BDN election page for our latest coverage of local, state and national races.
Mainers have several voter guides to lean on as they finish their homework before Tuesday’s election, ranging from a personalized digital sample ballot to a plain-language PDF.
The guides could help you at the end of a crowded cycle. Voters will settle the U.S. Senate race that could decide control of the chamber, fill the 2nd District seat opened by U.S. Rep. Jared Golden’s departure and pick a successor to term-limited Gov. Janet Mills.
We decided to make you a guide to those guides. Here they are.
Maine Trust for Local News
The most detailed option comes from the Maine Trust for Local News, which owns the Portland Press Herald and sister papers. Its ballot lookup tool builds a sample ballot from your address, running from the Senate race down to city council, school board and local referendums.
Readers can check off their picks and print a copy. Not every candidate filled out the guide’s questionnaire. The holdouts include many legislative candidates and both 2nd District candidates, Democrat Matt Dunlap and Republican former Gov. Paul LePage.
The Maine Monitor
The Maine Monitor, a nonprofit newsroom, has pages for the top races, every county and every legislative district, which voters can find through another address lookup tool.
In partnership with C-SPAN, it has video interviews with the candidates for governor and the 1st District. The Senate and 2nd District campaigns didn’t make candidates available, so the Monitor compiled clips. It also tracks campaign fundraising down to the legislative level.
Maine Public
Maine Public’s Your Vote 2026 page is built around long-form “Maine Calling” interviews with host Jennifer Rooks. They cover the candidates for governor, both 1st District candidates, Dunlap and Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Troy Jackson, the former Maine Senate president.
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and LePage get only links to their campaign websites after they did not sit for interviews. Rooks addressed the senator’s absence during Jackson’s interview. The page also carries video of the station’s Oct. 15 Senate debate in Bangor.
Guides.vote
Guides.vote, a national project, takes a research-heavy approach to the Senate race. It sorts Collins’ and Jackson’s records into 14 issues, including abortion, taxes and the war in Iran, and links each position to a vote, statement or news story.
It’s available in Spanish and as a PDF. The Senate race is its only Maine guide this year.
League of Women Voters of Maine
The low-tech option is the League of Women Voters of Maine’s guide. It explains registration, absentee voting, ranked-choice voting and accessible voting machines in plain language.
It also prints candidates’ unedited answers to two questions. Three Republicans didn’t respond: gubernatorial nominee Bobby Charles, LePage and 1st District challenger Ron Russell. For legislative, county and local races, the league points readers to Vote411.org.

title: Why some Maine hunters struggled to call in bull moose this year
text:
Of all my assorted big game hunts, the celebrated Maine moose hunt gets top billing for plain fun, challenges and, at times, downright frustration. Over the years, I have either hunted with a permit or been part of a moose hunting party. Most of my hunts have been cow hunts, except for two bull hunts. My last hunt, this fall, was a bull hunt, and I was invited along as a guest with my chainsaw-powered winch.
Moose sign was as plentiful as I have ever seen, but sightings were scarce. At least three times, we had bulls answering our cow-in-heat calls, only to “hang up” just out of range or in thick cover. Frustrating! Common sense said that our calling strategy or techniques were just not up to snuff. What were we doing wrong?
I went to the experts to try to get an answer to that question.
In his 2006 book “Moose Hunting,” moose guide Dave Kelso devotes a chapter to moose calling. His advice carries weight because he has worked with Maryo Peppin and studied moose in captivity at the Buck Expert Research Center.
Effective calling involves many variables, and hunters need to adjust their vocalizations to the situation, Kelso explains.
Although cows are in heat for just 24 hours, bulls can still be called long after the rut. It is wrong to assume otherwise, Kelso says. The key to a good cow-in-heat call is a quivering tone that softly fades out.
There are two important bull grunts: the fight grunt and the love grunt. Hunters should learn the difference, Kelso advises. When answering a bull with brush raking or the volume of a call, try to sound bigger than he is. He considers mouth or voice calls the best option. Raking brush is also an art form when communicating with an incoming bull. Always pause between rakes. A bull will not rake and call at the same time.
Moose guide Tenley Skofield has many hunts under her belt. Here are some of her thoughts.
Once you have scouted or discovered a productive area to hunt, be aware of wind direction and keep it in your face. Start by lightly tickling brush with a scapula, antler or antler imitation. In the stillness of breaking dawn, that little bit of brush rustling will sometimes be enough to get a conversation started. Too often, a calling sequence begins too loudly and too frequently, pushing moose away rather than pulling them in.
The same goes for first calls. If you are making your first call in an area and are unsure whether moose are in the vicinity, call lightly at first in each of the four directions. Listen, then call again every 15 minutes or so as you move slowly and quietly. Gradually increase the volume.
There may or may not be a moose within earshot. Continue calling for at least an hour. Two hours is not too much time to invest in opening a conversation with a moose, especially one coming in silently. You may only know those moose are approaching by the sound of a snapped branch or antlers moving through the brush.
The most underrated element of calling is being quiet. Have a plan in place as you begin, communicate with your party using hand signals and whisper only if absolutely necessary. Unnatural sounds, such as talking, clanging shooting sticks, zippers and crackling packs and wrappers, will spook a moose and ruin any chance of calling one in to shooting range.
Highly experienced moose guide Nathan Theriault of OMM Outfitters offers similar advice. Cow calls should not be too loud or frequent. Instead, hunters should focus on a slow, drawn-out, nasal tone and proper cadence to attract bulls during the peak of the rut.
Pacing and patience are equally important, Theriault says. Bulls move slowly and may take hours to approach while checking the wind. Sit tight and avoid moving prematurely, which could spook the animal.
Wind direction and setup also matter. Always set up with the wind in your face. Mature bulls typically circle downwind before appearing, so position your caller and shooter accordingly.
Mouth calling and horns offer another advantage over electronic callers, allowing hunters to adjust pitch, volume and cadence in real time based on a bull’s reactions and behavior, Theriault says.
My final thought: A Maine moose hunting permit is a gift that could mean a once-in-a-lifetime hunt. It pays to be ready. Calling is critical, especially during the rut. Consider doing more homework and practicing the art of moose calling. Only then will you truly be ready. I plan to heed my own advice on this one.

title: UMaine SDS leads ‘March Against ICE’ protest, calls for university action
text:
On Oct. 30, Students for a Democratic Society (SDS), a progressive student activist organization at the University of Maine, led a “March Against ICE” protest on the steps of Fogler Library to speak out against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). During the march, current and former faculty members, student organizations and SDS members spoke with the Maine Campus about the importance of protests in fostering civic engagement.
Four SDS members spoke at the event and President Gabriel Veilleux said the protest took three weeks to plan. He began his speech by leading the group in a chant: “Winter is coming, salt the ICE.”
Veilleux began by stating that SDS wanted to present concerns to UMaine President Joan Ferrini-Mundy in April, but according to Veilleux, those concerns have remained unaddressed since then. He said that SDS tried to meet with the president throughout the summer and this semester but received no response from the administration.
“We are hoping that this protest can land us attention with admin and make our asks very clear. We’re hoping that this action specifically can land a meeting with admin and open dialogue to what our goals are,” Veilleux said.
Veilleux said SDS would continue its efforts until members were granted a voice and the learning environment was safe, something the organization believes has not been guaranteed.
Veilleux said SDS plans to continue protesting despite these challenges, stating that “rain or shine we are still going to turn out, because it’s really the cause that’s important to us.”
“We strongly believe that admin needs to do a better job communicating with the student body. We believe that distinction between public and private spaces should really be marked on campus so students can know where their legal protections extend to,” Veilleux said.
Veilleux encouraged students to get organized as a way to stay involved and mentioned that he helped bring SDS back to campus after almost 60 years. The group meets on Tuesdays at 6:30 p.m.
One of the speakers, Sofia Carrasquillo, a member of SDS and an officer in the Caribbean and Latinx Student Alliance (CALSA), was the third to speak. Carrasquillo said everyone should have the freedom to exist without having to consistently defend that freedom. She also mentioned that although the system cannot change in one day, she was grateful for the presence of those who attended.
During the march, Stephen Coghlan, a wildlife ecology professor at UMaine and the adviser for SDS, discussed how faculty should respond to the ongoing political climate.
“We have a responsibility in an institution here of learning and open inquiry. Freedom of thought, freedom of speech, freedom of questioning,” Coghlan said. “We have much more important things to worry about than our grants.”
Coghlan recognized that while some instructors, adjuncts, teaching assistants and students lack job security, those who feel comfortable speaking up should do so.
“We have the power but we’re not using it as a whole faculty,” Coghlan said. “If they are silent, they are complicit.”
Doug Allen was a professor of philosophy at UMaine for 46 years before retiring from full-time teaching seven years ago. Allen described himself as “retired but still active” and continues to attend marches and other civic engagement events in his community.
Allen said he is not afraid to speak about what he believes but recognizes that although some professors remain silent, it takes courage to get involved.
In a conversation with the Maine Campus, Coghlan and Allen agreed that while it is important for faculty to remain involved and not stay silent, there are different ways of doing so without necessarily blaming one party.
“We have to organize to have a voice. You have to have a voice and that’s what SDS is doing, trying to reclaim that you’re not just a student. It’s important to have your own voice, that people hear you and they take seriously what you have to say,” Allen said.
CALSA officer Micaela Cateriano attended the march and spoke about the importance of Latin representation on campus.
“We need to be present for the people who can’t be here because they fear that their faces are going to be in public. Sofia and I feel comfortable enough to be here for our loved ones that are not here right now, and important to show the people that we are a big, powerful community here and they are more than welcome,” Cateriano said.
CALSA meets Mondays at 5:30 p.m. in Room 312 of the Memorial Union.
The Maine Campus also spoke with three students who shared their opinions on why students should be involved in activism.
SDS committee organizer Wyatt de Mott said that when people get involved with the campaign, it “keeps the energy up,” giving students a chance to communicate important concerns to university administration.
Antonio Tobias Berletti said that while he does not attend meetings often, he remains active in SDS events. Berletti believes that as society grows tired of an older system, people are beginning to organize as a way to break out of the political system.
“I show up because I think it is important to get involved, to show your solidarity with oppressed people everywhere. Every struggle is a struggle worth dealing upon,” Berletti said.
SDS member Matt Hinds believes protests are important in the face of continued media coverage surrounding “the terrible things ICE is doing.”
“It doesn’t have nearly as much weight as when there’s a large group of people chanting against it and making their voices heard and giving speeches. It’s important to say people are upset about this. We want policy changes, please at least meet with us,” Hinds said.

title: College students need to talk about politics
text:
EDITORIAL: Tuesday, Nov. 3 is the big day. We are going to find out who will represent us in Washington and Augusta as Mainers. The influence and power that these political positions hold over your lives cannot be overstated. Sadly, it still seems that many students are unaware of the stakes and the candidates who lie in front of them. This is something that cannot continue. College students need to be aware of the world around them and the impact their decisions have — and they need to spread that awareness to others.
College students usually fall into the age bracket of 18 to 29, which has the lowest voter turnout rate in the country. One might wonder: What is the cause for such a low turnout? While there are multiple factors and theories as to why this is, a major component is unequivocally youthful, blissful ignorance.
A lot of people our age don’t realize the power their voice and vote hold. Life to them has always been relatively okay, and they might think who’s in office doesn’t affect them, that life is going to keep on going the way it’s been. Even if that is the case, which it probably isn’t, chances are there are groups of people whose quality of life will be impacted. You, the voter, have a say if those lives are going to improve or worsen, and you owe it to your fellow Americans to make an educated decision about the future of the country you share. Beyond that, the right to decide the leaders of your country is not something that everyone in the world gets to do, so make the best of it.
It’s hard to have political conversations with your friends. The environment surrounding this election and politics in general has become extreme — but that’s because it matters. We’re not saying you need to get into screaming matches with your friends, but you should encourage political discourse with the people you care about, even if it’s uncomfortable. It is the people you love whose lives are going to be affected by the outcome of political elections, as well as your own. If you really care about your friends and family, you have to do what’s best for them, even if that’s uncomfortable.
Talking to your partner is also an obstacle many run into, but it’s one that you have to overcome. Politics is something that looms in relationships, and in heterosexual relationships, that shadow probably feels like it’s looming larger than ever. Differences in political beliefs between men and women among people under 30 have grown over recent years, and are projected to grow further in the next election. Men have always leaned to the right and women to the left; however, women have moved significantly to the left in recent years.
This can make talking about politics with your partner scary, because you don’t want to tip the boat and cause something that could end the relationship. If that’s the case, the relationship probably isn’t the one for you. You have to be able to have difficult, honest conversations with your partner, especially when you’re having a disagreement. The outcome of the conversation doesn’t need to end in agreement, but it’s important that you have a conversation about something that is so integral to the character of the person you’re dating, especially if there is an issue that is paramount to you. If you can’t do that, it’s not a relationship worth being in.
You and your friends can’t be unaware of the world around you. We’re not kids anymore. Our decisions, whether they involve voting for a certain candidate or not voting at all, have major consequences. We as a campus need to know the options the candidates are giving us as voters and make the best decision for ourselves and the people around us.

title: 'Heat' director Michael Mann sustains 'superficial injury' at gun range
text:
'Heat' director Michael Mann sustains 'superficial injury' at gun range
Filmmaker Michael Mann was injured at a gun range on Saturday in Los Angeles. He was taken to a hospital where he was treated and is being released, his representative told The Associated Press on Sunday.
Mann sustained what his representative described as a superficial injury after a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered.
The 83-year-old filmmaker behind crime classics like “Heat,” “Collateral” and “Thief” has apparently been an experienced target shooter for decades, and the accident happened at a sanctioned gun range.
Mann continues to be quite active in Hollywood in his 80s. He most recently directed the film “Ferrari,” with Adam Driver, and is developing a sequel to “Heat,” which is supposed to begin filming early next year.

title: China is a potential enemy
text:
To the Editor:
President Trump should be wary of communist China, a country that wants to spread its communist ideology around the world.
A prime example of China's anti-American foreign policy is the assistance it is providing Iran in its war with the United States.
It appears China is providing satellite imagery data to Iran, which allows Iran to more precisely target ships in the Strait of Hormuz and U.S. and other military bases in the Middle East. In essence, China is helping Iran injure and kill U.S. service members.
According to news reports, China has made 1,300 shipments of parts to Iran that can be used in the manufacture of drones and missiles.
Communist China is a sworn adversary of the Unites States and the democracies of the world. It should be treated as an adversary and potential enemy. We should be trying to weaken China economically to impede the buildup of its military and the development of new and advanced weapons. China currently has the largest navy in the world by ship count, is expanding its nuclear weapons capabilities and has extensive cyber warfare systems.
We need to support our allies in the Far East, especially Japan, Taiwan, the Philippines and Australia, to ensure they have strong militaries to help deter China's aggressive policies.
We must also be wary of Russia and North Korea, two countries who are potential enemies.
Donald Moskowitz
Londonderry, N.H.

title: Falmouth chiropractor relocates to larger lease in Portland
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Alchemy Chiropractic LLC, led by Dr. Sergey Terrio, relocated from 251 U.S. Route 1 in Falmouth to a larger space at 222 Auburn St. in Portland.
The solo practice leased 1,368 square feet of professional office space under a five-year lease agreement with MSP Professionals LLC.
Michael Atienza of Atienza Commercial & Residential Real Estate Brokers represented Alchemy Chiropractic in the transaction and assisted in evaluating the solo practice’s space requirements, identifying a suitable location and navigating the commercial leasing process.
John Doyon of Malone Commercial Brokers represented the landlord, MSP Professionals.
The location has private treatment rooms, natural light, skylights, a reception and waiting area, updated interior finishes and elevator access.
Terrio has been in practice more than five years. The site search took only a few weeks.
“This space is bigger and better in terms of location,” said Terrio. “I now have more rooms and the aesthetic/environment of the place serves better for healing as well.”

title: Despite higher paychecks, Americans still have less money to spend, Labor Department report says
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) - Although Americans are seeing bigger paychecks on paper, they still have less money to spend.
According to the U.S. Department of Labor’s Employment Cost Index, the total compensation for civilian workers, including wages and benefits, rose 3.4% over the last 12 months, ending in September. Wages and salaries were up 3.1%, while benefit costs climbed 3.9%.
After adjusting for inflation, however, wages are effectively shrinking, according to the report.
For private-sector workers, inflation-adjusted wages and salaries fell 0.6% over the past year, according to the Labor Department. For state and local government workers, real wages slipped 0.5%. That means price increases are outpacing pay gains, lowering workers’ purchasing power even as employers appear to be spending more on compensation.
The report shows that pay raises are not keeping up with the cost of living, which is a major frustration for many American households. The report also highlights a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is trying to tame inflation without triggering a sharp slowdown in hiring or wage growth.
Last month, the government reported that consumer inflation accelerated in September as goods and services became more expensive, according to the Associated Press.
The Employment Cost Index is one of the Federal Reserve’s closely watched barometers of underlying wage and benefit pressures in the economy.
The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time since 2023 six weeks ago. It was an effort to tame high inflation. It said another rate hike could happen later this year.

title: Casco’s first full-time fire chief retires
text:
Brian Cole, Casco’s first full-time fire chief, has retired after 36 years with the department, including nine as chief, and is set to become the Fire/EMS coordinator for Cumberland County.
Cole began working at Casco Fire Rescue, which operates as a combination of per diem, full-time, and call company firefighters, in August 1990, according to a Facebook post honoring Cole’s retirement. In 2017, Cole, then a deputy chief, was asked to step into the role of fire chief following the retirement of his predecessor, Jason Moen. David Morton, town manager at the time, thought Cole was a “good fit” for the role, and appointed him to the role permanently.
In 2020, Cole became the town’s first full-time fire chief. Cole recalled how the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted the fire department’s routines, and led to discussions about bringing the department up to national standards by adding a full-time position.
Cole has been succeeded as fire chief by interim chief Jon Morrison.
Town Manager Anthony Ward said having a full-time fire chief has provided Casco with more consistent fire services and a solid leadership base for department staff.
“There’s a clear message of where we’re going,” said Ward, “and the chief is a key part of that dialogue and ensuring those standards are met.”
Ward praised Cole’s role in starting dialogue regarding mutual aid and sharing of equipment among Casco and neighboring communities including his role in establishing a cross-town “fly car” program, shared with Windham, Gray and Raymond, to assist town emergency response teams amid a paramedic shortage. Had it not been for the presence of a full-time fire chief, many of those cross-town dialogues would not have occurred, said Ward.
Following his retirement, Cole said, the Cumberland County manager asked him to serve as the county’s Fire/EMS coordinator, a new position designed to “streamline and centralize” key operations within the county’s fire and emergency services.
Cole said he was selected due to his experience and connections with fire chiefs across the county. He said the role is focused on coordinating fire and EMS, such as organizing information for cross-town purchases, and organizing conversations and capital improvement plans to improve service delivery across the county. Cole said he is available to assist in “any way within his realm” across the county.
Cumberland County Manager Jim Gailey praised Cole, noting how he came with a vast knowledge of the work that the county’s fire chiefs and town managers have done over the years, and calling him a “valuable asset” for the Fire/EMS coordinator position.

title: Midcoast clammers and sea farms could feel impacts of algae bloom for years
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
September’s algae bloom has faded from the waters around Harpswell, but harvesters and growers are still taking stock of the damage.
Some of the most vulnerable species, like worms and softshell clams, appear to have been wiped out in certain areas, while hard clams and oysters mostly survived. But with the bloom happening just before winter, growers and harvesters say they will have to wait for spring to know if the stress and lack of nutrients will lead to more losses.
Clam diggers and others started seeing signs of the bloom around Sept. 8 and 9. Dead and dying shellfish and worms were found on mudflats at the head of Middle Bay, in Long Cove, and in other areas, while some places in Harpswell saw no impacts at all. Maine’s Department of Marine Resources and other authorities soon confirmed that the bloom was spreading from Casco Bay as far south as New Hampshire and Massachusetts.
Tests revealed that the bloom contained the plankton Karenia mikimotoi, which is toxic to shellfish but not dangerous to humans. In addition to the plankton’s toxicity, any large algae bloom uses up oxygen, suffocating marine life. Those decomposing animals further deplete oxygen, both in the water and the mud, and can increase acidity.
The near-shore bloom seemed to peak around the middle of September. There were fears that a large storm that moved up the East Coast in the last week of September might push offshore algae back into Maine’s bays, but the storm ultimately tracked away from land and had minimal impact on Harpswell.
On Oct. 9, Harpswell Harbormaster Darcie Couture reported on Facebook that there were no more visible signs of the bloom, even offshore.
Harpswell clam digger David Wilson, who chairs the town’s Marine Resources Committee, said that in Long Cove and Middle Bay, he and other harvesters have found that larger quahogs, also known as hard clams, survived the event, while younger clams and seed clams did not.
Wilson said it could take as many as seven years for populations to rebuild. And he worries that even the clams that did survive the bloom might not make it through the winter if they haven’t built up their fat stores sufficiently.
Bloom’s impact extends to sea farms
Harpswell has more than 100 aquaculture leases, with oysters as the main crop, and farmers reported mixed experiences of the bloom.
Kat Lipp, general manager of Mere Point Oyster Co., on Middle Bay in Brunswick, estimated that the farm lost about 20% of its oysters from the bloom. The farm discovered the harm early on, before the bloom was fully evident. When the extent of the threat became clear, Lipp said, staff stopped handling the oysters to reduce stress on them and give them the best chance of survival.
Like Wilson, she said it remains to be seen how many of the oysters will survive the winter.
Snow Island Oysters, which farms oysters on Harpswell Sound near the north end of Orr’s Island, has not seen an unusual die-off, according to Tait Nygaard, farm manager. The farm has been cautious about handling oysters, he said. He speculated that its location closer to the open ocean may have been a safer spot than farther up in the bays.
Another oyster farmer, Seth White, said his shellfish near Little Birch Island in Middle Bay seem to be doing OK. But his other crop, urchins, was hit hard. White said that when he pulled them up in the middle of September, he found many dead urchins. Some of the live ones didn’t look so good either.
White said he only knows of one other urchin farm, in Portland, and he heard that it survived the bloom. He said it may be a few years before he can try to grow urchins again, because their seed can cost 40 times as much as oyster seed.
He got his urchin seed from the University of Maine through a grant. This was his first time trying to grow them, and he had hoped they would be ready to sell next season. Now he’ll have to wait years to see if urchins can be an economically viable crop.
A more immediate concern for many in the aquaculture and harvesting industries is the immediate loss of income. White said that when oyster farms decided to take a break from their usual schedule of harvesting and handling oysters to give the shellfish a better chance of surviving the bloom, farm workers saw their hours cut. He knew of a dozen or more people at the end of September who hadn’t had any work to do.
At Mere Point Oyster Co., Lipp had a similar message. “The folks out there really being affected by this are the diggers, the farmers, the wild harvesters — the individuals, not the companies,” she said. It will likely be months more before the full effects on workers is known.

title: Red Sox’s Chad Tracy a finalist for manager of the year
text:
NEW YORK — Milwaukee Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski is among four members of the World Series champions who are finalists for baseball’s biggest individual awards.
The Miz, a heavy favorite to win the NL Cy Young Award, was one of the top three vote-getters in balloting for the prize by the Baseball Writers’ Association of America at the conclusion of the regular season.
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy, who took over in April after Alex Cora was fired, and led Boston tot he playoffs, is a finalist for AL Manger of the Year along with Kevin Cash of the AL champion Rays and Will Venable of the White Sox.
Also, Red Sox starting pitcher Payton Tolle is a finalists for Rookie of the Year. Tolle went 9-6 with a 3.03 ERA in 26 starts. Cleveland pitcher Parker Messick and Detroit infielder Kevin McGonigleher are the other finalists.
Finalists for all the major BBWAA awards were announced Monday night on MLB Network. Winners will be revealed next week.
Gold Glove second baseman Brice Turang is in the running for National League MVP, and Milwaukee skipper Pat Murphy could become the first to win three consecutive Manager of the Year awards. Brewers closer Trevor Megill is a finalist for NL Relief Pitcher of the Year, a new category this year in both leagues.
Here are the finalist for the other awards:
AL MVP
Houston slugger Yordan Alvarez is the favorite to win. Third baseman Junior Caminero from the AL champion Tampa Bay Rays and shortstop Bobby Witt Jr. of the Kansas City Royals are the other finalists.
NL MVP
Gold Glove center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Chicago Cubs is expected to win after batting .280 with 45 home runs and 41 stolen bases, becoming the seventh member of the 40-40 club. Turang and four-time MVP Shohei Ohtani of the Los Angeles Dodgers are also finalists.
AL Cy Young

title: Trump is giving his closing midterm pitch at problem-plagued Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is making his closing pitch of the midterm elections at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, pushing his slow, expensive and problem-plagued efforts to repair it back into the spotlight on the eve of Election Day.
In comments to reporters as he deplaned from Air Force One for a Sunday rally in Iowa, Trump said his speaking at the site would “show how beautiful it is.”
“We might hold it tomorrow or something,” the president added, without giving specifics. Hours later, the White House formally announced he’d be giving a speech there Monday afternoon.
Rather than using Monday to travel to key states and try to energize his “Make America Great Again” supporters as his Republican Party tries to maintain control of Congress, Trump opted for an event at a Washington renovation project that has been embarrassing and contentious.
The unusual move marks a departure from Trump’s month-long race to stage more than 25 rallies in largely conservative areas, hoping the GOP can overcome his own low approval ratings and polls predicting that the Iran war, high energy prices and cost of living increases could spell a strong election night for Democrats.
Trump wrote on his social media site that his Sunday evening rally in Kansas — which followed his Iowa visit — was “my last stop.”
The presidewnt spent a lot of time at those rallies talking about his second-term focus on molding the White House and the surrounding nation’s capital in his own image. He crammed the Oval Office with gold flourishes, demolishing the East Wing to construct a sprawling ballroom, converting the Rose Garden into a patio space reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago estate and erecting a sprawling South Lawn helipad.
Trump also closed the Kennedy Center after failed attempts to add his name to the building, has planned a towering arch just outside the city and is pushing to revamp a century-old public golf course.
He has bristled at criticisms from former President Barack Obama and other Democrats that he’s spent too much time focused on construction projects — insisting that renovations relax him and that he does them quickly and without requiring too much planning time.
Trump said the Reflecting Pool fix would be fast and inexpensive
His Reflecting Pool saga began in April when Trump said he wanted to change its color and would use contractors he knew to fix the monument in mere days and for about $1.5 million before Independence Day.
The repairs wrapped up nearly three months behind schedule and the budget ballooned to more than 10 times Trump’s early estimate — and that’s assuming no more additional work will need to be done in the future.
Trump had initially declared the work was complete in June. But after unveiling the overhaul, the pool was soon choked with algae blooms, and its “American-flag blue” liner began peeling off in sections. The pool was quickly drained anew for repairs in mid-July.
Trump has repeatedly blamed vandals, but the office of U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia — former Fox News host and longtime Trump ally Jeanine Pirro — said the problems were caused by shoddy workmanship.
In his comments Sunday, Trump continued to insist that the Reflecting Pool “was vandalized badly.” He said that security cameras have since been added to stop that.
Still, a particularly ignominious moment came when the Justice Department charged former Olympian David Hearn with intentionally damaging the Reflecting Pool — then abruptly dropped the case this summer — determining he was not responsible.
A judge later permanently dismissed it.
That prompted Trump to fume that Pirro “choked,” and that he was “disappointed with Jeanine Pirro, really disappointed. She folded like an umbrella” — though he stopped short of firing her.

title: Penobscot County budget drops to $41M after legal review
text:
Penobscot County’s plan to recoup $1 million through next year’s budget was found to be illegal, dropping the county’s proposal for next year to $41.5 million.
After the million-dollar bump was added to Penobscot County’s budget proposal last week, a lawyer found that the plan went against state law, County Administrator Blair Tinkham said.
County officials will present the new proposal to its budget advisory committee on Wednesday, Nov. 4. The drop in the overall amount still puts the county on pace for a 24% hike next year from the current budget.
The plan was brought forward as part of a budget that fully funds the Penobscot County Jail, which has gone underfunded since 2021. Underbudgeting for jail expenses has bled more than $11 million from county reserve accounts, but officials have said there are few ways to recoup those funds quickly.
Penobscot County Commissioners David Marshall and Andre Cushing approved adding the money to the proposed budget last week to help refill the county’s depleted reserves. The addition was not needed to fund the Penobscot County Jail despite being added to one of the facility’s budget lines.
County Commissioner Dan Tremble voted against the proposed budget.
At the time, Tinkham said he was unsure if the additional funds would be legal, but thought they would be.
“Our read was, if we undertax, we should be able to recoup it in the following years,” Tinkham told the Bangor Daily News on Friday.
Since 2021, Penobscot County has not taxed municipalities as much as it could for jail operations. Taxing below the allowed amount, which is set by the state, lowered tax rates for residents but left the county with depleted reserves, Tinkham said.
Another portion of the proposed budget is still under legal review.
County officials have had to borrow from some of its own accounts, including opioid and COVID-relief funds, early in the year when there is not enough money on hand to operate. As part of next year’s budget, Penobscot County was going to pay back 20% of the $1.4 million officials took from the county’s unorganized territory department.
Not repaying the borrowed money would not affect any services or resources in the unorganized territory, Tinkham said, but it’s unclear if the funds have to be paid back in a single year or not.
Lawyers are still reviewing the proposal. If it is found to be illegal, nearly $1.1 million will be added to the budget.
If passed as proposed, next year’s budget would go up $6 million from 2026. That would mean an $85 jump in taxes for a home worth $245,000 in Bangor. Residents of other towns, including Brewer, Hampden and Hermon, would see a bump of more than $100 a year in county taxes.
Tinkham compared the spike in county taxes to the cost of a meal from McDonald’s being added to homeowners’ tax bills every month.
The budget advisory committee will meet next week to review the plan. Last year, the committee scrutinized the 2026 budget over two lengthy meetings and ultimately asked for $1 million to be cut.
County officials need the committee to approve a budget by Nov. 5 so commissioners can finalize it on Nov. 18. That will allow County Treasurer Glenn Mower to start the process of obtaining a loan for the beginning of 2027.
If the budget isn’t approved on this timeline, it may not give the county enough time to secure a loan. Without a loan, the county would not have the $3.5 million needed to fund services in January, meaning it would not be able to pay expenses or payroll.
That option is not “on the table,” Tinkham said.
Tremble, who was critical of the budget proposal, said he expects the committee to request cuts because of rising local taxes and the fear that residents won’t be able to afford the added burden.
“I think we’ve got a long way to go before we get to stuff that the budget committee is going to be comfortable with,” Tremble said.
Budget committee members said part of the reason last year’s meetings took so long was because information about expenses wasn’t shared until just days before it met. This year, county officials shared that information earlier and added more detail, Tinkham said.
That transparency, coupled with explanations that will be given at next week’s meeting, should allow the meeting to go smoothly, despite people’s disagreement with the rising budget, Tinkham said.
“We’re doing our due diligence,” Tinkham said. “People don’t like the number. I don’t like the number.”

title: Gout: Causes, warning signs and what you can do
text:
(Aging Untold) — Gout is common, painful and sometimes missed at first, but it is treatable.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, is explaining what gout is, what can trigger it and how to confirm it early.
What gout is
Gout starts with uric acid building up in the blood and crystals forming in the joints and other tissues, Rogers said.
“It triggers a very inflammatory, painful response,” Rogers said.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says gout is painful type of arthritis that will usually affect a single joint at a time.
When most people think of gout, they picture a big toe that is red and throbbing — podagra, Rogers said.
Why the pain is so intense
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said her youngest daughter has had gout twice and describes it as feeling like a shard of glass. Even walking near her daughter’s foot caused her pain, Cradduck said.
Cradduck said the crystal itself is not what causes the pain.
“It’s not actually the crystal. It’s the immune system that’s coming after to attack that,” she said.
Rogers said the immune system treats the crystal as a foreign object.
What gout can signal about your health
And a uric acid buildup can point to something bigger, Rogers said.
“It really is telling you something else. It can be a very significant signal for underlying metabolic disease,” Rogers said.
Many people with gout also have insulin resistance, diabetes or cardiovascular issues, Rogers said.
Uric acid also lowers nitric oxide, which makes arteries relax, Rogers said.
“It’s the same mechanism that’s involved with atherosclerosis, or hardening of the arteries,” Rogers said. “That’s why it’s so significant to recognize.”
Why men get gout more often than women
Men get gout more than women and Rogers said that is because of estradiol.
“Estradiol is protective,” Rogers said.
Premenopausal women have that protection and men do not have the same level of estradiol. Men get some estradiol from the conversion of testosterone, Rogers said.
As men age, they tend to have less testosterone and carry more visceral fat, Rogers said.
For women, the picture changes after menopause.
“After menopause, when the estradiol drops, then that gap closes,” Rogers said.
Diet, lifestyle and getting checked
Gout has long been called “the disease of kings,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said, and has been linked at times to rich foods and alcohol.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said it comes back to what you put in your body and what you do to keep your body healthy.
She said that in her experience, men do not seek treatment as quickly as women. Her advice: If you have a husband, partner or brother, nudge him to see a doctor.
When treating patients, Rogers said some doctors will put them on allopurinol.
“But that same mechanism of action of lowering uric acid with vitamin C, quercetin and luteolin, the three together, there’s some, products that have all three together that you take that will naturally lower the uric acid,” Rogers said.
As always, consult your health care provider for medical advice.
Sugary food and sugary drinks are some of the quickest ways to raise fructose, and that is one of the quickest ways to push insulin high and hold onto uric acid, Rogers said.
Learn more
Learn more about gout through Alliance for Gout Awareness.

title: 5 injured in Halloween night shootings near Michigan State campus, police say
text:
EAST LANSING, Mich. (WILX/Gray News) - An investigation is underway after two shootings on Halloween night near the Michigan State University campus left five people injured, authorities said.
At a press conference Sunday afternoon, East Lansing Police Chief Jennifer Brown said the department responded to four separate incidents, including two shootings that left a total of five people injured.
Police officers were called to a reported shooting near the intersection of M.A.C. Avenue and Linden Street.
Multiple shots were fired in that incident and three people were taken to the hospital with gunshot wounds, according to Brown.
Officials said two of the victims were listed in stable condition, while the condition of the third was not immediately known.
The chief said later that night, a second shooting was reported and police responded to the area of Stoddard and Frye Avenues, where two more people were shot.
Those two victims are now listed in stable condition. The chief said multiple guns were recovered from the scene, but officials were not sure whether they were the weapons used in the shooting.
Brown said “several individuals were taken into custody” in connection with the violence.
Police have not said whether the shootings are connected. It is unclear whether any of the victims are MSU students.
A spokesperson for MSU said the Department of Police and Public Safety did assist ELPD in response to shootings, but “the criminal activity did not involve a threat to campus and did not take place on MSU’s campus.”
Brown said the East Lansing Fire Department also responded to 91 total incidents over a 24-hour span, including 75 incidents into Halloween night.

title: Martha Stewart says she 'really screwed up' with homeless Halloween costume
text:
Martha Stewart says she ‘really screwed up’ with homeless Halloween costume
Martha Stewart has said she is "distressed" and "sorry," after her choice of Halloween costume sparked a backlash.
In a since-deleted image on Instagram, the TV personality, entrepreneur and author — who is America's first self-made female billionaire — appeared dressed as a homeless person, wearing a black hat, distressed jeans and a cardigan, with black marks smeared across her face, as she held up a sign that read "I AM HUNGRY HELP ME!!" In the post's caption, Stewart promoted her candle collection.
Critics soon weighed in on social media, with one saying, "I think that Martha Stewart wins this year for the most tone-deaf Halloween costume."
Another described the move as "grotesque, disgusting, morally bankrupt, incredibly wrong," adding, "What in the 'let them eat cake' is this costume?"
More than 700,000 people in the US are homeless, according to official data.
Addressing the uproar the following day, Stewart said her look was meant to raise awareness.
Related video: Boy with rare form of muscular dystrophy receives Star Wars-themed wheelchair costume
"I am distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people, which was never my intention," she told Page Six on Sunday.
"Homelessness continues to remain one of America's greatest challenges and ongoing crises, something that I care deeply about and I have spent a significant amount of time and effort supporting charities that combat this ongoing social epidemic," Stewart added.
Later that day, she issued an apology in a statement released on her Instagram story.
"It's hard to admit when you've really screwed up," Stewart wrote. "My earlier statement didn't go far enough. I know many people are suffering economically. Wearing a costume like I did was insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry."
CNN has reached out to her representatives for further comment.
Stewart's costume was not the first to spark controversy this year. In August, Target apologized and stopped selling a Halloween costume that depicted a circus clown after critics said it evoked Blackface and minstrel shows.

Bangor

title: Israeli officials say elections will stand after Netanyahu claimed Arabs stole vote
text:
TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ‘s efforts to question last week’s elections weakened Sunday as officials said the vote would not be undermined by the allegations and a court ordered suspects in one case released.
In an image that indicated officials were on the same page, the head of Israel’s elections committee was shown sitting between Israel’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet intelligence service for a statement making clear that even if claims of foreign interference raised last week are substantiated, the vote would stand.
Netanyahu’s Likud party has said, without giving evidence, that Arab-led parties “stole” the elections in which Netanyahu’s bloc lost its majority of seats in parliament. By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appears to be trying to block any potential alliance in the opposition with the Arab parties that could force him from office.
Likud has cited a handful of cases, including the arrests of three political activists before polls opened on Oct. 27 with envelopes of cash, allegedly to bribe voters. Two days later, police arrested four more suspects. Police said the suspects were connected to the Islamist party Ra’am, which denied that it was involved.
A judge on Sunday questioned or rejected police requests for further restrictions on the three suspects. Police later said one was released subject to unspecified “conditions” and another was ordered to remain on house arrest for eight days. The detention of the third suspect was extended for two days.
Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra’am party, which won eight seats in the Knesset, denounced the arrests as undemocratic and “an attempt to influence the election results.”
Netanyahu suggests joining with Arab parties is treason
Netanyahu saw his parliamentary bloc of allies drop to 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, down from a peak of 68 in the outgoing parliament.
A bloc of parties led by his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, won 48 seats, while Arab-led parties, including Ra’am, won the remaining 19 seats. Together, those two blocs opposing Netanyahu have enough seats to form a new government, though it remains unclear whether they will agree to do so.
The results are due to be officially certified this week, and President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday will begin meeting with each of the parties elected to parliament after that to see who they prefer to be the next prime minister.
Following those consultations, he will choose the candidate — most likely Netanyahu or Eisenkot — who he believes has the best chance of forming a coalition government.
That would set the stage for weeks of negotiations. If they are unsuccessful, Herzog could ask another candidate to try. Otherwise, the country would be plunged into a new election early next year.
Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for Eisenkot to join with Arab parties. Some Israelis agree. A few dozen people protested outside Eisenkot’s home on Sunday night.
“We have a tiny country, a very tiny Jewish country. We want to keep it as a Jewish country,” said one protester, Shoshana Idasis. Other, larger rallies in recent days have called for a Jewish-Arab coalition.
Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of trying to delegitimize the vote
Likud also has alleged foreign interference in the vote. The Shin Bet security service, at the request of Israel’s election commission, has opened an investigation.
But the head of the elections committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said that “our position is that even if the suspicions are substantiated, this would not undermine the integrity of the electoral process or the election results as a whole.”
Likud quickly issued a statement asking how the committee chief can acknowledge there are serious allegations while saying there will be no effect on the final outcome.
Eisenkot on Sunday accused Netanyahu of launching an “orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results” by insinuating that Qatar had supported opposition parties to unseat Netanyahu. Eisenkot said that Shin Bet briefed him on the investigation into foreign interference.
Qatar has denied funding any activities meant to influence the election’s outcome. Many Israelis see the Gulf Arab country as a patron of Hamas, and allegations of its influence have roiled Israeli politics in other cases, including one in which close aides of Netanyahu allegedly accepted money from Qatar while working for the prime minister’s office.
Netanyahu’s opponents have accused him of using scare tactics and trying to create a narrative to further discriminate against Arab-led parties and Israel’s Arab citizens, who make up 20% of the population.
Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List of Arab parties, which won 11 seats, noted last week that more than half the content published by Likud and Netanyahu on election day was directed against Arab voters as a tactic to encourage right-wing Israelis to vote.
“In moments of crisis, he reverts to his familiar tactic: racist incitement and the delegitimization of the Arab public,” he said.
