title: Everybody in Maine needs to get serious about homelessness
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rich Hooks Wayman is chair of the Statewide Homeless Council and CEO of VOA Northern New England.
Last month, more than 40 state agency directors, nonprofit executives, planners, data specialists, advocates and people with lived experience gathered for Maine’s second Interagency Summit on Homelessness. Convened by the Statewide Homeless Council and the Maine Continuum of Care, the summit assessed Maine’s response to homelessness.
Homelessness is both a personal crisis and a public one. It affects individuals, families with children, veterans, older adults and people with disabilities in every Maine county. Residents see encampments and panhandling; communities confront shelter closures and strained emergency services. Yet Maine has a functioning homelessness response system, accountable data and interventions that produce measurable results.
Maine’s Homeless Management Information System and regional service network give us a statewide picture. Nine service hubs coordinate intake, assess needs and maintain by-name lists of people seeking help across Maine.
In 2025, more than 4,170 people experienced homelessness and sought support. More than 3,450 entered shelters, where they received services and help finding housing. Maine’s shelters help about 1,040 people move into safe, permanent housing each year. Over 96% of all supportive housing tenants remain stably housed for more than 12 months. That is meaningful progress.
The data also show where Maine is falling short. Average shelter stays have increased from roughly two months in 2022 to more than three months in 2025 as people seek housing in a shrinking market. The burden of homelessness falls disproportionately on people with disabilities, including veterans; young people with histories of neglect; and racial minorities, who are nine times more likely to experience homelessness than white Mainers.
Geography matters, too: although Maine has 1,314 shelter beds, 284 transitional housing units, 562 rapid-rehousing or subsidized units and 2,180 permanent supportive housing apartments, rural communities and entire counties face serious gaps and lack of units.
In response to public health concerns, each winter, Maine stands up warming centers — more than 520 crisis spaces in winter 2026. While laudable, warming centers would not be necessary if Maine had adequate shelter and housing capacity in our state’s homelessness response system.
Homelessness is driven by poverty, a severe shortage of affordable housing and health systems that do not meet everyone’s needs. Family conflict, domestic violence, social isolation, incarceration, mental illness and addiction can compound the crisis. Subsequently, Maine’s homelessness response system and community-based nonprofits are focused on strategies that move individuals from homelessness into stable housing and that improves health and well-being.
Community programs require sustainable, annual investments. The public will pay for homelessness one way or another: through expensive crisis responses, overcrowded jails and emergency rooms or through services and housing that help people regain stability. Maine should choose the approach that is more humane and effective. While the federal government contributes around $60 million per year to support homelessness services in Maine, continued state support is desperately needed.
The role our state plays is even more important now. Federal policy proposed by HUD could eliminate 470 supportive housing units in Maine next year. HUD is now emphasizing greater reliance on law enforcement, civil commitment or treatment requirements as conditions of housing.
We all agree that public safety must be maintained by law enforcement and that large encampments should be addressed with outreach engagement, swift responses to imminent hazards and housing referrals. However, locking up people does not solve homelessness and is a costly approach.
Maine needs the Legislature and next governor to invest more in high-quality, health-focused shelter services and a major expansion of permanent supportive housing construction and social services. Those investments must be paired with better planning, accountability and disciplined use of public dollars.
Government cannot do this work alone. It’s easy to become frustrated by the lack of progress. However, our citizens must play a role and can contribute to meaningful change. Maine residents can urge local, state and federal officials to protect homelessness services. They can support candidates who make those priorities real.
Everyone can say, “Yes! Come to my community,” when affordable and supportive housing is proposed in towns or cities. They can take part in Maine’s homeless-response hubs and learn more through the Maine Homeless Planning website. You can also volunteer with organizations providing outreach, shelter, food and housing support, and contribute private resources generously.
Maine has the structure, data and committed partners needed to improve. Now we need the public investment to expand shelter capacity and build permanent supportive housing, alongside private generosity, volunteer time and persistent advocacy. A new state plan to address homelessness could hold all of us accountable.
Maine can do better — and every one of us has a contribution to make.

title: Bangor Mall condemned; Dick’s Sporting Goods, JCPenney remain accessible
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - With the exception of two anchor stores, the Bangor Mall is officially off-limits Monday after being deemed by the City as unfit for human occupation.
The city posted condemnation placards outside the property Monday.
Bangor officials declined comment to WABI Monday, instead referring us to the postings at the mall.
Dick’s Sporting Goods and JCPenney are still accessible through their own entrances.
Some Theatre Company, which is based inside the mall, shared the following post on Facebook. The closure comes as their team prepares for a production of Les Miserables.
The theatre’s owner tells WABI they had no advanced warning before the property was condemned.
Kathy Harvey owner of Furniture, Mattresses & More said she’s seen work underway at the property, and is confused by the timing of the closure.
“They came in and saw me also and explained that they were shutting the inside of the Bangor Mall, not Dick’s and not JCPenney and not me because I own my building,” Harvey said. “I’m not a part of the mall, so I own my own building, the land that it’s sitting on, but the mall itself on the inside, they said they’d shut it down until they got future repairs done such as the roof and things, but I have saw roofers on the roof for several weeks and electrical, so the timing is a little odd.”
Harvey also organizes the craft fair scheduled for this weekend and next weekend, which takes place at the mall. She says the craft fair, which features over 300 vendors is still on. Harvey says she cleared out her space at Furniture, Mattresses & More for a backup plan to keep the craft fair going and provide an opportunity for locals to support their neighbors.
We have reached out to Namdar Realty Group, who owns the mall, for comment.
This is a developing story and we will have further information when it becomes available.

title: Butterfly Kisses Alliance changes the way families are supported after the loss of a child
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (Aging Untold) — Families navigating the tragic and unexpected loss of a baby are receiving an additional support system from the Butterfly Kisses Alliance.
A group of nurses in St. Louis founded the nonprofit in 2023 to offer support and resources to families and people impacted by the death of a baby, whether before, during or shortly after birth.
Kayla Hollingshead, Jennifer Koskela, Janie Mullinnax and Jeannette Hickey work together as labor and delivery nurses at Progress West Hospital. For each of them, the emotional toll of caring for mothers who had suffered a loss prompted them to create a way to help.
“We grieve with these families because we are there with them through the worst day of their life,” Hollingshead said. “We’re humans as well, we have emotions, and we got into nursing because we care and we love hard.”
Hollingshead said with most diagnoses, there is a standard of care within the medical profession, meaning there is a level of skill, knowledge and care a healthcare provider or support staff member is reasonably expected to provide given the situation.
However, she said, no real standard has ever existed for those who unexpectedly lose a baby.
“These families need to be given a standard amount of care and it should be standard across the country,” she said.
So, the women created a new standard of care that has been implemented at the hospital, ranging from how office staff speaks to families, to ultrasound technicians and beyond.
In addition to changing standards of care, the women also create comfort kits containing books, cards and self-care items that are mailed to families around the world.
Kelsey and Greg Fussner suffered an unconscionable loss of their own in 2023. After suffering a miscarriage 2021, Kelsey found out she was pregnant in July of 2022.
“It was such a relief because we made it past what everyone said,” she said. “Because we’d never made it that far before, so making it that far was really fantastic.”
From the beginning, she said her doctor told her she likely would deliver by 38 weeks. However, as the 38-week mark approached, she said her doctor told her she would be scheduled for a C-section at 39 weeks and one day.
But at Fussner’s final appointment before delivery, at 38 weeks and three days, she received unimaginable news.
“The ultrasound tech just looked at the doctor and shook her head and he [my husband] said, ‘No say it out loud, say it out loud,’ and then the doctor said there was no heartbeat,” she said.
Having eaten breakfast before her appointment, Fussner said the next eight hours were agonizing, as she waited for surgery to deliver her baby girl Nora.
“I wanted to see her, I couldn’t wait to see her and see what she looked like, but on the other side of it was completely devastating and hard to grasp that I’m not going to be able to take my baby home,” she said.
What Fussner didn’t know at the time was that her nursing staff consisted of the same women who founded Butterfly Kisses Alliance. Immediately, she said, they showed compassion by removing baby items from her hospital room and closing other patient doors when she walked the halls.
Then, forced to leave the hospital without her baby, the women offered Fussner a weighted stuffed animal, an elephant, stuffed to the exact weight of her daughter Nora, eight pounds, 13 ounces.
They also packed her a comfort kit full of memories of Nora, including her hospital blanket, footprints, a necklace, homemade quilt and pictures in the outfit she was meant to go home in.
“They took lots of pictures, which I hold so dear to me because it’s the only memory I have of her,” she said.
As the couple continued to grieve, a few months later, Kelsey got a surprise - she was pregnant.
“It was fast, and of course, you’re absolutely terrified,” she said. “It’s confusing because you want to celebrate, but at the same time, you feel bad celebrating.”
Under the care of a different doctor, Fussner was scheduled to deliver at 37 weeks via C-section. It just so happened, she said, to fall on April 10, the same month and day Nora was due.
“They asked if we wanted to change it and I said no,” she said.
On April 10, 2024, Kelsey gave birth to Abigail.
“I felt like this was meant to be, that this was Nora’s way of saying she is with us,” Fussner said. “She will always be part of our lives and she’s a part of our story and my life and she’s going to be part of Abigail’s too, just in a different way.”
The Butterfly Kisses Alliance offers online resources for families dealing with pregnancy loss, even when in-person support is not available.
The organization provides materials for mothers seeking advice about physical changes after pregnancy loss and fathers looking to honor their child. Resources are also available for siblings, grandparents and friends wanting to help their loved ones cope.
To learn more about the Butterfly Kisses Alliance, its mission, or to donate, visit here.

title: Washington reports first US bird flu death of 2026; health officials say risk to the public is low
text:
Washington reports first US bird flu death of 2026; health officials say risk to the public is low
A person in Yakima County, Washington, who caught bird flu after being exposed to infected dairy cows has died following a severe illness, county health officials said on Sunday.
Video above from 2024: First severe bird flu case in the U.S. reported
This is the first person in the U.S. to die from complications from avian influenza in 2026, and the third in the U.S. to die from bird flu since February 2024, when the virus jumped into dairy cattle for the first time. So far, the CDC has recorded bird flu cases in more than 70 people in the U.S. since 2024.
Most people who’ve become ill have worked on farms with infected cattle or poultry. Health officials say most cases have been mild and all have been so-called “dead-end” infections, where a virus jumps from an animal to a person but doesn’t spread farther.
So far, no human-to-human transmission of bird flu has been documented in the U.S. Health officials say the risk to the public remains low.
Yakima County health officials said they are closely monitoring the contacts of the person who died to ensure they didn’t pass the infection to anyone else.
On Oct. 31, the Yakima County Health District reported a person who had come into contact with infected cattle was hospitalized with a severe case of bird flu. The person had underlying health conditions, but the county did not specify what they were. On Nov. 1, the county reported the person had died.
Yakima County officials also said a third person exposed to infected cattle has tested positive. All three Washington cases have occurred since mid-October and resulted from exposure to infected cows. The third infected person has mild symptoms and has not been hospitalized, county health district officials said.
Since Oct. 8, 33 dairy herds infected with the H5N1 bird flu virus have been reported in Washington. The state is urging people who work at the dairies to wear personal protective equipment and report their symptoms if they feel ill.

title: The Best Places to Retire in Maine Might Surprise You

title: Pres. Trump focuses on Reflecting pool
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - With the 2026 midterms elections just a day away, President Trump on Monday touted the completion the repairs to the Reflecting Pool and also made his closing message to voters.
Off the campaign trail after nearly 30 rallies and with control of Congress at stake, President Donald Trump traveled from the White House to the Lincoln Memorial to tout the improvements to the Reflecting Pool.
It’s a project that took the Interior Department months to complete. The President repeated allegations there was vandalism involved.
“The people from Interior have been incredible. And the pool is now better and more beautiful than it’s ever been before. And we’re very proud of it.”
The President also made his closing message to voters- who will decide which party should control Congress for the next two years. “As you know, this is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime. The Democrat Party is nominated in the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history. These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up.”
While voters tell pollsters that their number one issue this election cycle is the high cost of living, the President did not address that issue during his remarks at the Reflecting Pool. Instead, the President touted what he described as a strong and resilient U.S. economy.
The President acknowledged that typically, historically the party in power loses seats during the Midterms. With a razor thin majority, the President and Republicans are hoping to defy that history. The final polls are pointing to significant Democrat success for the 2026 midterm elections.

title: Shop handmade and local at these 36 Maine holiday craft fairs

9 a.m.-2 p.m. Nov. 14. Seton Village Community Center, 1 Carver St., Waterville. On Facebook.
This fair features handmade crafts, baked goods, pickles and relish, hot dogs and refreshments.
10 a.m.-3 p.m. Nov. 14. Breakwater School, 856 Brighton Ave., Portland. mainemade.com.
Rosemont Artists Guild is teaming up with the Caravan Artist Market for a fair that will feature more than 30 artists and makers. Bard Coffee will be on site with beverages and pastries.
10 a.m.-4 p.m. Nov. 14. Bear Mountain Inn + Barn, 364 Waterford Road, Waterford. mainemade.com.
Bear Mountain Inn + Barn in Waterford will host a holiday market featuring local makers and artisans, free photos with Santa, cookie decorating for kids and live music.
10 a.m.-4 p.m. Nov. 14, 10 a.m.-3 p.m. Nov. 15. Costello Sports Complex at the University of Southern Maine, 37 College Ave., Gorham. mainemade.com.
This is a huge annual fair that features dozens of local artisans and crafters.

9 a.m.-4 p.m. Dec. 5. Westcustogo Hall & Community Center, 120 Memorial Highway, North Yarmouth. mainemade.com.

11 a.m.-2 p.m. Dec. 5. Cliff House, 591 Shore Road, Cape Neddick. On Instagram.

title: Supreme Court rejects Trump administration push to set aside thousands of California ballots
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected a push for California to set aside thousands of mail ballots from people President Donald Trump’s administration claims are noncitizens, a decision that comes on the eve of the final day of voting in the pivotal midterm elections.
The high court refused to intervene in a case involving 20,000 people the Republican administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the largely Democratic state’s voter rolls.
The swift rejection was the latest in a flurry of election-related litigation the day before the elections, which will decide control of Congress for the last two years of Trump’s second term. No justices publicly dissented.
In California, the Trump administration had asked the high court to set aside the challenged ballots until the voters’ citizenship status could be verified. But officials there said that the list appeared to be filled with errors and that setting the ballots aside could effectively disenfranchise legal voters.
The high court did not detail its reasoning, as is common in emergency decisions. The justices previously rejected Trump’s push to restrict mail ballots around the country in September, even though the justices have sided with his administration in a series of other emergency docket appeals.
The Republican Trump administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite them being rare.
A district court judge previously denied the Justice Department’s request and warned that the demand could disenfranchise citizens.
Also on Monday in Washington, another federal judge ruled against the administration’s efforts to make last-minute demands of California election officials, finding they violated the U.S. Constitution.
“The Executive Branch has likely violated the Constitution’s Elections Clause, which commits authority over election rules to the states and Congress alone,” wrote Chief Judge James Boasberg.
The administration, for its part, said segregating the ballots was a modest request that would eventually allow legal votes to still be counted.
The administration has faced a remarkable string of losses in court in its push, as well as criticism for waiting until a few weeks before the election to make its demands of California election officials with a list that even the Department of Justice admits is not entirely reliable.
During a hearing over whether to lift her own order forbidding the administration from threatening to prosecute election workers who let potentially illegal voters cast ballots, District Court Judge Trina Thompson drilled down on reports of widespread inaccuracies in the Justice Department’s data.
“Would you agree there’s a high error rate?” Thompson asked Kenneth Kao, a Justice Department attorney.
“That’s a fair statement,” Kao said. “That’s why we ask for the registrars’ aid in verifying these are all valid voters.”
At the same time, Bill Essayli, the federal prosecutor running the Justice Department’s Los Angeles office, said at a news conference he was highly confident the people on the list were not entitled to vote.
“This isn’t speculation. This isn’t a theory,” Essayli said, later conceding there may be errors on the list.
Voting has been underway in California, a largely Democratic state, since early October. All of the state’s roughly 23 million registered voters are mailed a ballot. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. California election officials have said that finding and setting aside the challenged ballots now would be logistically impossible.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said the appeal “reeks of desperation and is another attempt to undermine our elections and trample on the rule of law.”
Lower courts have sided with the state, with a district judge warning that segregating ballots would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections and erode trust in the democratic process.
“If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” wrote U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who was nominated by President Bill Clinton, a Democrat.
A 2-1 appeals court panel upheld his order, with one judge appointed by Trump and another appointed by President Joe Biden, a Democrat, voting in favor. The third judge on the panel, also appointed by Trump, argued in a dissent that California’s unwillingness to separate the ballots encourages the “violation of federal law.”
The Justice Department has sought to move the case along quickly, unsuccessfully asking an appeals court to intervene early.
___
Associated Press writers Sophie Austin in Sacramento and Safiyah Riddle in Los Angeles contributed to this report.
___
Follow the AP’s coverage of the U.S. Supreme Court at https://apnews.com/hub/us-supreme-court.

title: Man grabs trick-or-treating girl, follows other children in van on Halloween night, police say
text:
KELSO, Wash. (KPTV/Gray News) - Authorities say they are investigating after reports of a man in a white van trying to grab a child and following children on Halloween evening.
According to the Kelso Police Department, officers were called just before 7 p.m. to a neighborhood after a man reportedly grabbed a girl by the arm while she was out trick-or-treating.
The girl said the man in question was wearing a black hoodie and dark jeans, and that he got out of a white utility van that had been following her.
Police said the girl told them that she was able to get away from him after kicking him in the groin.
Officers checked the area but did not find any matching vehicles or suspects.
Shortly after the report in Kelso, officers with the Longview Police Department said they also received word of a van following children who were out trick-or-treating.
Kelso police said security footage from the neighborhood was being checked and urged anyone with further information to contact them at 360-423-1270.

title: Victims of Florida jet crash include 20-year-old copilot and tech entrepreneur and his family
text:
Victims of Florida jet crash include 20-year-old copilot and tech entrepreneur and his family
A tech entrepreneur, his wife and their two young children were among the nine people killed in a jet crash Sunday in Florida, as was a co-pilot who got her license at 17, the victims' families said.
One of the two pilots of the Learjet 60 was a 20-year-old named Nathalia Filgueiras, her mother told The New York Times. 
Adam Robinson, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their children, 4-year-old Emma and 2-year-old Charlie, were identified as victims by their families. Anita Maria Cetina, who helped care for the children, also died.
Two more victims were identified as Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr. The identity of the other pilot was not immediately disclosed.
"Our hearts are also with the families of the pilots, who are grieving alongside us," the families of the seven said.
Authorities have not yet publicly confirmed the victims of the crash.
It hasn't been confirmed which pilot was flying the plane when it started descending. Filgueiras' pilot's license showed she had the rating to fly that model of Learjet but not to be in command of the flight, The Associated Press reported.
Plane may have started breaking up before impact
The Bahamas-bound aircraft fell from the sky before hitting the ground and exploding in a residential area of Greenacres, about 7 miles southwest of West Palm Beach.
A federal investigator said Monday that parts of the business jet appear to have broken off before the aircraft crashed in South Florida and erupted into a ball of flames.
“It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said. “It looked like a missile going down.”
“We do have some indication that the aircraft was breaking up before impact,” National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said at a news conference Monday. “We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site.”
Weather conditions will be a major focus of the investigation, Chapman said. One of the pilots had told air traffic control about ice conditions amid rain in the region on Sunday.
Co-pilot was 17 when she got her pilot's license
Filgueiras started flying during high school and earned her private pilot’s license in 2023, when she was just 17 years old and a senior at West Boca Raton Community High School, CBS 12 in Florida reported that year. In addition to attending ground school, she learned firsthand from her father, who started flying for fun in 2018.
The outlet wrote that Filgueiras’ “ultimate dream” was to become a commercial airline pilot or pilot jets.
Filgueiras had logged more than 1,300 hours of flight time, Camila Corteleti told the Times, saying she worked for Upper Jets, a private charter firm based in Fort Lauderdale.
Her mother told CNN Brasil that her daughter was the co-pilot.
“She was a very good girl — responsible, hardworking,” Corteleti said. “She was the co-pilot and couldn’t make any decisions.”
NASA administrator Jared Isaacman, writing in his "personal capacity," warned against speculation over the crash's causes on X.
"The charter industry routinely hires commercial pilots very early in their careers to gain experience alongside an ATP-qualified captain before they move up to the airlines," he wrote. "She would still have the appropriate training, qualifications, and checkouts by an FAA examiner or designee."
He criticized "troubling" commentary on the crash.
"She was the second-in-command (SIC), and while she was empowered to point out mistakes as part of good crew resource management, she was doing her job, communicating with ATC right to the end in a terrifying situation," Isaacman wrote. "She likely knew before many of those calls that she was going to die."
Her mother said Filgueiras announced she wanted to be a pilot when she was 12.
“She loved the freedom,” Corteleti told the Times. “It was completely different seeing the world from the top.”
Families share joint statement on victims
"Adam and Helen were devoted parents, and Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, were the light of their lives," a joint statement from the victims' families said. "Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever."
"Anita Maria cared for Emma and Charlie with tenderness and devotion, and she was truly part of the family," the statement said.
Fehr and Reed “loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation,” the statement said. “From the moment they met, they were all in on each other and the life they were building.”
Robinson was a co-founder of Robly, an email marketing platform, and founder of Retention.com.
“I feel like I’m living the dream,” Robinson, 45, said on a recent episode of the podcast ProfitLed. He said he and his family lived in Aspen, Colorado.
“I love the fact that I get to see my kids in the morning and the evening, and I don’t have to travel for work that much, and I get to live in this place that’s always been my dream,” he said. “And my wife is super happy because she can be a full-time artist."

title: The billion-dollar problem in firehouses: Potentially toxic gear, tight budgets and a fight over who pays to replace it
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — When a vintage B-17 bomber went down during a living history flight at Bradley International Airport in 2019, the response put firefighter and Connecticut fire union representative Chris Albani right in the thick of it.
After racing to the scene, it was his job to coat the wreckage with a special foam used to quickly smother airplane fires.
That foam contains PFAS — man-made, toxic chemicals touted for their ability to resist heat and fire. They’re a lifesaver in aviation disasters, but also a health hazard, with studies linking PFAS to cancer.
Those chemicals that put him at risk aren’t limited to the foam Albani uses in a crisis. PFAS has also been found in the specialized equipment he and thousands of other first responders wear daily on the job.
“It’s in the gear,” Albani said. “It’s the PFAS that is intentionally put in the gear. And it’s poisoning members.”
And court documents show the manufacturers have known for decades that PFAS are toxic but kept that information hidden.
But recent academic research on PFAS that highlighted the link to cancer has raised alarms at firehouses.
Even so, InvestigateTV discovered firefighters across the country are still wearing potentially toxic turnout gear that contains the chemicals – with a battle brewing from coast to coast over the cost of replacement and who should pay it, leaving first responders in limbo.
The cost of protecting the protectors
Cancer fears have long haunted firefighters like Albani, and for good reasons. The disease is the leading cause of line-of-duty deaths for firefighters, according to the International Association of Fire Fighters.
Albani said that fear has stayed with him.
“It’s just that unknown,” he said. “I have 15 years on, and cancer isn’t an immediate thing. It’s a long-term thing. So, I might not know until I’m 60. The mindset people have now - it’s not about if I get cancer, it’s when.”
Those concerns about risks associated with turnout gear were amplified in 2020. That’s when a study from Notre Dame confirmed high levels of PFAS in both new and used turnout gear, with the potential for the cancer-linked chemicals to leach out and soak into first responders’ skin.
But six years later, InvestigateTV found hundreds of thousands of firefighters nationwide are still wearing gear that contains PFAS. Many want to get rid of it, but replacing it could cost billions — and leave taxpayers on the hook.
“Gear - a baseline pants and jacket is anywhere up to $3,000,” Albani said. “And then you start throwing in a helmet, gloves - looking at $5,000-8,000 per member. If you have a department of 200 people, do the math. It’s a big money ticket item for a municipality to cover.”
Massive lawsuit aims to make manufacturers pay
For many departments, it’s a cost they can’t bear.
InvestigateTV surveyed fire departments across the country - half of the chiefs that responded said they haven’t made the switch because their towns and cities can’t afford the cost. Many believe they shouldn’t have to. That’s where a massive class action lawsuit comes in.
“The defendants understood the dangers of PFAS,” said Jennifer Sclar, an attorney representing a growing number of fire unions and municipalities on the East Coast. “This is not like it came out of the sky in 2018. The defendants have long understood what the dangers of PFAS were and are.”
Sclar is suing more than a dozen companies that manufacture turnout gear or the materials and chemicals used to make it. Every company listed in the filing was contacted for comment by InvestigateTV on numerous occasions. Most — including big names like 3M and DuPont — wouldn’t comment.
In legal filings, 3M has argued that it didn’t manufacture any of the gear worn by the firefighters and there’s no proof of a direct link between the company and protective fire gear - also saying firefighters haven’t made allegations of any physical injuries. DuPont previously told another media outlet the complaints were without merit.
Still, the lawsuit against those companies and others claims they knew about health risks with PFAS chemicals and the gear that contains it but kept saying it was safe.
“That never should have happened,” Sclar said. “And it can’t continue to happen. You have to protect the protectors.”
The goal of the recent legal actions isn’t just to get firefighters out of their toxic threads – they seek to make the manufacturers to foot the bill for replacement gear.
Five class action lawsuits filed by cities and towns now have been consolidated into a single case in Minnesota.
“When this first came to light and firehouses started asking some of the defendants, ‘Hey - I’m hearing PFAS may have had some bad health effects, you know what’s the deal?’” Sclar said. “The defendants told these firemen, ‘Don’t worry about it. There’s nothing to worry about. Nothing to see here’. And they knew that wasn’t true.”
Lawsuit claims secrets about PFAS kept for decades
Dozens of documents made public by the Environmental Working Group, cited in the class action suit and analyzed by InvestigateTV, show 3M and DuPont specifically were long aware of the risks associated with PFAS.
Those records show the companies were internally labeling PFAS as “toxic” as far back as the 1960s and 70s.
By the 1980s, documents InvestigateTV examined show both companies started moving women of child-bearing age off certain assignments to limit PFAS exposure. And in the 1990s, their own records show scientists and studies were finding links between PFAS and cancer.
“We want to make sure that these manufacturers who knew full well that this dangerous chemical was harmful to human beings but yet infused that into our gear for decades - that they’re paying for this gear that we need to replace,” said Ed Kelly, who runs the nation’s largest fire union — the International Association of Fire Fighters.
But replacement is complicated. Getting firefighters from coast to coast into PFAS-free gear means giving millions more to the same companies many believe burned them already.
“They can’t be trusted,” Kelly said. “We have to take that gear and get it independently tested to ensure not only that there’s no PFAS but there’s no other negative health impacts infused into this gear.”
Kelly’s skepticism is grounded in reality.
In 2025, the fire department in Quincy, Massachusetts paid millions for new, supposedly PFAS-free gear — only to have independent tests that same year reveal high levels of the chemicals.
“Outrageous,” Mayor Thomas Koch said at a press conference where the discovery was revealed.
The company involved in manufacturing the gear said in a public statement it eliminated PFAS from all of its textiles the same year Quincy bought its gear and recently told InvestigateTV the chemicals were not intentionally added during manufacturing — with testing turning up very low levels.
But the case still captured national headlines and left fire chiefs even more confused and worried.
In InvestigateTV’s national survey, some leaders said there are too many unknowns with the PFAS alternatives, and not enough proof their crews will be protected if they change gear.
“We know we were lied to,” Albani said. “So, we don’t have a level of trust with those companies. We were deceived. We’ve had members pay the ultimate sacrifice because of it. It’s a problem.”
The potential health threat of PFAS is something firefighters like Chris Albani have to face every time they put on their turnout gear.
Walking through the firehouse and looking at the gear, Albani said he tries not even to touch the jackets and pants he knows contain the chemicals until it’s absolutely necessary. It’s a drastic change after decades of donning the suit for every call.
But firefighters are being forced to break old routines because of new science - waiting for safe gear that lets them save lives — without potentially putting their own at risk.

title: Encaustic, multi-media artist Helene Farrar at the Gilley
text:
SOUTHWEST HARBOR — Contemporary multi-media artist Hélène Farrar is the People-Nature-Art presenter at the Wendell Gilley Museum, with an in-person artist’s reception at 6 p.m. and her presentation at 7 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 10. Her talk will be offered both in person and online. Attendance is free but registration is required. Sign up at wendellgilleymuseum.org/calendar.
Farrar is the museum’s first featured artist whose work is largely encaustic, a form of painting that involves a heated wax medium (often beeswax and resin) to which colored pigments have been added. The molten mix is applied to a surface, usually prepared wood, and tools can be used to shape the wax. Her colorful paintings reflect themes from both the natural world and her observations of people, and they have a depth and luminousness achieved through careful attention to texture and surface quality. She considers her work part of a conversation about humanity, beauty and nature. Farrar’s unique style is playful but also serious. “I’m very serious about my silly work,” she says. “I take it very seriously.”

title: How fundraising in Maine's Senate races compares to other battleground contests
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How fundraising in Maine's Senate races compares to other battleground contests
Despite entering the race late, Democrat Troy Jackson has raised more than incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins
How fundraising in Maine's Senate races compares to other battleground contests
Despite entering the race late, Democrat Troy Jackson has raised more than incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins
Maine’s Senate race is one of five closely watched battleground contests that are considered toss-ups. According to the latest Federal Election Commission filings, candidates in those races have raised nearly $437 million combined.
Despite entering the race late, Democrat Troy Jackson has raised more than incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
Collins raised $25.2 million this election cycle, while Jackson raised $26.8 million. Together, they brought in more than $52 million.
That total is slightly higher than the amount raised by candidates in Alaska’s Senate race, but lower than the totals in three other toss-up races: Michigan, Ohio and Texas.
In Texas, Democratic candidate James Talarico alone reported raising more than $146.3 million, more than twice the combined total raised by the Maine candidates.
Across all five states, Democratic candidates are leading in fundraising, bringing in 76% of the nearly $437 million total, excluding fundraising by Political Action Committees.

title: IDEXX posts double-digit jump in Q3 results, raises full-year outlook
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
IDEXX Laboratories Inc. (Nasdaq: IDXX) posted double-digit increases in third-quarter earnings and revenue that exceeded market expectations and raised its full-year financial outlook.
The Westbrook-based maker of veterinary diagnostics and software posted diluted earnings per share of $4.01, representing an increase of 18% as reported and 22% on a comparable basis.
Earnings per share were boosted in part by a non-operating gain on an equity investment, tax benefits from share-based compensation and year-over-year currency changes, all while absorbing acquisition impacts, the company said.
The earnings per share figure is above the $3.71 per share consensus estimate of analysts polled by Zacks Investment Research.
Net income attributable to stockholders rose to $317.1 million, up from $274.6 million a year earlier.
IDEXX posted quarterly revenue of $1.21 billion, an increase of 10% as reported and organic amid growth in the company’s Companion Animal Group division. The revenue figure was 2.21% above the Zacks consensus forecast.
Mike Erickson, who took the helm as IDEXX’s president and CEO earlier this year, said the latest results reflect innovations that are helping veterinary practices detect disease earlier and work more efficiently.
He also noted that the company advanced its software capabilities through the recent acquisition of CoVetAI Inc., a Canadian-based company.
“IDEXX delivered exceptional third-quarter results, reflecting strong commercial execution and momentum from our innovation-driven growth strategy,” Erickson said in Monday’s earnings release.
As of Friday’s close on Wall Street, IDEXX shares had a market value of around $43.4 billion. The stock is trading 24% lower than a year ago.
Updated guidance
In its updated outlook for the full year, IDEXX is projecting earnings per share to be in the range of $14.96 to $15.16. That represents a 25-cent increase at the midpoint level over the previous guidance.
IDEXX also expects full-year revenue growth to be in the range of $4.74 billion to $4.76 billion, or reported growth of 10.1% to 10.8%. That represents an increase of $32 million at midpoint, including $5 million related to the recent CoVet acquisition.

title: InvestigateTV+: A solution to blood shortages?
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A Kansas City doctor is testing a new way to fight severe blood loss with ingredients that sound more like your grocery list. InvestigateTV+ explains how it works and why some in the medical community are hopeful that the discovery can ease blood shortages.
Then, volunteers show us how they turn donated clothing into a boost of self-esteem for young students.
Plus, we get an up-close look at how teamwork on the tarmac gets flights in the air safely and on time.
Better than blood?
A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.”
When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death.
Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock.
Bringing education to eager students
It’s not unusual to see students working on college-level coursework, earnestly taking notes from the professor.
But some of the lessons being taught by Rhodes College professors aren’t being delivered in a lecture hall, or even on a school campus, but inside a facility at the West Tennessee State Penitentiary.
Airport brothers
Brothers Bobby and Lance Snyder have a combined eight decades of service with American Airlines at Charlotte Douglas International Airport.
They help make sure planes arrive and depart safely and on time at the airline’s second-largest hub. Their commitment is inspiring their younger co-workers.
These boxes help children
A Virginia nonprofit is using volunteers to pack personalized boxes of clothing and other items for children who lack access to proper clothes.
Boxes of Basics founder Sarah Tyndall started the organization in 2018. A thousand volunteers have since built custom care packages for more than 8,500 children across Virginia.

title: Manufactured homes are wrong for Kennebunk
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
As a longtime resident of the Kennebunks, I know firsthand that our community urgently needs affordable housing. Our children are being priced out of the town they grew up in. Abode’s proposed trailer park in Kennebunk is the wrong solution for a legitimate need for affordable housing.
According to the engineers at the Oct. 26 community meeting, the “manufactured homes” come in on a flatbed and only need to be hooked into utilities. Unlike traditional stick-built homes, there is not much local job creation from this project.
More concerning is the business model. Residents will not truly own their home or land—they will rent the lot from an out-of-state venture capital firm. While land fees may be frozen for the first five years, abode can—and likely will—raise rent significantly afterward on captive residents. Furthermore, manufactured homes are depreciating assets. Instead of building equity, buyers face potential long-term financial traps. Is that what we want for our children?
Baas (the parent company of Abode) is based in Utah and won’t have to live with the consequences of this development. Kennebunk residents will. We must reject this ill-conceived plan from an out-of-state investment group and focus on true, sustainable housing solutions for our community.
Shawn Magaw
Kennebunk

title: Where the governor's race stands heading into Election Day
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Where the Maine governor's race stands heading into Election Day
Nearly two dozen candidates entered the race to become the 76th governor of Maine, and 13 candidates qualified for the ballot in the June 9 primary.
A ranked-choice voting tabulation was needed to decide the primary winners. Former Maine House Speaker Hannah Pingree won the five-way Democratic primary race, while Bobby Charles, a former assistant U.S. secretary of state, won an eight-way Republican primary.
State Sen. Rick Bennett, a Republican-turned-independent, submitted enough signatures to qualify for the general election ballot.
Bennett said he is focusing on making things such as housing, healthcare and childcare more affordable.
"Maine and Maine people deserve a functioning government and a governor who will put them first," Bennett said.
Charles has also made affordability a focus of his campaign, and his slogan is "cut crime, cut taxes, no nonsense."
"At a certain point in time, you get to an age and you say, 'You know what? I need to start giving back,'" Charles said.
During the primary campaign, Charles faced criticism from fellow Republicans about some of his proposals, such as cutting $4 billion from the state budget — something he has since walked back.
Pingree also wants to bring down costs for Mainers, rolling out plans on education, healthcare and housing.
After becoming the youngest woman in the United States to ever serve as a state house speaker (2008-10), Pingree served as the director of Policy Innovation and the Future in the Mills administration from January 2019 to May 2025. Pingree said she is ready to work across the aisle when necessary.
"I'm ready to work with anybody who cares about Maine's future," Pingree said. "I'm ready to get the job done."
All three gubernatorial candidates participated in WMTW's debate on Oct. 14, and the tension was high. During that debate, and in the last few weeks, Charles has doubled down on allegations regarding Pingree's involvement in a grant that her community received for affordable housing. Charles claims that Pingree's family profited off that grant. Maine's Total Coverage has repeatedly fact-checked the claim and found that Pingree and her father did not get paid by the nonprofit organization that received the grant. Her sister's domestic partner is the nonprofit's executive director, and he does get paid by the organization.

title: Rhodes College professors bringing elite education to inmates
text:
HENNING, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - It’s not unusual to see students working on college-level coursework, earnestly taking notes from the professor.
But some of the lessons being taught by Rhodes College professors aren’t being delivered in a lecture hall, or even on a school campus, but inside a facility at the West Tennessee State Penitentiary.
“It was the last decade of 15 years of my career here was looming and I wanted to do something maybe different, challenging,” said Dr. Stephen Haynes, a 30-year professor of religious studies and humanities at Rhodes College.
Haynes is the director of the college’s “Liberal Arts in Prison” program.
“People who were involved in higher education and prison are 43% less likely to go back to prison,” Haynes said.
The program started as a Great Books Discussion Group in the fall of 2016 with about 25 women interested.
Dr. Haynes said it soon became apparent what the inmates really wanted was a program that gave them college credit.
Now, every week, a group of Rhodes professors and students gather on campus at the statue of former college president Charles Diehl to begin their trek to the Women’s Therapeutic Residential Center in Henning, Tennessee, a low-security rehabilitation-focused prison where instructors teach the hallmarks of a Rhodes College curriculum.
“And so, we were able to develop a certificate program,” Haynes said. “At the end, by May, we’ll have about 45 women who have graduated with these certificates of liberal arts.”
Women like inmate Jameshia Davis — serving a 24-year sentence for drug and firearm possession.
“I thought it was hard at first, because when you hear Rhodes College, it makes you think of like Harvard or something,” Davis said. “Education, if you would have mentioned education to me before I came to prison, I would have probably looked at you like you was crazy.”
Davis not only completed the program but also became a tutor for other incarcerated women.
“I would just like to encourage anyone who’s either discouraged about school, education, whatever it may be, to just challenge yourself and to just know that you can do anything that you put your mind to,” Davis said.
Rhodes English professor Dr. Lori Garner has been part of the prison program for about five years.
“I really think they make me a better teacher. When I learn their perspectives, I can bring them back into my classes at Rhodes. And that really helps everyone,” Garner said. “They bring really diverse life experiences to these same stories that I’ve been teaching for decades.”
Rhodes seniors Sophie Stevenson and Laurel Phillips work closely with the inmates, leading discussion groups and other organizational activities — two of the more than 70 students who’ve volunteered for the program.
Both say over the two to three years they’ve been involved, they’ve come to see the women as friends.
“We hear about their kids and their grandkids and the pets and the birthdays and special occasions and when they are going up for parole and like potentially going to be released,” Phillips said.
The student helpers say the program has not only changed their perspectives about prisons and prisoners but also their own lives.
“I would love to keep working in prisons after this, and I’m really grateful to have gotten this opportunity. I think this is not something that I came to college thinking about or knowing was an option, and now it’s sort of defined my entire college career,” Stevenson said.
For inmates like Davis — who has a parole hearing in May — these classes provide a chance to change their futures and perhaps even the futures of those they love.
“I don’t know, it was kind of really encouraging for my oldest son because he’s in high school and he just...when they see good things that I’m doing, it makes them be like, ‘Hey. If mama can do it, I can do it,’” Davis said.
As of spring of 2025, 92 incarcerated women at WTRC had accumulated 765 Rhodes credits, with 32 earning certificates.
It’s a lesson that extends far beyond the walls of a prison.
“They’re human beings with a future. They’re not the worst thing they’ve ever done. Most of them will get out and they have a lot of potential and it’s great to see that potential being realized,” Haynes said.
Jameshia Davis plans to continue her education toward a bachelor’s degree when she gets released.
And thanks to a $500,000 Mellon Foundation grant, a new Bachelor of Arts in Liberal Studies will be offered at WRTC and support the expansion of educational programming in the men’s facility at West Tennessee State Penitentiary.
That means, starting this summer, WTRC inmates will be able to enroll in a full four-year degree program as part of the Liberal Arts in Prison initiative.
Professor Haynes said the program sponsors are looking for ways to help sustain the program into the future and are looking for donors who want to see it succeed.

title: Alert issued for missing, endangered 6-year-old boy in Kentucky
text:

Roman Heilman was reported missing in Louisa, Kentucky. He’s described as weighing 60 pounds, with blonde hair and blue eyes. He was last seen wearing a green fur jacket, red and white monster pajama pants, and Crocs.
He was last seen at 3:45 p.m. Sunday at 948 Tadpole Road. According to the Lawrence County Emergency Management’s Facebook post, the missing child is known to respond to the song “If You’re Happy and You Know It.”

title: WABI Matinee: Director Jim Merkel talks award-winning documentary ‘Saving Walden’s World’
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Award-winning filmmaker and Belfast native Jim Merkel sat down with WABI to discuss his documentary, “Saving Walden’s World.”
Released in 2024, the film has screened at 23 international film festivals across four continents and received 14 awards, including selections in Barcelona, Kolkata, Mexico, and Venezuela.
The documentary follows Merkel, a former military engineer turned sustainability activist, as he raises his son Walden on an off-grid homestead in Maine. The film also documents his travels to Kerala, India; Cuba; and Slovenia to highlight women-led communities that have improved quality of life by prioritizing healthcare, literacy, and reproductive freedom.

title: Timing is everything in rutting season
text:
Many sportsmen count the November deer hunt as the highlight of all of their outdoor passions. It is a special time. Frosty mornings and quiet moments in a tree stand with hand warmers, a thermos of hot coffee mixed with the anticipation of a big buck in the crosshairs is a deer hunter’s daydream. Or, for the most hardy and driven among the hunt fraternity, the dream is to follow a big, dew-clawed track on fresh snow.
And, of course, the Maine deer camp is also the centerpiece of the hunt, part of the heritage and the history. These camps come in all sizes and description and locales, many of them passed along from generation to generation, along with unique histories and huntin’ yarns that get carried on year after year.

title: Large fire burning hundreds of acres along the Maine-New Hampshire border
text:
Large fire burning hundreds of acres along the Maine-New Hampshire border
A large fire has already burned hundreds of acres in the White Mountain National Forest in Coos County, New Hampshire, along the border with Maine.
The Wild River Fire is just southeast of Gorham, New Hampshire, and just south of Gilead, Maine. As of about 3:30 p.m. on Monday, the fire had burned about 300 acres. The fire was first reported at about 1 p.m. on Sunday and was not contained on Monday.
The Saco Valley Fire Association said the fire was at Wild River and Evans Notch and that there was a lot of fire in the area.
The area remains in a drought and officials say the fire is burning in timber, snags, and leaf litter.
Firefighters were working on Monday to try to establish a perimeter as quickly as possible, but access to the area is difficult due to the steep and rugged terrain. As of 7 p.m. on Monday, the fire was 11% contained.
National Forest officials said more than 40 people were assigned to the Wild River Fire as of Monday afternoon.
The cause of the fire was under investigation. Officials said there were no significant threats to property.
The fire danger was low to moderate across New Hampshire. In Maine, the fire danger was high across the southern half of the state.
On Sunday, a fire caused by a tree that fell on a power line burned nearly 20 acres in Casco.

title: Man completes 28-year, 31,000-mile walk around the world
text:
HULL, England (AP) — Karl Bushby embraced his weeping mother in his arms Monday as he returned to his northern England home to complete a 28-year odyssey to walk around the world.
“Where have you been?” his mother, Angela, asked as he arrived outside the home he left in 1998 that was now decked with a banner saying “Welcome Home Son.”
He didn’t need to tell her.
Bushby set out from Punta Arenas, Chile, on Nov. 1, 1998, and walked 31,000 miles (50,000 kilometers) across four continents and 30 countries to get home. He navigated shifting ice over the Bering Strait and swam across the Caspian Sea and English Channel to avoid taking a boat or plane — or any transport — to propel him forward.
He vowed not to return until he could complete the journey on foot. It was an eye-opening adventure full of danger and drudgery that was interrupted for years at a time by the unexpected: the 2008 financial crash that sapped funding from sponsors, the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic and mountains of bureaucratic red tape to get across international borders.
A trek made possible by kind strangers
On the final day of the journey, Bushby pushed his cart toward a hero’s welcome at City Hall before setting off for the last stretch to see his mother.
“Sorry to keep you waiting,” he joked to the crowd of hundreds who cheered his arrival. “Is that it, is it done?”
The ex-paratrooper said he looked like he was 10 years old when he left his mother’s row house at the age of 29. He returned at 57 — softer, grayer and weathered, but far more worldly.
“They say it takes a village but literally it took a world to get me here,” Bushby said. “The kindness of strangers, so many, from individuals to nation states to get me back here today. I didn’t do this alone. There was a big team. The biggest team. Earth.”
The idea started with a birthday card from his dad
Bushby had a thirst for adventure, but his mission only came into focus when his father, Keith, sent him a birthday card in the mid-90s. His dad, an army veteran himself, mentioned an argument two special forces troops had about the possibility of walking from London to New York over the Bering land bridge, believed by some scientists to have been used by early humans to migrate from Asia to the Americas at a time of lower sea levels.
Perilous jungles, scorching deserts and frozen tundra slowed him down, but bureaucratic holdups brought his adventure to a halt for long periods.
Bushby originally calculated the distance could be covered in about five years, but he knew that was unrealistic.
“You just dump a whole bucket full of reality on that,” he said. “We suspected that it was 12 years plus. And the plus was a big plus. But never in our wildest dreams would we ever have imagined 28 years.”
Danger on land and sea followed by border problems
He dodged Colombia’s armed conflict in the dangerous Darién Gap, the roadless and rugged jungle, rainforest and mountains between South and Central America in 2001, and was then jailed for 18 days after crossing a restricted border zone in Panama.
After being airlifted to safety during the 56-mile (90-kilometer) Bering Strait crossing in 2006 with American adventurer Dimitry Kieffer, they started again and faced a standoff with a polar bear, survived near-death plunges into freezing waters and almost lost all their supplies when their sleds plunged in the sea. After managing the rare crossing, the pair were jailed and faced deportation for entering Russia illegally.
It took Bushby almost 10 years to make his way through Russia in fits and starts because of visa struggles and weather that only allowed travel a few months a year. When Russia denied him a visa in 2012, Bushby walked in protest from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., which eventually led to him getting the proper paperwork.
Family firsts and a long-awaited reunion
Bushby has met several times over the decades with family members who have met up with him on his journey. He was greeted on the beach in Dover by his father and brothers after crossing the channel last month.
He reunited with Adam, his 36-year-old son from an early marriage whom he had rarely seen, and he met his 12-year-old granddaughter for the first time, which he said was amazing.
Bushby hadn’t seen his mother in a decade, setting the stage for an emotional and somewhat awkward reunion captured amid a throng of cameras and a documentary film crew.
“Behave yourself, mother,” he joked, as his mother wrapped her arms around him and wept. “Get yourself together.”
He said he had long tried to imagine that moment he would return to find his mother at the gate where he left her so long ago. He said it was an emotional reunion that was “one great, big, blurry mess” he was trying to process.
“It was kind of almost shocking to see my mother after so long,” he said at a news conference later. “She’s changed a lot. We’ve all changed a lot in that time.”
Next steps for a man who walked millions
In the final days of his trip, Bushby spoke of his anxiety over the trip ending, not knowing what he would do next and coming to terms with having to live in his mom’s basement.
“It’s like stepping across the event horizon into a black hole,” he told The Associated Press. “I have no idea what’s about to happen in my life.”
There will be plenty to keep him busy. Six speaking engagements are scheduled in the next two months, a sequel to his memoir “Giant Steps” is due and German filmmaker Werner Herzog is making a documentary on his trek.
He expects to struggle with the ups and downs other adventurers have experienced after long journeys.
“The only way I think, you know, you get over that is just get another mission, another passion and get busy,” he said. “That’s what I intend on doing.”

title: Ellsworth’s historic bowling alley gets a makeover after raising $340K online
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Ellsworth’s historic candlepin bowling alley has replaced its aging flooring, carpeting and seating after netting more than $340,000 in donations.
The latest changes follow the nostalgic bowling alley’s feature on CBS News Sunday Morning in August, after which more than 4,000 donors around the country contributed to a GoFundMe campaign started by the business’ owner, Autumn Mowery.
The bowling alley has long been a fixture in Ellsworth’s social scene, hosting first dates, birthday parties and bowling leagues throughout the year.
Mowery — who was only 18 when she took over Ellsworth Candlepin Bowling Alley in 2021— previously said she planned to use the funds to renovate the family-friendly business, which has operated since 1974 under various owners. The business is one of a dwindling number of candlepin bowling alleys across Maine.
By the end of October, a portion of the roughly $342,000 raised online was used on replacing the bowling alley’s dated flooring with new hardwood and neon carpeting, according to the business’ Facebook page.
“When I look around this building and see how much has changed, it’s hard to believe how far we’ve come,” Mowery said on Facebook. “There’s still so much more I want to accomplish, but seeing everything slowly come together has been incredibly rewarding. This building has been around for decades, and my goal has never been to take away its history or character. I want to preserve what makes this place special while giving it the love and attention it deserves.”
The funds have also been used to buy and install new retro-inspired seating at the foot of each bowling lane and new ramps to expand accessibility to the bowling areas.
Nearly all of the alley’s new heat pumps have also been installed, according to the Facebook post.
Next, Mowery intends on professionally refinishing each of the bowling lanes over the spring.
Mowery herself has fixed much of the business’ aging equipment, which dates back to the 1940s, and she now offers behind-the-scenes tours of the bowling alley’s historic pinsetters.
Mowery did not respond Monday to inquiries from the Bangor Daily News.
